September 17, 2025

The Honorable Brooke Rollins Secretary U.S. Department of Agriculture 1400 Independence Avenue SW Washington, DC 20250

Secretary Rollins,

California and the United States Department of the Agriculture (USDA), and its United States Forest Service (US Forest Service) have long enjoyed a cooperative relationship to sustain the health and productivity of the federal forest lands in California. Given this shared responsibility, it is imperative that USDA ensure opportunities for meaningful public input and thoroughly study potential impacts before rescinding the Roadless Rule.

We oppose the proposed wholesale rescission of the Roadless Rule. The rule protects almost 4 million acres of roadless areas across 10 national forests, from the Klamath Mountains to the Sierra Nevada to southern ranges, including the San Jacinto, and San Bernardino mountains. These areas are essential for clean water for communities across the state and protect the headwaters of the rivers that support our agricultural and fishery economies and drive the state’s \$74 billion recreation economy.

To address today’s forest management challenges, California is accelerating projects, improving practices in the wildland–urban interface, and using fire as a natural process through prescribed burning. The Roadless Rule has not hindered these efforts in designated areas. In fact, more than 240,000 acres of roadless land in California have undergone vegetation treatments to reduce wildfire risk and protect nearby communities. For example, in Caples Creek, a designated roadless area, fuels management work helped shield communities during the 2021 Caldor Fire. This is one of over two thousand vegetation management and wildfire resilience projects completed or underway across the state.

Science and experience demonstrate that fire threat increases in areas with established roads due to human-caused ignitions. While access can aid fire response and prevention work, the potential to increase fire risk must be carefully weighed and considered prior to rescinding the Roadless Rule. Last year, fires in California cost the state at least \$250B. Opening inventoried roadless areas to road construction, clear-cut timber harvest, and mining may put rural communities at increased risk of fire and significantly increase firefighting costs of California. We simply cannot afford to ignore the potential costs of more fires that could result from rescinding the roadless rule.

The proposed rescission represents a major shift in the longstanding management of federal forests lands across the country. As with other significant federal land policy changes, tribal governments, local landowners and managers, recreational users and rural communities who have a real stake in their local forest lands should have the opportunity for meaningful participation and input before such a change is made.

Given the protection that the current roadless rule provides to California’s natural resources, any effort to modify that rule must fully account for the evidence of protection and thoroughly study any potential adverse impacts. Therefore, before proposing any such rescission, the US Forest Service should fully study impacts such as water quality, potential introduction of invasive species, increased wildfire, impacts to endangered species, and others. The US Forest Service should also consider less damaging alternatives, such as adjustments to the rule instead of full rescission.

Instead of completely rescinding the roadless rule, we ask that USDA follow best available science, maintain roadless area protections and increase investment in the partnership between the state and the US Forest Service as detailed above. The Roadless Rule has proven effective in protecting communities, managing fire, and increasing forest health.

Sincerely,

Dear Secretary Rollins,

I write to express my concern with the recent efforts to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and the potential impact this change may have to the Los Padres National Forest, which crosses Ventura County, California. As a member of the Ventura County Board of Supervisors and someone dedicated to advancing long-term environmental stewardship and enhancing wildfire resilience in our region, I am concerned this change could adversely impact our community and other communities across the Country.

In general, it has been shown that roadless areas not only protect environmental habitats and watersheds, but also benefit local economies as recreation destinations and can promote fire resilience.

The Los Padres National Forest covers 1.75 million acres of chaparral, oak woodland, grassland, and conifer forests across the Transverse Ranges and southern Coast Ranges in Southern California. The Forest also contains 37 “inventoried roadless areas” -- totaling 635,106 acres -- that span Ventura, Santa Barbara, Kern, San Luis Obispo, and Monterey Counties.<sup>1</sup> Nearly one million visitors visit the forest each year, generating more than \$75 million in annual revenue while supporting over 1,500 jobs and contributing approximately \$103.4 million in yearly income for local workers and businesses.

In recent years, wildfires have significantly affected our area, causing widespread damage and heightened concern throughout our community. I fear rescinding the Roadless Rule may intensify wildfire-related and environmental challenges for our region. According to the U.S. Forest Service, “[b]uilding roads into inventoried roadless areas would likely increase the chance of human-caused fires due to the increased

presence of people.”<sup>2</sup> More recently, analysis of 30 years of fire data shows that on national forest lands, fires were found to be four times more likely to ignite in areas with roads than in roadless tracts.<sup>3</sup> Furthermore, it is my understanding the Roadless Rule already contains commonsense provisions to allow road construction to protect public health and safety. The Roadless Rule allows fuel reduction and fire management projects, and in Los Padres National Forest, projects like Tecuya Ridge and Pine Mountain have proceeded under the Roadless Rule’s protections.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,

September 19, 2025

The Honorable Brooke Rollins Secretary of Agriculture U.S. Department of Agriculture 1400 Independence Avenue, S.W. Washington, D.C. 20250

RE: Proposed Rulemaking: Recission of 2001 Roadless Rule

Docket Number: FS-2025–0001

Sent via: https://www.regulations.gov/document/FS-2025-0001-0001

Dear Madam Secretary,

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (“USDA") is initiating an environmental impact statement (EIS) and rulemaking concerning management of inventoried roadless areas on approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System lands, including Alaska. The proposed rule would rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (“2001 Roadless Rule"),1 which prohibits road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas, with limited exceptions.

Consistent with the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA") the USDA is soliciting public comment on the alternatives and effects of the proposed action, as well as useful information, studies, and data. Humboldt County, Nevada, (“the County") is pleased to respond to this request.

Humboldt County is significantly affected by the proposed action. Of the State of Nevada's 5,833,000 acres of National Forest System Lands, 3,186,000 of these acres (or 54.6%) are Inventoried Roadless Areas.2 In Humboldt County, the Santa Rosa Ranger District of the Humbolt-Toiyabe National Forest comprises more than 280,000 acres, the vast majority of which are Inventoried Roadless Areas (“IRAs") or Wilderness Areas. Because Humboldt County's natural resource economy and valued rural lifestyle depend on multiple uses of the surrounding public lands such as grazing, mineral extraction, many forms of recreation—and the access within our National Forests necessary to carry out these activities—the County will strongly benefit from the USDA's

proposed rulemaking. Moreover, by lifting the blanket ban on road construction and reconstruction on IRAs, the proposed rulemaking will make our forests and communities significantly safer by enabling efficient and effective firefighting response as well as enabling forest management projects like timber thinning to help increase fire resistance and resiliency.

## Issues to be Considered in the EIS

## 1. What is the Impact on Fighting Fire and Minimizing Fire Risk on Nevada's National Forests?

According to USDA data,3 the State of Nevada has the highest fire risk in the U.S. Northern Nevada (which includes Humboldt County and the Santa Rosa Ranger District) has the highest risk of wildfire within the state, as well as the highest fire risk to homes.4 In short, Humboldt County suffers some of the highest wildfire risk in the nation, endangering human lives, private property, infrastructure, rangeland, wildlife, and the timber resource.

Roadless Areas have limited road access and are subject to a blanket ban on timber harvesting and extreme restrictions on timber management. It is therefore not surprising that forty percent of lands within inventoried roadless areas are classified as having high or very-high wildfire hazard potential Between 1984 and 2024, 13 percent of Roadless Areas (5.5 million acres) experienced wildfires of high or moderate severity. Additionally, approximately 23 percent (10.2 million acres) of inventoried roadless areas managed under the 2001 Roadless Rule are located within the wildland-urban interface (WUI) in close proximity to property, homes, and humans.5

The No Action alternative would negatively impact Humboldt County by continuing the blanket ban on road construction, reconstruction, and timber sales, and extreme limitations on timber management. Strategic road building and road improvements are critical for swift and efficient fire incident response on National Forests and for the safety of firefighters, some of whom are from locally based Rangeland Fire Protection Agencies (RFPAs) and Rural Fire Departments. Moreover, road improvements and access are essential for implementing forest management projects like tree thinning, fine fuels reduction, and application of herbicides. By banning the strategic building and rebuilding (improvement) of key access roads on Roadless Areas and restricting timber management, the No Action Alternative impedes critical fire management activities, in conflict with direction from Executive Order 14308 Empowering Commonsense Wildfire Prevention and Response.6 By contrast, the Proposed Action would give the local Ranger District and Forest Manager—in

cooperation with other federal agencies, local governments, Tribes, and affected parties—the ability to determine the best fire attack and risk management needs for local Forest Service roads and access, taking into consideration local circumstances.

## 2. What is the Impact to National Forest Lands for Multiple Use Activities?

Under the National Forest Management Act (“NFMA"), the National Forests are explicitly mandated to be managed according to the principles of multiple use and sustained yield:

"In developing, maintaining, and revising plans for units of the National Forest System pursuant to this section, the Secretary shall assure that such plans [...] provide for multiple use and sustained yield of the products and services obtained therefrom in accordance with the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act of 1960 [16 U.S.C. 528–531], and, in particular, include coordination of outdoor recreation, range, timber, watershed, wildlife and fish, and wilderness..."

16 U.S.C. § 1604(e)(1)

Many products and services—including but not limited to livestock grazing, mineral resources, timber, and many forms of recreation—make the National Forests vital to rural communities like Humboldt County both as sources of economic prosperity and for personal enjoyment. Notably, three mining districts (the National District, the Rebel Creek Placer District, and the Paradise District) all reside within the Santa Rosa Ranger District, as well as twelve grazing allotments and abundant opportunities for recreation. Nearly all multiple uses (with the exception of primitive backcountry hiking) require safe and reliable access on maintained roads.

The No Action alternative undermines the multiple use / sustained yield character of the National Forests by banning road construction, reconstruction, and timber harvest on over 58 million acres (or 30%) of all National Forest System lands. In Nevada, this percentage is even higher—54.6% of Nevada's National Forests are within Roadless Areas. The blanket ban on road construction and reconstruction (i.e. improvement) frustrates access for vehicles necessary for livestock management, mining, timber harvest, fire management, and many recreational activities. When the public loses access to forests and their resources, it impedes the multiple use of Forest Service lands and resources. By contrast, the Proposed Alternative allows the local Ranger District and Forest Manager—in consultation with state and local government agencies, Tribes, and affected partiesthe ability to determine the best management of Forest Service roads and resources, taking into consideration local circumstances and needs. This, in turn, allows the National Forest System to fulfil its multiple use conservation mission, including timber production, recreation, wildfire suppression, and fuel reduction treatments.

## 3. What is the Impact on Social Justice Issues?

While the Roadless Rule allows certain limited road maintenance actions, the blanket ban on road building and rebuilding (improvement) effectively freezes in time the road system on huge swathes of National Forest land and creates an added pretext for decommissioning (closing) Forest Service roads. In Humboldt County, we are sensible that many members of the public who use and enjoy the National Forests are disabled, elderly, or have limited or low income, and are not physically or financially able to participate in roadless primitive backcountry experiences. Consequently, properlysited roads are essential for providing safe and reliable access for all members of the public, irrespective of age, ability, or income. The No Action alternative would negatively impact disadvantaged members of the public by permanently sealing off areas of the National Forests with no current road access, effectively managing these areas as de facto Wilderness Areas. By contrast, while the Proposed Alternative does not by itself authorize the building of any specific roads, it leaves the decision making of whether and where to build new access roads up to the local Ranger District and Forest Manager, in consultation with State and local governments, Tribes, and the public.

## 4. How Would the Alternatives Impact Local Decision Making?

NFMA commands that the management of the National Forests shall incorporate local input, both from State and local governments and the public:

Y "The Secretary shall provide for public participation in the development, review, and revision of land management plans, including consultation with State and local governments and other interested parties." 16 U.S.C. § 1604(d)

"Land management plans for units of the National Forest System shall be coordinated with the land and resource management planning processes of State and local governments." 16 U.S.C. § 1604(a)

In conflict with these mandates, the 2001 Roadless Rule handed down key Forest management decisions for IRAs on all National Forests from its Washington Office. This cookie-cutter, centralized approach has unnecessarily and adversely tied the hands of the local Ranger District and Forest Supervisor, who are unable to exercise management discretion. However, well-informed land management requires the flexibility to respond to local land and resource conditions.

The No Action alternative would prolong 24 years of top-down, centralized planning that ignores local conditions and circumstances and input from local governments and the public, including but not limited to, coordination with local government planning as mandated by 16 U.S.C. § 1604(a). By contrast, the Proposed Alternative would provide discretion for local land managers to tailor management, as appropriate, to local land conditions. Most importantly, this latitude allows local managers to provide critical access for firefighting, fuels management, and strategic multiple uses of Forest resources. Moreover, the Proposed Action allows, consistent with NFMA, for important resource values on inventoried roadless areas to be effectively conserved through local decision making and planning without restrictive and unnecessary national prohibitions.

## 5. Conclusion

Humboldt County supports the USDA's proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule and return management decisions to local Forest Managers in partnership with local governments and the public. Local oversight is essential, given evolving conditions on National Forest lands such as increased wildland-urban interfaces, greater wildfire, drought, pest challenges, and ongoing maintenance needs since 2001. As the Proposed Action would not compel amendment or revision of any land management plan, or approve any specific road or timber projects, we find that the potential environmental impacts of the Proposed Action are negligible, while the benefits for future management would be significant. We are also mindful that any subsequent proposed projects will be individually subject to NEPA environmental review and land use plan consistency.

If the USDA has any questions regarding the above comments, please contact Humboldt County Manager Don Kalkoske or Humboldt County Public Lands Consultant Andy Rieber.

Sincerely,

Secretary Rollins,

On behalf of the Round Valley County Water District Board of Directors, I urge you not to rescind the Roadless Rule. The 45 million acres of remote, wild and roadless forests across our country are the few pockets of unbroken forest where nature can flourish undisturbed. Their disturbance would have deleterious impacts in our rural community in particular. Rolling back the Roadless Rule will not protect communities from wildfire and may in fact lead to more wildfires. Wildfires are four times as likely to start in areas with roads than in roadless forest tracts and 90 percent of all wildfires nationwide started within half a mile of a road.

As elected officials charged with defending and conserving water resources and the ecologies that depend of them, the Round Valley County Water District Board strongly encourages efforts to overturn the Roadless Rule. We shouldn’t jeopardize the wildlife, habitat connectivity, recreation and clean water that these beloved intact forests provide by opening them to road-building, commercial logging, mining and drilling. Please leave America’s last wild forests alone.

## RE: U.S. Department of Agriculture Intent to Rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule—Docket No. FS-2025-0001

Dear Acting Director Kinder:

The Association of California Water Agencies (ACWA) respectfully submits comments regarding the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) intent to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.<sup>1</sup> ACWA appreciates USDA efforts that support active forest management strategies to help reduce wildfire risk, restore forest health, and protect watersheds and critical water infrastructure.

ACWA is the largest statewide coalition of public water agencies in the United States. ACWA represents approximately 470 member agencies that are responsible for delivering about 90 percent of the water to communities, farms, and businesses in California. ACWA represents water management entities in every sector of water supply, including municipal and agricultural water, water recycling, water reuse, wastewater management, and stormwater management. ACWA and its members are dedicated to providing a high-quality, reliable water supply in an environmentally sustainable and fiscally responsible manner.

Effective management of Inventoried Roadless Areas can decrease damage to roads, forests, water sources, wildlife habitat, and recreation sites. ACWA therefore urges USFS to consider the following as it proposed to rescind the Roadless Rule and develop an Environmental Impact Statement.

## I. Increase Management on Forest Service Lands to Enhance Wildfire Prevention and Response Capacity

As a subdivision of USDA, U.S. Forest Service (USFS) operations are important to ACWA members and millions of California water users. California encompasses the second largest allotment of USFS land in the nation with over 20.8 million acres of land.<sup>2</sup> These 20.8 million acres make up about 20 percent of the total land mass in California and are the source of approximately half of its surface water. Of California’s nearly 21 million national forest lands, 4,416,000 acres are Inventoried Roadless Areas.<sup>3</sup>

Many of California’s municipal and agricultural water supplies originate in National Forest lands, particularly in the Sierra Nevada and Cascade Ranges. These source watersheds are increasingly vulnerable to severe wildfire, pest outbreaks, and post fire erosion. Additionally, the challenges posed by catastrophic wildfires, deteriorating forest conditions, and restricted land management have become increasingly urgent in recent years. Catastrophic wildfires over the past decade— including the 2017 Tubbs Fire, 2018 Camp Fire, 2020 North Complex, and 2025 Palisades Fire and Eaton Fire<sup>4</sup>—have underscored the urgent need for increased access and forest treatment capacity in California’s upland watersheds. In 2025 to date, there are more than 47,000 wildfire incidents that have burned more than 4 million acres.<sup>5</sup>

Roadless areas are already largely overgrown. To help reduce wildfire risk, restore forest health, and protect water infrastructure, long-term sustainability of critical headwater areas—many of which fall within lands governed by the Roadless Rule—depends on the ability of land managers to access and perform fuels reduction activities. Proper access to care for roadless areas can spur decreased risks. For example, during the August 2021 Caldor Fire that began in Eldorado National Forest, USFS reported that proactive fuels reduction treatment efforts, such as forest thinning and prescribed burns, helped protect some communities from wildfire devastation in South Lake Tahoe<sup>6</sup>; flame lengths in untreated areas were observed between 100 to 150 feet while areas with fuels treatments had flame lengths reduced to 20 feet or less.<sup>7</sup> Access to roadless areas to properly manage national forest lands are also needed to perform other fuels reduction activities like mechanical thinning that help prevent and mitigate catastrophic wildfires.

ACWA values the natural environment but believes its preservation depends on better management of our land and water resources. The Roadless Rule has constrained the ability of federal land managers and local partners to implement active forest management strategies in critical headwater regions. These constraints limit opportunities for strategic road access and fuel reduction projects that are essential for sustaining healthy forests and protecting water quality and supply. While the Roadless Rule was intended to preserve wilderness character, it has become increasingly clear that restricted access hinders proactive fire mitigation and rapid response capabilities. Rescinding the rule would allow fire agencies, utilities, and local water providers to better plan and implement landscape-scale treatments and protect water supply infrastructure from wildfire-related damage. ACWA therefore realizes USDA’s intent to rescind the Roadless rule to remove prohibitions on road construction, reconstruction, and timber harvesting on the nearly 59 million acres—or 30%—of national forest lands that make up Inventoried Roadless Areas.

## II. Collaborate with Local Partnerships to Ensure Forest Stewardship

California water providers, communities, farms, businesses, and ecosystems rely on a strong partnership with USFS. ACWA is concerned that USFS “does not anticipate designating any Federal, State, Tribal, or local agencies as cooperating or participating agencies” and “only encourages input through public comment opportunities.” Numerous ACWA members have partnered with USFS to conduct forest health treatments on USFS lands.<sup>8</sup> ACWA members have dedicated significant financial resources, time and personnel to protecting watersheds and improving forest health on federal lands. ACWA is grateful for these partnerships and encourages USFS to coordinate with all impacted parties, especially water managers, to ensure the health of national forest lands—both in California and nationwide.

Additionally, understanding local conditions is extremely important to determine when, where, and what type of forest health treatments are needed—especially among the various landscapes with California alone. Local officials best understand the needs of the community. ACWA realizes that efforts by USDA to remove prohibitions for road construction and reconstruction in roadless areas would provide discretion to local land managers to tailor management, as appropriate, to local land conditions. This provides opportunities for USFS to work with ACWA member agencies and others to implement forest stewardship strategies. ACWA urges USFS to reconsider its coordination with essential players that safeguard national forest lands.

Partners and public engagement are essential to shape and improve practical forest management strategies. ACWA encourages USFS to initiate proactive, enhanced outreach to land managers and water utilities, as well as local, state, and tribal leaders as it drafts the proposed Roadless Rule and develops an Environmental Impact Statement. These are significant policy developments that necessitate a collaborative process. As water utilities like ACWA member agencies are and will be impacted by USFS regulations, their engagement in forest-related efforts is essential.

## III. Establish a Western Hub Office in California

California is currently home to numerous USDA regional operations, including the U.S. Forest Service regional office in Vallejo, California. ACWA is concerned that USDA’s proposed transition of hub locations outside California outlined in its reorganization plan <sup>9</sup> could inadvertently make the development and execution of contracts and permits more difficult and create unnecessary challenges for water managers and agricultural producers. ACWA urges USDA to ensure any reorganization preserves and enhances commitments to the evolving needs of agricultural producers, rural communities, and water managers, and is responsive to the growing threats posed by poor forest health on federal lands.

The greatest successes have occurred when ACWA members have been able to establish trusting relationships with national forest supervisors and their superiors at the region level. ACWA is concerned that moving a USFS regional office outside of California will hinder forest health work on federal lands and place critical watersheds, and the communities and farms that depend on this water, at risk.

If USDA moves forward with the reorganization ACWA requests that USDA establish a western hub office in California. ACWA believes establishing a western hub in California is aligned with the underlying goals of Secretary Memorandum 1078-015. Section 4, Principle 2 discusses the importance of bringing USDA closer to its customers. USDA has a significant customer base in California. Also, as mentioned above, there is more USFS land in California than in any other state in the Continental United States.

## IV. Maintain a Capable Workforce

ACWA recognizes the importance of efficient federal operations through a capable USDA workforce, and supports efforts to improve administrative efficiency, reduce duplication, and strengthen field-level responses. However, ACWA is concerned that USDA’s reorganization of personnel could hinder engagement with local water agencies, support for multi-benefit watershed projects, forest health treatments, and administration of critical financial and technical assistance for water managers and agricultural providers. The shift of experienced USDA staff could dimmish knowledge of regional and local conditions, technical expertise, knowledge of ongoing projects, historical precedents, and interagency coordination. ACWA is concerned that this may lead to inefficiencies and create challenges for water providers and others in the regulated community. For example, decreased forest work efforts may lead to higher chances of catastrophic wildfires that can have a severe economic impact on those who live in these areas as well as nationally.

## V. Extend the Comment Period Deadline

ACWA appreciates USDA providing an opportunity to comment on its intent to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. Due to the technical nature of this notice and its large-scale implications on forest management and water resources nationwide, ACWA encourages USDA to extend this comment period by at least an additional 30 days. Extending the comment period will allow USDA to consider adequate responses from more impacted parties.

The current 21-day timeframe is challenging for many small water utilities—including some ACWA member agencies—who may lack the resources to develop sufficient comments within the imposed deadline. Nevertheless, those directly affected by USFS activities under USDA jurisdiction have important real-world information to share that this short timeframe will likely hinder.

## Conclusion

Thank you for considering ACWA’s comments. ACWA stands ready to work with USDA and USFS leadership to support active forest management strategies to help reduce wildfire risk, restore forest health, and protect water infrastructure. Please let us know if we can provide additional information and resources. If you have any questions or would like to follow up on this matter, please contact ACWA Federal Relations Representative, Caleb Raspler, at calebr@acwa.com or (202) 434 - 4762.

Respectfully,

Re: Notice of Intent to prepare an environmental impact statement rescinding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Federal Register Doc. 2025-16581)

## Dear Secretary Rollins,

As Supervisor for Santa Barbara County’s First District, I take public safety and public access very seriously. California’s 20 million acres of national forests are vital to the efforts of both. So I speak for my constituents: we oppose the proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule) that prohibits new road construction and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas (with limited exceptions).

The #1 reason we oppose the revocation is because Roadless Areas promote fire safety and resilience. According to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) 2024 Wildfire Activity Statistics report, 97% of wildfire ignitions statewide were humancaused and occurred within 500 feet of road edges, which includes unimproved forest roads. Roads are ignition zones. In my district, the stakes are high, and a single spark can have devastating consequences.

Roadless areas, in contrast, serve as essential buffers and are a critical part of fire safety and resilience strategies. We just saw this with the recent Madre and Gifford Fires in the Cuyama Valley this summer: after a dragging chain sparked a roadside wildfire, a largely rural and roadless area in the Los Padres National Forest burned for a combined 210,000 acres burned. Fortunately – and due to the roadless nature of the land -- no lives were lost and the damage to property and industry was minimal.

In terms of fire-safety, the Roadless Rule does not stand in the way of fuel reduction and fire management projects. The U.S. Forest Service has approved multiple projects in roadless areas of Los Padres National Forest in recent years (including on Tecuya Ridge in Kern County and Pine Mountain in Ventura County), demonstrating that fire-related work can and does move forward under current protections.

I urge you to retain the Roadless Rule and carry on America’s Best Idea: preserving forests and wilderness as untouched beacons of safety and recreation. Every mile of roadless wilderness is one less ignition source and one more step toward keeping people safe.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,

## Dear Secretary Rollins,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the United States Department of Agriculture’s (“USDA”) proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule. More than 551,000 acres of four national forests are within Mesa County and of that acreage, more than 51% is inaccessible due to the Colorado Roadless Rule. While we understand that the Colorado Rule is not being considered in this Environmental Impact Statement (“EIS”), we appreciate being able to share our concerns and propose solutions to ensure our forests are actively managed rather than treated as de facto wilderness.

As is becoming more common, wildland fire crews have been battling large wildfires across western Colorado this summer. While years of continued drought is a factor in the number, size and intensity of these fires, overstocked and diseased forests, coupled with reductions in timber harvests, is also largely to blame for the billions being spent annually on suppression and recovery efforts.

Mesa County is now confronting our own recovery challenges following the Turner Gulch Fire that burned through nearly 32,000 acres, including forest identified as Colorado Roadless and Tier 1 Roadless areas. The fire has impacted a nearby community that depends on these forests for grazing cattle. Due to the loss of summer pasture, two large producers have had to relocate six hundred head of cattle to another allotment more than ten miles away. While this is an extremely difficult situation for these families, we are grateful for the willingness of our local USFS Ranger and staff to provide support and solutions to those affected.

While Colorado’s 2012 Roadless Rule has provided stability through changing administrative policies, we would like to advocate for allowing additional provisions. In partnership with the local USFS districts, allowing counties to collaborate in work related to fuels reduction, wildfire mitigation, and watershed maintenance would provide crucial active management that our forests urgently need. A similar agreement is working in Montana where counties have signed

Memoranda of Understand (“MOUs”) with the Forest Service to coordinate forest health efforts while respecting environmental concerns.

This request is not about opening these lands to development- but to provide better access to protect our communities and the water sources that we in the west rely so heavily on. Colorado’s counties have the tools, personnel, and collaborative spirit needed to contribute meaningfully to this effort. Our goal is to complement, not conflict with, the values embedded in the Roadless Rule by adding flexibility where it’s needed most.

We believe that communities need every tool available to combat the growing threat of increased fire activity. These fires test the limits of our emergency response systems, impact air quality, raise insurance rates, and threaten our rural economies and recreational assets. Counties want to be part of the solution—and we believe this framework offers a balanced, bipartisan way forward.

We thank you for your continued leadership in ensuring local voices are heard by our federal partners. We believe the Roadless Rule recension will benefit all western states as we address critical forest needs, and we hope that Colorado will be granted the same opportunity.

Sincerely,

Re: Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule (66 FR 3244, 36 CFR Subpart B (2001)) Public Comments

Dear Acting Director Kinder,

Boulder County appreciates the opportunity to provide public comments regarding the rescinding of the 2011 Roadless Rule. The Roadless Rule, first established in 2001, prohibits road construction, logging, and mining across more than 58 million acres of national forest land.

The Roadless Rule has been essential in protecting wildlife habitat, biodiversity, and drinking water quality, while also reducing soil erosion. A 2020 U.S. Forest Service study (https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/61251)—based on nearly 20 years of monitoring data— concluded that roads do not improve forest health through increased fire management activities. The study found that the absence of roads has not prevented fire prevention measures from occurring. Historical fire maps further demonstrate that forests with and without roads have burned at similar rates. In fact, areas with roads often experience more fires due to increased human-caused ignitions, which offset any benefits from easier access for firefighting.

The disadvantages of rescinding the Roadless Rule are numerous and well-documented:

• Roads accelerate the spread of invasive plant species.

• Roads cause significant erosion, degrading water quality.

Roads encourage development within watersheds, leading to reduced water quality and more expensive drinking water treatment.

• In many western states, roadless areas are the primary source of municipal drinking water.

There is no evidence that roadless protections impede national forest planning. According to CalWild (calwild.org), roadless designations actually help guide forest management planning. Importantly, the Forest Service retains access to all available fire suppression tools in roadless areas, including bulldozers and helicopters. Data show that roadless areas experience disproportionately fewer wildfires than roaded areas.

Because of topographical grades, roads are often constructed alongside stream and river corridors. Therefore, the recission of this rule may disproportionately impact beaver

Commissioner Claire Levy • Commissioner Marta Loachamin • Commissioner Ashley Stolzmann

Boulder County Courthouse • 1325 Pearl Street • Boulder, Colorado 80302

Mailing Address: P.O. Box 471 • Boulder, CO 80306 • www.BoulderCounty.gov

Commissioners@bouldercounty.gov • Telephone: 303.441.3500 • Fax: 303.441.4525 complexes within stream corridors. If these beaver complexes are impacted, we lose all the ecosystem services associated with beavers including flood mitigation, wildfire suppression, drought resiliency and the beaver-created habitat that supports many species of wildlife, including fish, birds and amphibians.

In summary, Boulder County does not believe rescinding the Roadless Rule will reduce wildfires or improve forest health. On the contrary, rescission would:

• Decrease biodiversity,

• Negatively impact wildlife,

• Degrade water quality,

• Increase invasive species spread,

• Accelerate soil erosion, and

• Heighten the risk of human-caused fires.

For these reasons, Boulder County strongly opposes rescinding the Roadless Rule. The 2001 Rule was established through an extensive public involvement process, and attempting to rescind it after only a limited two-week public comment period does not reflect the public’s will. Moreover, rescinding the rule would pave the way for taxpayer-funded logging roads that prioritize commercial logging at the expense of environmental protection, community use of the land for hunting, fishing, and recreation, and the preservation of water quality.

## Dear Secretary Rollins:

As the Board of County Commissioners for La Plata County, Colorado, we write to express our strong opposition to the proposed rescission of the federal Roadless Area Conservation Rule. Our county is home to 428,000 acres of the San Juan National Forest, whose 1.8 million acres spans 10 counties in Southwest Colorado. These lands provide essential wildlife habitat, watershed protection, recreation opportunities and economic vitality. The Roadless Rule has long been a cornerstone of protecting our environment, economy, and way of life.

## Local Impacts on Water and Forest Health

Roadless areas in and around La Plata County safeguard critical headwaters that supply clean drinking water to our residents, farms, and businesses. These watersheds are among the most sensitive landscapes in the region. Opening them to new road construction or industrial logging increases the risk of erosion, sedimentation, and long-term degradation of water quality.

## Wildfire and Public Safety

We recognize the urgent need to reduce wildfire risk in our forests. However, scientific research consistently shows that road building often increases human ignition sources and exacerbates fire spread. The Roadless Rule already allows for necessary exceptions—such as fire suppression and insect/disease control—while limiting unnecessary development in fragile areas. Rolling back the rule undercuts balanced, science-driven wildfire management.

## Economic and Cultural Concerns

La Plata County’s economy and identity are deeply tied to outdoor recreation, tourism, and the quality of life that comes from having accessible but intact public lands. Roadless areas draw hunters, anglers, hikers, and visitors from around the world. Their protection sustains businesses, jobs, and cultural traditions. Removing these protections threatens not only ecosystems but also the economic resilience of our communities.

## Climate Resilience and Long-Term Stewardship

Undisturbed forests play an irreplaceable role in carbon storage and climate resilience. At a time when Colorado and the Southwest face intensifying drought, wildfire, and extreme weather, it is shortsighted to reduce protections for landscapes that help buffer us from these impacts. The Roadless Rule provides a consistent, national framework that prevents piecemeal management and ensures these lands remain intact for future generations.

On behalf of the people of La Plata County, we urge the USDA and Forest Service to maintain the Roadless Rule in full effect. Rescinding this safeguard would risk irreversible harm to our water, wildlife, economy, and cultural heritage. We ask that you instead strengthen collaborative approaches to forest management that balance ecological integrity with community needs.

Thank you for considering our comments and for your commitment to the stewardship of our nation's forests.

Sincerely,

LA PLATA COUNTY

Ms. Brooke Rollins, Secretary United States Department of Agriculture U.S. Department of Agriculture 1400 Independence Ave., S.W. Washington, DC 20250

RE: Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

Dear Secretary Rollins:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Proposed Action to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule and to support upholding it. The only acceptable action for the USFS to take is the “No Action” Alternative to retain the U.S. Forest Service’s (USFS) 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.<sup>1</sup>

I am an Ouray County Commissioner and have held various leadership positions on our Colorado Counties Inc. and National Association of Counties public lands commitees over the last 14 years. I have served multiple terms on the Bureau of Land Management’s Southwest Colorado Regional Advisory Council and have participated as a representative for a cooperating agency in numerous planning and project processes with the United States Forest Service (USFS) and Bureau of Land Management (BLM). These roles involved participating as a knowledgeable local expert and local government liaison as part of these public lands management agencies’ coordination, collaboration, consultation, and cooperation eforts with local government stakeholders in all the phases of pre-scoping, scoping, draft, final, and objection in developing plans or projects with Environmental Impact Statements or Environmental Assessments as required by the National Environmental Protection Act (NEPA). I have atended and even assisted in planning and hosting public town hall events with USFS and BLM for their major planning or project actions.

In my capacity as Ouray County Commissioner, I am writing to provide comment on the Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (Notice) for proposed rulemaking on Roadless Area Conservation to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

Ouray County is a mountainous county located at the intersection of the northern San Juan Mountain range, the Colorado Plateau, and the Colorado Mineral Belt in southwestern Colorado. Elevations range from about 6,300 feet in the Uncompahgre River valley near Colona to over 14,000 feet at the tops of Mount Snefels and Weterhorn Peak. It comprises 542 square miles, with just 2 square miles (0.04%) of that being water. Ouray County has approximately 46 percent federal public land. Our population is about 5,100 people, and our density is less than 10 people per square mile.

Ouray County oficially recognizes in our 2025 revised Master Plan that our most precious resource is our natural environment. In fact, since our first Master Plan in 1971, we have recognized the importance of our natural resources and the strain that development and tourism have on our natural environment.<sup>2</sup>

Since 1971, we have framed the purpose and need for our Master Plan, our zoning, and our Land Use Code with this preamble:

“The area encompassed by Ouray County is a quiet land of awesome beauty, even today nearly untouched and unspoiled . . . It ranges from the magnificent San Juan Mountains on the south across the Uncompahgre Valley, and on in to the rolling foothills and mesas covering the northern parts of the county. Ouray County, then, possesses a rare combination of assets; a priceless and varied natural environment, ranging from unique wilderness to more hospitable areas, and a population which is aware of the value and delicacy of the physical seting surrounding it. Ouray County is now becoming known to people from all areas as a winter and summer recreation area . . . In the face of such potential popularity, how can the unique environment for living, including the delicate natural environment, be protected? How can the County accommodate the inevitable development pressures, without leting these pressures negate or even destroy the unique and irreplaceable qualities that atracted them in the first place?”<sup>3</sup>

The USFS Travel Management Rule and Roadless Rule together accomplish what local governments do with our public development of sound planning and zoning regulations. That is, we guide and manage development, growth, infrastructure, and transportation to ensure public health, safety, and welfare by reducing conflicts and degradation. By appropriately managing land use, balancing growth and land uses with community needs, providing adequate public services, protecting natural resources, and enhancing the overall quality of life for residents, we are ensuring that we are acting eficiently within our authority and our capacity.

Regarding the importance of retaining areas managed by the United States Forest Service (USFS) designated as “Roadless” under the 2012 Roadless Rule, I will be using examples from the State and places I know best, Colorado, the Grand Mesa, Uncompahgre, and Gunnison (GMUG) National Forests, and the adjacent San Juan National Forest (SJNF). I realize that the Roadless Rule rescission says it currently does not afect the Colorado Roadless Rule; however, without an understanding of what the Roadless Rule means and does, we might be next. Regardless, USFS lands provide essential ecosystem services, natural resources, watershed health, forest health, and multiple-use recreation to all Americans and our native plant and animal species.

I am strongly opposed to the Proposed Action of rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule and I am writing in support of upholding the 2001 Roadless Rule. I support the “No Action” Alternative to retain U.S. Forest Service’s (USFS) 2001 Roadless Area for the very reasons why the Roadless Rule was created in 2001.

The proposed rule would rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule) (66 FR 3244, 36 CFR Subpart B (2001)), which prohibits road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas, with limited exceptions.

The general rationale for this proposed rescission appears to be based on ideas that the Roadless rule bans road construction and suitable timber harvest, and therefore is related to increases in wildfires.<sup>4,5</sup> Current data and research refute that harvesting timber from Roadless Areas is necessary for industry or wildfire. There is also abundant data and robust support from diverse stakeholders and the American public for the Roadless Rule and its outcomes.

Important background information: The United States Forest Service (USFS) manages approximately 14.5 million acres of public lands in Colorado distributed among eight National Forests and two National Grasslands in Colorado. Of this, the Forest Service designated about 4.2 million acres (about 29 percent) as CRAs under the 2012 Colorado Roadless Rule. This tracks with the national average of Inventoried Roadless Areas outside of Colorado and Idaho. According to the summary information posted for this docket in the Federal Register, “Today, inventoried roadless areas total approximately 58.2 million acres, or about 30 percent of all National Forest System lands.”<sup>6</sup>

## 1. Both of the major premises for rescission of the Roadless Rule are false.

a. Timber harvests have increased (not harmfully decreased) in Colorado after the Roadless Rule was enacted. In Colorado, after the passage of the Roadless Rule, timber harvests on USFS lands continue to increase. For example, the USDA wrote in 2025 that “2020 timber harvests from private timberlands were 159 percent higher than in 2016 while timber harvests from National Forest System lands were 33 percent higher.”<sup>7</sup>

In 2003, a Colorado State University research report about “forests and water” reviewed all forested lands in Colorado, regardless of ownership, and stated, “Forests occupy 22.6 million acres in Colorado, or 32 percent of the land area, and nearly three-quarters of the forest lands in Colorado are in public ownership. About 55 percent of the forested area is considered suitable for forest harvest. National forests comprise nearly half of the forested area, and approximately 60 percent of the area is considered suitable for forest harvest. There are no significant, privately owned, industrial forest lands in Colorado.”<sup>8</sup>

The USFS calculations of suitable timber change over time based on changes in methods and harvesting technology. Non-reserved timberland is forest land that is both productive enough to be harvested for wood products and is not legally protected from timber harvesting. In 2020, a USFS report found that 70.3 percent of USFS land in Colorado was non-reserved timberland.<sup>9</sup> This equates to 10.1 million acres out of 14.5 million acres of USFS lands in the state, even with the 2012 Colorado Roadless Rule in efect.

b. USFS research also contradicts the government's assertion that building more roads will help combat wildfires. A 2020 Forest Service study concluded, after nearly 20 years of monitoring data, that additional roads do not beneficially improve forest health or enhance fire management eforts.<sup>10</sup>

In fact, the study found that the abundance of human-caused fires was more common in roaded areas than in non-roaded areas. To quote the study:

“Agency management records show that a lack of roads has not stopped fire prevention measures; fuel management activities in roadless areas have actually been more numerous on a per-square kilometer basis than elsewhere in the National Forest System, although activities in areas with roads cover larger areas. Historical fire maps indicate that forests with and without roads have burned at similar rates since the Rule took efect. The apparent neutrality of roads with respect to fire occurrence may be due to higher rates of human caused ignition near roads ofseting advantages related to more agile positioning of fire-fighting assets.”

The increased density of wildfire starts near roads vs. other lands is also described by The Wilderness Society in a 2025 paper.<sup>11</sup>

The Forest Service is already permited to conduct thinning and other fuel reduction projects in roadless areas to help mitigate wildfires and improve important habitat.<sup>12</sup> In many locations, existing roads provide adequate access for both wildfire mitigation and community defense. According to findings by the USDA Ofice of Inspector General,<sup>13</sup> the current road infrastructure has suficient access for fire suppression in nearly all high-risk areas, including those that are roadless.

2. Motorized and non-motorized stakeholder groups agree that Roadless Areas do not exclude motorized trail construction and maintenance. For example, in oficial comments shared by Colorado OHV Coalition, Trails Preservation Alliance, and Colorado Snowmobile Association, these organizations stated in 2018 to the GMUG: “1) While Roadless areas have limitations on road construction and heavy maintenance, multiple-use trails are entirely outside the scope of the Colorado Roadless Rule, 2) Trail networks to include motorized trails may be constructed and expanded in Colorado Roadless areas.”<sup>14</sup>

3. The proposed rescission will negatively afect runof and water supplies if more roads are constructed in high-elevation areas. It is common sense to acknowledge that plowing roads and introducing dust accelerates early snow melting. Changes in land cover and contour changes runof paterns. In 2003, a Colorado State University research report about “forests and water” found, “Most of the runof in Colorado comes from forest and alpine areas above approximately 9,000 ft (2730 m) in elevation, and is generated by snowmelt from approximately mid-April to mid-July.” <sup>15</sup>

It is well-known that due to climate change, Colorado has experienced dramatically warmer winter temperatures and increases in precipitation falling as rain instead of snow over the last 25 years. These changes make the runof from USFS-managed forest lands even more precious in the greater Colorado River basin.<sup>16</sup> Our headwater communities and agriculture will be harmed by further accelerating snow melting.

It is well-documented that Colorado's peak runof is shifting to earlier in the spring, occurring before the main growing season for many crops, due to climate change and warming temperatures. This earlier runof is characterized by a reduced overall snowpack and earlier peak streamflow timing by 1-4 weeks, impacting water management, agriculture, and reservoir operations statewide. Other contributing factors can include dust-on-snow events, which reduce snow reflectivity and accelerate melting.

Roadless areas provide an essential bufer from worsening impacts and challenges due to reductions in water availability, including intake by thirsty soils and vegetation, agricultural stress, reduced water supplies for water storage, and increased fire vulnerability.<sup>17</sup>

4. The rescission will negate years of public engagement and stakeholder input and overturn Roadless Areas that balance conservation and active management in areas important to the public and the economy. If the USDA reneges on its “commitment to the public collaborative process and respects the stakeholders' good faith compromises and engagement during the original efort to develop the 2012 Colorado Roadless Rule,”<sup>18</sup> there will certainly be a chilling efect on future collaborative processes and partnerships, which the USFS relies on to fulfill its mission.

The highly collaborative process that led to the Roadless Rule and Colorado’s 2012 Roadless Rule should be honored and preserved. As recorded in the Federal Register, <sup>19</sup>

a. “The State of Colorado, USDA, Forest Service, and the public worked in partnership for many years to find a balance between conserving roadless area characteristics for future generations and allowing management activities—including the construction of temporary roads that would not foreclose coal exploration and development—within CRAs that are important to Colorado's citizens and the economy. Throughout the

rulemaking process, a total of five formal comment periods were held by the State and Forest Service resulting in 27 public meetings and more than 312,000 comments. In addition, five meetings open to the public were held by the Roadless Area Conservation National Advisory Commitee, which provided recommendations to the Secretary of Agriculture… The final amount of CRA and upper tier acreage was arrived at through a collaborative process between the Forest Service and stakeholders… demonstrates USDA's commitment to the public collaborative process and respects the stakeholders' good faith compromises and engagement during the original efort to develop the 2012 Colorado Roadless Rule.”

5. The rescission ignores that Roadless Areas perform important functions. As summarized in the Federal Register<sup>20</sup>,

“In its petition to the Secretary of Agriculture, the State of Colorado indicated a need to develop State-specific regulations for the management of Colorado's roadless areas for the following reasons:

Roadless areas are important because they are, among other things, sources of drinking water, important fish and wildlife habitat, semi-primitive or primitive recreation areas that include both motorized and non-motorized recreation opportunities, and naturally appearing landscapes. A need exists to provide for the conservation and management of roadless area characteristics.

The USDA, the Forest Service, and the State of Colorado recognize that timber cuting, sale, or removal and road construction/reconstruction have the greatest likelihood of altering and fragmenting landscapes, resulting in immediate, longterm loss of roadless area characteristics. Therefore, there is a need to generally prohibit these activities in roadless areas.”

6. Colorado’s Roadless Rule demonstrates that state-specific Roadless Rules are beneficial to manage Roadless Areas, and Roadless Areas are desired and needed. The proposed rescission should not resort to a unilateral rescission. It could instead analyze, in a NEPA process, an alternative that opens the door for additional state-specific Roadless Rules using Colorado as a model. As articulated in the Federal Register,

“The 2012 Colorado Roadless Rule also addressed State-specific concerns that are important to the citizens and economy of Colorado. These concerns included: (1) Reducing the risk of wildfire to communities and municipal water supply systems, (2) permiting construction and maintenance of water conveyance structures, (3) restricting linear construction zones, (4) accommodating ski areas, and (5) facilitating exploration and development of coal resources in the North Fork Coal Mining Area. Providing for the State-specific concerns generally allows for tree cuting and road construction/reconstruction beyond what was allowed under the 2001 Roadless Rule.”

“The Colorado Roadless Rule includes regulatory provisions to mitigate impacts of road construction within CRAs. Specifically:

Within a native cuthroat trout catchment or identified recovery watershed, road construction will not diminish, over the long-term, conditions in the water influence zone and the extent of the occupied native cuthroat trout habitat (36 CFR 294.43(c)(2)(iv)).

Watershed conservation practices will be applied to all projects occurring in native cuthroat trout habitat (36 CFR 294.43(c)(2)(v)).

Conduct road construction in a manner that reduces efects on surface resources and prevents unnecessary or unreasonable surface disturbance (36 CFR 294.43(d)(1)).

Decommission any road and restore the afected landscape when it is determined that the road is no longer needed for the established purpose prior to, or upon termination or expiration of a contract, authorization, or permit, if possible. Require the inclusion of a road decommissioning provision in all contracts or permits. Design decommissioning to stabilize, restore, and revegetate unneeded roads to a more natural state to protect resources and enhance roadless area characteristics (36 CFR 294.43(d)(2)).”

The above provisions were negotiated and implemented in good faith between the USDA, the State of Colorado, stakeholders, and citizens.

7. The rescission is unnecessary and will be costly in dollars to implement and manage. Despite the confusing name, “Roadless Areas,” these areas do actually have pre-existing roads, routes, and trails providing high-quality multiuse benefits while also reducing levels of efort and road maintenance costs that the USFS and gateway communities cannot aford. Gateway communities also provide health, safety, welfare, search and rescue, and additional gateway community services. Gateway communities and counties provide maintenance of local roads that lead to USFS system roads. If the USFS dramatically increases its system roads, that will cause an unfunded mandate on gateway communities, many of which are rural or frontier rural with very limited capacity and resources.

The 2005 Travel Management Rule<sup>21</sup> is essential to retain, along with the Roadless Rule.

8. I am incorporating by reference the full comments provided by Winter Wildlands Alliance for this docket. The excellent and well-researched points made by Winter Wildlands Alliance include:

a. Wildfire Management Should Maximize the Defensive Value of Existing Road Infrastructure.

b. The Roadless Rule Already Supports Flexible, Multiple-Use Management.

c. The Roadless Rule Is Vital to Creating Meaningful Outdoor Experiences Across User Groups.

i. I especially want to emphasize the importance of Roadless Areas to supporting Ouray County’s outdoor recreation-based economy and our dedication to environmental quality and integrity for humans and wildlife. Ouray County, particularly the City of Ouray, is often referred to as the “Outdoor Recreation Capital of Colorado” due to its more than 60 recreational activities that residents and visitors can enjoy.<sup>22</sup> Ouray County’s unique outdoor experiences depend on the pristine forests, rock outcrops, dark skies, and wild lands supporting hunting, hiking, mountaineering, mountain biking, backcountry skiing, rock and ice climbing, in our remote and technical terrain within Roadless Areas. According to Colorado’s Outdoor Recreation Industry Ofice within the Ofice of Economic Development and International Trade (OEDIT), “Colorado’s outdoor recreation industry accounts for \$13.9 billion in value-added (GDP) annually and contributed 130,000 direct jobs in 2022. According to the 2017 SCORP report, 92% of Colorado residents participate in outdoor recreation each year.”<sup>23</sup> Twenty-nine percent of Colorado is within Roadless Areas, which provides high-quality outdoor recreation and hunting opportunities that reduce conflicts with other types of uses while also balancing essential conservation and water resource needs.

ii. Roadless areas also support the country’s \$1.2 trillion outdoor recreation economy, which represents 2.3% of the U.S. GDP and supports 5 million jobs.<sup>24</sup> In the winter, people travel from all over the country to areas where they can ski, snowshoe, snowboard, and snowmobile, with backcountry tourism playing a vital role in supporting rural mountain communities across the American West where many of these roadless areas are. All afected communities must receive locality-specific analyses on socio-economic and cultural impacts from the proposed rescission rule before implementing any alternative other than Alternative A, the No Action Alternative.

iii. The Travel Management Rule requires the Forest Service to designate specific areas for motorized and non-motorized winter use under Subpart C.15 This

process is designed to balance recreation access, protect natural resources, and minimize user conflicts. Roadless areas are essential to this framework as they preserve undeveloped terrain necessary for both motorized and non-motorized opportunities while ensuring that travel planning decisions remain efective.

iv. If the Roadless Rule were rescinded, new road construction would undermine the integrity and intent of Subpart C travel management planning. It would increase user conflicts, degrade undeveloped recreation setings, and constrain the agency’s ability to provide diverse recreation opportunities consistent with federal policy.

d. Roads Fragment Ecosystems, Afect Water Quality, and Reduce Biodiversity.

e. Rescinding the Roadless Rule Undermines Precedent for Public Participation in Land Management.

f. Roads Construction and Maintenance Is Costly.

In closing, the Forest Service must adopt the No Action Alternative.

Respectfully,

<s>

Lynn Padget

County Commissioner

Ouray County, Colorado

lpadget@ourayco.gov

# BCC 2025-146 Sept. '11, 2025

U.S. Forest Service Attn: Director, Ecosystem Management Coordination 201 14th Street SW, Mailstop <sub>1</sub> 108 Washington, DC 20250-1 124

RE: Proposal to Rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (docket number FS-2025- 0001)

Dear Secretary Rollins,

Missoula County submits this comment to express our opposition to the proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. While we share concerns about wildfire risk and forest health, the proposed rollback of critical protections for inventoried roadless areas presents significant threats to our communities, ecosystems and the long{erm resilience of our public lands.

Missoula County is privileged to be surrounded by vast expanses of national forest <sub>lands,</sub> including inventoried roadless areas, that provide clean water, habitat for native wildlife, and iconic wildlands for recreation, tourism and quality of life. We are concerned about the ecological and environmental risks associated with building new roads in these areas, including creating fragmented ecosystems, increased erosion and invasive species spread, and threatened sensitive plants and wildlife habitat.

Research also suggests that roads can actually increase wildfire ignition and severity rather than reduce risk. A recent study (2025) analyzing three decades of wildfire data across contiguous U.S. national forests found wildfire ignition density was highest within 50 meters of roads versus much lower densities farther away, resulting in clear findings that most wildfires started near roads not in roadless areas. Furthermore, existing allowances in the rule already permit emergency fire suppression and hazard response.

Conversely, increased road building will burden already strained Forest Service budgets with insurmountable infrastructure maintenance costs with increased risk to public safety and water quality. GAO confirmed \$4.85 billion in deferred maintenance for roads (FY2022), and more recent USFS data from FY2024 indicates \$5.373 billion in road maintenance backlogs alone (excluding bridges). These backlogs are already presenting public safety and water quality concerns for Missoula County.

![](images/17a47b55fa0b3bd1d36a6364e4e51d38ca6bfdd7a81aa1e8ffc2f04daee98e63.jpg)

The 2001 Roadless Rule emerged from nearly 1.6 million public comments and more than 600 hearings, making it one of the most participatory federal rulemakings in history. Revoking such a widely vetted and enduring rule without equally robust public engagement undermines trust and transparency. Missoula County is aware that an Environmental lmpact Statement (ElS) is forthcoming, anticipating a draft in winter 2026 and final decisions by late 2026, and we want to emphasize the need for careful, science-based review, not hasty rescission.

We urge the Forest Service to maintain the integrity of the 2001 Roadless Rule, preserving roadless protections that safeguard critical values.

At minimum, any changes to the rule must be preceded by full, transparent and inclusive public engagement, including local communities, stakeholders, interest groups and local, state and tribal governments.

Decisions regarding road construction must continue to require site-specific Environmental Assessments or Environmental lmpact Statements, consistent with the National Environmental Policy Act and existing land management plans.

Thank you for your attention and consideration

Sincerely,

BOARD OF COUNTY COMMISSIONERS

SANDERS COUNTY BOARDOF COMMISSIONERS

## Re: Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule

Dear Secretary Rollins,

Sanders and Mineral County have entered into a Memorandum Of Understanding to work together to assist in the formulation of federal agency planning and project development. The commissioners have identified that most issues facing both counties are similar, if not identical and the issues set forth in the Mineral County Resource Use Plan apply to most the lands in Sanders County as well.

The following input is provided jointly by Mineral and Sanders Counties in support of the USDA’s actions to rescind the Roadless Rule.

We strongly support President Trump’s Executive Order 14192 to eliminate overcomplicated, burdensome barriers that hamper American business, fire suppression, multiple use forest management, and innovation and we applaud the USDA actions to rescind the ill-conceived, obstructive 2001 Roadless Rule purportedly put in place to “protect” over 59 million acres of NFS lands, a flawed notion that has proven to be catastrophically incorrect.

The Roadless Rule effectively barred active forest management across nearly 60 million acres of our National Forest System lands. Predictably, now these forests are overstocked and stressed as they compete for limited water and nutrients, conditions that make them increasingly susceptible to insect and disease infestations and the inevitable ensuing wildfires. Nearly half of all roadless acres are located in areas rated as high or very high wildfire risk with dead or dying trees dominating the landscape creating ideal conditions for a disastrous increase in high-severity wildfires. Already more than 8 million acres of roadless forests have burned since the Roadless Rule was enacted including areas within the Wildland Urban Interface (WUI) threatening life and public and private property.

The 2001 roadless rule along with the Endangered Species Act, and the related litigation and flawed court decisions have caused the disastrous loss of our natural resource dependent industries across the west devastating communities, citizens, schools, hospitals, and counties. Here in Mineral and Sanders Counties we are most effected by the loss of our forest products industry. Since 1990 we have lost 36 forest products industries along with thousands of directly related high paying jobs in Montana.

The reference to the lands within the Roadless Rule here in Montana as “roadless” is erroneous and misleading. There are thousands of miles of existing roads within lands designated under the 2001 Roadless Rule, including National Forest System roads as well as county, state, or other ownerships. Additionally, in many cases they are either adjacent to or very near freeways, railroads, high voltage power lines, and communities. They extend into the WUI butting up against private land ownerships.

Insect and disease and wildfire activity, especially within the WUI, affects important resources, neighboring infrastructure, and communities and threatens life and property.

The evidence is clear, the 2001 Roadless Rule does not now nor has it ever provided appropriate mandated actions to manage our National Forests for the benefits of all Americans. Rescinding the roadless rule will place management decisions back in the hands of local land management agencies and personnel with local knowledge and expertise guided by land management plans without restrictive and unnecessary national prohibitions.

Once the IRA’s are rescinded, local professional land managers will manage those areas as directed by Forest Plans and NEPA guidelines. While there can be no doubt there will be an increase in road construction, logging and other resource management activities, including recreation, and fire mitigation activities, it will not result in unrestrained road building and logging activities as some would have us believe.

While we appreciate the opportunity for the public to provide input on this action, we hope the USDA will use this information to help inform and substantiate their decision to rescind the roadless rule only, not to decide whether to rescind the rule. Our forests are in crisis and an emergency situation has been determined. Immediate action is needed, now is not the time for procrastination. This should not be a collaborative action or majority vote; the decision should lie squarely within the USDA.

A great deal of good work is already being done with more planned in the near future to reduce bureaucratic layers and place management decisions back in the hands of local land management agencies and personnel with local knowledge and expertise. However, we are concerned about implementation.

Four difficult barriers have not yet been addressed that are obstructing the agencies ability to implement new programs and policies:

1. Managing ESA species (most specifically grizzlies and bull trout in our area) is and will continue to hamper project development. Grizzlies should be delisted and we need to have a serious discussion about our ability to ever see the recovery of bull trout without aggressively dealing with the invasive species issue. Bull trout in the Clark Fork River drainage can not be recovered managing habitat only. 2. litigation continues to obstruct project development and implementation.

3. Agency personnel are struggling with the “new era” concept and implementation of new policies and programs providing us with the tools to accomplish recent directions mandated by Executive Orders, Secretarial Memos, Associate Chiefs Implementation Directive, and the National Active Forest Management Strategy. The concept of developing larger projects, maximizing the number of acres for commercial treatments within each project, treating more volume per acre, and utilizing all the tools made available to overcome roadblocks to accomplish this work is proving difficult for agency personnel to wrap their arms around.

4. We also are impaired by dealing with a shortage of private sector infrastructure to facilitate or accomplish multiple use benefits.

Respectfully Submitted,

Mineral and Sanders Counties

Subject: Comments on the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule

Dear Secretary Rollins and Chief Shultz,

On behalf of the citizens of Ravalli County, we write to provide our perspective on the U.S. Forest Service and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's review of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (the ''Roadless Rule"). As local stakeholders who live and work alongside these public lands, we believe our community's experience offers valuable insights for your consideration.

Since its implementation over two decades ago, the Road less Rule has significantly affected forest management practices in our region. The rule's restrictions on road construction and reconstruction have negatively impacted public safety for our citizens, firefighters and visitors as well as limiting various management activities, including thinning, prescribed burns and sanitation harvesting. Ravalli County has observed the following impacts:

The Bitterroot National Forest has the highest fire hazard watersheds in the nation due to hazardous fuels loads, insect infestation and disease.

Ravalli County has 1, 126,604 acres of USDA Bitterroot National Forest Service land in our jurisdiction, which include:

• 403,438 acres of Inventoried Road less Area

• 483,882 acres of Wilderness Area

• 103,370 acres of Wilderness Study Area)

• 105,876 acres IRA (road construction allowed)

• 219,485 acres IRA (No road construction allowed)

• 77,077 acres IRA (within Recommended Wilderness AreaM/SA)

The Bitterroot National Forest is hamstrung when you consider that 81 % of the forestland in our jurisdiction has a special use designation. These designations significantly limit opportunities for fire suppression, forest management and recreational pursuits.

Ungulate populations live and thrive in healthy forest stands with adequate forage and utilize roads as game trails. Dense, over-grown stands support higher predator populations, which in turn, drive ungulate populations onto working agricultural lands.

Ravalli County has experienced nearly one million acres of catastrophic wildfires since 2000, much of which has been in special designation areas (Wilderness, Recommended Wilderness, WSA, IRA).

Based on the above reasons, we support proposed changes to the Roadless Rule.

We appreciate the opportunity to provide input on this important policy and request that you consider the unique conditions and needs of our community in your deliberations. Ravalli County looks forward to working constructively with federal land managers to achieve outcomes that serve both local and national interests.

Respectfully,

Subiect: Support for Rescinding the Roadless Rule in the Willow Creek Watershed Area.

Dear To Whom lt May Concern,

We are writing to express our strong support for rescinding the application of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule) in the Willow Creek Watershed Area located in White Sulphur Springs, MT.

While we recognize the importance of conservation, we believe the current restrictions imposed by the Roadless Rule in this particular region are overly broad and counterproductive to the long-term environmental and economic health of our communities.

The Willow Creek Watershed Area is a vital resource not only for water supply but also for forest management, wildfire mitigation, recreation, and responsible economic development. Maintaining roadless status hinders essential access for active forest management, especially as we face increasing threats from catastrophic wildfires due to fuel accumulation and climate-driven weather extremes. Carefully planned and constructed roads are criticalfor thinning overgrown forests, conducting emergency operations, and ensuring that first responders can act quickly to protect both natural resources and human life.

Moreover, local industries that depend on access to forestlands-such as sustainable logging, mining, and tourism-have been hampered by the inflexibllity of the Roadless Rule. With modern environmental oversight and improved best practices, we can ensure development occurs in a responsible way that balances conservation with community needs.
