Brad Kinder, Acting Director United States Department of Agriculture Ecosystem Management Coordination 201 14th Street SW, Mailstop 1108 Washington, DC 20250-1124

Re: Docket # FS-2025-001 Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement

Dear Director Kinder,

Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks (“FWP”) appreciates the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (“Department’s) invitation to submit written comments on its initiation of an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) and rulemaking attendant to the proposed recission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Rule). As stewards of Montana’s fish, wildlife, and recreational resources, FWP agrees that the proposal to rescind the Roadless Rule requires a robust environmental analysis, particularly considering the increasing pressure from human development and recreation. In the same stewardship role, FWP recognizes the need to manage forests for long-term resilience and health — particularly in the face of increasingly severe wildfire seasons.

## Elk

Roadless areas in Montana provide critical habitat for many of the state’s iconic and sensitive wildlife species. Repealing the 2001 Roadless Rule would likely result in increased road construction. The relationships between elk, elk habitat, and roads are well-researched and documented. Incorporating relevant elements of that existing science into the NEPA analysis before any final rule determination would both inform and enhance the strength of any final decision. FWP stands ready to provide more details if necessary.

## Grizzly Bears and Other Species

Like elk, the relationship between roads and grizzly bears is well-established in science. And like elk, due consideration of that science should be a component of any environmental review. Different from statemanaged elk, the ongoing effort to delist recovered grizzly bear populations still listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) in the lower 48 states adds credence to the thoughtful consideration of all available science, recovery efforts, and commitments already made by the

![](images/ae5ffcbe7de2fc66626890c563b72cbe8d240027626b0254ae48944cb4a8485b.jpg)

Department to date. Again, FWP stands ready to provide more details if necessary. Other ESA-listed species, including wolverines, lynx, and bull trout, are also present in current roadless areas.

## Recreation

FWP recommends reviewing and considering the goals in Montana’s 2026-2030 Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (SCORP) when preparing the Environmental Impact Statement. The purpose of the SCORP is to guide recreation planning, management, and investment among local, tribal, state, and federal partners. This includes balancing recreation access with wildlife habitat conservation, which is an important consideration in the EIS. The final SCORP will be available January 1, 2026.

## Conclusion and Recommendations

The proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (36 CFR Subpart B, 66 FR 3244) has the potential to impact a wide array of wildlife, fisheries, habitat, and recreational opportunities. FWP urges the U.S. Forest Service, through a rigorous environmental review, to explore supported and long-lasting opportunities for targeted, science-based forest management that balances habitat conservation (and potential improvement) and recreation with forest resilience health goals. This approach will benefit both wildlife and people using National Forest lands in Montana today and in the future.

Sincerely,

Christy Clark

Director

## Director Kinder,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA)’s Notice of Intent to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) and rulemaking concerning management of inventoried roadless areas on approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System lands. The effort of the USDA and the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) to return decision making for road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas to local officials, in conjunction with Forest-level land management planning, is long overdue.

On behalf of the Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation (DNRC), we support the recission of the inventoried roadless areas rule, more commonly referred to as the “roadless rule.” Since 2001, the roadless rule has significantly restricted common sense active forest management on National Forest System lands. The impact across the western United States has been significant. For Montana, this has meant 58 percent of USFS lands in our state have been directly affected by this designation. During this period, we have witnessed declining forest health, higher intensity wildfires, and restricted access for federal and state land management agencies to meaningfully address excessive fuels and respond to wildfires.

In light of our forest health crisis, the State of Montana, thanks to leadership from Governor Greg Gianforte, has been focused on expanding forest management efforts including on federal lands. The Governor and Chief Tom Schultz recently entered into a historic Shared Stewardship Agreement (SSA) with the USFS. This agreement proposes several landmark measures, including the State managing a 200,000-acre landscape utilizing Good Neighbor Authority (GNA).

Montana’s State Forest Action Plan, which was developed by the DNRC in coordination with the USFS, the Natural Resources Conservation Service, the Bureau of Land Management, and a 23-member citizen advisory committee, identified areas at the highest risk of fire and degraded forest health. The risk of wildfire to lives, property, and natural resources is ever present in Montana, with over 20 million acres at an elevated risk of wildfire, including 3.8 million acres in the Priority Areas for Focused Attention. The Priority Areas for Focused Attention represent 3.8 million acres of forested land in Montana. Notably, this includes approximately 500,000 acres in the wildland-urban interface, or WUI, and 123,000 acres in drinking water source watersheds.

About 23 percent (approximately 10.2 million acres) of inventoried roadless areas managed under the 2001 Roadless Rule are within the WUI, areas where human development intermixes with the wildland, based on the definition of WUI set out in the Healthy Forests Restoration Act of 2003 (16 U.S.C. 6511(16)). An additional 4.8 million areas are within one mile of the WUI, totaling about 35 percent of these inventoried roadless area acres. These inventoried roadless areas pose a much higher risk for catastrophic fire than areas that are accessible for fuels mitigation treatments.

When considering wildfire risk in relation to inventoried roadless areas, it is important to recognize that adjacency to these lands can significantly increase WUI risk.

Inventoried roadless areas are adjacent to the WUI, creating unique wildfire management challenges. The Suppression Difficulty Index (SDI), detailed by the USFS Research and Development, provides a science-based metric for assessing how landscape factors like topography, fuels, and road access influence the difficulty of suppressing wildfires in these regions. USFS frameworks such as Potential Operational Delineations (PODs) explicitly integrate SDI, mapping out strategic fire management zones using boundaries like roads and natural barriers—features especially relevant when protecting highly valued resources and assets near the WUI. These connections are discussed in “Using Potential Operational Delal Operational Delineations (PODs) on Your Forest,” “Suppression Difficulty Index | US Forest Service Research and Development,” and the Rocky Mountain Research Station's PODs overview, which collectively demonstrate that fires in inventoried roadless areas and adjacent to WUI communities are more difficult to suppress, creating a high wildfire risk when access is not present. The science is clear that access for forest health and wildfire hazard reduction is critical and lowers overall wildfire risk to communities and infrastructure.

There are 393,337.58 inventoried roadless acres within State Forest Action Plan priority areas. These inventoried roadless areas pose a much higher risk for catastrophic fire than areas that are accessible for forest health projects and wildfire risk reduction.

This has a tangible impact on the overall costs for implementing active forest management projects to mitigate fire risks. For instance, the Basin Creek-Butte Watershed project, which is being implemented by the USFS, DNRC, and the City and County of Butte-Silver Bow, lies partially within the Basin Creek Inventoried Roadless Area. Because of that, it is more complex and expensive than a typical fuel reduction project. Planning the project required additional considerations for the roadless area, and a substantial process to allow effective fuel reduction treatment within the roadless area units. With limitations on road building, implementation options for our contractors were limited to very long forwarding distances and/or helicopter operations. These operations require specialized equipment and skills, slow the pace of work, and limit the pool of contractors who can complete the work.

The Basin Creek Phase 2 contract is estimated to treat 1,550 acres for \$3,787,751. At over \$2,400 per acre, this work is more than quadruple the average paid by DNRC for recent fuel reduction work. Because road building and conventional harvesting operations were not considered or available to bidders on the project, we do not have exact costs for comparison. That said, we are confident that the flexibility to build temporary roads and consider other harvesting systems would have encouraged additional bidders and resulted in a lower cost for treatment.

Lastly, the roadless rule has a direct effect on the ability of partners to respond to wildfires. This past June, we witnessed the Jericho Mountain fire from our state’s capital. The response from the USFS, along with interagency partners, was focused, thoughtful, and aggressive, with resources visibly being deployed to respond to the incident. For a multitude of reasons, this is a challenging landscape to navigate. However, the top challenge that shaped the overall response was the fact that this is a roadless area. We were fortunate that favorable weather conditions, in conjunction with an aggressive response effort, led to the fire being contained. The reality is that the roadless rule shapes and ultimately places restrictions on fire suppression tools and techniques that are necessary to aggressively and safely respond to fires.

We appreciate the opportunity to offer comments. As you continue to work through this effort, the State of Montana would welcome the opportunity to assist you. If you have additional questions, please contact Shawn Thomas, Montana State Forester, at sthomas@mt.gov or 406-444-4978.

## Executive Summary

The Montana Natural Resource Coalition strongly supports the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and the return of decision-making to the local level. However, we have some concerns that we wish to raise with our expectation that the responsible official(s) will be responsive to those concerns.

The United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) is initiating proposed rulemaking to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and prepare an environmental impact statement (EIS) concerning management of approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System lands in the United States, including Alaska. The rule at 36 CFR Subpart B prohibits road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas, with limited exceptions.

The closure of roads throughout the National Forest System (NFS) along with the restriction preventing construction of any new roads within inventoried roadless areas (IRAs) since 2001 has had deleterious effects on recreation, timber harvest potential, mineral location and extraction, livestock grazing, and other important multiple uses. Congress requires the management of public lands in recognition of a “domestic source of minerals, food, timber, and fiber from the public lands including implementation of the Mining and Minerals Policy Act of 1970 (84 Stat. 1876, 30 USC 21a) as it pertains to the public lands.”<sup>1</sup>

For decades federal agencies have incrementally sequestered increasing amounts of natural resources on federal lands, causing the nation to become more dependent upon foreign sources of minerals, timber, and other materials. This creates international trade disadvantages and impediments to crucial local economic development and activity.

The proposed rescission would return planning to local levels.

Concurrently, the Department of the Interior Bureau of Land Management (BLM) is proposing to rescind its Conservation and Landscape Health Rule (CLHR) that was issued as a final rule on May 9, 2024.

In our research we discovered that the forested lands managed by the BLM and the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) lands affected by the 2001 Roadless rule were both subject to executive orders, some of which were not called out in the Federal Register notice of intent, mandating increased production of forest products and minerals for reasons of national security and economic resilience, both of which are matters of overriding public interest, the nature of which means that these concerns take precedence over normal considerations for public lands management, as reinforced by USDA Secretary’s Memorandum 1078-006, which designated an emergency situation on National Forest System Lands.

We fear that this oversight will lead to a missed opportunity to solicit comments relating to the consideration of the executive branch’s national security and economic resiliency concerns and the management practices necessary to mitigate those concerns.

The proposed rulemaking and EIS development are taking place at a time of intense government-wide regulatory reform actions and in the context of the authority of agency employees to interpret law being significantly curtailed as a result of recent judicial decisions and executive actions. Agency officials working on this process will need training in how to accomplish rulemaking and NEPA analysis not only for new NEPA process requirements but also for reduced authority to interpret law.

Despite the 2001 agency commitment to seek input and participation by State, local, and Tribal officials in the early stages of forest and project planning regarding subsequent decisions for inventoried roadless areas, the current notice of intent states that the agency will not offer such participation by those officials, improperly relegating them to being passive public commenters. We provide the responsible official(s) with tools in this document to correct this error before it becomes an issue for judicial review.

## Introduction

These comments are responsive to the 90 FR 42179 Notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement and rulemaking to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule<sup>2</sup> (2001 Roadless Rule). The 2001 Roadless Rule prohibits road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas (IRAs), with limited exceptions. The Tongass National Forest and state-specific roadless rules for Idaho and Colorado are excluded from this process which would return decision-making for road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in IRAs to local officials in conjunction with Forest-level land management planning.

The EIS will evaluate the impacts of the proposed rule rescission and study alternatives for roadless area conservation on National Forest System lands, including the Tongass National Forest, in the context of multiple use resource management.

The primary statutory authority controlling the U.S. Forest Service is found in the Organic Act of 1897, now codified at 16 USC § 475:

“…No national forest shall be established, except to improve and protect the forest within the boundaries, or for the purpose of securing favorable conditions of water flows, and to furnish a continuous supply of timber for the use and necessities of citizens of the United States; but it is not the purpose or intent of these provisions, or of said section, to authorize the inclusion therein of lands more valuable for the mineral therein, or for agricultural purposes, than for forest purposes.”<sup>3</sup>

It is the express intent of Congress that the 154 national forests in the National Forest System be managed so as not to affect productive utilization of timber, access for exploration and extraction of the higher value mineral estate, opportunities for domestic livestock grazing on Taylor Grazing Act - Chiefly Valuable for Grazing Districts (CVG Districts) situated throughout the National Forest System, or recreational opportunities.

16 USC § 475 applies both delegation and non-delegation doctrine prescriptive mandates. Congress delegated authority to USFS to accomplish four purposes but denied authority to incorporate lands containing higher value mineral resources or that would be managed for agricultural purposes.

16 USC § 528, Development and Administration of Renewable Surface Resources for Multiple-Use and Sustained-Yield

In the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act of 1960 (MUSYA), Congress expanded and elaborated upon the Organic Act of 1897 statute, and both laws continue to form the mission and purpose behind the existence of the U.S. Forest Service as a civil service agency.

MUSYA established a productive hierarchy for resource management concentrated on natural resource productivity and utilization as opposed to sequestration. Conservation occurs within and is a byproduct of productive multiple land and resource use principles. Consequently, forest monitoring, management, and inventory programs reflect values that prioritize for productive and multiple use.

“It is the policy of the Congress that the national forests are established and shall be administered for outdoor recreation, range, timber, watershed, and wildlife and fish purposes. The purposes of sections 528 to 531 of this title are declared to be supplemental to, but not in derogation of, the purposes for which the national forests were established as set forth in section 475 of this title. Nothing herein shall be construed so as to affect the use or administration of the mineral resources of national forest lands or to affect the use or administration of Federal lands not within national forests.”<sup>4</sup>

## 16 USC § 531, Definition of Multiple Use and Sustained Yield

As used in sections 528 to 531 of this title the following terms shall have the following meanings:

(a) “Multiple use” means: The management of all the various renewable surface resources of the national forests so that they are utilized in the combination that will best meet the needs of the American people; making the most judicious use of the land for some or all of these resources or related services over areas large enough to provide sufficient latitude for periodic adjustments in use to conform to changing needs and conditions; that some land will be used for less than all of the resources; and harmonious and coordinated management of the various resources, each with the other, without impairment of the productivity of the land, with consideration being given to the relative values of the various resources, and not necessarily the combination of uses that will give the greatest dollar return or the greatest unit output.”

(b) “Sustained yield of the several products and services” means the achievement and maintenance in perpetuity of a high-level annual or regular periodic output of the various renewable resources of the national forests without impairment of the productivity of the land.”<sup>5</sup>

USFS transition of land use planning to landscape-scale biodiversity and ecosystem management principles contravenes the statutorily authorized mandates and goals of inventory and assessment for the purposes of multiple use and sustained yield.<sup>6</sup>

Many forest communities have been economically hamstrung by limiting or precluding access and utilization for multiple use purposes and timber sources for the wood products industry. This despite language in the Forest Service’s Organic Act of 1897, as echoed at 36 CFR § 221.3 Timber Management Planning:

“Provide, so far as feasible, an even flow of national forest timber in order to facilitate the stabilization of communities and of opportunities for employment.” (Emphasis added)<sup>7</sup>

For the past three decades, administrative policy and regulations that implement non-delegated policy have been embedded in agency culture and practice. Some of these directives cannot be traced to controlling authorities, raising legitimacy and compliance questions. In the case of the roadless rule, there was a marked shift away from multiple-use sustained-yield priorities toward passive preservation and biodiversity to the neglect of the human environment.

## Recent Related Federal Register Notices

Since the publication of 90 FR 42179 – USFS Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands – Notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement,<sup>8</sup> there have been two additional Federal Register notices related to the notice of intent regarding rescission of the 2001 Roadless

Rule. The Montana Natural Resource Coalition (MtNRC) has reviewed these notices and include information from them as they pertain to the proposed 2001 Roadless Rule rescission rulemaking and EIS development processes.

90 FR 42432, September 2, 2025, Notice of Adoption of Categorical Exclusions Under Section 109 of the National Environmental Policy Act

The Department of the Interior’s Office of the Secretary notified the public and documented the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM’s) adoption of several categorical exclusions from several federal agencies, including nine from the USFS:

1. 36 CFR 220.6(d)(4), which applies to the repair and maintenance of roads, trails, and landline boundaries;

2. 36 CFR 220.6(d)(8), which applies to the approval, modification, or continuation of minor, short-term special uses;

3. 36 CFR 220.6(d)(11), which applies to the issuance of a new special use authorization;

4. 36 CFR 220.6(e)(3), which applies to the approval, modification, or continuation of minor special uses of National Forest Service lands that require less than 20 contiguous acres of land;

5. 36 CFR 220.6(e)(6), which applies to timber stand and wildlife habitat improvement activities, subject to limitations on the use of herbicides and road construction;

6. 36 CFR 220.6(e)(8), which applies to mineral energy, geophysical, and geothermal investigations of one year or less involving no more than one mile of temporary road;

7. 36 CFR 220.6(e)(19), which applies to removing and relocating debris and sediment following a disturbance event;

8. 36 CFR 220.6(e)(24), which applies to the construction and realignment of up to two miles of road and associated parking areas; and

9. 36 CFR 220.6(e)(25), which applies to forest and grassland management activities.<sup>9</sup>

Consistent with 36 CFR 220.6(e), the USFS, when relying on these categorical exclusions, develops a supporting record and a decision memo. The documentation the BLM will develop when it relies on one of these adopted categorical exclusions will be similar to the USFS documentation and the BLM will publish the documentation on its National NEPA Register.

At 90 FR 42432 the BLM describes its forest management program:

“The BLM manages close to 58 million acres of forest and woodlands across 12 Western States and Alaska. BLM forests are managed for sustained yield timber production under the Oregon and California Railroad Grant Lands Act of 1937 and the Federal Land Policy Management Act of 1976 (FLPMA) for the 2.4 million acres in western Oregon, and under the multiple-use and sustained-yield principles of FLPMA for the balance of public lands. The BLM manages forests to maintain healthy forest ecosystems that provide ecosystem services such as clean water, fish and wildlife habitats, economic opportunities from recreational use, and the harvest of forest products. A significant management issue in many forest types is overly dense conditions that are susceptible to high-severity wildfire, insect epidemics, and sensitivity to drought. Thinning treatments to reduce crown fire potential have been proven effective at preventing the loss of forest while also maintaining key ecosystem and habitat components.”<sup>10</sup>

## 90 FR 43990, September 11, 2025, Rescission of Conservation and Landscape Health Rule<sup>11</sup>

The Department of the Interior’s (DOI) Bureau of Land Management (BLM) is proposing to rescind the Conservation and Landscape Health Rule (CLHR), issued as a final rule on May 9, 2024.

BLM determined that the 2024 Rule is unnecessary and violates existing statutory mandates. It is unnecessary to facilitate, and even undermines, BLM management of public lands under applicable law, including the direction in FLPMA to manage public land for multiple-use and sustained-yield, except where it is dedicated to a specific use by other provisions of law. The rule constrains management flexibility.

These concurrent USDA and DOI actions demonstrate similar programs and objectives acting together in response to executive actions and other considerations responsive to conditions affecting the federal lands they manage. Several of the statutes that provide authority and direction for the agencies mandate coordinated action between the secretaries of Agriculture and the Interior. These actions should not be considered in isolation from one another.

For that reason, and for these comments, The Montana Natural Resource Coalition considers their ongoing programs and proposed actions as responsive to statutes interpreted in pari materia.

## Recent Constraints on Agency Statutory Interpretation Discretion

The 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule that the proposed actions at 90 FR 42179 are intended to rescind was promulgated at a time when Chevron deference provided broad discretion for agencies to interpret statutes when engaging in rulemaking and policy actions. Recent judicial and executive actions have curtailed agency discretion for statutory interpretation. We provide a brief overview of some of these to ensure USFS officials are aware of these changes at this stage of the rulemaking and EIS processes.

Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. (2024),<sup>12</sup> Certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.

The Court held that:

“…Chevron is overruled. Courts must exercise their independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority, as the APA requires. Careful attention to the judgment of the Executive Branch may help inform that inquiry. And when a particular statute delegates authority to an agency consistent with constitutional limits, courts must respect the delegation, while ensuring the agency acts within it. But courts need not and under the APA may not defer to an agency interpretation of the law simply because a statute is ambiguous.

Because the D.C. and First Circuits relied on Chevron in deciding whether to uphold the Rule, their judgments are vacated, and the cases are remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. 13

Any further action on remand must be decided consistent with the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision of June 28, 2024. On remand the D.C. Circuit ordered supplemental briefing and re-argument. The parties submitted supplemental briefs and the Court heard argument in November 2024.

On July 16, 2025, the parties submitted a joint motion for abeyance<sup>14</sup> to engage in settlement discussions to pursue a resolution of the underlying matter without the need for the Court to decide the appeal. The appeal does not affect the Supreme Court’s decision of June 28, 2024, overruling Chevron, which stands independent of the case’s underlying matter.

## Executive Orders

Presidential executive orders are formal directives issued by the President to manage operations within the government. They carry the force and effect of law and primarily direct and bind employees within the executive branch of the government. Compliance is required because executive orders govern the actions of executive branch officials, ensuring implementation of presidential policies.

## Executive Order 14215 of February 18, 2025 — Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies

Sec. 7. Rules of Conduct Guiding Federal Employees’ Interpretation of the Law. The President and the Attorney General, subject to the President’s supervision and control, shall provide authoritative interpretations of law for the executive branch. The President and the Attorney General’s opinions on questions of law are controlling on all employees in the conduct of their official duties. No employee of the executive branch acting in their official capacity may advance an interpretation of the law as the position of the United States that contravenes the President or the Attorney General’s opinion on a matter of law, including but not limited to the issuance of regulations, guidance, and positions advanced in litigation, unless authorized to do so by the President or in writing by the Attorney General.<sup>15</sup>

Executive Order 14219 of February 19, 2025 — Ensuring Lawful Governance and Implementing the President’s “Department of Government Efficiency” Deregulatory Initiative

Sec. 2. Rescinding Unlawful Regulations and Regulations That Undermine the National Interest. (a) Agency heads shall, in coordination with their DOGE Team Leads and the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, initiate a process to review all regulations subject to their sole or joint jurisdiction for consistency with law and Administration policy. … agency heads shall, in consultation with the Attorney General as appropriate, identify the following classes of regulations: …

(iii) regulations that are based on anything other than the best reading of the underlying authority or prohibition;

(iv) regulations that implicate matters of social, political, or economic significance that are not authorized by clear statutory authority; …

Sec. 3. Enforcement Discretion to Ensure Lawful Governance.

(a) Subject to their paramount obligation to discharge their legal obligations, protect public safety, and advance the national interest, agencies shall preserve their limited enforcement resources by generally de-prioritizing actions to enforce regulations that are based on anything other than the best reading of a statute …

Sec. 4. Promulgation of New Regulations. Agencies shall continue to follow the processes set out in Executive Order 12866 for submitting regulations for review by OIRA … In evaluating potential new regulations, agency heads, DOGE Team Leads, and the Administrator of OIRA shall consider, in addition to the factors set out in Executive Order 12866, the factors set out in section 2(a) of this order. …

Sec. 6. Definitions. … (e) “Regulation” shall have the meaning given to “regulatory action” in section 3(e) of Executive Order 12866, and also includes any “guidance document” as defined in Executive Order 13422 of January 18, 2007 (Further Amendment to Executive Order 12866 on Regulatory Planning and Review”).<sup>16</sup>

Each of the above judicial actions and executive orders demonstrate that, in contrast to many decades of deference to agency officials’ interpretations of statutory and administrative law, the judicial and legislative branches, and the leadership of the executive branch of the U.S. Government are reasserting their constitutional authorities and are limiting the latitude for interpretations of law previously afforded to executive branch officials at agency levels.

## MtNRC Statutory Interpretation Practices

When working with and preparing responses to Federal Register notices and other actions, the Montana Natural Resource Coalition researches statutory and administrative law and authoritative policy documents, interpreting them through the lens of interpretive doctrines, canons of construction, rules, and other authoritative sources informing judicial review. These include but are not limited to:

## Whole Code Rule/Doctrine<sup>17</sup>

Justice Scalia formalized the whole code rule as part of the whole-text canon, calling on judicial interpreters to consider the entire text, in view of its structure and of the physical and logical relation to its many parts.<sup>18</sup>

## In pari materia<sup>19</sup>

The doctrine of in pari materia originates in English common law and is applied in American jurisprudence to interpret statutes on the same subject together for consistency and to ascertain legislative intent. The in para materia canon of statutory construction requires that all like-kind statutes are to be interpreted as a whole. “Statutes,” Justice Frankfurter once wrote, “cannot be read intelligently if the eye is closed to considerations evidenced in affiliated statutes.”<sup>20</sup>

## Plain Meaning Rule<sup>21</sup>

The rule prioritizes textual clarity to promote predictability and limit judicial discretion.

## Incorporations by Reference

The hyperlinked documents in this MtNRC response to the Federal Register notice at 90 FR 42179 are incorporated as integral parts of its initial participation as an instrumentality of its member government in this formal process.

## Origin of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule

The 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule traces its roots to USFS efforts between the 1930s and 1960s, when undeveloped “primitive areas” were first identified for potential wilderness designation. After passage of the Wilderness Act of 1964, Congress reserved to itself the authority to designate wilderness, requiring USFS to evaluate and inventory remaining undeveloped lands. This process culminated in the Roadless Area Review and Evaluation (RARE I, 1971–73; RARE II, 1977–79), which mapped millions of acres but was invalidated by litigation. Nevertheless, these inventories became the foundation for later policy.

Roadless areas were managed through individual forest plans into the 1990s under the National Forest Management Act of 1976, with discretion at the local level. Mounting litigation over old-growth logging, ESA listing of the northern spotted owl, and salmon habitat fueled demand for broader forest protections.

In response, President Clinton convened the 1993 Forest Conference,<sup>22</sup> leading to the Northwest Forest Plan (NWFP), which applied to 24.5 million acres of federal forests in Washington, Oregon, and Northern California. It created late-successional and riparian reserves to protect spotted owl and salmon habitat, still allowing limited timber harvest and is a region-wide ESA-driven overlay, separate from national roadless policy.

Later, recognizing fragmentation and litigation surrounding roadless area decisions across the country, President Clinton directed that USDA create a nationwide policy in October 1999. After more than 600 public hearings and 1.6 million comments, the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule was adopted, prohibiting most new roadbuilding, rebuilding, and timber harvest on 58.5 million acres of inventoried roadless areas, roughly 30% of the National Forest System. Unlike the NWFP, the 2001 Roadless Rule was a broad administrative regulation, not tied to a specific ESA listing but intended to safeguard biodiversity, water quality, recreation, and agency budgets.

As executive action rather than legislation, the 2001 Roadless Rule was controversial. Supporters argued it was necessary to protect biodiversity, water quality, and recreation opportunities while avoiding costly new road maintenance. Critics argued it created “de facto wilderness” without congressional approval, contrary to multiple-use and sustained-yield mandates in statutes such as the Organic Act of 1897, the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act of 1960 (MUSYA), and the National Forest Management Act of 1976 (NFMA). Years of litigation followed until the Tenth Circuit upheld the 2001 Roadless Rule as valid in 2011.<sup>23</sup>

Congress never defined conservation as preservation-only. Under the Organic Act of 1897, MUSYA, and NFMA, conservation means active management for multiple-use and sustained-yield. The proposed rescission is an opportunity to restore lawful forest management that balances access to timber, water, wildlife, mineral resources, and recreation, within the statutory framework Congress intended.

## Associated Impacts of the 2001 Roadless Rule

The 2001 Roadless Rule arose out of the political stalemate created by litigation over old-growth logging and the northern spotted owl. Environmental groups used litigation to force preservation of roadless areas as de facto old-growth reserves, substituting litigation-driven preservation for the congressionally mandated statutory framework of multiple-use and sustained-yield.

The proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule would return decision-making for roadless area management to local forest plans under NFMA. In Washington State, the Northwest Forest Plan of 1994 remains a regional overlay controlling all national forests from the Canadian border to Northern California. Unless the NWFP is revised, 24.5 million acres of NFS lands in Washington would remain bound in its late-successional and riparian reserve structure, even after the 2001 Roadless Rule is rescinded. To ensure that forest planning becomes fully decentralized again, a future separate action for that purpose would need to be undertaken.

The State of Montana and other states have experienced post roadless rule forest planning which has systematically closed thousands of miles of roads and trails throughout the NFS. According to a study by the Environmental Quality Council on the loss of access to our public lands that has occurred since 1995:

‘. . .the Forest Service has closed an astounding 21,951 miles of roads on land they manage in Montana. Each and every one of these roads was important for recreation and management of this land. In Montana our population demographics show an ageing population. With this increase in age comes a greater need and desire for some type of mechanized and motorized transport in order to recreate on our public lands.’<sup>24</sup>

Old-growth preservation for biodiversity and storing carbon to offset climate change as reserved component of the 2001 Roadless Rule conflicts with NFMA at 16 USC § 1604(m)(1):

The Secretary shall establish-

(1) standards to insure that, prior to harvest, stands of trees throughout the National Forest System shall generally have reached the culmination of mean annual increment of growth (calculated on the basis of cubic measurement or other methods of calculation at the discretion of the Secretary): Provided, That these standards shall not preclude the use of sound silvicultural practices, such as thinning or other stand improvement measures: Provided further, That these standards shall not preclude the Secretary from salvage or sanitation harvesting of timber stands which are substantially damaged by fire, windthrow or other catastrophe, or which are in imminent danger from insect or disease attack …<sup>25</sup>

Large-scale sequestration and protection of old-growth stands is an exception that must meet the standards mandated at 16 USC 1604(m)(2) after consideration has been given to statutory multiple-use and sustainedyield principles and mandates.

The 2001 Roadless Rule administratively prioritized biodiversity and ecosystem services over existing statutory purposes, creating wilderness-like restrictions without congressional action. Rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule corrects this inconsistency by returning consideration of biodiversity and ecosystem services to the forest-level planning process where they can be weighed alongside multiple-use, sustainedyield and other statutorily mandated uses.

While the 2001 Roadless Rule did not significantly change grazing availability in the IRAs, it did demonstrate how administrative overlays can create uncertainty concerning congressionally mandated uses on NFS lands. Returning full management authority to local forest planning processes will remove that uncertainty and restore access to the full range of multiple-use availability.

Together, the spotted owl listing and the 2001 Roadless Rule created the perception that the ESA and protection of the environment beyond lawful requirements could displace statutory NFS management mandates. The reality is that protection of species and old growth forests must take place in the context of USFS managing the NFS to provide protection and improvement of the forests, ensure favorable conditions of water flows, and furnish a continuous supply of timber, minerals, and other forest products.

## Exercise of Police Powers by State and Local Governments

Extensive roadless areas on NFS lands have deleterious effects on State and local government exercise of their police powers for public health, safety, and welfare. Law enforcement and search and rescue response by county sheriffs, wildfire response, and more are adversely affected by the lack of road access to NFS lands within the boundaries of the inventoried roadless areas. States and their political subdivisions possess police powers, but federal agencies do not.

“State governments have the authority and responsibility to protect the public health, safety, and welfare. This authority is an inherent attribute of State governmental sovereignty and is shared with local governments” “… Substantive due process is the constitutional doctrine that legislation must be fair and reasonable in content and designed so that it furthers a legitimate governmental objective. The doctrine of substantive due process is based on the recognition that the social compact upon which our government is founded provides protections beyond those that are expressly stated in the U.S. Constitution against the flagrant abuse of government power. Calder v Bull, 3 U.S. 386 (1798).”<sup>26</sup>

Long extant federal statutes<sup>27</sup> also reinforce the principle that police power is reserved to the State and local governments. Title 7 of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA)<sup>28</sup> at 43 USC 1701, note(g)(6) states that,

“Nothing in this Act shall be construed as limiting or restricting the power and authority of the United States or - (6) as a limitation upon any State criminal statute or upon the police power of the respective States, or as derogating the authority of a local police officer in the performance of his duties ... on the national resource lands.”<sup>29</sup>

The 2001 Roadless Rule acts as an impediment to State and local government exercise of their police power for public health, safety, and welfare.

Rights-of-Way Established Prior to the Enactment of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 Must Continue to Provide Public Access

Many rights-of-way on public lands have their origins in Section 8 of the Mining Act of 1866:

“The right of way for the construction of highways over public lands, not reserved for public uses, is hereby granted.”<sup>30</sup>

The now-repealed statute was self-executing, meaning that no application or federal approval was required. If any road, trail, or byway was constructed on unreserved federal land prior to FLPMA’s enactment on October 21, 1976, its right-of-way was automatically granted to the public or local authority under state law. Such rights-of-way remain valid unless otherwise legally abandoned. If a valid right-of-way exists, it cannot be invalidated by administrative rule.<sup>31</sup>

## National Security and Economic Resilience

The rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule is a crucial national security and economic resilience issue. Recent executive orders, secretarial memoranda, and other executive branch actions highlight this as a matter of overriding public concern. Examples include but are not limited to:

Executive Order 14241 – Immediate Measures To Increase American Mineral Production — “Our national and economic security are now acutely threatened by our reliance upon hostile foreign powers’ mineral production. It is imperative for our national security that the United States take immediate action to facilitate domestic mineral production to the maximum possible extent.”<sup>32</sup>

Executive Order 14223 – Addressing the Threat to National Security From Imports of Timber, Lumber, and Their Derivative Products — “The wood products industry, composed of timber, lumber, and their derivative products (such as paper products, furniture, and cabinetry) is a critical manufacturing industry essential to the national security, economic strength, and industrial resilience of the United States.”<sup>33</sup>

Executive Order 14225 – Immediate Expansion of American Timber Production — “The United States has an abundance of timber resources that are more than adequate to meet our domestic timber production needs, but heavy-handed Federal policies have prevented full utilization of these resources and made us reliant on foreign producers.”<sup>34</sup>

Secretary’s Memorandum 1078-006 – Increasing Timber Production and Designating and Emergency Situation on National Forest System Lands — “Immediate action is needed to mitigate risk, protect public health and safety and critical infrastructure, support local and rural economies, and mitigate threats to natural resources on NFS lands. We can do more to contribute to American prosperity and protect our national and economic security.”<sup>35</sup>

The national security concern arises from geopolitical tensions resulting in increased difficulty in obtaining resources, such as rare earth minerals sourced in China, in an environment where increased access to those resources is necessary to meet the needs of emerging technologies moving from prototype to production materials demand levels. Vulnerabilities stem from overregulation limiting extraction on mineral-rich NFS lands, leading to dependence on adversarial suppliers. Minerals production on NFS lands supports technologies, energy infrastructure, and economic dominance. Executive Order 14241 and related policies prioritize domestic sourcing to counter these threats.

Access to timber resources has been complicated by potential reductions in access to, for example, Canadian timber, in response to political/diplomatic tensions between national governments and other trade factors. Foreign dumping erodes the U.S. manufacturing base, reducing industrial resilience, and unfair trade practices impair competitiveness. Excess reliance on foreign sources also heightens vulnerabilities in domestic timber supply chains.

MtNRC urges the Secretaries of Agriculture and the Interior to work closely with their fellow cabinet Secretaries to ensure that necessary policy support is directed toward restoring milling and refining infrastructure to accommodate the anticipated increases in raw materials availability from the public lands. Such industrial facilities are important to the human environment and local economies of our member counties.

The example executive orders and the Secretary’s memorandum illustrate the domestic policy drivers that make access to National Forest System lands and resources an overriding matter of public concern.

Restoring access and policy to the IRAs is a matter of priority as a necessary first step in responding to the Federal government’s valid national security concerns and for increasing the nation’s economic resilience. Restoring full access to the IRAs would result in reduced tensions between competing nations, even before production increases occur, ensuring improved national security and economic resilience positions.

## Federalism and Consultation with Local Governments on Proposed Agency Actions

The final rule and record of decision establishing the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule was published in the Federal Register at 66 FR 3244 on January 12, 2001. The notice’s section on Federalism and Consultation with Tribal Governments appeared at 66 FR 3271:

“The agency considered this rule under the requirements of Executive Order 12612 and found the rule will not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. Therefore, the agency determined that no further assessment on federalism implications is necessary at this time. In addition, the consultation requirements under Executive Order 13132, effective November 2, 1999, were reviewed. This new Order calls for enhanced consultation with State and local government officials and emphasizes increased sensitivity to their concerns.

Forest Service line officers in the field were asked to make contact with Tribes to ensure awareness of the initiative and of the rulemaking process. Outreach to Tribes has been conducted at the national forest and grassland level, which is how Forest Service government-to-government dialog with Tribes is typically conducted.

Outreach to State and local governments has taken place both in the field and Washington offices. Forest Service officials have contacted State and local governmental officials and staffs to explain the notice of intent and the rulemaking process. The agency met with and responded to a variety of information requests from local officials and State organizations, such as the National Governors Association and the Western Governors Association.

In the development of this rule comments received from States, Tribes, and local governments in response to the notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement published October 19, 1999 (64 FR 56306) were carefully considered. Following publication of the proposed rule, the agency met with State, Tribal, and local government officials to explain and clarify the proposed rule and the accompanying environmental impact statement. The extent to which additional consultation was appropriate under Executive Order 13132 was considered. In addition, the Forest Service responsible official will seek input and participation by State, local, and Tribal officials in the early stages of forest and project planning regarding subsequent decisions for inventoried roadless 36 areas.

This stands in contrast to the USFS statement regarding State and local governments appearing at 90 FR 42182 in the notice at 90 FR 42179:

“The USDA Forest Service does not anticipate designating any Federal, State, Tribal, or local agencies as cooperating or participating agencies. These organizations are encouraged to provide input through the public comment opportunities for this notice of intent, as well as the proposed rule and draft EIS.”<sup>37</sup>

The rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule is at least as, if not more than, consequential as its initial establishment, so the rigor of its administrative procedure process should also be at least as rigorous and compliant with statutory and administrative policies. Unfortunately, the responsible officials are choosing not to fulfill their predecessors’ commitment that:

“…the Forest Service responsible official will seek input and participation by State, local, and Tribal officials in the early stages of forest and project planning regarding subsequent decisions for inventoried roadless areas. 38

Then, after stating that tribal governments would not be allowed as cooperating or participating agencies, in the very next column at 90 FR 42182, the Federal Register NOI offers that:

“Tribal governments and Alaska Native Corporations will have an opportunity to be engaged during rulemaking and EIS development through various coordination and consultation events.”<sup>39</sup>

The sum of these statements adds up to a situation where the agency would, unless it alters course, procedurally disenfranchise subnational sovereigns (i.e., States, and counties as extensions of State sovereignty), improperly treating them as non-jurisdictional actors throughout the rulemaking and EIS development processes.<sup>40</sup>

Executive Order 13132 Section 1 Definitions

(a) “Policies that have federalism implications” refers to regulations, legislative comments or proposed legislation, and other policy statements or actions that have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.

(b) “State” or “States” refer to the States of the United States of America, individually or collectively, and, where relevant, to State governments, including units of local government and other political subdivisions established by the States. 41

The process of reducing local governments (political subdivisions of their States under the Tenth Amendment and their State constitutions) from formal participatory status to equivalence with private citizens in administrative proceedings would constitute a deliberate withholding of mandated meaningful engagement, relegating sovereign governmental entities to passive public commenters. Such participatory demotion would be an evasion of Executive Order 13132’s governance-wide principles, would interfere with the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government, and would constitute federalism circumvention.

Refusing the cooperating agency designation would be a denial of access to joint EIS preparation and information-sharing which would constitute cooperating agency exclusion.

Excluding State and local governments from meaningful participation in two major administrative processes while ensuring full access to those administrative processes by tribal governments and Alaska Native Corporations would be unjust to the affected State and local governments.

On June 27, 2025, the Administrative Conference of the United States (ACUS), a federal agency in the executive branch charged with identifying and promoting improvements in the efficiency, adequacy, and fairness of the procedures by which federal agencies conduct regulatory programs, published a Federal Register notice of adoption of recommendations at 90 FR 27515.<sup>42</sup> Administrative Conference Recommendation 2025-2, Consultation With State, Local, and Tribal Governments in Regulatory Policymaking begins at 90 FR 27517. These recommendations were adopted subsequent to a report ACUS commissioned, Final Report to the Administrative Conference of the United States, Consultation with State, Local, and Tribal Governments in Regulatory Policymaking.<sup>43</sup>

MtNRC is a strong advocate for government reforms that support full actualization of the principles of federalism in United States governance. We engaged with ACUS in support of this effort.

ACUS initiated a follow-on project, Federal Agency Collaboration with State, local, Tribal, and Territorial Governments (SLTTGs) on May 27, 2025, at 90 FR 22224.<sup>44</sup> The project focuses on federal agency collaboration and coordination with SLTTGs and is ongoing.

ACUS recommendation 2025-2 provides best practices to help agencies develop rules, policies, and practices that promote effective consultation with state, local, and tribal governments. It encourages agencies to be transparent about their policies, adopt practices that foster meaningful consultation, and establish mechanisms for assessing performance. Further, the recommendation also identifies potential actions for consideration by OMB, consistent with its mission and resources, and by Congress, which may improve consultation between federal agencies and state, local, and tribal governments in regulatory policymaking and implementation.

This rescission, rulemaking, and EIS process represents significant potential for enduring regulatory reform in USFS land management programs. It represents a unique and timely opportunity for USFS to also take leadership in stepping up to engage local governments in meaningful consultation and coordination in accordance with the ACUS 2025-2 recommendation and the forthcoming collaboration and coordination recommendation.

MtNRC stands ready to work with USFS for the rulemaking and EIS development processes and includes both the ACUS report and ACUS Recommendation 2025-2 by reference as integral to these comments.

We are in a time where regulatory reform is seen not only as a possibility but also as a priority. In that light, there is a mechanism whereby USDA and USFS could provide an innovative platform that can include meaningful government-to-government participation by MtNRC and includes the use of the previously described methods of statutory interpretation.

There are statutes mandating that the Secretaries of Agriculture and Interior work collaboratively on programs. Wildfire management is one. Livestock grazing on public lands is another. MtNRC sees no reason this could not happen with the 2001 Roadless Rule rescission or the concurrent CLHR Rule rescission process.

The Secretary of the Interior could be invited, in accordance with 42 USC § 4336a(a)(1)(A), to participate with the Secretary of Agriculture where USDA has the lead agency. This would then allow the Secretaries to appoint MtNRC as a joint lead agency in accordance with 42 USC § 4336a(B).

There are also numerous sections in 7 CFR 1b (90 FR 29646) where lead agencies can appoint local governments, such as MtNRC, to positions for meaningful government-to-government participation.

## 2001 Roadless Rule Rescission Rulemaking and EIS Processes

Rulemaking under Administrative Procedure Act mandates is necessary to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule. 90 FR 42179 states that the proposed EIS will evaluate the impacts of the proposed rule rescission and study alternatives for roadless area conservation on the NFS lands, including the Tongass National Forest, in the context of multiple use resource management. The proposed rule and EIS would be developed concurrently.

The Federal Register NOI states that the proposed rule is expected to be released by March 2026, accompanied by the draft EIS. MtNRC recognizes that the EIS will be prepared under the mandates of the USDA National Environmental Policy Act Interim Final Rule of July 3, 2025, at 90 FR 29632, codified as 7 CFR Part 1b, and we are prepared to meaningfully participate with USFS in developing the EIS.

As noted above, MtNRC is prepared and requests formal consultation as mandated in Executive Order 13132 and as recommended by the Administrative Conference of the United States Recommendation 2025- 2. MtNRC specifically requests meaningful formal government-to-government participation with USFS for both the 2001 Roadless Rule rescission rulemaking and the development process for the accompanying proposed environmental impact statement.

MtNRC notes that tribal governments are being offered extensive consultation and coordination opportunities throughout the development processes for both the proposed rule and the proposed EIS, but that USFS does not intend to offer similar opportunities to State and local governments at this time. We strongly request that USFS reconsider this omission of affected local governments from the governmentto-government interactions.

MtNRC has expertise in federal administrative process, NEPA, the National Forest System within Montana and the jurisdictional boundaries of its member counties, and upholds federalism as a core pillar of United States governance. Several of MtNRC’s member counties would be materially affected by both the final rule and the final EIS and its record of decision.

## Findings and Recommendations

I The US Forest Service should recalibrate this administrative process to ensure that issues of national security and economic resiliency are a priority.

MtNRC finds that the Federal Register notice at 90 FR 42179, while including some pertinent executive orders in justifying the purpose and need for action, missed including others, specifically Executive Order 14241 Immediate Measures To Increase Mineral Production<sup>45</sup> and Executive Order 14223 Addressing the Threat to National Security From Imports of Timber, Lumber, and Their Derivative Products.<sup>46</sup> When added to those included in the NOI, the picture changes from one focused primarily on the 2001 Roadless Rule itself to one where the most pressing need for the proposed action are the related issues of national security and economic resilience.

This lapse means that the largest portion of submitted comments will be addressing a range of issues that will not address the most critical issues facing the nation that the administration is seeking to resolve, in part with this proposed action, the concurrent rescission of the Department of the Interior’s proposed rescission of the BLM’s CLHR Rule, and other administrative actions.

MtNRC further finds that placing the focus of the proposed action squarely where the national need is the greatest, that of national security and economic resilience, the EIS list of proposed actions would differ significantly from that list if the proposed rulemaking and EIS development processes are focused solely on the 2001 Roadless Rule Rescission itself to the exclusion of very real and significant overriding issues of public concern.

MtNRC strongly recommends that USDA and USDA Forest Service recalibrate this administrative process to ensure that the overriding issues of national security and economic resiliency are placed in the priority position as the primary purpose and need for the proposed action.

## The Secretaries of the Departments of Interior and Agriculture should collaborate for consistent land management frameworks.

MtNRC finds that the 2001 Roadless Rule rescission rulemaking and EIS administrative process is not occurring in isolation because the Department of the Interior noticed its proposed rescission of the BLM Conservation and Landscape Health Rule at 90 FR 43990 on September 11, 2025. As with the proposed 2001 Roadless Rule rescission process, a core purpose of the proposed DOI action is to lift a range of conservation restrictions from what were originally designated as working lands. There are several statutes where the Secretaries of Agriculture and the Interior are mandated to work together. While that may not apply in this instance, 42 USC § 4336a does provide for timely and unified federal reviews.

The uses for the NFS lands and the BLM-managed lands are very similar in nature and lands administered by the two departments often abut one another, so the outcome of the two rescission processes would better serve the nation, particularly in respect to national security and economic resiliency if the outcomes of those rescission processes result in federally managed lands with very similar frameworks.

MtNRC recommends that the Secretaries of the Departments of Interior and Agriculture enter an agreement to work together to ensure the functional management of federal lands currently operating under the mandates of the 2001 Roadless Rule and the Conservation and Landscape Health Rule is as similar as possible to seamless across boundaries. For the 2001 Roadless Rule rescission the Secretary of Agriculture would be the preferred lead based on consideration of USDA’s involvement using 42 USC § 4336a for timely and unified reviews as the basis for that determination.

## III USDA should grant meaningful government-to-government consultation and participation in the 2001 Roadless Rule rescission and EIS processes to state and local governments.

MtNRC finds that USDA, through its statement concerning cooperating and participating agencies at 90 FR 42182, runs the risk of improperly circumventing federalism via participatory demotion of State and local governments, reducing inter-level power distribution to informal input by procedurally disenfranchising political subdivisions (county governments in this instance) of the State of Montana, relegating them to the status of passive public commenters. Tribal governments and Alaska Native Corporations, in contrast, are being invited to participate in opportunities to be engaged during rulemaking and EIS development through various coordination and consultation events.

When the 2001 Roadless Rule was promulgated, the responsible official made a commitment that:

“…the Forest Service responsible official will seek input and participation by State, local, and Tribal officials in the early stages of forest and project planning regarding subsequent decisions for inventoried roadless areas. 47

24 years later, that commitment is no longer being honored by the federal government.

MtNRC and its member counties, having expertise in governance, the human and natural environments, and local economies within its member counties’ jurisdictions, and possessing police power for public health, safety, and welfare request meaningful government-to-government consultation and meaningful participation in the 2001 Roadless Rule rescission rulemaking and EIS processes. There are multiple statutory (i.e., NEPA), executive order (especially E.O. 13132), and administrative law mandates requiring or allowing meaningful consultation, coordination, and other forms of meaningful participation in administrative processes. Administrative Conference of the United States Recommendation 2025-2, Consultation With State, Local, and Tribal Governments in Regulatory Policymaking, adopted June 12, 2025, at 90 FR 27515, June 27, 2025, page 27517 provides information summarizing executive branch agency responsibilities for meaningful engagement with State, Local, and Tribal governments. The recommendation provides agencies with best practices to help agencies develop rules, policies, and practices that promote effective consultation with state, local, and tribal governments. It encourages agencies to be transparent about their policies, adopt practices that foster meaningful consultation, and establish mechanisms for assessing performance.

MtNRC recommends that USDA and its responsible official(s) grant meaningful government-togovernment consultation and participation in the 2001 Roadless Rule rescission and EIS processes as the most appropriate means of mitigating the risk posed by its initial intent to demote States and their political subdivision governments to the status of passive commenters for these processes.

IV USDA should adhere to the U.S. Supreme Court’s opinion in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, Executive Order 14215 Section 7, and the best reading of the underlying authorities in its rulemaking and EIS preparation.

MtNRC finds that, since the time the 2001 Roadless Rule was promulgated, judicial and executive actions have substantially diminished executive branch agency authority to interpret United States law, most recently with the decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Section 7 of Executive Order 14215, Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies. Both actions constrain agency interpretation of the law for the purposes of the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule and the preparation of the EIS.

MtNRC further finds that Section 4, Promulgation of New Regulations, of Executive Order 14219 mandates that new regulations (regulatory actions) be based only on the best reading of the underlying authority or prohibition. This is an implementation of the Plain Meaning Rule, which is a foundational canon of statutory interpretation that instructs courts to apply the ordinary common-sense meaning of a statute’s text when it is clear and unambiguous, without resorting to extrinsic aids such as legislative history, purpose, or intent.

MtNRC recommends that USDA require its responsible official(s) to adhere to the U.S. Supreme Court’s opinion in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, Executive Order 14215 Section 7, and the best reading of the underlying authorities in its rulemaking and EIS preparation for the proposed 2001 Roadless Rule rescission.

AGENcY: Administrative Conference of the United States.

ACTION: Notice.

sUMMARY: The Assembly of the Administrative Conference of the United States adopted three recommendations at its hybrid (virtual and in-person) Eighty-third Plenary Session: Agency Investigative Procedures; Consultation with State, Local, and Tribal Governments in Regulatory Policymaking; and Public Participation in Agency Adjudication.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: FOr Recommendation 2025–1, Adam Cline; Recommendation 2025-2, Becaja Caldwell; and Recommendation 2025-3, Lea Robbins. For each of these recommendations the address and telephone number are: Administrative Conference of the United States, Suite 706 South, 1120 20th Street NW. Washington, DC 20036; Telephone 202– 480–2080.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The Administrative Conference Act, 5 U.S.C. 591-596, established the Administrative Conference of the United States. The Conference studies the efficiency, adequacy, and fairness of the administrative procedures used by Federal agencies and makes recommendations to agencies, the President, Congress, and the Judicial Conference of the United States for procedural improvements (5 U.S.C. 594(1)). For further information about the Conference and its activities, see www.acus.gov.

The Assembly of the Conference met during its Eighty-third Plenary Session on June 12, 2025, to consider three proposed recommendations and conduct other business. All three recommendations were adopted.

Recommendation 2025-1, Agency Investigative Procedures. This recommendation provides best practices for agencies that promote accuracy, efficiency, and fairness in investigations of specific regulated entities. It provides guidance on initiating investigations; exchanging and considering evidence and arguments; issuing subpoenas and warrants; and deciding whether to terminate an investigation, negotiate with the subject of an investigation, or pursue an action in an administrative or judicial tribunal.

Recommendation 2025–2, Consultation with State, Local, and Tribal Governments in Regulatory Policymaking. This recommendation provides agencies with best practices regarding consultation with state, local, and tribal governments in the development and implementation of regulatory policies. It provides guidance on developing policies for consultation; designating officials responsible for overseeing and facilitating consultation; publicizing consultation opportunities; and adopting procedures to promote effective consultation with state, local, and tribal officials.

Recommendation 2025-3, Public Participation in Agency Adjudication This recommendation provides agencies with best practices regarding public participation in administrative adjudications. It provides guidance on circumstances in which public participation may be appropriate; options for public participation; and methods for facilitating public participation effectively.

The Conference based its recommendations on research reports and prior history that are posted at: https://www.acus.gov/event/83rdplenary-session.
