September 17, 2025

The Honorable Secretary Brooke L. Rollins U.S. Department of Agriculture 1400 Independence Ave. SW Washington, D.C. 20250-0108

Comments on Docket Number FS-2025-001; submitted electronically through the Federal eRulemaking Portal https://www.regulations.gov

Dear Secretary Rollins:

The New Mexico Energy Minerals and Natural Resources Department (EMNRD) Forestry Division and New Mexico Department of Game and Fish (DGF) submit this letter in response to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) request for comments on the proposed rescission 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule) (66 FR 3244, 36 CFR Subpart B (2001)), which prohibits road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas, with limited exceptions. Through this comment, the EMNRD Forestry Division and DGF expresses deep concern regarding the proposed recission of the 2001 Roadless Rule.

EMNRD Forestry Division’s mission is to address the critical needs of New Mexico’s 24.7 million acres of forests and watersheds by reducing the fuels that increase the dangers of wildland fires, supplying wood products to New Mexico wood processors and residents, identifying invasive insects that lead to mortality and disease, conserving rare plants, and promoting healthy forests and watersheds for generations to come. EMNRD Forestry Division is the lead state agency for wildland fire management on 43 million acres of non-federal, nontribal, and non-municipal lands, with responsibility to maintain fire suppression capacities and ensure public and firefighters’ safety.

DGF’s mission is to conserve, regulate, propagate and protect the wildlife and fish within the state of New Mexico, using a flexible management system that ensures sustainable use for public food supply, recreation and safety and to provide for off-highway motor vehicle recreation that recognizes cultural, historic and resource values while ensuring public safety. DGF is the lead agency in conserving and managing fish and wildlife populations across the state of New Mexico, including making best practice recommendations for ways to mitigate impacts of development activities on state-protected species.

The USDA purpose and need for proposing to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule is “provide discretion for local land managers to tailor management, as appropriate, to local land conditions.” In New Mexico, the 2001 Roadless Rule applies to 1,549,469 acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRA), which is approximately 15% of the National Forest System lands in the New Mexico, and about 2% of all lands in the state. The New Mexico Forest Action Plan identified the top 500 watersheds with the highest risk of catastrophic wildfire that would negatively affect communities, wildlife habitat and water supplies, and 80% of the IRA are in the watersheds with high risk of wildfire.

EMNRD Forestry Division and DGF are concerned about long-term mitigation of wildfire risk in IRA but feel the exceptions in the 2001 Roadless Rule are sufficient to allow the necessary fuels reduction work.

EMNRD Forestry Division and DGF support aggressive and strategic hazardous fuels removal to reduce the risk of catastrophic wildfire and long-term damage to watersheds that are critical for habitat and water supply and reliability (see caveats for wildlife-friendly practices below).

The 2001 Roadless Rule already allows for road construction under circumstances wherein “a road is needed to protect public health and safety in cases of an imminent threat of flood, fire, or other catastrophic event that, without intervention, would cause the loss of life or property.” Furthermore, the 2001 Roadless Rule also allows timber harvesting “to maintain or restore the characteristics of ecosystem composition and structure, such as to reduce the risk of uncharacteristic wildfire effects, within the range of variability that would be expected to occur under natural disturbance regimes of the current climatic period.”

To achieve its purpose in rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule, which is to provide discretion for local land management to tailor management to local land conditions, the USDA Forest Service will need to carefully consider and minimize unintended impacts to wildlife and their habitats. DGF expresses deep concern regarding the proposed recission of the 2001 Roadless Rule and has the following more specific comments regarding this proposed recission.

1) Impacts of roads on wildlife and their habitats: The scientific literature very clearly indicates the threat to biodiversity as a whole (e.g., Findlay and Bourdages 2000) and to different taxonomic groups (e.g., birds, Holbrook and Vaughan 1985; fishes, Franklin et al. 2024; insects, Muñoz et al. 2015; mammals, Oxley et al. 1974, Lyon 1979; reptiles and amphibians, Fahrig et al. 1995, USFWS 2013, Andrews et al. 2015) from roads. Threats from roads come in the form of direct mortality resulting from wildlife-vehicle collisions (e.g., Fahrig et al. 1995, Cramer et al. 2022) and indirect threats associated with increasing human access to otherwise undisturbed areas and related increases in harvest or poaching (e.g., Holbrook and Vaughan 1985, DGF comments in USDA 2000, Haines et al. 2012), introduction of invasive species (e.g., Tyser and Worley 1992, Greenberg et al. 1997, Christen and Matlack 2009), and habitat fragmentation/loss of habitat connectivity (e.g., Reed et al. 1996, Warren and Pardew 1998, Theobald et al. 2011). It also clearly indicates the value of structures that increase permeability of roads (e.g., culverts, Yanes et al. 1995, openbox crossings, Warren and Pardew 1998). Further, there are at least 131 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) as identified in the 2025 State Wildlife Action Plan for New

Mexico (SWAP) and 66 state-listed species that have either been observed in or may be found in, based on local habitat types, the roughly 1,500,000 acres of inventoried roadless areas currently in New Mexico (see Appendix A). This is a minimum count of SGCN potentially present in these areas as spatial occurrence data are not yet available for all 505 SGCN identified in the 2025 SWAP. Additionally, the final rule and record of decision for the 2001 Roadless Rule (USDA 2001) indicates that the U.S. Forest Service receives insufficient funds to maintain the existing road infrastructure on National Forest System lands; it is not logical to create more roads that cannot be maintained, especially given their anticipated impacts on wildlife. DGF requests discussion of these impacts from roads on wildlife and their habitats in the proposed EIS.

2) Impacts of timber cutting on wildlife and their habitats: There is evidence of the impacts of timber cutting and removal on different taxonomic groups (e.g., birds, Franzreb and Ohmart 1978; insects, Baker et al. 2015; mammals, Zwolak 2009; reptiles and amphibians, Todd and Andrews 2008, USFWS 2013). Effects are especially notable for clear cutting that does not retain sufficient unlogged patches or suitable forest habitat. Threats from timber cutting include loss of key habitat features (e.g., forage sites and prey, Franzreb and Ohmart 1978). Given the potential for timber cutting to negatively impact a diversity of wildlife, DGF encourages incorporation of more wildlife-friendly thinning approaches in the proposed EIS, relevant to any areas where timber cutting is undertaken (e.g., Ponderosa Pine Restoration Guidelines to Benefit Wildlife, Reynolds et al. 1992, Darr et al. 2022).

3) Relationship of roads to wildfire ignition and frequency: On page 42180, the NOI states the following: 1) “Between 1984 and 2024, 13 percent of inventoried roadless areas (5.5 million acres) experienced high or moderate severity wildfire”; 2) “Currently, forty percent of lands within inventoried roadless areas have a high or very-high wildfire hazard potential…”; and 3) “…the area encompassing the WUI [Wildland-Urban Interface] has increased alongside increased insect and disease and wildfire activity throughout the National Forest System, including within inventoried roadless areas”. The Department requests the specific data sources supporting these statements. Further, on page 42181, the NOI states that “the proposed rule responds to the need for national forests to take swift and immediate action to reduce wildfire risk…”. These statements in the NOI imply that greater access to current inventoried roadless areas, through road construction and timber harvest, is required to address high wildfire risk in these areas. As stated previously, the 2001 Roadless Rule (36 CFR Part 294.13.b.1.ii) already allows for cutting, sale, and removal of timber in order to “maintain or restore the characteristics of ecosystem composition and structure, such as to reduce the risk of uncharacteristic wildfire effects, within the range of variability that would be expected to occur under natural disturbance regimes of the current climatic period;”, thus allowing for treatments to address wildfire risk in inventoried roadless areas. There is also mixed evidence regarding the relationship between road presence and wildfire occurrence. For example, there is evidence that the presence of roads, even minor roads, and increased road density can increase fire ignition frequency (Faivre et al. 2014) and that most wildfires are human caused and occur within 0.5 miles of a road; only 3% of fires start in wilderness or backcountry areas far from roads (Morrison 2007). Conversely, there is evidence that roads are poor predictors of fire ignition (Fusco et al. 2016) and that, while human-caused ignitions are concentrated near roads, fires occurring in roaded areas are smaller than those occurring in roadless and wilderness areas (Narayanaraj and Wimberly 2012). There are also factors other than tree density driving changes in fire occurrence; while wildfires have become increasingly large (i.e., burn area has increased), more severe (i.e., area burned at high severity has increased), more frequent, and last longer in the western U.S. than they did historically, these changes have been documented to be associated with warmer temperatures, earlier spring snowmelt, and drought (Westerling et al. 2006, Westerling 2016, Parks and Abatzoglou 2020). Increasing access via roads to current inventoried roadless areas will not alleviate the climate-related causes of these trends toward higher wildfire frequency and severity may in fact increase the risk of wildfire ignition as described above. Additionally, whenever feasible, DGF encourages the use of less invasive approaches to implementing forest treatments to reduce wildfire risk (e.g., hand thinning) in currently undisturbed or less disturbed areas, as opposed to the more invasive approaches associated with the large equipment for which roads provide access. Even if roads that are constructed to allow for forest treatments are temporary, it is often hard to close roads and maintain them as closed (DGF comments in USDA 2000). For the proposed EIS, DGF requests clarification of the relationship between the presence of roads and wildfire frequency and severity and an emphasis on the use of the least invasive methods possible and minimizing the use of roads, even temporary roads, when conducting forest treatments to reduce the potential for severe wildfire occurrence.

## Conclusion

EMNRD Forestry Division and DGF deeply value the partnership with USDA, Forest Service and the five National Forests in New Mexico. We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule and hope that it is one of many such opportunities to provide feedback on how the rescission will affect New Mexico’s human and wildlife communities. If you have questions related to these comments, please contact Mr. Jacob Pederson at (505) 629-6643 or Jacob.Pederson@emnrd.nm.gov or Dr. Virginia Seamster at (505) 629-7738 or Virginia.Seamster@dgf.nm.gov.

Sincerely,

Secretary Brooke Rollins

Secretary of the U.S. Department of Agriculture

U.S Department of Agriculture

1400 Independence Ave, S.W.

Washington, DC 20250

Dear Secretary Rollins,

I respectfully urge you to reconsider rescinding the Roadless Area Conservation Rule. The Roadless Area Conservation Rule was implemented in 2001 to protect roughly 58 million acres of National Forest and Grasslands from roadbuilding, mining, drilling, and logging. These roadless areas provide clean drinking water for millions of Americans and protect precious habitats for endangered species and plants.

For more than two decades, the Roadless Area Conservation Rule has survived multiple legal challenges, including Wyoming v. U.S. Department of Agriculture, 661 F.3d 1209 (10th Cir. 2011). In that case, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit ruled that this rule did not violate the Wilderness Act of 1964 and that the rule was not "arbitrary and capricious" since the Forest Service has a legitimate interest in protecting clean water sources and precious wildlife.

Rescinding the Roadless Area Conservation Rule will have far-reaching environmental and economic consequences. By opening these protected lands up to development, water sources that millions of Americans depend on will be threatened by erosion and chemical runoff from road building and other industrial activity. Additionally, rescinding this rule will expand the Forest Service's already multibillion-dollar road maintenance backlog and will deprive the country of revenue generated from recreation and tourism.

Given the strong legal precedent of this rule and the consequences this decision will have, I respectfully urge the Department of Agriculture to reconsider rescinding the Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

Sincerely,

# North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission

# M. Kyle Briggs, Executive Director

September 18, 2025

Brooke Rollins Secretary of Agriculture US Department of Agriculture

SUBJECT: NCWRC input on Notice of Intent to prepare EIS to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Docket Number FS-2025-0001)

Dear Secretary Rollins:

Biologists with the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission (NCWRC) have reviewed the US Forest Service (USFS)’s Notice of Intent to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule). The NCWRC is charged by statute with management, regulation, protection and conservation of wildlife resources and inland fisheries in North Carolina (General Statute 113-132). The NCWRC’s mission includes conserving North Carolina’s wildlife resources and their habitats.

NCWRC staff assist the USFS in assessing and managing wildlife resources on Forest lands and are familiar with the ecology, structure, and composition of forests in North Carolina. We offer the following input on the proposal to rescind the Roadless Rule to aid in the development of the EIS:

Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) focus on providing large contiguous areas where developed infrastructure is limited and natural disturbance processes drive forest dynamics. In some areas like the western US, natural disturbances are the primary drivers of change. This is critical for maintaining ecosystem diversity. IRAs often have less non-native invasive plants due to the lack of roads and other pathways generally associated with their spread and distribution.

Conversely, the lack of management within IRAs can have undesirable consequences. This outcome is particularly true in the eastern United States where relatively few places remain “untouched” by humans, and most forest has regenerated from historical logging and past land clearing activities, as in most currently designated IRAs. While large landscapes of relatively undisturbed and intact forest can be beneficial for some forest interior wildlife species, managing IRAs with a hands-off approach can lead to challenges such as the spread of forest diseases and pests, lack of structural and compositional diversity, and limited ability to restore and maintain fire-adapted forest communities. This hands-off approach can also contribute to the excessive buildup of forest fuel loads that can lead to catastrophic wildfire, as well as hinder the USFS’ ability to implement wildfire suppression measures such as prescribed burning.

The Roadless Rule has been in place for almost 25 years, and land management plans have been developed and implemented within the context of this rule. In North Carolina, the recently finalized land management plan for the Nantahala-Pisgah National Forest was developed through a careful and long-term collaborative process with local stakeholders, resulting in a plan that balances the needs of natural communities, wildlife, recreation, and the local economy. Currently, the proposal would not require specific changes to existing land management plans, and authority to make adjustments to plans and management would be left to the discretion of the local forest land managers. If this rule is rescinded, we strongly recommend that the management of these areas continue to be guided by current land management plans and by local land managers. Land management is best determined by local forest planning processes and decision-makers.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide input on Roadless Rule. Please contact me at (919) 707-4055 or david.cox@ncwildlife.org if I can provide any further assistance.

Sincerely,

# North Carolina General Assembly 16 WEST JONES STREET, RALEIGH, NC 27601

September 19, 2025

Re: Docket (FS-2025-0001) Environmental Impact Statements; Availability, etc.: Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands

Dear Chief Schultz,

We, the undersigned North Carolina Legislators, representing millions of constituents, urge you to keep the Roadless Conservation Area Rule (Roadless Rule) in place in order to continue to protect the wildest parts of our public forests.

The plan to rescind this rule jeopardizes nearly 45 million acres of heritage forestland managed by the U.S. Forest Service, comprising nearly a quarter of the territory in our national forest system.

Wild forests protected by Inventoried Roadless Area status provide the following benefits to the American public by providing:

• Vital Habitat for Imperiled Species

• Protecting Migration Corridors and Game Habitat

• Protecting Vital Sources for America’s Drinking Water

• Subsistence and Cultural Values

• Outdoor Recreation

• Climate Mitigation

Rescinding roadless area protection would undermine all of the benefits listed above as well as endanger communities and put a financial burden on communities and taxpayers by:

• Increasing Risk of Wildfires

• Creating Financial Burdens for Local Communities

Putting taxpayers on the Hook for Expense of Building Unnecessary Roads (Even with the Roadless Rule in place, the Forest Service already has a 360,000-mile road system – twice as long as the nation’s highway system – crisscrossing national forests.)

## Regarding North Carolina Specifically, Roadless Areas Are Vital to Our Economy and Environment:

• The Roadless Rule is a critical policy that prohibits new road building and timber cutting in roadless areas of the national forests, with common sense exceptions, like for wildfire management.

• North Carolina’s roadless areas are some of the wildest, most intact forest areas in the Southern Appalachian Mountains. These places are home to world-class hiking and mountain biking trails, oldgrowth forests, crystal-clear trout fishing streams, and habitat for rare wildlife.

• North Carolina’s rural communities and economies thrive on tourism that is anchored by recreation in roadless areas. Trout fishing in western NC creates over a billion dollars in annual economic impact, and whitewater paddling, rock climbing, and mountain biking in the Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests add over \$100 million more. These local economies depend on the backcountry settings provided by roadless areas.

In addition, downstream communities rely on roadless areas for clean water. Two million North Carolinians can trace their drinking water directly to a roadless area that would lose protection under the proposed repeal.

• And roadless areas are essential habitat for rare species. The roadless areas of the Nantahala and Pisgah national forests contain 58 and nearly 9,000 acres of the rarest natural communities delineated by the State’s Natural Heritage Program.

## Losing the Roadless Rule Threatens What Makes North Carolina Special

• Fragmentation by roads is a serious threat to North Carolina’s most special places.

Once a road is built into an area it is almost never taken out, which is how the Forest Service wound up with a 370,000-acre road system (enough to drive to the moon and halfway back) and a multi-billiondollar maintenance backlog. North Carolina’s national forests have only about 13% of the funding needed to fully maintain their roads.

These unnecessary and poorly maintained roads do long-lasting damage to our forests. They increase sediment pollution in mountain streams, block the movement of fish and other wildlife, spread invasive plants, and increase the risk of wildfire ignitions.

• Roads and logging in these steep areas also increases flooding and landslide risk, which would exacerbate damage from storms like Hurricane Helene.

• Before the Roadless Rule was adopted, many of North Carolina’s roadless areas were fragmented or entirely whittled away by Forest Service road construction. For example, Cheoah Bald, once our state’s largest roadless area, shrank by almost 17,000 acres, and the Wildcat roadless area, part of the Appalachian Trail corridor, isn’t even on the map anymore.

• Our remaining roadless areas could suffer a similar fate. Of our 172,000 roadless acres, 144,000 acres— more than 83 percent—would lose protection if the Roadless Rule is rescinded. (See attached map.)

Americans have the right to explore tens of millions of acres of wild backcountry lands where there are no roads – only open land, clean water, and peace of mind. Indeed, roadless areas in national forests are some of the last places in the country where that is still possible. These lands are universally enjoyed and they belong to everyone. Please protect them for the American public today and for future generations.

Sincerely,

Director, Ecosystem Management Coordination 201 14th Street SW, Mailstop 1108 Washington, DC 20250-1124

Secretary Rollins, Under Secretary Sleeper, and Chief Schultz,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Roadless Rule rescission. For the record, I am a Union County Commissioner in in Northeast Oregon. Union County is home to the Wallowa Whitman & Umatilla National Forests. Union County also hosts a good portion of Oregon's largest (Eagle Cap) wilderness area.

Nearly half of all roadless acres are located in areas rated as high or very high wildfire risk. Since the Roadless Rule was enacted, more than eight million acres of roadless forests have burned—highlighting the consequences of limiting access and management.

The Roadless Rule effectively barred active forest management across nearly 60 million acres, or almost one-third of the National Forest System. In effect this made these areas quasi-wilderness areas. This designation was fodder for litigation. This approach simply hasn't worked. I would include the East Side Screens in the same category – a failed policy the has been disproved by science and affirmed by the courts. Many of these forests are now overstocked with dead or dying trees, creating ideal conditions for insects, disease, and ultimately more high-severity wildfires. Rescinding the rule will give our public lands managers more opportunities to use science-based tools—like thinning, prescribed burning, and selective harvesting—to improve forest health and reduce ecological stress. Why would we continue to limit the tools available to our land managers?

Road access is necessary not only for management but also for maintaining recreation infrastructure, water systems, and search-and-rescue operations. The rule even prevented temporary road construction in areas where roads were critical for stewardship and public safety. Without access, firefighters can't reach ignition points, build containment lines, or safely evacuate visitors and residents. Rescinding the rule allows land managers to reduce fuels and restore healthier, more fire-resilient forests. Rescinding the rule doesn't mandate roadbuilding. It simply allows roads to be considered where they're needed.

I spent over 20 years as a seasonal wildland firefighter. The Forest Service routinely restricts access to certain roads using gates, locks, and barriers—especially in areas with sensitive wildlife or fire concerns. Rescinding the Roadless Rule does not mean unlimited public access. Not all roads are open to the public. Roads can be managed to reduce ignition risks. Agencies can control access to prevent human-caused ignitions while maintaining roads for emergency response, fuels treatment, and maintenance. Poor access is a top obstacle to fire suppression. In nearly every major wildfire over the past 15-20 years, the Forest Service has identified lack of road access as a key barrier to effective response. Road infrastructure supports rapid suppression. Having roads in place—especially ones that are closed but can be quickly reopened—allows firefighting crews to access ignition points faster and prevent small fires from becoming large, destructive events.

Current policy is leading to road loss, not expansion. The Forest Service is losing more than 1,000 miles of road access every year due to policy restrictions or lack of maintenance funding—further limiting its ability to manage forests and respond to fire Building new roads mid-crisis is inefficient and dangerous. When fires start in remote areas, it often takes days for the Forest Service to build temporary roads just to get equipment on-site. Maintaining access in advance saves valuable time and resources. A one-size-fits-all mandate doesn't work across 60 million acres of diverse landscapes. Rescinding the rule gives local land managers and stakeholders flexibility to tailor solutions based on forest conditions, fire risk, and ecological needs.

Tribes, states, counties and local stakeholders will be consulted and engaged throughout the process to ensure broad input collaboration, cooperation and coordination. For too long we have tried the methods of preservationists, obstructionists and serial litigants; let's try using scientifically sound forest management practices.

Sincerely,

lad Adares

Paul M. Anderes

Union County Commissioner

Mr. Brad Kinder Acting Director, Ecosystem Management Coordination United States Department of Agriculture, Forest Service 201 14th Street SW, Mailstop 1108 Washington DC 20250-1124

RE; Comments on Initiating an Environmental Impact Statement and Rulemaking Concerning Management of Inventoried Roadless Areas on National Forest System Lands, Docket No. FS-2025-0001-0001

Dear Mr. Kinder:

We, the Jackson County Board of Commissioners, appreciate the opportunity to comment on the United States Department of Agriculture's (USDA) proposal to initiate an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) and rulemaking concerning the management of inventoried roadless areas on National Forest System lands. Jackson County supports rescinding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule) for numerous reasons, and believes that the rescission is in the best interest of the National Forest System lands and the public for the following reasons:

First, the 2001 Roadless Rule has raised concerns about wildfire and public safety. Nearly half of the roadless areas are located on National Forest System lands rated as having high or very high wildfire risk. Since the 2001 Roadless Rule was adopted, nearly 8,000,000 acres of roadless National Forest System lands have burned. Roads are essential for safe and effective wildfire response. Simply put, if wildland firefighters cannot access an area, they cannot respond to a wildfire effectively, which impacts the public's health and safety.

Second, the 2001 Roadless Rule was not a science-based decision, and left nearly 60,000,000 acres unmanaged. This has led to overstocked, dead, and dying trees, the ideal condition for insects, diseases, and wildfire, which impact the public's health and safety. Rescinding this unscientific "Rule" will allow public lands managers the opportunity to use science-based tools to improve the health of the forests.

Third, opening up road access is necessary not only for management but also for recreation, infrastructure, water systems, and search and rescue. As applied, the 2001 Roadless Rule has prevented even temporary roads deemed critical for management or public safety. Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule does not mandate unfettered road construction and allows road construction and maintenance where needed.

Fourth, simply rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule is not going to result in unrestrained logging. Roaded or roadless, logging, and any other activities must still comply with the myriad of Federal laws and regulations related to those activities, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act of 1973, the Clean Water Act, and adopted forest management plans. Projects will still need to comply with environmental review, public input, and scientific analysis. Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule allows for the implementation of projects, as a practical matter, if those projects comply with applicable Federal laws and regulations.

Rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule removes the current "one-size-fits-all" regulation of millions of acres of National Forest System lands and allows public land managers to truly manage the public's lands.

Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

Sincerely,

JACKSON COUNTY BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS

Dear Secretary Rollins:

The State of Oregon is writing to provide formal comments on the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule). Oregon values its longstanding and productive partnership with the USDA, particularly in the stewardship of our 11 National Forests, which span over 16 million acres – more than a quarter of our state’s land area. The process and scope of the Roadless Rule rescission, however, has the potential to undermine this partnership and the progress we have made with the regional offices of the U.S. Forest Service in Oregon to promote healthier and more resilient forests.

Oregon’s identity and culture is rooted in our collective love for our public lands. The Roadless Rule covers approximately two million acres of federally owned forestland in Oregon. For decades, the rule has effectively protected these lands so that they can provide exceptional recreational opportunities to the public and serve as critical anchor areas for clean water and unaltered fish and wildlife habitat. Oregonians have a significant stake in the final outcome of the rule as we have integrated these lands into our everyday lives and local economies and have championed their collaborative management. The proposed rule ignores these connections and places decades of progress in jeopardy.

I urge the USDA to consider and act on the recommendations provided by Oregon’s agencies, particularly the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife and the Oregon Department of Forestry. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

The Honorable Brooke Rollins Secretary of Agriculture U.S. Department of Agriculture 1400 Independence Avenue, SW Washington, DC 20250

RE: Comments on Proposed Rule – Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands (Docket No. USDA–FS–2025–0001)

Dear Secretary Rollins,

On behalf of the State of Oregon, we are writing to provide formal comments on the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. Oregon values its longstanding and productive partnership with the USDA, particularly in the stewardship of our 11 National Forests, which span over 16 million acres—more than a quarter of our state’s land area. Approximately 2 million of those acres are designated as inventoried roadless areas.

We recognize the USDA’s intent to provide local flexibility in forest management. However, we urge the Department to pursue a more targeted, collaborative approach that maintains the core conservation benefits of the 2001 Roadless Rule while addressing specific, localized barriers to wildfire resilience and forest restoration where local communities deem it necessary.

## Wildfire resilience and forest management goals can be met through strategic, local processes.

Oregon has worked collaboratively with the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) and other federal land managers since 2019, under our Shared Stewardship Agreement, to develop a 20-Year Landscape Resilience Strategy. Rather than pursuing a blanket, one-size-fits all recission of the 2001 Roadless Rule, this deep collaboration on wildfire resilience strategy leaves Oregon well prepared to work with local forests on the most strategically important areas for fire treatment and identification of the barriers to achieving those treatments. If the roadless areas are an actual barrier, targeted removal of roadless designations, or other flexible uses of the forest could be employed locally to support fire suppression and ecological restoration.

Roadless areas are not road-free—as the federal register notice indicates, many roadless areas are within a half-mile of existing roads. Considering that the USFS is not currently able maintain the network of existing roads, we support an approach to wildfire resilience that focuses on maximizing the use of existing roads. We support limited flexibility for road construction or reconstruction only where it is clearly justified through a thoughtful siting process, starting with the local, strategic need and placing roads in ways that minimize habitat degradation. However, such flexibility must be paired with strong travel management planning to minimize ecological impacts and human disturbance throughout the year.

## Increased road density and road use has the potential increase fire ignitions.

Many analyses have demonstrated that building roads into undeveloped areas significantly increases wildfire risk. Human-caused wildfires—by far the most common type—occur disproportionately near roads, with over 53% more ignitions in the first 200 meters from roads than would be expected by chance. While roads can aid firefighter and restoration access, they also invite ignition sources such as recreationists, vehicle sparks, and even arson. The likely effect of expanding road networks is a substantial increase in wildfire ignitions, which far outweighs the marginal benefits of increased access. Protecting roadless areas is a practical strategy for reducing wildfire risk and safeguarding communities, ecosystems, and public resources.

## High road density and motorized vehicle use on National Forests pushes wildlife on to private lands, increasing economic damage.

High road density and motorized vehicle use on National Forest lands have indirect and significant consequences for wildlife and rural communities. Species like elk are particularly sensitive to human disturbance and are displaced from federal lands by motorized vehicle traffic onto quieter adjacent private lands, where they cause substantial damage to crops and rangelands. This displacement creates significant economic hardship for landowners. Maintaining roadless areas and travel management on existing roads is essential to providing undisturbed habitat for elk and other sensitive species—a critical use of public lands. As referenced above, USDA has not provided evidence that the 2001 Roadless Rule precludes active forest management in strategically important areas in Oregon. There is ample opportunity to implement habitat restoration, hazardous fuels reduction, and forest health treatments using the existing road network—without expanding it.

## A blanket recission maintains the one-size-fits all approach.

The 2001 Roadless Rule has provided consistent, science-based protections for ecologically important landscapes. In many places, it is working well. Rescinding the rule outright would impose a significant regulatory burden on local forests, requiring them to re-establish protections through individual planning processes. A more efficient and effective solution would be to surgically amend the rule—allowing local forest managers to work with their communities to identify areas where the modern fire context requires flexibility to support forest resilience, timber goals, or community protection, while retaining protections elsewhere.

## State Involvement and Consistency Across Forests

We strongly encourage the USDA to formalize a role for states in shaping how roadless area management is implemented locally. Oregon’s experience managing state forests has shown the value of consistent, landscape-scale planning—such as Oregon’s 20-Year Landscape Resilience Strategy and Good Neighbor Authority. Without the unifying framework of the 2001 Roadless Rule, there is a risk of fragmented decision-making across National Forests. We urge the Department to ensure that any new approach includes:

• State-level coordination to guide implementation;

• Smart siting standards for road density and location;

• Travel management to reduce road use during critical times for wildlife;

• Clear mechanisms for managing motorized access and seasonal use;

• Balanced consideration of ecological, economic, and community needs.

## Environmental Impact Statement Scope

The USDA’s notice states that the proposed rule does not compel changes to land management plans or authorize specific projects. However, by removing the prohibitions on road construction, reconstruction, and timber harvest, the rule change would enable a range of future actions by each forest. The Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) must therefore evaluate a full spectrum of reasonably foreseeable impacts, including:

• Increased road construction and timber harvest under Executive Order 14255;

• Effects of a range of road construction volumes on threatened, endangered, and sensitive species;

• Impacts to water quality, soil stability, and scenic integrity;

• Changes in public access, recreation, and cultural resource protection;

• Economic implications for local and regional communities.

We also note that the Forest Service receives less than 20% of the funding needed to maintain its existing road network. Adding new roads without addressing this backlog would exacerbate maintenance challenges and environmental degradation, which should be accounted for in the EIS.

## National Direction Remains Necessary

In the 2001 federal register notice, USDA stated that, “the past two decades of litigation, appeals, and congressional debate underscore the importance of a consistent national framework for roadless area management.” We believe that this statement remains true. The 2001 Roadless Rule provides clarity, reduced conflict, and protection for some of the most ecologically valuable lands in the National Forest System. While we support adaptive management and local flexibility, we caution against a full return to forest-by-forest decision-making, which risks undermining both conservation outcomes and public trust.

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on this important proposal and look forward to continued collaboration with the USDA to ensure that Oregon’s forests remain healthy, resilient, and well-managed for future generations.

Sincerely,

## Mr. Kinder,

The Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) offers the following comments on the proposed action by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) (90 FR 42197). This action by the USDA Forest Service is a notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement and rulemaking “concerning management of inventoried roadless areas on approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System lands, including in Alaska. The proposed rule would rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, also referred to as the 2001 Roadless Rules (66 FR 3244, 36 CFR Subpart B (2001)), which prohibits road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas, with limited exceptions” (FR Doc. 2025-16581).

For twenty-five years, existing inventoried roadless areas on US Forest Service (USFS) lands have been protected from further development and industrial activity. These lands are an important buffer against human impacts in designated wilderness areas in the state of Oregon. USFS lands, in general, play a key role in maintaining and restoring water and air quality in Oregon, throughout the Pacific Northwest, and nationwide. USFS-administered lands offer the critical uninterrupted natural spaces for providing compliance with Clean Water Act and Clean Air Act standards, support of beneficial uses of natural resources, and protection of ecosystems. The historic efforts of the USFS to protect wilderness and roadless areas are key to this superior performance. The landscape position and extent of inventoried roadless areas mean they supplement designated wilderness areas and function as anchors for air and water resources and the forest ecosystems upon which those resources depend.

Oregon DEQ is supportive of additional actions to reduce wildfire risk, but we are concerned with the lack of transparency into the decision-making of the USFS, the speed of the proposed repeal of the roadless rule, and the apparent decision to remove the rule without proper consideration of the environmental impacts of the decision. DEQ encourages the USFS to reconsider moving forward with this environmental impact statement (EIS) and proposed rule. Repealing the 2001 Roadless Rule does not align with the federal and state efforts to manage inventoried roadless areas, nor has it been coordinated with adequate engagement from states. The current comment period for the notice is unusually short. DEQ would like confirmation that should the USFS continue with the EIS, there will be a 30-day time period for objections upon publication of the legal notice of the EIS as required by 36 CFR 218.32(a). The USFS should provide an extension so that States, particularly western states like Oregon, which has nearly 2 million acres of inventoried roadless areas, will have time to analyze the EIS and offer recommendations on potential impacts.

Due to the severity of this proposed rule repeal, DEQ stresses the importance that USDA follow the planning requirements in 36 CFR Part 219. USFS states that this action is not subject to the objection process of 36 CFR 218.7, without providing the basis for reaching such a conclusion. What about this action permits it to be exempt from the process specified? Does the USDA consider this repeal a hazardous fuel reduction project per 36 CFR 218.7(a)? DEQ has serious concerns as to how rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule would impact the agency’s efforts to protect both water and air quality.

## Repeal of the Roadless Rule will have detrimental impacts to Oregon’s rivers and streams

Oregon has streams and rivers throughout the state, listed<sup>1</sup> as impaired under Section 303(d) of the Clean Water Act, either in need of a Total Maximum Daily Load or with a TMDL in effect (40 CFR 130.7). Current Forest Service management approaches, such as roadless areas, the Aquatic Conservation Strategy under the Northwest Forest Plan, and PACFISH/INFISH approaches on the eastern side of the state, are yielding gains for improving water quality and restoring aquatic ecosystems. Monitoring data from Oregon DEQ shows that federal forests consistently provide higher water quality than industrial forests, agricultural land, and urban areas, making federal forest policy the cornerstone of water quality in the state. Increasing the reach of roads and industrial extraction on federal forests threatens this progress and puts aquatic ecosystems and drinking and irrigation water for millions of Oregonians at risk. We urge you to reconsider this course of action, keep the 2001 Roadless Rule in place, and look for active management opportunities in parts of the National Forests in need of combined restoration and thinning activities.

Roads are the keystone human disturbance that facilitates other disturbances. Roads and crossings require disturbance and removal of habitat in the near-stream area. Roads themselves create chronic sedimentation in near-stream areas and at crossings. Preventing and reducing this pollution requires expensive maintenance. Roads and river crossings disturb natural areas, channel excess stormwater, decrease water retention in soils, and contribute to further erosion of waterways. They also create avenues for anthropogenic sources of pollution like garbage, sediment, metals, and petroleum products. Western Oregon especially has a high density of streams, so new road construction by necessity will create impacts across the stream network. Road building and subsequent management activities, such as timber harvest in Inventoried Roadless Areas, further complicate the area’s hydrology and increase wildfire hazards. DEQ encourages USFS to consider the ecological and financial cost of road construction in the EIS.

Extensive timber harvest changes the hydrology of streams and rivers by reducing canopy interception of precipitation, facilitating rapid snowmelt, and eliminating evapotranspiration from the harvested tree stands. The net effect in the near term is increased streamflow and erosion of stream beds and banks. In the long term, intensive timber harvest reduces streamflow in the summer and early fall compared to older, complex forests, as fast-growing young trees consume large volumes of water. This reduces water available for fish, drinking water, and irrigation while contributing to high stream temperatures during the time most dangerous for salmon and amphibians. DEQ encourages USFS to consider the hydrological impacts of increased harvest in the EIS.

Roads bring human ignition sources farther into the forest landscape. Human-caused wildfire is a large enough problem (along with garbage dumping and vandalism) that many private forestland owners have eliminated open public access and switched to permit systems for land access.

Given that the vast majority of wildfires are human-caused (Balch et al. 2017)<sup>2</sup>, creating this kind of human access deep into forest landscapes is a major increase in risk to life, property, natural resources, and timber volumes on public and adjacent private lands.

## Repeal of the Roadless Rule will have impacts on the air quality of Oregon communities

DEQ understands the need for forest management, as the severity of wildfires have increased in past years; Oregon has been working to manage areas that are high risk for wildfires. Oregon participates in the National Interagency Fire Center along with the USFS to develop interagency strategies to manage wildfires. The data gathered in the multi-agency efforts have shown that most wildfires are ignited within a half mile of a road. The cost-benefit analysis within the EIS needs to adequately represent the increased risk of wildfire ignition posed by increasing roadways in national forest lands. Cost-benefit analysis in the EIS also needs to reflect the cost of road maintenance, which was provided as evidence for the establishment of the roadless rules in 2001.

The EIS should specify what impact additional roads in the current inventory area would have on the ability of neighboring airsheds to attain and maintain the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS). Road construction and maintenance create emissions of what the Clean Air Act refers to as criteria pollutants<sup>3</sup>, such as particulate matter and ozone precursors like volatile organic compounds, that can be transported to areas outside of the wilderness area boundaries. Communities in Oregon have worked hard to attain all NAAQS, and we are working even harder to maintain the quality of our air. The Klamath Falls airshed has recently had a submission for EPA’s consideration to be listed as a maintenance area (Klamath Falls PM2.5 Maintenance Plan). Fine particulate matter will be set airborne within the airshed or transported to it during new road construction, and along the roadways due to vehicle traffic and human-caused wildfires. Should this cause the area to fall back into nonattainment, the economic burden to the community will be felt through the contingency measures that will be required to be put in place for the region. Such potential outcomes need to be considered in the EIS.

Road construction and vehicle use on new roads constructed as a result of the roadless rule repeal also have the potential to reverse improvements made by Oregon to improve visibility in our Class I areas (twelve wilderness areas and national parks). Sections 169A and 169B of the Clean Air Act require States to develop and submit plans to bring visibility in our Class I areas back to natural conditions by 2064. Introducing additional emissions of haze-forming pollutants within Class I areas will impact Oregon’s ability to maintain reasonable progress and may require additional reductions from sources outside the Class I area. These tribal, local, state, and federal coordinated efforts would be among the most impacted by the rescission of the roadless rule. Oregon’s existing federally approved Regional Haze Plan relies on the roadless rules as a baseline condition. The increased impact to visibility as a result of this proposal would require additional action by USFS to mitigate the impact and maintain our progress. This type of assessment is necessary and has not been included in the proposal.

## Conclusion

The Preliminary Description of Proposed Actions states that local land management planning will provide the basis for conservation of inventoried roadless areas.

Will the repeal require the same decision-making process to be followed for development projects in roadless areas? How will USFS comprehensively evaluate current local land management planning during the EIS process? How will USFS evaluate how those local policies may impact current inventoried roadless areas in terms of future development, including impacts to NAAQS, Visibility, and CWA requirements; impacts to watershed management; impacts to threatened, endangered, and sensitive species; and other resources as noted in the Preliminary List of Substantive Issues and Summary of Expected Impacts?

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this action. Oregon DEQ looks forward to USFS's responses and further collaboration on the EIS. Should anyone wish to follow up with Oregon DEQ regarding these comments, please contact Graham Bates at graham.bates@deq.oregon.gov.

Sincerely,

Re: Federal Register Doc 2025-16581

To Whom it May Concern:

Meade County, SD strongly supports the proposed action to rescind the 2001 road less rule including the road less area designation in Beaver Park. While the concept of setting aside lands for resource protection is appealing to some, the designation of Beaver Park and many other road less areas has increased the risk of catastrophic fire and risk to human health and safety to those that live near these areas.

The designation of Beaver Park as a road less area was motivated by a desire by USFS to designate a roadless area in the Black Hills based on the 2001 road less rule. The designation was pushed on a fast track without full consideration of the impacts to landowners, recreation, the presence of a national trail, numerous existing roads and the potential for increase wildfire risk.

Beaver Park lies within a high-use and high-growth region of Meade County that supports a diverse mix of economic, recreational, and agricultural activities. The area's proximity to the 1- 90 urban corridor, its adjacency to private lands and the Black Hills National Cemetery, and the need to support forest health through ongoing fire mitigation projects make it incompatible with a roadless designation.

The hands off approach associated with the road less rule directly conflict with Meade County's priorities for economic diversity, which depend on a balanced approach to land use that includes recreation, timber, agriculture, responsible development, and fire safety.

Meade County strongly supports responsible stewardship of public lands, but that stewardship must also account for the needs and realities of the communities who live, work, and recreate near them. The Beaver Park area has long been managed as general forest land and should be returned to a management approach where multiple use and proper forest management can occur.

Please consider and address the enclosed comments as part of the Environmental Impact Statement (EIS).

Regards,

Comments from Meade County South Dakota.

Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement to Rescind the USFS Roadless Rule Federal Register Doc. 2025-16581

To: USDA, USFS Director, Ecosystem Management Coordination, 20114<sup>th</sup> St. SW Mailstop 1108, Washington DC 20250-1124

Comment 1: The 2001 roadless designation of Beaver Park has resulted in a hands-off approach in terms of forest health and mitigation of wildfire risk. As an example, in 2021, Beaver Park was removed from the USFS Chimera forest and fuels treatment project. While areas around Beaver Park are being actively treated and managed under the project, Beaver Park now remains an enclave of thickly stocked pine prone to large fires.

Comment 2: In 2022, USFS identified the Beaver Park and the Sturgis fire shed that surround it as one of 21 high risk areas in the western US. The reason for this rating was the proximately to critical infrastructure, homes and the potential impacts to natural resources from large scale wildfire. Within Beaver Park itself, over 80% of the forest has high to very high wildfire severity hazard rating. A southwest wind driven wildfire during high to extreme fire danger conditions would endanger thousands of people who live in the 1-90 Corridor between Sturgis and Tilford. The lack of management in Beaver Park from the current roadless designation has resulted in densely stocked ponderosa pine with many areas exceeding 200 sq. feet of basal per acre. Fires that burn in these conditions tend to crown and then blow up if weather conditions are right. Comment 3: The road less rule infringes upon the property rights of adjacent landowners and makes management of grazing, control of weeds and other management tasks more difficult. It limits access for adjacent landowners and grazing permittees who rely on these lands for their livelihoods.

Comment 4: The Federal Register Notice discusses the increased risk of catastrophic fire, forest health concerns and risks to human health and safety as a result of the Road less Rule designations. To keep this planning process on track, we request that these problems be identified as formal planning issues in the EIS. With the exception of the required "no action" alternative, any alternative that is developed should specifically address these issues.

Comment 5: We support rescinding the road less rule in its entirety and urge against the temptation to implement half measures that would keep the designation but reduce restrictions and allow equipment use in these areas. We also emphasize that maintaining the road less area but allowing local management control of the Black Hills National Forest is not an answer as the scrutiny associated with road less designation will hang over the head of the decision maker and result in lack of timely decisions. Fully rescinding the Beaver Park roadless designation is the only approach that truly addresses the issues identified above.

## Subject: Support for the Repeal of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule

Dear Secretary Rollins and Chief Shultz,

On behalf of the citizens and the economic future of Uintah County, Utah, the Uintah County Commission writes to voice its strong support for the repeal of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule ("Roadless Rule"). For more than twenty years, this rigid federal rule has actively undermined the health of our forests, increased the risk of catastrophic wildfire, and created insurmountable barriers to the economic and recreational development that is vital to our community's survival.

The Roadless Rule has inflicted severe environmental damage seen across the region. By prohibiting road access for active management, it has left our forests dense, diseased, and dying The bark beetle epidemic has turned vast portions of our backcountry into a standing tinderbox of dead timber, creating a severe and unacceptable wildfire risk to our communities, watersheds, and wildlife. Our local land managers are prevented from implementing the very projects—such as thinning, commercial timber harvest, and sanitation harvesting—that could restore forest health and mitigate these dangers

To understand the Roadless Rule's reach in Uintah County, we have included this map in our letter that shows all of the IRA in the county, which is primarily located on our northern border

![](images/e504e6854f3a088a664799bbe6c0fb6912c6e08999216eab1926b8fff4e19f6c.jpg)

The darker shade of green on this map shows the vast amount of IRA land within our county. As evident, Uintah County has been trapped and surrounded by unworkable federal land designations on its northern end which prevent human and economic growth. Specifically, the areas designated as IRA are our key watersheds for our citizenry. For these reasons, Uintah County has opposed the roadless rule since its inception.

This lack of management also degrades habitat for key wildlife species and harms our ranching partners. Unhealthy, overgrown forests provide poor forage for wildlife, while the inability to maintain range infrastructure harms the sustainable grazing operations that are part of our heritage and economy.

Just in the past two decades since the roadless rule's inception, significant catastrophic fires have occurred in the surrounding region that have burned thousands of acres in the IRAs due to the fuel load buildup on these lands. These fires include, but are not limited to, the Neola North fire, the East Fork fire, the Dollar Ridge fire, and the recent Speirs fire. This affects our citizenry economically, ecologically, and from a public health perspective

Repealing the Roadless Rule is not a call for widespread road building or unchecked development. It is a necessary call to restore common-sense, localized management to our public lands. We must empower local Forest Service managers, in collaboration with counties, to make site-specific decisions that improve forest health, reduce wildfire danger, and allow for carefully planned recreational and economic projects that can sustain our communities.

Uintah County strongly urges you to proceed with repealing this failed and destructive policy Let us work together collaboratively for our forests, our wildlife, and our people.

Respectfully,

Uintah County Gommissioners

## Subject: Support for the Repeal of the Roadless Rule

Dear Secretary Rollins and Chief Shultz,

On behalf of the citizens, economy, and natural resources of Duchesne County, Utah, the Duchesne County Commission writes to express its support for the U.S. Forest Service and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's efforts to repeal the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (the "Roadless Rule"). For over two decades, this federal mandate has imposed a one-size-fits-all restriction on our public lands that has proven to be counterproductive, economically devastating, and environmentally harmful to the forests within our county.

The Roadless Rule was implemented with the intention that it would improve the landscape and offer a backcountry experience for recreators, but its practical consequences have been catastrophic for the health of our forests. By prohibiting road construction and reconstruction, the rule has effectively paralyzed active forest management across vast landscapes. This careless approach has prevented our local land managers from implementing crucial projects, such as thinning, prescribed burns, and sanitation harvesting. As a result, our forests have become unnaturally dense, overgrown, and dangerously susceptible to disease andinsect infestation. The fuel load has reached unprecedented levels, turning our beautiful mountains into a tinderbox awaiting a spark. The very "protection" offered by the rule has created the conditions for the catastrophic, landscape-scale wildfires we now face year after year.

A drive through the Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) within the Ashley National Forest in our county provides a stark and tragic visual. These are not the pristine, healthy ecosystems envisioned by the rule's authors. Instead, nearly all of these areas are now a beetle-kill wasteland. Vast expanses of standing dead timber cover our mountainsides—a direct result of a bark beetle epidemic that foresters were powerless to combat due to the access restrictions imposed by the Roadless Rule. We were forced to watch helplessly as the infestation spread, with no ability to remove infected trees or salvage the dead timber before it became a fire hazard and lost all economic value

To understand the Roadless Rule's reach in Duchesne County, we have included this map in our letter:

![](images/174609de927a9429ef2a8df0a715db500b7f24fdf9d976da26eed62763850385.jpg)

The darkest shade of green is congressionally designated wilderness. The middle shade of green is inventoried Roadless Areas. The lightest shade of green is forest lands that are subject to multiple use and sustained yield under the National Forest Management Act. As you can see, most of the forest lands in Duchesne County are locked up either through wilderness areas or under the Roadless Rule, ultimately resulting in over 360,000 acres of locked up IRA lands in our County. This leaves our county with very few options and opportunities in our northern and southern regions for trails, roads, pipelines, and other recreational opportunities.

This forced inaction has hamstrung our local timber industry. Duchesne County once had a thriving forest products sector with sawmills that provided multi-generational, family-wage jobs. The Roadless Rule, by locking up access to manageable timber, was a primary driver in the decimation of this industry. The economic ripple effect has harmed our entire community. Furthermore, the rule has prevented or unnecessarily complicated many other vital projects, including mineral resource development, water infrastructure improvements, and even the enhancement of recreational access for our citizens.

The negative impacts extend directly to wildlife and grazing. A healthy forest is a diverse forest, with a mosaic of young and old growth, meadows, and clearings. The unmanaged, dying forests created by the Roadless Rule are a monoculture of dense, dead trees that provide poor habitat for species like elk, mule deer, and sage grouse, which depend on varied forage habitats. Similarly, our local ranchers, who are vital stewards of the land, have been harmed. The rule impedes their ability to maintain and improve range infrastructure, such as fences and water developments, which are essential for sustainable grazing management, and the wildfires that result from the fuel loads caused by the roadless rule can leave their allotments in shambles

As a result of the dense and dead tree buildup caused by the Roadless Rule, Duchesne County has had several catastrophic wildfires since the Roadless Rule was finalized, resulting in millions of dollars in costs to our citizens, the State of Utah, and the federal government. Some noteworthy fires in Duchesne County include the East Fork Fire (burned approximately 90,000 acres, much of which was in roadless areas), the Dollar Ridge Fire (burned nearly 70,000 acres, partially in roadless areas), and the Neola North Fire (burned over 40,000 acres, partially in roadless areas). For these reasons, Duchesne County has been calling for its repeal for over a decade.

Ultimately, under the U.S. Forest Service's Organic Act of 1897, Congress declared that it is the central policy of the Forest Service to “protect and improve the forests for the purpose of securing a permanent supply of timber for the people and insuring conditions favorable to continuous water flow." The roadless rule is in direct conflict with the Forest Service's statutory mandate, and Duchesne County appreciates your efforts to right the ship

Repealing the Roadless Rule is not a call for unchecked development. It is a call for the restoration of common-sense, active management of our public lands. It is a request to return decision-making authority to the local Forest Service managers who understand the specific needs of our forests, in collaboration with state and local governments. We need to provide these managers with the tools and flexibility to address forest health crises, mitigate wildfire risk, restore wildlife habitat, and support our rural economies.

Duchesne County strongly urges you to move forward with repealing this failed policy. Let us work together to manage our forests for true health, resilience, and multi-use productivity,

Respectfully,

The Duchesne County Commission

RE: Recission of the 2001 Roadless Rule, Docket number FS-2025-0001.

Beaver County, Utah, would like to submit comments relating to the proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. This administrative rule, adopted by regulation by the United States Forest Service (USFS), has been the subject of numerous legal challenges and was seen at the time by many, as a scandalous way of circumventing congress to create the equivalent of Wilderness Areas. Millions of acres of National Forest were suddenly locked up under this restrictive contrivance and any existing roads within its boundaries were immediately closed down. The fact that roads existed within these inventoried areas belies the “roadless” moniker used to reclassify the status of National Forest System lands. Thereafter, timber harvesting in these areas was halted, traditional uses were hampered and active forest management was severely impaired.

Beaver County has a deeply held antagonism towards the Roadless Rule from its inception. National Forest System lands were taken out of production for timber harvesting, mining, and many other pursuits which impacted our communities economically. The opportunity to recreate on these newly designated lands was suddenly halted for all but a very few people. Ironically, the productivity of these lands were suspended and the purposes for which the National Forest System was created was overturned.

The National Forest Management Act of 1976 (NFMA) was passed by congress to give the U.S. Forest Service direction in managing the National Forest, to set standards for timber sales and to create policies to regulate timber harvesting. The underlying purpose for creating the National Forest System was to provide timber products for America. The tone and tenor of the Roadless Rule was, in stark contrast, a mandate to end forest productivity through hands-off protectionism. Throughout this Roadless

Rule, there is a clear conservation emphasis that, in fact, without active forest management, has left these forests in overgrown, decadent and hazardous conditions.

The Roadless Rule fails to consider the distinct forest types and local management needs within the National Forest System. In our area, the large catastrophic fires we experience are a result of old, overgrown timber stands that are no longer healthy and resilient to insect infestations. The need to harvest, thin, and proactively manage for forest health is undeniable. In our estimation, the biggest threat to our forests is to place them behind a locked gate without active management. A “wilderness” is not the objective, rather, healthy and resilient forests should be the prime objective.

The U.S. Forest Service produced a report entitled “Mature and Old-Growth Forests: Analysis of Threats on Lands Managed by the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management, June 2024.” Thi report found that the greatest threat to old and mature forests was wildfire. Yet, the obvious glaring solution for protecting the forest and preventing wildfires is to actively manage it with silvacultural methods like timber harvesting and reducing the quantity of trees per acres. It is common knowledge that as a forest ecosystem becomes old and degenerate, the forces of nature will renew the ecosystem by the natural cycle of death, fire and regrowth. It is a natural process that old trees die and become a fuel load for the inevitable wildfire, which in turn brings new growth. Proper forest management can delay or manipulate this process by infusing new growth while removing fuel loads. Proper active management can interrupt or replace this cycle. The goal is to have a healthy and resilient forest, NOT a collection of dead trees in a “Roadless Area”!

In Beaver County, we have a strong working relationship with our local Ranger District. We coordinate plans and goals to improve our local forest, to provide timber products, to improve watershed health, to improve grazing, and to provide access for numerous recreational activities. Through the Shared Stewardship Program, our district has accounted for millions of dollars in on-the-ground projects that benefit our forest. This proactive approach is working and is a model for other regions to emulate. However, the Roadless Areas are essentially out of reach. Forest managers must go through so many hoops to do any work within an Inventoried Roadless Area that it effectively stifles any effort to do so. The amazing success we see in forest management and health on the rest of the forest is juxtaposed by the inactivity and decadence within the roadless areas.

National Forest System lands should be accessible and provide a benefit to local communities. They should also contribute to local economies. The primary focus of the Forest Service should be forest health and productivity. Sadly, these goals are not emphasized in the Inventoried Roadless Areas. The lack of timber harvesting and other management activities within the roadless areas has left many of them in very poor health and susceptible to catastrophic wildfire. With the ongoing droughts, threats of climate change, increasing wildfire scope and frequency and their threat to communities and Wildland Urban

Interface (WUI) areas, we simply must do something to remediate the forest condition within those areas set aside as Inventoried Roadless Areas. In fact, as proposed, we believe the best solution is to rescind the Roadless Rule and allow full and proper management of these lands. The local Ranger Districts should be allowed full discretion in forest level planning and management of lands within their jurisdictional boundaries. The goal of “multiple use and sustained yield” should apply to the entire forest with few exceptions.

Beaver County encourages Secretary Rollins and the U.S. Forest Service to formally rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule to allow full and proper management of our National Forest System Lands.

Sincerely,

San Juan County supports the preparation of an EIS to analyze the effects of a proposed rule to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule.

The Honorable Brooke Rollins U. S. Secretary of Agriculture U.S. Department of Agriculture 1400 Independence Avenue, SW Washington, DC 20250

RE: Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands

Dear Secretary Rollins:

The State of Utah (State), through the Public Lands Coordinating Office, has reviewed the Notice of Intent to prepare an environmental impact statement (EIS) and rulemaking, published in the Federal Register on August 29, 2025, regarding management of inventoried roadless areas on approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System lands, including in Alaska. The proposed rule would rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule) (66 FR 3244, 36 CFR Subpart B (2001), which prohibits road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas, with limited exceptions. The State offers these comments on the scope of the EIS and proposed rulemaking to assist the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) in developing a rule that is well-reasoned, legally sound, and addresses the concerns of the State of Utah.

Utah's forests are grappling with a confluence of serious issues, most notably beetle kill and dangerously high fuel loads. Decades of fire suppression and other management practices have led to unnaturally dense forests, which are highly susceptible to insect infestations, disease, and wildfire. The "fuel load" drastically increases the risk of unwanted wildfires, which pose a significant threat to communities, watersheds, and air quality. Complicating these forest health issues is the federal Roadless Area Conservation Rule. While the rule has some

exceptions, active forest management is severely hindered. As such, the State supports the full rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

## 1. Localized Decision-Making

The State supports a shift to localized decision-making for the management of roadless areas. The State requests that the EIS allow local Forest Service personnel to make decisions regarding roadless area management. Line officers are most familiar with the needs and challenges of each formally designated roadless area. The State advocates an approach that can be tailored to the unique ecological, economic, and social conditions of each Forest. A onesize-fits-all federal rule fails to account for the diverse landscapes and specific management needs across the country.

## 2. Forest Management, Air, and Water Quality

The EIS must analyze the impacts of rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule on forest health and its subsequent effects on air and water quality. The State contends that the current rule's restrictions have led to a significant decline in active forest management, contributing to unhealthy, overgrown forests. The State requests that the EIS examine how a more proactive management approach, facilitated by increased access, could lead to:

• Improved air quality by reducing the frequency and severity of large-scale wildfires, which are a major source of particulate matter and pollutants.

• Enhanced water quality through the prevention of severe soil erosion and sediment runoff that often follow high-intensity fires.

## 3. Wildfire Risk and Mitigation

The State urges the Forest Service to thoroughly evaluate and address the urgent need for fuels reduction in areas currently designated as roadless under the 2001 Roadless Rule. The EIS should consider how the proposed rule can facilitate active forest management to mitigate wildfire risks.

## 4. Wildlife Management and Data Collection

Utah has one of the largest habitat restoration programs in the United States, with hundreds of thousands of acres treated each year. The temporary use of roads facilitates the movement of restoration equipment and crews. The proposed rule change could increase the number of acres that can be restored on forest lands in the state but could undermine long-term habitat restoration goals if permanent roads are created.

The rule change could also increase timber harvest throughout the state, which may have a positive impact on big game species. Timber harvest can increase the quantity and quality of summer habitat for mule deer and elk, which in turn can improve their body condition going into winter. This factor is an important predictor of survival for big game in Utah.

However, the DWR is concerned about how forest roads will be used and the impacts of creating new roads if the rule is repealed. Roadless areas in Utah conserve a significant portion of the state’s mule deer and elk populations. Roads with high traffic volumes and/or constant use can have significant negative impacts on wildlife and their habitats. The negative effects of roads are well-documented and include increased mortality from vehicle collisions and the loss, fragmentation, and degradation of habitats and migration corridors.

Roads and related infrastructure may also negatively impact trout and other aquatic species by increasing sediment loading, altering stream channels, fragmenting habitat, and acting as a barrier to migration.

Increasing permanent roads creates a greater risk of spur route development by OHVs, transport of invasive species, and increased human-caused wildfire in crucial mule deer and elk habitat.

If the rule is repealed, DWR recommends limiting the development of forest roads to temporary or infrequent activities to protect wildlife and their habitats. If you have questions, please contact Daniel Olson, Impact Analysis Coordinator, in our Salt Lake Office, at 385-415- 4010.

## 5. Efficient Management of Water Rights

The Utah Division of Water Rights (DWRi) advocates for revisions to federal policies and local land use plans to better accommodate the management of water resources. DWRi emphasizes the necessity of ensuring access to both existing and future water-related infrastructure, which includes the ability to:

• Construct, operate, and regulate water storage and diversion facilities.

• Measure and monitor water flows and conditions.

• Utilize telemetry and related equipment for remote operation and data collection.

Although the current roadless rule (§294.12) provides some justification for these activities, DWRi maintains that repealing the rule would enable greater flexibility. Increased coordination at the local level would allow for a more effective and efficient administration of water rights in Utah.

## 6. Forest Health and Economic Benefits

The State requests that the EIS examine how the proposed rule could lead to an improvement in overall forest health. Specifically, an analysis should be conducted on the economic and ecological benefits of allowing for the salvage and harvesting of dead and diseased trees, as well as other forest thinning activities. Increased accessibility would enable these critical management practices, which are currently restricted, leading to more resilient forests and a reduction in the risk of catastrophic wildfires and insect infestations.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide scoping comments. The State looks forward to our continued collaboration with the Forest Service to ensure that federal lands are managed for a wide range of sustainable uses, contributing to the health and vitality of our forests.

Please do not hesitate to contact me if you have any questions.

Sincerely,
