RE: Docket No. FS-2025-0001

Dear Acting Director Kinder,

On behalf of the Salt Lake City Department of Public Utilities (SLCDPU), I write in response to the Notice of Intent (NOI) published by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) U.S. Forest Service (USFS) entitled “Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands."I appreciate the opportunity to inform the development of an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) and express concerns on the Administration's planned proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule or "Roadless Rule." Our community opposes any federal action that could put our regionalwater quality at risk for 400,000 users throughout the Salt Lake City metropolitan area.

SLCDPU is a municipal water, sewer, and stormwater provider serving the capital city and neighboring communities along theWasatch Front. Our drinking water service area is 141 square miles in the fastest growing metropolitan area in the State of Utah. TheWasatch Mountains east of Salt Lake City provide 60% of our daily water supply. We have the great honor and distinction of being one of the oldest retail water providers in the Western United States

At the turn of the century, the leaders of Salt Lake City asked the federal government for help in protecting its drinking water source. President Theodore Roosevelt created the Salt Lake Forest Reserve in 1905. Now part of the Uinta-Wasatch-Cache National Forest, these lands are primarily managed for the provision of drinking water to the valley below. A large range of partners, ranging from canyon residents to USFS, collaborate in keeping these canyons healthy to provide clean drinking water. We are carefully managing the replacement and rehabilitation of aging infrastructure, the protection of our water sources. and the protection of the environment for now and future generations

Roadless forests are protected lands administered by USFS that fall within critical watersheds our system depends on to provide clean drinking water to more than 400,000 regional users throughout Salt Lake County. Approximately four million acres of inventoried roadless areas in Utah, including over 600,000 acres in the Wasatch Range, could be impacted and exposed to potential overdevelopment if the Roadless Rule is rescinded. A lack of protections along the Wasatch Front could pose a threat to the environment and our vital drinking water sources by increasing access with limited resources for maintenance and enforcement of watershed restrictions. Furthermore, infrastructure development that disturbs the ground can cause sedimentation and other negative water quality impacts. With millions of visitors annually to the canyons along the Wasatch Front, human activity can have far reaching impacts to our drinking water quality. While watersheds elsewhere in America have been closed to the public to prevent pollution, the Wasatch Front Watershed has remained open while maintaining a pristine water supply due to careful stewardship.

USDA stresses that "the nation's largest single source of water is the National Forest System, the network of national forests stewarded by the USDA Forest Service."<sup>1</sup> The agency notes that more than 60 million Americans nationwide rely on drinking water from river and aquifer systems that have sources within our national forests. Efforts to conserve forests are eficient, cost-efective eforts to protect critical supplies and ensure the delivery of clean water.

The rescission of the Roadless Rule may inhibit our ability to continue ensuring this careful stewardship amongst intergovernmental partners and the public. While our community recognizes the need for fire suppression and mitigation activities on our public lands, adding roads may increase the potential for fire ignitions in our area due to the high usage and popularity of these canyons. We encourage policymakers to take a balanced approach in consideration of the fact that sustaining these forests helps to address other hazards and needs, like flood control and water availability respectively. We ask the Administration to ensure adequate consultation with local governments as this process moves forward.

Protecting our water quality and our public health is the foremost responsibility of our work at SLCDPU. In alignment with that mission, we respectfully ask USFS to keep these potential impacts to municipal drinking water in mind as the agency develops an EIS. We encourage the Administration to withdraw this current proposal to rescind the Roadless Rule. Thank you for your time and consideration of our concerns.

Sincerely,

Director, EcosystemManagement Coordination:

Dear Director,

I am writing to urge final approval of the proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule. Utah counties like mine have been disproportionately harmed by this outdated regulation. By restricting access across 4 million acres of national forest in Utah, the rule has prevented us from maintaining critical watersheds, supporting sustainable grazing, and improving recreation opportunities for Utah families.

Our watersheds are the lifeblood of small towns, yet the Roadless Rule often made it impossible to treat diseased stands or construct limited-access roads to maintain water infrastructure. Ranchers have faced reduced grazing allotments because land managers lacked the flexibility to maintain forage areas. Recreation, an industry that sustains many Utah counties, has been hobbled by the inability to build and maintain the very roads and trails families use to enjoy our forests. These are not hypothetical harms; they are real economic and social im pacts we have lived with for two decades. The Trump administration's proposal finally recognizes that federal rules written in 2001 do not serve the realities of 2025.

Thank you for moving this commonsense reform forward.

Sincerely, Marvin Kenison Juab County Commission Chair

## Formal Comment of the Kane County Commission

Re: FS-2025-0001, Notice of Intent to Prepare <sub>an</sub> Environmental Impact Statement and Rulemaking Regarding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule

## Submitted by: Kane County Commission

Dear Secretary Rollins and USDA Forest Service Officials

The Kane County Commission respectfully submits the following comments regarding the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. Kane County strongly supports this proposed action and urges the U.S. Forest Service to finalize rescission  quickly  possible.

## About Kane County

Kane County, Utah, is  90 percent federally managed land, with only  small private tax base. Federal policies directly  disproportionately affect  livelihoods,  and public safety. residents depend  National  System lands for grazing, forest products, recreation, utilities, and tourism. Restrictive federal rules, including the Roadless Rule, have left rural counties like ours unable to properly manage forest health, protect communities, and sustain economic activity.

## Legal and Historical Foundations

The Organic Administration Act of 1897 established that national forests were created for two purposes: (1) to conserve water flows, and (2) to furnish a continuous supply of timber for the American people. The U.S. Supreme Court in United States v. New Mexico (1978) reaffirmed that national forests were never intended to be set aside as parks for non-use, but to serve vital economic and resource needs. The Roadless Rule, by prohibiting road construction, reconstruction, and timber harvest, is inconsistent with these statutory purposes and has contributed to catastrophic wildfire and economic decline.

## Alignment with the Forest Service's Proposal

The Forest Service has acknowledged in its Notice of Intent that the "one-size-fits-all" approach of the 2001 Roadless Rule is  longer appropriate. Kane County agrees. Conditions  the ground have dramatically changed, with increasedwildfire, drought, and insect infestations. The Roadless Rule has contributed to these problems by limiting proactive management. We support rescission and return of decision-making to local land managers. The Roadless Rule has:

• Restricted access needed for fuel breaks, thinning, and forest health treatments.

• Undermined local emergency response capacity

• Suppressed timber and wood product industries vital to rural jobs.

Increased <sub>costs</sub> and delays for water, power, and communication infrastructure.

Concentrated recreation in limited areas, harming both the land and tourism-based businesses.

Created millions of acres of de facto wilderness without Congressional approval.

## Recent Wildfire Examples

The effects of the Roadless Rule <sub>are</sub> evident <sub>in</sub> recent catastrophic wildfires in and around Kane County and Southern Utah. In 2025, the Monroe Canyon Fire burned <sub>more</sub> than 73,000 <sub>acres</sub> in Fishlake National Forest, destroying power transmission lines and cutting electricity <sub>to</sub> Wayne County. The France Canyon Fire burned nearly 35,000 acres of the Dixie National Forest in Garfield and Kane Counties, impacting nearby communities and tourism. Just south of Kane County, the Dragon Bravo scorched over 145,000 acres  the Kaibab Plateau, destroying the historic Grand Canyon Lodge. These mega fires underscore the urgent need for proactive forest management and access, which the Roadless Rule prevents.

## Consistency with Kane County's Resource Management Plan

County's  Management  (RMP), adopted  Code §17-27a-401, emphasizes multiple-use management and adequate  for forest health, grazing, wildfire suppression, and recreation. The RMP requires coordination with federal agencies   consistency. Federal law, including FLPMA §1712(c)(9) and the National Forest Management Act, requires the Forest Service to coordinate its plans with state and local governments <sub>to</sub> the maximum extent possible. The Roadless Rule has ignored these mandates. Rescission will allow the Forest Service to realign with <sub>our</sub> RMP and the law by restoring flexibility for local managers and respecting county-adopted policies.

Economic and Community Harm in Kane County

Since implementation of the Roadless Rule:

Timber harvests have collapsed, contributing to the closure of mills and loss of family-wage jobs.

•Ranching operations have suffered as ranchers cannot maintain or access water infrastructure and range improvements.

Tourism opportunities have been constrained by the inability to develop <sub>or</sub> maintain recreation infrastructure that disperses visitors.

Infrastructure projects (water lines, power corridors,  towers) have faced excessive delays <sub>or</sub> denials, raising costs for rural residents.

• Wildfire suppression costs and risks have grown, straining local budgets for search-and-rescue and emergency response.

## Conclusion

Kane County strongly supports USDA's proposal <sub>to</sub> rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule. The Rule has harmed economy, increased wildfire risks, created de facto wilderness without Congressional approval, and conflicted with <sub>our</sub> Resource Management Plan. We urge the Forest Service to finalize rescission and restore management authority to local decision-makers, working in coordination with counties and states.

thank USDA for initiating this  and stand ready  provide further data, examples, and partnership <sub>as</sub> the EIS proceeds.

## RE: Docket No. FS-2025-0001

## Dear Acting Director Kinder:

On behalf of the Salt Lake County (Utah) Mayor's Office, I am writing in response to the Notice of Intent published by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) entitled “Special Areas: Rogdless Areg Conservgtion; National Forest System Lands" regarding an environmental impact statement and rulemaking process concerning management of inventoried roadless areas. My office appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the Administration's planned proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule or “Roadless Rule."Respectfully, we oppose the proposed nationwide recission of the Roadless Rule, Utah is comprised of nearly four million acres of inventoried roadless areas. Approximately 29,000 of those acres fall within Salt Lake County -- concentrated in the Wasatch Mountains, including Big Cottonwood, Little Cottonwood and Millcreek canyons These locations are indispensable to our region's drinking water security, outdoor recreation economy, wildlife habitat, effective emergency management practices and wildfire resilience. Removing long-standing protections against permanent roads and industrial activity would harm these landscapes and the communities that rely on them.

Salt Lake County is Utah's most populous county, home to over 1.2 million residents from the region's urban and suburban core to canyon communities and canyon-adjacent communities, such as Millcreek, Holladay, Cottonwood Heights, Sandy, Draper, Alta, and Brighton. Our Salt Lake County government delivers essential services including public health and safety, watershed management, emergency response, parks and trail recreation programs,roadway planning, and land-use regulation. In addition, the County manages important andvalued public amenities, while promoting sustainable growth, economic development, community resiliency and environmental stewardship. As the regional government, we support the leadership of the Salt Lake City Department of Public Utilities in safeguarding the essential water supply that serves more than 400,000 residents within a 141-square-mile service area. These users represent a significant share of Salt Lake County's population, and their water security depends on the Wasatch Mountains. Rescinding the Roadless Rule could jeopardize this critical resource and undermine the health and safety of our region.

## Utah's Forests and Impact on Communities

## Drinking Water Access and Quality

The Wasatch canvon areas serve as critical source water protection zones. More than 60 percent of Salt Lake City's municipal water supply originates in these headwaters. Even

SL SALT LAKE COUNTY

Jennifer Wilson Mayor

Erin Litvack Deputy Mayor, County Services

Darrin Casper Deputy Mayor, Finánce and Administration

Catherine Kanter Deputy Mayor, Regional Operations

Andrew Roberts Chief of Staff

limited disturbance in these sensitive areas accelerates sedimentation, increases nutrient loading, and introduces pollutants such as hydrocarbons and heavy metals into our water supply. Increased human access through new roads further elevates the risks of unauthorized camping, trash dumping, and waste contamination, all of which directly degrade water quality and increase treatment costs.

In addition, road construction and logging reduce the natural water storage and filtration capacity of these forests, diminishing resilience to drought and climate variability. Erosion from disturbed slopes also shortens the lifespan of downstream reservoirs by reducing storage capacity, thereby compounding both water supply and flood control challenges.

Recognizing that our forests serve as natural water filters (by trapping sediment and promoting the delivery of clean drinking water), Salt Lake City, Salt Lake County and the USFS have successfully managed our forests for over a century. Road construction, logging and grazing operations introduce erosion, sedimentation, and other pollutants into streams, lakes and reservoirs jeopardizing the health of this precious resource. The preservation of local headwaters and our sensitive watershed curbs these threats.

## Recreational Access/Impact to Economy

Our state's renowned outdoor opportunities are central to Utah's identity. Activities such as hiking, camping, climbing, backcountry skiing, mountain biking, fishing and hunting depend on undeveloped, road-free natural landscapes. Logging scars and new roads would destroy the scenery, limit solitude, and drive down tourism revenue from outdoor sports, retail, guide services, and hospitality businesses. Diminished recreational value and increased pollution undermine community resilience and our local economy, creating a major socioeconomic vulnerability. Preserving these landscapes supports the USFS goal of providing sustainable recreational access for present and future generations.

## Habitat

Utah's roadless areas provide refuge for numerous at-risk species ranging from elk and black bears to sensitive nesting raptors and local plant species. Permanent roads carve corridors into natural habitats which can disrupt migration routes and invite invasive species by way of increased human traffic. Once fragmented, these ecosystems cannot be restored to their undisturbed condition, exposing the state's natural landscape and undermining decades of conservation progress. Maintaining intact habitat and biodiversity aligns with USFS's commitment to sustaining forest productivity and wildlife values.

## Emergency Management

Beyond wildfire management, intact roadless areas play an essential role in reducing flood hazards and protecting public safety during high stream flows and annual spring runoff events. These headwaters provide natural attenuation of peak flows, slowing runoff and reducing downstream flood severity. Disturbances caused by road construction or slope clearing increase erosion, debris flows, and sedimentation, which can overwhelm downstream flood control facilities, clog culverts and channels, and heighten flood risk in canyon-adjacent communities. In 2023, Salt Lake County actually experienced a serious risk of this type of flooding due to a historically high level of spring run-off that year.

When road networks are cut into steep canyon terrain, they not only destabilize slopesbut also create false access corridors that quickly become impassable during floods, avalanches, or debris flows, consequently increasing demand for emergency rescues and diverting scarce resources.

Current wildfire strategy and emergency management efforts are most effective when concentrating on precision oriented “at risk"areas such as theWildland-Urban Interface (WUI), rather than on remote roadless areas. Prioritizing WUI management strategies (with their direct connection and proximity to already developed structures) while protecting remote inventoried roadless areas directly advances USFS wildfire resilience objectives.

## Wildfire Risk

## Recommendation

In summary, the Salt Lake County Mayor's Office sincerely urges the Administration to maintain the Roadless Rule in full. These protections safeguard 60 percent of the water supply to our capital city and the regional water supply serving more than 400,000 County residents, ensuring the health and safety of our communities. Salt Lake County acknowledges the importance of fire suppression and mitigation strategies in forest areas and we fully support efforts to reduce wildfire risks. That laudable goal, however, should not be relied upon as a primary (or even secondary) justification for rescinding the Roadless Rule -- particularly given the risk that allowing roads within these pristine environments will actually only exacerbate the threat of forest fires. Furthermore, good public policy warrants balancing other critically important objectives, such as water quality,recreation access, economic vitality, wildlife preservation and emergency management, against any suggested benefit to wildfire prevention. Furthermore, retaining the Roadless Rule protections directly aligns with the USFS's goals to sustain healthy, diverse, and resilient forests and the USDA's mission to conserve natural resources and safeguard public health.

As such, a healthy and robust forest provides emergency management benefits. If these landscapes are compromised, Salt Lake County could face substantially higher demands on both routine responses and disaster recovery operations

Understanding the exceptions to the current Roadless Rule and the allowances this gives to mitigation and public safety activities, Salt Lake County is highly concerned with a complete rescission of the rule. Construction of new road networks could exacerbate Utah's severe risk of wildfires. While proponents suggest that new roads will actually facilitate wildfire management, data suggest otherwise. 85 percent of our nation's wildfires are humancaused and often ignited along roads and trails. Intact roadless areas limit ignition sources and potentially slow fire spread. Although it is possible that new roads could serve as temporary fire breaks and provide additional access for fire suppression, the expansion of road networks and logging debris fields would introduce new ignition points, exacerbating Utah's high risk for wildfire.

Re: FS-2025-0001-0001

The Port of Port Angeles is a county-wide Port District in Clallam County, Washington. The Port has a long history of supporting the sustainable and active management of forest lands in western Washington, including the Olympic National Forest. Many of the services we provide for our customers rely on a viable forest products industry, Because of this, we support the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. This proposal represents a necessary step toward restoring responsible, science-based forest management and addressing the growing threat of catastrophic wildfire across our public lands

For nearly a quarter of a century, the Roadless Rule has imposed blanket restrictions on road construction across almost 60 million acres of National Forest System lands. This rigid, one-size-fits-all policy has made it more difficult for land managers to carry out critical wildfire mitigation, restoration, and infrastructure maintenance—even in areas facing extreme fire risk or located near communities. As a result, many of these forests have become overgrown and unhealthy, fueling more severe fires that threaten lives, property, wildlife habitat, and water supplies. Since the rule was enacted, more than8 million acres of roadless forests have burned, and nearly half of all roadless acres are now classified as having a high or very high risk of wildfire. In many cases, firefighters have been unable to quickly access ignition points, delaying suppression efforts and increasing the scale and intensity of wildfires.

Even today, in what is considered the “wet National Forest – The Olympic National Forest." many in our local communities have been enduring poor air quality and other impacts from the Bear Gulch fire, While some of the fire footprint does have roads within it, much of the fire is located in areas with little to no access and wilderness areas. Much like the Roadless Rule, these limitations and prohibitions on management have allowed this fire to grow to over 8,000 acres.

Rescinding the Roadless Rule does not authorize unchecked logging or eliminate environmental safeguards, All projects must still comply with the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, and existing forest management plans. Rescinding this “one-size-fits-all" rule will restore flexibility for local land managers to consider road access where necessary to protect forests, communities, and public resources.

We urge the US Forest Service to move forward with this common-sense reform, supporting the health, safety, and resilience of our national forests and local communities.

Sincerely,

# RE: Comment on EIS of the proposed rescission to the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule - Docket No. FS-2025-0001.

SENT VIA: Regular USPS Mail, and Electronically

Dear Director,

On behalf of the Walla Walla City Council, thank you for the opportunity to comment on the initiation of an environmental impact statement (EIS) and rulemaking concerning the management of inventoried roadless areas of National Forest Service lands.

The City of Walla Walla is located in eastern Washington state and sits at the base of the Blue Mountains of the Umatilla National Forest located in southeast Washington and northeast Oregon. Within the Umatilla National Forest is the Mill Creek watershed , which flows into the Walla Walla River and ultimately the Columbia River.

The Mill Creek Watershed is a 36 square mile area at the upper end of the headwaters of Mill Creek and is the primary source of drinking water for over 35,000 residents. The watershed is closed to the public and protected through a 1918 cooperative agreement between the City of Walla Walla and the Department of Agriculture. A majority of the Mill Creek Watershed lies within the area mapped as Inventoried Roadless Areas designated by the 2001 Roadless Rule. It is the City's continued interest to protect the Mill Creek watershed as a precious source of drinking water for City residents.

The Federal Register Notice and request for public comment, published in Vol. 90, No 166 / Friday, August 29, 2025, provides a preliminary list of substantive issues and summary of expected impacts the EIS will evaluate, which are considered reasonably foreseeable social, economic, and environmental impacts of the proposed recission. Notably, not listed or summarized are the social, economic, and environmental impacts that recission of the rule may have on water quality, quantity, and seasonal flows for drinking water. The City of Walla Walla respectfully submits that those impacts are reasonably foreseeable and should be analyzed and evaluated in the proposed EIS.

The City encourages the U.S. Department of Agriculture to consider the adverse social, economic, and environmental impacts that rescinding the 2001 "Roadless Rule" may have on municipal watersheds, such as the City of Walla Walla's, which provides clean, and reliable drinking water to our residents . To this end, the City of Walla Walla is opposed to any recission or change to the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule .

![](images/6a09a2070b03aafe819d215f5aa765576a7be3f08194d158c4cdab3cb53ad400.jpg)

The August 29, 2025 Federal Register Notice states, that the proposed rule, accompanied by a draft EIS, is expected by March 2026 along with a request for additional public comments. The City of Walla Walla reserves the right to provide additional comment when the proposed rule and draft EIS are prepared. We therefore ask that the City of Walla Walla be added to the interested party list and receive further notification of additional comment periods at the appropriate time.

Notification of future actions should be sent to the following mailing address:

City of Walla Walla Attn: Elizabeth Chamberlain, City Manager 15 N. 3<sup>rd</sup> Avenue Walla Walla, WA 99362

and by email to the following address: echamberlain@wallawallawa.gov

Thank you again for the opportunity to provide comments on this matter.

Re: Docket FS-2025-0001 — Proposal to Rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule

## U.S. Department of Agriculture / U.S. Forest Service:

Washington’s national forests contain approximately 9,215,000 acres of U.S. Forest Service lands, including approximately 2,015,000 acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs), about 22% of the state’s federal forests. These IRAs include about 336,000 acres in the Mt. Baker– Snoqualmie NF, 403,000 acres in the Okanogan–Wenatchee NF, 151,000 acres in the Gifford Pinchot NF, 182,000 acres in the Colville NF, and 86,000 acres in the Olympic NF. These figures derive from the Forest Service’s own state and forest-level IRA maps and Forest Plan records.

## Ecological Risks of Opening IRAs to Road Construction and Harvest

• Aquatic resources and ESA-listed salmonids: New or reopened roads elevate fine sediment delivery, alter hydrology, and create fish-passage barriers, degrading habitat for salmon, steelhead, and bull trout, contrary to watershed recovery goals.

• Late-seral wildlife (northern spotted owl, marbled murrelet): Added road edges and associated entries fragment interior conditions; murrelet nesting habitat has already declined, roughly 20% since 1988 with increased edge exposure. Rescission would worsen fragmentation trends.

• Wide-ranging carnivores (wolverine, lynx, grizzly): Elevated road density and human access reduce secure habitat and permeability, undermining recovery efforts in the North Cascades and Northeast WA linkages.

## Management Practicality and Fiscal Prudence

The Forest Service already manages between 371,000–386,000 miles of roads nationally with about 90,000 miles across Oregon and Washington but has roughly 15% of the budget needed for maintenance of these roads. On the Okanogan–Wenatchee NF alone more than 6,000 miles lack adequate maintenance or decommissioning plans. Authorizing net new roads into currently undeveloped IRAs would deepen the backlog and divert funding from high-priority aquatic and safety repairs.

## Requested Actions

1. Retain Roadless Rule protections in Washington; do not authorize new permanent roads in IRAs without decommissioning the same miles of current undermaintained roads.

2. If site-specific access is essential for public safety or ecological restoration, restrict to reopening existing roads or temporary roads with enforceable timelines for decommissioning and full hydrologic reclamation.

3. Establish IRA-specific road density caps and secure habitat standards in known carnivore movement zones and late-seral wildlife cores.

4. Prohibit new stream crossings in key watersheds/critical habitat absent a clear, sciencebased finding of net ecological benefit; otherwise require fish-passage compliant designs and sediment-control storm-proofing.

5. Treat distance-to-road as a wildfire risk factor; apply seasonal closures/gating and

prevention programs where roads are opened.

6. Demonstrate life-cycle funding to maintain any proposed new miles without degrading performance on the legacy maintenance backlog; where funding is insufficient, deny authorizations.

I appreciate the opportunity to comment and am available to collaborate on IRA-compatible restoration that improves watershed function, fish passage, fuels in the WUI, and climate resilience without expanding the permanent road system.

Sincerely,

Brandon Austin

Forest Habitats Section Manager

Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife

# STATE OF WASHINGTON OFFICE OF GOVERNOR BOB FERGUSON

September 18, 2025

The Honorable Brooke Rollins Secretary U.S. Department of Agriculture 1400 Independence Ave. SW Washington D.C. 20250

Re: Comments on Proposed Rescission of Roadless Rule

Dear Secretary Rollins:

The Roadless Area Conservation Rule has safeguarded some of our nation’s most ecologically and culturally important landscapes for more than two decades. In Washington state, these protections sustain clean water, fish and wildlife habitat, tribal treaty and cultural resources, and an outdoor recreation economy vital to our state’s identity.

The proposal to rescind the Roadless Rule creates significant uncertainty and concern. The U.S. Forest Service has not provided a clear framework for how equivalent protections would be maintained if the rule were rescinded. Additionally, the abbreviated comment period and lack of Tribal consultation is concerning. Without clarity, our state is left questioning how investments in salmon recovery, protection of Tribal treaty rights, critical values, ecological integrity, climate resilience, cultural resources, and recreation will be secured in the long term.

Any reconsideration of the Roadless Rule must be accompanied by a transparent plan that demonstrates how these landscapes will continue to be protected. Absent such assurances, rescission risks undermining stability, predictability, and trust that communities, Tribes, and states rely upon.

Washington urges the Department of Agriculture to either retain the Roadless Rule or clearly articulate how its rescission will not compromise the values and protections it has long provided.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Sincerely,

# WISCONSIN LEGISLATURE

# P.O. BOX 8952 • MADISON, WI 53708

## Hello,

Today, we are writing in opposition to the proposed rollback of the 2001 Roadless Rule. This rule has prevented construction of roads and other developments on millions of acres of public land for the past 25 years. The USDA’s plan would leave 44.7 million acres vulnerable. For Wisconsinites, this means a treasured national forest, Chequamegon-Nicolet, would be impacted.

This rule was enacted under the Bush Administration after hundreds of public meetings and 1.6 million public comments with overwhelming support for roadless protections.

The National Forest System already contains twice as many miles of roads as the U.S. Interstate Highway System and expanding the network will only increase wildlife risk as approximately 85% of wildfires are caused by human activity and 90% ignite within half a mile of a road.

According to the USDA’s own website, National Forests face threats from drought, mortality, insect-borne disease, and wildfire. Active management of these areas is a valid concern for wildfire risk, and should be taken seriously. However, even under the roadless rule, habitat restoration and wildfire prevention projects are still able to be built, as are temporary roads for emergency purposes.

Our National Forests also serve as important watershed areas, and more than sixty million Americans depend on them for their drinking water. A healthy water table is the most important tool we have in staving off wildfire, drought, and human suffering due to climate change.

Our National Forests also grant access to millions of acres for hunting, fishing, camping and other recreational activities. An annual forest pass for Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest in Wisconsin for example, costs thirty dollars and a day pass cost just five dollars. We want people to be able to visit and appreciate these lands at a cost that is accessible to every American. If we open our lands to private interests, visitors and their families will have to compete with the deep pockets of corporate America, driving prices upward and pricing lower-income families out.

A full repeal of the Roadless Rule might provide short term benefits for private interests, but will do long term damage to these vital ecosystems that the public fought to be maintained 25 years ago. We ask that you uphold the Roadless Rule and prioritize the rights of the general public over those of corporate interests.

In Service,

RE: USDA-FS-2025-0001 Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement – Roadless Area Conservation.

Dear Director Kinder:

On behalf of the Wyoming State Forestry Division (WSFD), we respectfully submit comments on the Notice of Intent (NOI) to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) published in the Federal Register on August 29, 2025 (Vol. 90, No. 166).

We are supportive and fully endorse the current proposal to return management discretion of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) to local land management planning processes. Wyoming's forests face unique challenges, including extensive insect and disease outbreaks, diverse forest types, and varying community needs that cannot be effectively addressed under a single national framework. Local planning, grounded in the National Forest Management Act and informed by stakeholder input, provides the flexibility needed to balance conservation with active management.

Wyoming has a long history of legal contests trying to stop the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (RACR) filing suit in Federal Court in 2001 and 2007. The cases concluded in 2012 after the Supreme Court denied certiorari. Wyoming's national forests have numerous areas incorrectly identified as "roadless" contained in IRAs. The current RACR does not give local forest managers the flexibility to address forest management needs, protect critical watersheds and old growth forests, proactively manage for fire, noxious/invasive weeds, and insect and disease outbreaks.

In these comments, WSFD addresses key concerns, provides recommendations, and poses questions for consideration as a partnering land management agency.

Wyoming contains portions of two U.S. Forest Service Regions with approximately 9.2 million acres of National Forest and Grasslands. The Rocky Mountain Region (Region 2) manages the Black Hills, Bighorn, Shoshone, and Medicine Bow-Routt National Forests and the Thunder Basin National Grassland. The Intermountain Region (Region 4) manages the Bridger-Teton, Uinta-Wasatch-Cache, Caribou-Targhee, and Ashley National Forests. Within Wyoming's National Forests, approximately 3 million acres are designated as Wilderness and an additional 3.2 million acres are managed as IRAs. This means that 67% of the National Forest and Grasslands are set aside for preservation that includes severe limitations on active management.

Many of Wyoming's current National Forest Land Management Plans were developed while the 2001 RACR was enjoined in Wyoming District Court. In 2011 the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals lifted theWyoming District court injunction and put the 2001 RACR back into effect. Out of the eight National Forests and one National Grassland, only two National Forests, the Shoshone and Ashley National Forests, have Land Management Plans that include and recognize the 2001 RACR IRAs

The Black Hills and Bridger-Teton National Forests are currently in the beginning stages of Land Management Plan revisions and are already set to address roadless area conservation needs through the locally led, transparent processes required by the 2012 Planning Rule. The proposed RACR rescission would allow an opportunity to revisit IRA designations at the local level while collaborative Land Management Plan revisions are ongoing

While WSFD acknowledges the intent of this NOI, we offer several recommendations to ensure that implementation of the new direction is place-based, durable across future administrations, and consistent with statutory and regulatory frameworks.

## 1. Localized Land Management is Essential

The 2001 RACR imposed a one-size-fits-all approach that did not reflect Wyoming's diverse ecological or community needs. The 2001 RACR left Wyoming's government, land management agencies, and citizens out of the decisions that impacted Wyoming the most. As the Honorable US District Judge Clarence Brimmer was quoted saying in reference to why he allowed the enjoining of 2001 RACR that was imposed on Wyoming, “I feel we have to play the cards face up." Even Wyoming's Wilderness areas were designated through a collaborative process. Forest planning under the 2012 Planning Rule ensures that roadless considerations are integrated into broader land management objectives, including timber, recreation, grazing, fuels reduction, and watershed protection

## Recommendation:

The Forest Service should ensure that IRA decisions are made through the 2012 Planning Rule process, led by Forest Supervisors, with states and local governments engaged as cooperating agencies. The 2012 Planning Rule is newer than the 2001 RACRitself and provides a modernized approach that ensures national forests are managed to a desired condition that has input from all local, state, and national stakeholders.

## 2. Inaccurate IRA Mapping and Risks to Forest Health Must be Addressed

As is often the case with national rules and mandates, Wyoming's National Forests contain known inaccuracies in IRA mapping, including areas with existing roads (such as a State Highway or County roads) or other historic access routes that were nonetheless designated as "roadless." The RACR utilized outdated maps that are currently over four decades old and irrelevant. For example, the Bighorn National Forest's IRA contains 390 miles of system roads. It is 2025 and WSFD insists Wyoming's National Forests manage with up-to-date science and mapping to rightly implement management objectives and monitoring. The Forest Service utilizes highly technical drones that provide timely data to make on-the ground management decisions and yet continues to accept outdated, improper mapping for RACR

Many of Wyoming's IRAs are in high-risk wildfire zones that include municipal watersheds (Bighorn National Forest IRAs contain 7 municipalities water sources). Specifically, 2.1 million acres (66%) of Wyoming's IRAs are in the designated Forest Health and Fuels Emergency Lands (FHFEL). These inaccuracies prevent managers from addressing pressing forest health and wildfire concerns

## Recommendation:

The decision should establish a process for reviewing and correcting mapping errors at the local level, specifically honoring designated roadless areas within Wyoming's Land Management Plans. Wyoming does not need a top-down national US Forest Service rule to designate roadless areas, as our Land Management Plans established a balanced approach for conservation, forest management, and multiple use through a collaborative process. Requiring National Forest supervisors and regional leadership to go through an onerous corrections process is a waste of taxpayer time, that could be better spent focused on implementing Land Management Plans

## 3. A Stepwise Framework for Roadless Evaluation

WSFD supports a structured process for evaluating roadless areas during Land Management Plan revisions, using the Wilderness Evaluation framework. Through an evaluation process already in place, areas fit for roadless area conservation can also be evaluated

## Recommendation:

The Forest Service should continue to utilize the wilderness framework while also including an evaluation of Inventoried Roadless Areas through land management planning revisions. For example, in Chapter 3 of the Bighorn National Forest Plan, roadless areas are evaluated and designated through this framework. This structured process is completed nationwide, and ensures each step occurs within the context of local forest Land Management Plan revisions.

## Recommended Framework:

• Step 1 — Inventory: Define metrics to trigger review of potential IRA designation.

• Step 2 – Evaluation: Assess whether areas meet IRA characteristics (absence of roads, infeasible access, natural conditions).

• Step 3 – Comment and Decision: Present findings in a draft plan/EIS with no fewer than 90 days for public review

• Step 4 – Recommendation: Determine whether areas should be managed as roadless or for other management objectives consistent with the 2012 Planning Rule.

## 4. Impacts: Loss of Opportunities to Manage Forests Properly

Due to the 2001 RACR, 3.2 million acres of Wyoming National Forest lands have been excluded from important management opportunities. It is impossible to holistically manage for a municipal watershed when portions (in some cases in Wyoming, over two-thirds) of the watershed is in designated IRA. There are lost opportunities to effectively mitigate wildfire and manage forests' health and resilience, leaving multiple municipal watersheds and Wyoming's communities at risk of losing clean drinking water. It is also very difficult to mitigate postwildfire impacts in municipal watersheds located within IRAs, as no categorical exclusion exists to do so. Wyoming communities deserve better and necessitate the opportunity to act effectively and efficiently in recovering our water sources after a devastating wildfire.

Another crucial loss is the opportunity to rehabilitate forested lands for wildlife habitat needs Wyoming is facing a steady decline in mule deer populations, and many of Wyoming's IRAs are within areas prioritized to improve wildlife habitat for multiple big game species. After analyzing Wyoming's Terrestrial Restoration Habitat Priority Areas, you will find that roughly 78% or 2.6 million acres of these areas are found in designated IRAs. These areas are defined by 3 metrics: 1) areas that need to be protected or conserved to maintain viable healthy populations of terrestrial and aquatic wildlife for the present and future, 2) areas where there is a high potential in the 5 years after the Statewide Habitat Plan is published to successfully address wildlife habitat issues by improving, enhancing, or restoring wildlife habitats, and 3) migration corridors and fish passages that need to be protected or enhanced to maintain or improve connectivity. Without the flexibility needed to manage these landscapes, creating and maintaining critical habitat for species that need early seral forests (which can provide necessary forage), such as mule deer, becomes increasingly challenging if not impossible.

We would be remiss not to bring up that the 2001 RACR has led to years of lost opportunities to protect critical old growth forests as well as Whitebark Pine, a threatened tree species native to Wyoming. It is important to have the flexibility to manage areas in order to maintain and care for old growth areas as well as Whitebark Pine trees. Choosing the management method of “leave it alone" isn't always the best management strategy to maintain the integrity and protect these areas or species. The US Forest Service/WSFD aerial survey observations from 2001 - 2024 in Wyoming's IRAs totaled 1,207,322 acres of tree mortality attributed to insects and diseases. Additionally, 814,398 acres within Wyoming IRAs are at risk of a 25% loss in standing live basal area trees greater than 1" DBH in the next 15 years. This means that over 2 million acres of Wyoming's IRAs (66%) have already been affected or will be affected by insect and disease outbreaks due to lack of management and proves the "leave it alone" method does not regularly achieve desired condition objectives.

We have witnessed an overwhelming increase in Wyoming's dead and dying forests (millions upon millions of acres) over the last two decades due to severe management limitations.

Because of these limitations, we have watched our forests die and will have to watch these unhealthy forests burn up over the next several decades. Having the ability to adapt management strategies within 3.2 million acres of Wyoming's IRA would be a viable solution to prevent future losses, which can be revisited if the 2001 RACR is rescinded

## Recommendation:

Allow locally led management decisions that align with current Land Management Plans. Where opportunities have been lost, new approaches can be adopted to better manage forests toward desired conditions. Flexibility fosters innovation and enables the modern solutions necessary to meet today's forest management challenges.

## 5. Alignment with National Policy and Executive Orders

Recent Executive Orders highlight the importance of flexibility, deregulation, and active forest management:

Executive Order 14192 – Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation

Executive Order 14225 – Immediate Expansion of American Timber Production

• Executive Order 14154 – Unleashing American Energy

Secretary's Memorandum 1078-006 – Increasing Timber Production and Designating an Emergency Situation on National Forest System Lands

Wyoming Executive Order:

• Executive Order 2025-04 - Increase of Active Forest Management in Wyoming

Retaining outdated IRA restrictions directly conflicts with these priorities and limits the Forest Service's ability to fulfill its multiple-use mandate.

## Recommendation:

The decision should explicitly recognize the need to balance conservation with timber, energy, and community uses, consistent with these Executive Orders and with the statutory obligations of the National Forest Management Act.

## 6. State-Specific Designated Inventoried Roadless Rule Areas

When the 2001 RACR was put into effect, an alternative option was provided for states.

“§ 294.12 State petitions

The Governor of any State or territory that contains National Forest System lands may petition the Secretary of Agriculture to promulgate regulations establishing management requirements for all or any portion of National Forest System inventoried roadless areas within that State or territory. Any such petition must be submitted to the Secretary of Agriculture not later than November 13, 2006."

If the US Forest Service rescinds the 2001 RACR, there should be similar opportunities for states to create their own IRAs. WSFD supports reopening the opportunity for state-specific IRAs, as successfully implemented in Colorado and Idaho. Such rules provide durability,

accountability, and flexibility, ensuring decisions reflect local conditions and stakeholder priorities.

## Recommendation:

The Forest Service should allow states to pursue state-specific rules and provide assurance that these rules remain durable across administrations, balancing ecological, social, and economic considerations. The date for such a petition has been expired for almost 9 years, and we recommend reopening the opportunity to petition as an appropriate alternative for states postrule rescission.

## 7. Utilizing Cooperating Agencies Will Lead to Better Results

WSFD believes that cooperating agencies must be fully engaged in the EIS process. Our involvement brings essential data, local expertise, and technical guidance that will lead to effective, durable outcomes. Inventoried roadless areas have already been collaboratively identified in existing Land Management Plans, and we remain committed to their continued management. Collaborative input is vital, as it ensures areas are accurately identified with all stakeholders' priorities in mind.

We ask the US Forest Service to consider the following questions:

• How will ongoing Land Management Plan revisions (e.g., Black Hills and Bridger-Teton) be aligned with the proposed rescission process?

• In the case of rescission, how will special designations be utilized for areas that were formerly IRAs?

• How will risks to municipal watersheds be prioritized within the EIS?

How will the Forest Service ensure that future inventoried roadless area evaluation processes are transparent and accessible to the public?

Will the Forest Service commit to providing states with the alternative option to pursue state-specific roadless area conservation rules?

• How will these rules be protected from being reopened with each administrative change?

## Recommendation:

The US Forest Service should respect existing protections and partnerships in Wyoming through the inclusion of Wyoming's cooperating agencies as much as possible through the EIS process and by deferring IRA decisions to collaborative, forest-level planning processes.

## Conclusion

The Wyoming State Forestry Division strongly supports returning IRA identification and management decisions to the local National Forest level under the 2012 Planning Rule

Wyoming's forests already operate under robust conservation protections and Land Management Plans that incorporate stakeholder input. National, one-size-fits-all restrictions are unnecessary, duplicative, and harmful to the active management needed to address wildfire, insects, disease, and other forest health challenges

We respectfully request the US Forest Service adopt the recommendations outlined in this letter and ensure that Wyoming remains an active partner throughout the EIS process

Thank you for the opportunity to comment and for your continued partnership.

Sincerely,

RE: Wyoming Dept. of Environmental Quality Comments - Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands (90 FR 42179)

Dear Mr. Kinder,

On behalf of the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality (WDEQ), we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed recission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (36 FR 3244, 36 CFR Subpart B (2001)).

It is important to note that WDEQ has been delegated primacy over multiple programs by the federal government including water, air, solid and hazardous waste, abandoned mine land reclamation, uranium mining and processing, and coal mining.

WDEQ supports the proper management of national forests, including the implementation of best management practices for activities such as road construction and timber harvesting to support both forest health and improved water quality. The proposed rule recission still requires site-specific impacts comply with applicable state and federal regulations, including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Clean Air Act (CAA), and Clean Water Act (CWA). As such, WDEQ will work with future project proponents to ensure that necessary permits are obtained, and applicable water and air quality standards are met.

WDEQ encourages the US Department of Agriculture to address various state and local authorities in the forthcoming EIS, including state primacy over natural resources such as air and water. Additionally, the requirement for future projects to acquire appropriate permits from state and local authorities should be addressed including National Pollutant Discharge System (NPDES) permits for discharges into surface waters, New Source Review (NSR) permits for air emissions, and other state specific requirements such as Wyoming’s regulations for fugitive dust control.

If you have any questions or need additional information, please feel free to contact Keith Guille at 307-777-6105 or keith.guille@wyo.gov.

Sincerely,

Re: Notice of Intent to prepare an environmental impact statement: Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands. 90 FR 42179: Docket No. FS-2025-16581

Dear Director Kinder,

I appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Notice of Intent (NOI) to prepare an environmental impact statement and rulemaking concerning the proposed rule to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule). I submit the following comments regarding the aforementioned Federal Register notice.

Wyoming fully supports efforts by the USDA to review the current 2001 Roadless Rule and return management of the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) Administered Lands back to local "Forest-level land management planning." This shift is crucial for several reasons, as forest-level local management offers a more nuanced and effective approach to land stewardship.

It is Wyoming's firm belief and experience that local management plans are inherently more responsive to the specific ecological, economic, and social conditions of individual forests. Unlike a broad, one-sizefits-all federal rule, local planning allows for tailored solutions that consider the unique biodiversity, wildlife, habitat, water resources, timber potential, recreational uses, and cultural heritage of each area. This localized approach fosters greater collaboration with state and local agencies, local communities, tribal governments, and stakeholders who possess invaluable on-the-ground knowledge and a vested interest in the long-term health of their surrounding forests. This will also guarantee the planning process recognizes the local authority granted to state agencies for managing wildlife, air quality, water rights, and water quality; thus ensuring state agencies manage the resources they are legally mandated to oversee.

Additionally, returning management to the forest-level can streamline decision-making processes, reducing bureaucratic hurdles and allowing for quicker adaptation to changing environmental conditions or emerging challenges. This includes the ability to implement more effective wildfire prevention and mitigation strategies, address insect and disease outbreaks promptly, and manage all resources in a way that benefits local economies and supports healthy forest management.

During the ongoing review process, I strongly advocate for and acknowledge the clear benefits of localized management and decision-making and the USDA's efforts for a thorough analysis, involving adequate opportunity for public comment and consultation with the state cooperating agencies. This approach will ensure not only the immediate effectiveness but also the long-term durability, resilience, and legal defensibility of the planning process, thereby safeguarding both ecological integrity and the public interest for years to come.

Finally, as mentioned above, Wyoming looks forward to early engagement in the NEPA process, exercising its rights and expertise as a cooperating agency. This early engagement will help the USDA develop strong language and alternatives that support a localized approach to forest management. In turn, this will help also ensure timely and durable, long-term planning for USFS-administered land in Wyoming.

Wyoming's support for this review is rooted in the belief that local expertise and engagement are paramount to achieving balanced and sustainable management of national forest lands. It represents a commitment to empowering those closest to the land to make informed decisions that reflect sound and sustainable management practices that support Wyoming and our local communities.

Thank you for considering Wyoming's perspective as the USDA moves forward in reviewing and evaluating the 2001 Roadless Rule. USDA should anticipate receiving comments from the following State of Wyoming agencies: Wyoming Department of Agriculture, Wyoming Game and Fish Department, Wyoming State Forestry Department, Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality, Wyoming State Parks and Cultural Resources. My office, along with Wyoming's state agencies, look forward to working with the USDA in a meaningful collaborative and cooperative manner.

If you have any questions or concerns please contact, Linda Cope, Senior Policy Advisor, at 307-777- 7942 or linda.cope3@wyo.gov

Sincerely, MansFurle

Mark Gordon

Governor of Wyoming

RE: USDA-FS-2025-0001 Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement – Roadless Area Conservation.

Dear Director Kinder:

On behalf of the Wyoming State Forestry Division (WSFD), we respectfully submit comments on the Notice of Intent (NOI) to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) published in the Federal Register on August 29, 2025 (Vol. 90, No. 166).

We are supportive and fully endorse the current proposal to return management discretion of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) to local land management planning processes. Wyoming's forests face unique challenges, including extensive insect and disease outbreaks, diverse forest types, and varying community needs that cannot be effectively addressed under a single national framework. Local planning, grounded in the National Forest Management Act and informed by stakeholder input, provides the flexibility needed to balance conservation with active management.

Wyoming has a long history of legal contests trying to stop the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (RACR) filing suit in Federal Court in 2001 and 2007. The cases concluded in 2012 after the Supreme Court denied certiorari. Wyoming's national forests have numerous areas incorrectly identified as "roadless" contained in IRAs. The current RACR does not give local forest managers the flexibility to address forest management needs, protect critical watersheds and old growth forests, proactively manage for fire, noxious/invasive weeds, and insect and disease outbreaks.

In these comments, WSFD addresses key concerns, provides recommendations, and poses questions for consideration as a partnering land management agency.

Wyoming contains portions of two U.S. Forest Service Regions with approximately 9.2 million acres of National Forest and Grasslands. The Rocky Mountain Region (Region 2) manages the Black Hills, Bighorn, Shoshone, and Medicine Bow-Routt National Forests and the Thunder Basin National Grassland. The Intermountain Region (Region 4) manages the Bridger-Teton, Uinta-Wasatch-Cache, Caribou-Targhee, and Ashley National Forests. Within Wyoming's National Forests, approximately 3 million acres are designated as Wilderness and an additional 3.2 million acres are managed as IRAs. This means that 67% of the National Forest and Grasslands are set aside for preservation that includes severe limitations on active management.

Many of Wyoming's current National Forest Land Management Plans were developed while the 2001 RACR was enjoined in Wyoming District Court. In 2011 the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals lifted theWyoming District court injunction and put the 2001 RACR back into effect Out of the eight National Forests and one National Grassland, only two National Forests, the Shoshone and Ashley National Forests, have Land Management Plans that include and recognize the 2001 RACR IRAs

The Black Hills and Bridger-Teton National Forests are currently in the beginning stages of Land Management Plan revisions and are already set to address roadless area conservation needs through the locally led, transparent processes required by the 2012 Planning Rule. The proposed RACR rescission would allow an opportunity to revisit IRA designations at the local level while collaborative Land Management Plan revisions are ongoing

While WSFD acknowledges the intent of this NOI, we offer several recommendations to ensure that implementation of the new direction is place-based, durable across future administrations, and consistent with statutory and regulatory frameworks.

## 1. Localized Land Management is Essential

The 2001 RACR imposed a one-size-fits-all approach that did not reflect Wyoming's diverse ecological or community needs. The 2001 RACR left Wyoming's government, land management agencies, and citizens out of the decisions that impacted Wyoming the most. As the Honorable US District Judge Clarence Brimmer was quoted saying in reference to why he allowed the enjoining of 2001 RACR that was imposed on Wyoming, “I feel we have to play the cards face up." Even Wyoming's Wilderness areas were designated through a collaborative process. Forest planning under the 2012 Planning Rule ensures that roadless considerations are integrated into broader land management objectives, including timber, recreation, grazing, fuels reduction, and watershed protection

## Recommendation:

The Forest Service should ensure that IRA decisions are made through the 2012 Planning Rule process, led by Forest Supervisors, with states and local governments engaged as cooperating agencies. The 2012 Planning Rule is newer than the 2001 RACRitself and provides a modernized approach that ensures national forests are managed to a desired condition that has input from all local, state, and national stakeholders.

## 2. Inaccurate IRA Mapping and Risks to Forest Health Must be Addressed

As is often the case with national rules and mandates, Wyoming's National Forests contain known inaccuracies in IRA mapping, including areas with existing roads (such as a State Highway or County roads) or other historic access routes that were nonetheless designated as "roadless." The RACR utilized outdated maps that are currently over four decades old and irrelevant. For example, the Bighorn National Forest's IRA contains 390 miles of system roads. It is 2025 and WSFD insists Wyoming's National Forests manage with up-to-date science and mapping to rightly implement management objectives and monitoring. The Forest Service utilizes highly technical drones that provide timely data to make on-the ground management decisions and yet continues to accept outdated, improper mapping for RACR

Many of Wyoming's IRAs are in high-risk wildfire zones that include municipal watersheds (Bighorn National Forest IRAs contain 7 municipalities water sources). Specifically, 2.1 million acres (66%) of Wyoming's IRAs are in the designated Forest Health and Fuels Emergency Lands (FHFEL). These inaccuracies prevent managers from addressing pressing forest health and wildfire concerns

## Recommendation:

The decision should establish a process for reviewing and correcting mapping errors at the local level, specifically honoring designated roadless areas within Wyoming's Land Management Plans. Wyoming does not need a top-down national US Forest Service rule to designate roadless areas, as our Land Management Plans established a balanced approach for conservation, forest management, and multiple use through a collaborative process. RequiringNational Forest supervisors and regional leadership to go through an onerous corrections process is a waste of taxpayer time, that could be better spent focused on implementing Land Management Plans

## 3. A Stepwise Framework for Roadless Evaluation

WSFD supports a structured process for evaluating roadless areas during Land Management Plan revisions, using the Wilderness Evaluation framework. Through an evaluation process already in place, areas fit for roadless area conservation can also be evaluated

## Recommendation:

The Forest Service should continue to utilize the wilderness framework while also including an evaluation of Inventoried Roadless Areas through land management planning revisions. For example, in Chapter 3 of the Bighorn National Forest Plan, roadless areas are evaluated and designated through this framework. This structured process is completed nationwide, and ensures each step occurs within the context of local forest Land Management Plan revisions.

## Recommended Framework:

• Step 1 — Inventory: Define metrics to trigger review of potential IRA designation.

• Step 2 – Evaluation: Assess whether areas meet IRA characteristics (absence of roads, infeasible access, natural conditions).

• Step 3 – Comment and Decision: Present findings in a draft plan/EIS with no fewer than 90 days for public review

• Step 4 – Recommendation: Determine whether areas should be managed as roadless or for other management objectives consistent with the 2012 Planning Rule.

## 4. Impacts: Loss of Opportunities to Manage Forests Properly

Due to the 2001 RACR, 3.2 million acres of Wyoming National Forest lands have been excluded from important management opportunities. It is impossible to holistically manage for a municipal watershed when portions (in some cases in Wyoming, over two-thirds) of the watershed is in designated IRA. There are lost opportunities to effectively mitigate wildfire and manage forests' health and resilience, leaving multiple municipal watersheds and Wyoming's communities at risk of losing clean drinking water. It is also very difficult to mitigate postwildfire impacts in municipal watersheds located within IRAs, as no categorical exclusion exists to do so. Wyoming communities deserve better and necessitate the opportunity to act effectively and efficiently in recovering our water sources after a devastating wildfire.

Another crucial loss is the opportunity to rehabilitate forested lands for wildlife habitat needs Wyoming is facing a steady decline in mule deer populations, and many of Wyoming's IRAs are within areas prioritized to improve wildlife habitat for multiple big game species. After analyzing Wyoming's Terrestrial Restoration Habitat Priority Areas, you will find that roughly 78% or 2.6 million acres of these areas are found in designated IRAs. These areas are defined by 3 metrics: 1) areas that need to be protected or conserved to maintain viable healthy populations of terrestrial and aquatic wildlife for the present and future, 2) areas where there is a high potential in the 5 years after the Statewide Habitat Plan is published to successfully address wildlife habitat issues by improving, enhancing, or restoring wildlife habitats, and 3) migration corridors and fish passages that need to be protected or enhanced to maintain or improve connectivity. Without the flexibility needed to manage these landscapes, creating and maintaining critical habitat for species that need early seral forests (which can provide necessary forage), such as mule deer, becomes increasingly challenging if not impossible.

We would be remiss not to bring up that the 2001 RACR has led to years of lost opportunities to protect critical old growth forests as well as Whitebark Pine, a threatened tree species native to Wyoming. It is important to have the flexibility to manage areas in order to maintain and care for old growth areas as well as Whitebark Pine trees. Choosing the management method of “leave it alone" isn't always the best management strategy to maintain the integrity and protect these areas or species. The US Forest Service/WSFD aerial survey observations from 2001 - 2024 in Wyoming's IRAs totaled 1,207,322 acres of tree mortality attributed to insects and diseases. Additionally, 814,398 acres within Wyoming IRAs are at risk of a 25% loss in standing live basal area trees greater than 1" DBH in the next 15 years. This means that over 2 million acres of Wyoming's IRAs (66%) have already been affected or will be affected by insect and disease outbreaks due to lack of management and proves the "leave it alone" method does not regularly achieve desired condition objectives.

We have witnessed an overwhelming increase in Wyoming's dead and dying forests (millions upon millions of acres) over the last two decades due to severe management limitations.

Because of these limitations, we have watched our forests die and will have to watch these unhealthy forests burn up over the next several decades. Having the ability to adapt management strategies within 3.2 million acres of Wyoming's IRA would be a viable solution to prevent future losses, which can be revisited if the 2001 RACR is rescinded

## Recommendation:

Allow locally led management decisions that align with current Land Management Plans. Where opportunities have been lost, new approaches can be adopted to better manage forests toward desired conditions. Flexibility fosters innovation and enables the modern solutions necessary to meet today's forest management challenges.

## 5. Alignment with National Policy and Executive Orders

Recent Executive Orders highlight the importance of flexibility, deregulation, and active forest management:

Executive Order 14192 – Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation

Executive Order 14225 – Immediate Expansion of American Timber Production

• Executive Order 14154 – Unleashing American Energy

Secretary's Memorandum 1078-006 – Increasing Timber Production and Designating an Emergency Situation on National Forest System Lands

Wyoming Executive Order:

• Executive Order 2025-04 - Increase of Active Forest Management in Wyoming

Retaining outdated IRA restrictions directly conflicts with these priorities and limits the Forest Service's ability to fulfill its multiple-use mandate.

## Recommendation:

The decision should explicitly recognize the need to balance conservation with timber, energy, and community uses, consistent with these Executive Orders and with the statutory obligations of the National Forest Management Act.

## 6. State-Specific Designated Inventoried Roadless Rule Areas

When the 2001 RACR was put into effect, an alternative option was provided for states.

“§ 294.12 State petitions

The Governor of any State or territory that contains National Forest System lands may petition the Secretary of Agriculture to promulgate regulations establishing management requirements for all or any portion of National Forest System inventoried roadless areas within that State or territory. Any such petition must be submitted to the Secretary of Agriculture not later than November 13, 2006."

If the US Forest Service rescinds the 2001 RACR, there should be similar opportunities for states to create their own IRAs. WSFD supports reopening the opportunity for state-specific IRAs, as successfully implemented in Colorado and Idaho. Such rules provide durability,

accountability, and flexibility, ensuring decisions reflect local conditions and stakeholder priorities.

## Recommendation:

The Forest Service should allow states to pursue state-specific rules and provide assurance that these rules remain durable across administrations, balancing ecological, social, and economic considerations. The date for such a petition has been expired for almost 9 years, and we recommend reopening the opportunity to petition as an appropriate alternative for states postrule rescission.

## 7. Utilizing Cooperating Agencies Will Lead to Better Results

WSFD believes that cooperating agencies must be fully engaged in the EIS process. Our involvement brings essential data, local expertise, and technical guidance that will lead to effective, durable outcomes. Inventoried roadless areas have already been collaboratively identified in existing Land Management Plans, and we remain committed to their continued management. Collaborative input is vital, as it ensures areas are accurately identified with all stakeholders' priorities in mind.

We ask the US Forest Service to consider the following questions:

• How will ongoing Land Management Plan revisions (e.g., Black Hills and Bridger-Teton) be aligned with the proposed rescission process?

• In the case of rescission, how will special designations be utilized for areas that were formerly IRAs?

• How will risks to municipal watersheds be prioritized within the EIS?

How will the Forest Service ensure that future inventoried roadless area evaluation processes are transparent and accessible to the public?

Will the Forest Service commit to providing states with the alternative option to pursue state-specific roadless area conservation rules?

• How will these rules be protected from being reopened with each administrative change?

## Recommendation:

The US Forest Service should respect existing protections and partnerships in Wyoming through the inclusion of Wyoming's cooperating agencies as much as possible through the EIS process and by deferring IRA decisions to collaborative, forest-level planning processes.

## Conclusion

The Wyoming State Forestry Division strongly supports returning IRA identification and management decisions to the local National Forest level under the 2012 Planning Rule

Wyoming's forests already operate under robust conservation protections and Land Management Plans that incorporate stakeholder input. National, one-size-fits-all restrictions are unnecessary, duplicative, and harmful to the active management needed to address wildfire, insects, disease, and other forest health challenges

We respectfully request the US Forest Service adopt the recommendations outlined in this letter and ensure that Wyoming remains an active partner throughout the EIS process

Thank you for the opportunity to comment and for your continued partnership.

Sincerely,
