# SARATOGA-ENCAMPMENT-RAWLINS CONSERVATION DISTRICT

September 25, 2025

Brad Kinder Acting Director, Ecosystem Management Coordination 201 14th Street SW Mailstop 1108 Washington, DC 20250-1124

Submitted Via: eplanning.blm.gov

RE: Notice of Intent to prepare an environmental impact statement – Roadless Area Conservation: Docket number FS-2025-0001

Dear Acting Director Kinder:

The Saratoga-Encampment-Rawlins Conservation District (SER CD or District), a local government entity with special expertise appreciates the opportunity to comment on the United States Department of Agriculture, United States Forest Service (USFS or Forest Service) Notice of Intent to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) concerning the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule) on National Forest System Lands.

## INTEREST JUSTIFICATION

SER CD’s comments are specific to our mission: “develop and direct programs to promote long-term conservation and enhancement of our natural resources while contributing to the economic stability of the district and its residents.” The Wyoming State Legislature passed an enabling act in March of 1941 to establish conservation districts in Wyoming. The law clearly states that conservation districts are legal governmental subdivisions of the state of Wyoming. Wyoming conservation districts have state statutory authority related to the conservation of soil and water resources, control and prevention of erosion, conservation, development, utilization and disposal of water, to stabilize the ranching or farming industry; preserve natural resources, protect the tax base, control floods, preserve wildlife, protect the public lands and protect and promote the health, safety and general welfare of the people of the State.<sup>1</sup>

Conservation districts are the only local government charged, specifically by state statute, with natural resource management. Each conservation district is governed by a board of five locally elected supervisors who serve without pay. District supervisors serve as the grass roots representatives of private landowners and the general public, providing leadership and direction in natural resource conservation programs. As the Roadless Rule has impacts on the conservation of our natural resources and the stability of the district and residents, we believe it is important you continue to inform us of future planning and decisions regarding docket number FS-2025-0001.

One of conservation districts’ greatest strengths is that we lead and support efforts and activities that are voluntary, locally-led, and incentive-based. We are leaders that help the public land managers get projects on the ground to maintain functioning, productive ecosystems. We have the structure to bring many partners to the table and leverage funds in a way that ecosystems and communities benefit. History has shown that locally led conservation is one of the most effective ways to help landowners and communities achieve their conservation goals.

Wyoming Conservation Districts are actively engaged in the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) processes to carry out their authorities as authorized by Wyoming statutes as it states:

When representing a conservation district as a cooperating agency in matters related to the National Environmental Policy Act and in federal land use planning, implementation and management actions, supervisors of a conservation district shall be deemed to have special expertise on all subject matters for which they have statutory responsibility as provided in W.S. 11-16-122 including but not limited to all subject matters directly or indirectly related to stabilization of the agriculture industry, protection of natural resources including but not limited to data and information, conservation of soil and water resources, control and prevention of soil erosion, flood prevention or the conservation, development, utilization and disposal of water within the district. Wyo. Stat. § 11-16-135.

Thus, Wyoming statutes clearly provide conservation districts the special expertise to act as a “cooperating agency” in the NEPA process.

The SER CD has partnered with planning and vegetation management projects on the Medicine Bow National Forest (Med Bow NF) for decades. The Record of Decision date for the current Med Bow NF plan was 12/29/2003. The Med Bow NF began the 2003 forest plan revision in 1999, prior to the adoption of the Roadless Rule. According to the FEIS (p 53), the Forest Service followed the planning process then in place but acknowledged the “uncertainty with the roadless issue” and conceded that “If the Roadless Rule goes into effect and is implemented it will override any agency policy and any management direction in this Plan.”

The cooperation to provide a working relationship during the implementation of the 2003 Med Bow NF Land and Resource Management Plan (Med Bow Plan) between the Forest Service, Medicine Bow-Routt National Forests and Thunder Basin National Grassland and the Southeastern Wyoming Conservation Districts was formalized in the recently reauthorized 2023 Memorandum of Understanding. The SER CD was a cooperating agency during the forest land management planning process and has continued with active participation during its ongoing implementation.

The Long Range Land Use and Natural Resource Management Plan for SER CD 2022-2026 (SER CD NRM Plan)<sup>2</sup> includes an extensive list of policy statements which are the basis for our comments. The SER CD NRM Plan was developed, open for public comment, adopted by the SER CD Board of Supervisors, and filed with the Carbon County Clerk. A few of the general expectation policy statements for any NEPA EIS process include:

Policy Expectations #3: Federal agencies shall conduct a consistency review with the Saratoga-Encampment-Rawlins Conservation District Long Range Land Use and Natural Resource Management Plan for every proposed National Environmental Policy Act decision an agency makes that may affect the District, the natural resources within the district, or its residents.

Policy Expectations #13: Saratoga-Encampment-Rawlins Conservation District’s special expertise is acknowledged regarding the natural resources as these policies are a key factor in proposed decisions.

Policy Expectations #14: Cooperation and open communication between federal agencies and Saratoga-Encampment-Rawlins Conservation District is achieved when assessing the effects of proposed federal actions within the district.

Policy Expectations #29: When determining the effects of any proposed action, those effects should be reasonably foreseeable and have a reasonably close causal relationship to the proposed action, including those effects that occur at the same time and place as the proposed action or alternatives and may include effects that are later in time or farther removed in distance from the proposed action or alternatives.

Policy Expectations #28: An "effect" when conducting a National Environmental Policy Act analysis should not be considered "significant" if the effect is remote in time, geographically remote, or the result of a lengthy causal chain.

## Specific Comments and Identified Impacts

1. The SER CD supports USFS’s efforts to rescind the Roadless Rule. We agree that many things have changed since the inception of the Roadless Rule. Forest health, wildland urban interface, forest fuel-loads, and recreation use conditions have and will continue to change over time. We agree that managing inventoried roadless areas to maintain their roadless character through a national rule no longer facilitates the maintenance of the long-term health and productivity of our individual national forests. While we support active forest management to maintain a healthy forest and strong local economy, we do not support placing roads or conducting commercial timber sales everywhere in the forest. Resource and social demands on each forest is a balancing act that is best addressed through decisions made as close to “on-the-ground” as possible, in coordination and cooperation with state and local governments.

The SERCD believes the Roadless Rule is an outdated administrative rule that contradicts the will of Congress and goes against the mandate of the Forest Service to sustain the health, diversity, and productivity of the nation's forests. The nationally imposed Roadless Rule adds unnecessary administrative burdens and does not efficiently support multiple use management of National Forest System lands. Rescinding this rule will remove top-down directives that impede the local forest managers from achieving the Forest Service multiple use conservation mission.

Rescinding the Roadless Rule will enhance forest management and economic opportunities for Wyoming. It will allow for locally-driven active forest management and promote decisions that are in-line with the local customs, cultures, values, and economies. The identification of management areas, including roadless areas, through the land management planning process as originally intended with NEPA and the National Forest Management Act (NFMA) will lead to improved forest health, reduced wildfire risks, reduced insect infestations, and the creation of jobs in sectors like logging, construction, and maintenance. Such activities contribute to Wyoming's economy and improve access for outdoor recreation and tourism.

Rescinding this rule will remove prohibitions on road construction, reconstruction, and allow for responsible timber production in response to ever-changing conditions, recreation opportunities, fuel reduction treatments, and wildfire suppression. Other projects that have nothing to do with timber production have been delayed because they are in inventoried roadless areas (IRAs), for example, clearing grazing allotment fences from all the downfall of dead trees killed by mountain pine beetles to allow for continued livestock grazing.

Rescinding the Roadless Rule would provide local land managers and local stakeholders to tailor management actions to address local land conditions and the needs of the local communities. Providing opportunities for local land managers to make decisions with less federal top-down regulation would increase rural economic opportunities and support the local economy. The flexibility to respond to the local land and resource conditions in a timely manner is paramount.

Individual forests and local communities are experts in knowing the management history of these nationa forest treasures that have significant impacts on local communities and counties. Priorities and workloads differ vastly from forest to forest, and the Forest Supervisors should have the authority to make decisions for prioritizing projects in relation to national, state, and local needs. The “most durable solution” needs to be developed locally with flexibility for adapting to changed conditions, whether those are from wildfire, insects, climate, or lessons learned from past active management.

The SER CD policies supporting this comment include: 1) Policy Socio-economics #1, “Federal agencies shall base all management decisions on the public land multiple use mandate of our public lands and implement actions that balance multiple uses for sustainable land health.”; 2) Policy Silviculture, Fire and Fuels #17, “Forest management shall follow the mandates of the Organic Administration Act and adhere to the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act of 1960, as well as the National Forest Management Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act.”; 3) Policy - Silviculture, Fire and Fuels #10, “Forest management should support a coordinated timber harvesting and thinning method to promote forest health, reduce disease and insect infestation, reduce wildfire impacts, and prevent waste of forest products.”; and 4) Policy Land Use & Realty #2, “Federal agencies should conduct any National Environmental Policy Act analysis using multiple-use principles that take into consideration all the resources such as, but not limited to, agriculture, air, energy, mineral extraction, range, recreation, socioeconomics, timber, tourism, wildlife, and water.”

2. The Notice of Intent requests public comment on the “impacts of rescinding the Roadless Rule.” Rescinding the Roadless Rule does not authorize any additional management decisions. Building roads or not building roads for commercial timber harvest is still a management decision that must comply with a Forest Plan, NEPA, and other environmental laws. However, rescinding the Roadless Rule would create opportunities to address a host of challenges and objectives across landscapes through proactive management.

There are also studies concerning the number of fires in IRA areas, severity of fires, where fires start, and burned acreages. While topography and the ability to address fires play a significant role, we have seen higher percentages of fires starting in IRA, a higher percentage of high-severity fires in IRA, a larger percentage of IRA acreage being burned than non-IRA acreage across the State.

The SER CD has seen the impacts from the implementation of the Roadless Rule. We saw quite a few mills in Wyoming close, including ones in Saratoga and Encampment after the Roadless Rule was implemented. The timber industry once was a large economic driver for Carbon County as timber was harvested for the railroad and transported down the river to make it easier to access. The mill in Saratoga was finally reopened after many years and joint efforts from many stakeholders. The timber industry has decreased significantly, however, the one sawmill in Saratoga, Saratoga Forest Management, is a large employer to the community. The sawmill provides lumber products and wood by-products.

The timber industry is still important to the economic stability of the District and vital component of proactive management of the forests in the District. To sustain a viable timber industry, it is imperative for access to economically feasible quantities of timber. As timber prices, extraction expenses, labor costs, and other costs fluctuate, the parameters for being economically feasible also fluctuate. During any federal forest land use planning, it is imperative to do a thorough socio-economic analysis based on current (at the time of the planning) and projected figures for these parameters. Lack of proactive forest management and logging can lead to less-than-ideal environmental conditions as experienced over the last 30 years. If logging of the beetle-killed trees isn’t done in a timely manner, consequences include forest-user safety and lack of access by humans, livestock, and wildlife to name a couple.

The SER CD policies supporting this comment include: 1) Policy Socio-economics #5, “Federal, state, and local agency plans or management recommendations shall include an appropriately detailed socio-economic impact description that addresses the effects on the Saratoga-Encampment-Rawlins Conservation District's natural resources, economies, and health and welfare of its citizens.”; 2) Policy Socio-economics #13, “Federal agencies consider Carbon County’s socioeconomic and economic viability in all federal decisions.”; and 3) Policy Land Use & Realty #7, “Federal agencies should support decisions that ensure the socioeconomic wellbeing of Saratoga-Encampment-Rawlins Conservation District citizens, maintain the culture and customs of the constituents, and consider natural resource health.”

3. SER CD believes it is imperative that the Forest Service engage with local and state cooperating agencies throughout the development of the EIS identified by docket number FS-2025-0001. SER CD looks forward to serving as an active partner throughout the development of the EIS to help the Forest Service in crafting a reasonable range of alternatives, ensuring a durable management framework, with the overarching goa of advancing locally supported forest management based on the needs of specific forests, community safety, resilient and working forests that meet the USFS’s multiple use and sustained yield mission.

The SER CD policies supporting this comment include: 1) Expectations Policy #2, “Federal agencies regularly coordinate and offer the ability for the Saratoga-Encampment-Rawlins Conservation District (Board) to participate as a cooperating agency for any federal action occurring within the district requiring National Environmental Policy Act analysis. The Board at its discretion, within its authority and resources available will consider the federal invitation and respond in writing to those projects which we feel we can be a productive team member.”; and 2) Expectations Policy #23, “Federal agencies should work with cooperating agencies in making sound natural resource decisions that are scientifically based, legally defensible, sensitive to resource health, and responsive to multiple-interest users.”

4. The SER CD asserts that the 2001 Roadless Rule has prevented vegetation treatments in areas of the Med Bow NF that suffer from hazardous fuel loading, diminished wildlife habitat, and less than an optimal recreation experience. While road infrastructure is present on the landscape, many of them were administratively closed after the implementation of the 2001 Roadless Rule finally went into effect after the litigation was completed. The Med Bow NF landscape had changed significantly from the time of the 1970s Roadless Area Review and Evaluation (RARE) I and RARE II IRAs mapping. There were no adjustments to the boundaries to reflect management actions that had occurred over the nearly thirtyyear period.

The Med Bow NF developed the Landscape Vegetation Analysis (LaVA) Project to respond to unprecedented landscape-level tree mortality from bark beetles that affected hundreds of thousands of acres across the Med Bow NF since the late 1990s leading to a lack of resilience to other disturbances and unsafe conditions in some locations.

The LaVA project is within the boundaries of a designated priority landscape area for treatment of insects and diseases, as defined by the Healthy Forests Restoration Act (HFRA). The Purpose and Need for the LaVA project includes mitigating hazardous fuel loading, providing for recovery of forest products, enhancing forest and rangeland resilience to future insect and disease infestations, protecting infrastructure and municipal water supplies, restoring wildlife habitat, enhancing access for forest visitors and permittees, and providing for human safety. The LaVA project was designed for multiple-benefit, active management on a landscape scale.

The LaVA Project includes up to 288,000 acres of vegetation management on the Med Bow NF, spanning multiple ranger districts, under one decision for 15 years from the August 2020 signed Record of Decision.

The Forest Service worked collaboratively alongside multiple federal, state, and local cooperating agencies and the public to plan the LaVA project. By working with cooperating agencies and the public, the Forest Service was able to develop a plan that addresses a diversity of stakeholder interests and mitigates risk to habitats, activities, and adjacent communities. The SER CD served as a cooperating agency during the development of the LaVA project and has continued an active role as a partner in conducting vegetation management for successful implementation of the LaVA.

In response to an objection, the Forest Supervisor excluded treatment inside IRAs from the decision, including IRAs where the project would have used existing roads that were Administratively closed. Since IRAs represented roughly 20 percent of the original LaVA treatment opportunity area acres, treatment acres were reduced by 20 percent. This removed roughly 123,000 acres, or 20 percent of treatment opportunity area acres from the project decision. It also reduced proposed treatment acres from 360,000 to 288,000 acres.

The SER CD policies supporting this comment include: 1) Policy - Silviculture, Fire and Fuels #7, “Federal and state land managers should implement proper management of forest and other public lands through Best Management Practices (BMPs) including, but not limited to, timbering, select cutting, fire management, and managed grazing practices for the prevention of catastrophic wildfires.”; and 2) Policy - Silviculture, Fire and Fuels #10, “Forest management should support a coordinated timber harvesting and thinning method to promote forest health, reduce disease and insect infestation, reduce wildfire impacts, and prevent waste of forest products.”

5. The Notice of Intent identified two alternatives, the No Action and the Proposed Action (rescission of the Roadless Rule). For all detailed environmental impact statements, under 42 U.S.C. 4332(C)(iii), there must be “a reasonable range of alternatives to the proposed agency action, including an analysis of any negative environmental impacts of not implementing the proposed agency action in the case of a no action alternatives, that are technically and economically feasible, and meet the purpose and need of the proposal.” The SER CD offers the following suggestions for consideration for an additional alternative for the EIS.

a. We suggest that in addition to a ‘No Action Alternative’ and a ‘Rescind the Roadless Rule’ alternatives that the Forest Service considers an alternative that rescinds the Roadless Rule and amends the 2012 Forest Planning Rule to include a simple directive saying that roadless areas will be taken into consideration as a specific management area during any forest land use planning effort process. This would ensure roadless area considerations and roadless discussions occur during the planning process.

b. We also suggest that the additional alternative provides a process for allowing for statespecific roadless conservation rules and how state-specific rules would account for national forests that span more than one state.

The SER CD agrees with the following statement in the federal register notice, “Land management plans and Agency directives provide a comprehensive framework with respect to inventoried roadless area decision making. Eliminating a cumbersome national level oversight process and returning authority to the local decisionmakers provides for efficiency as well as effectiveness for resource conservation. The important resource values of inventoried roadless areas can be effectively conserved through local decision making and planning without restrictive and unnecessary national prohibitions.” We assert that adding another alternative as suggested would strengthen the range of alternatives while accomplishing the stated purpose and need.

## Conclusion

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement on roadless area conservation. We look forward to continued engagement as the Forest Service allows. We sincerely hope the Forest Service considers engaging with cooperating agencies in the development of the environmental impact statement and updated roadless area conservation rule for the National Forest System Lands. The opportunity to serve as a Cooperating Agency is not just helping the NEPA process simply check a box. Cooperation is building and maintaining a meaningful relationship with federal partners in developing solutions to challenging social and environmental issues. This includes respectful timeframes and working to understand each party’s values for a thoughtful process.

The forests are more than just a place to visit for most Wyoming residents. They represent a part of the life blood of the communities and are interwoven into their very existence and stability. Local communities are connected to the forests whether it is through the ecosystem services they provide or the economic benefit they offer via livestock grazing, timber production, travel and tourism, or recreation opportunities. The health of the forest is vital to the stability of the communities and citizens. Ultimately, we will be partners on stewardship projects and continue leveraging funds to conduct proactive stewardship with the Forest Service to address local priorities of Wyoming forests while protecting the custom and culture, and economies of our rural communities.

The SER CD will continue cooperation with the Forest Service to cocreate durable solutions to managing national forests as the SER CD is committed to successful natural resource management throughout Wyoming and the United States.

Please feel free to contact us if you have questions about our comments.

Respectively,

RE: United States Department of Agriculture Forest Service Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement for Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands

Dear Secretary Rollins:

On behalf of the Crook County Board of Commissioners (“County") located in Sundance, Wyoming, I want to thank you for allowing us the opportunity to submit comments regarding for the United States Forest Service (USFS) Roadless Area Conservation Rule (RACR or Rule) Notice of Intent (NOI) to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS).1 Crook County's economic viability is highly dependent on federally managed lands for timber production and harvest, energy development, livestock grázing, wildlife, tourism, and recreation and this Rule reconsideration initiated by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) will have a significant impact on the socioeconomics, custom and culture of our County and State.

In Wyoming, counties serve as a legal arm of the state entrusted with carrying out statutory and regulatory goals at the local level. County governments are actively engaged in the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) processes to assist our federal partners to create management plans that encourage productive and enjoyable harmony between man and his environment. 42 U.S.C. §4321. Crook County takes our responsibility as a local government seriously and strives to ensure our

community is an economically vibrant, safe, and healthy place to live, work, and recreate. Wyo. Stat. § 18-5-208(b).

Crook County serves as a co-regulator and partner of thousands of acres of USFS federal surface that fall within our jurisdictional boundaries. Our County contains varying percentages of federal, state, and private land. which need thoughtful management at each jurisdictional level. The USFS lands in Crook County are part of the Black Hills National Forest (BKNF) and the Thunder Basin National Grasslands (TBNG). which eguates to approximately 9% of the total land in the County (200,000 acres and 320 acres respectively). These resources are important for the livelihoods of residents and the attraction of those traveling through. The BKNF and TBNG are included as affected areas and subject to this USFS Rule recission.

As co-regulators, Crook County has prepared Crook County Natural Resource Plan² to serve as the basis for communicating and coordinating with the federal government and its agencies on land and natural resource management issues, Wyo. Stat. § 18-5-208(b). Well managed forests are a crucial component to achieving our goals as local governments. Executive Order 14072 "Strengthening the Nation's Forests, Communities and Local Economies" (EO) recognizes this relationship and expressly connects local economies with forest management activities. Our plans, which the USFS should be consistent with, speak specifically about our local economy and the multiple uses within our federal, state, and private forested lands.

As partners, Crook County works diligently to support the work of our federal land managers to overcome shared challenges and achieve mutual goals. Our County actively participates with Wyoming USFS district offices and the regional office on NEPA projects, trainings and presentations, and special initiatives. Although RACR is a substantially different planning effort than is usually contemplated by the agency, we are committed to participate with the USFS and engage in this NEPA process in good-faith, to ensure federal agencies understand local environmental and socioeconomic impacts to proposed projects and plans, and that the NEPA documents contain up-to-date local information that only counties can provide.

Crook County also believes that land management decisions for the national forests in Wyoming are best made as close to “on-the-ground” as possible, in coordination and cooperation with state and local governments. The National Forest Management Act (NFMA) recognizes that forest direction should be ecologically sustainable, economically viable, and socially beneficial over the long term. The 2012 Forest Planning Rule operationalizes the NFMA at the local forest level with a commitment to cooperation with state and local governments, protecting our forests and communities from one-size-fits-all rules and

decisions from Washington, and strengthening federal decision making that can truly reflect the needs of individual forests and communities that rely on them

While the County fully supports the recission of RACR for reasons detailed below, we submit the following comments for the USFSs consideration as the agency moves forward with development the draft EIS:

## 1. General

• Wyoming County Commissioners Association (WCCA) - Crook County endorses, and incorporates by reference, comments submitted by WCCA.

State of Wyoming – Crook County endorses, and incorporates by reference, comments submitted by the State of Wyoming and its agencies.

## II. Background

Wyoming is home to the first national forest, the Shoshone, and portions, or the entirety, of seven other national forests: the Ashley, Bighorn, Black Hills, Bridger-Teton, Caribou-Targhee, Medicine Bow-Routt, and Uinta-Wasatch-Cache National Forests. National forest lands in Wyoming cover over 9.2 million acres, an area larger than New Jersey, Connecticut, and Delaware combined.

As stated above, the USFS lands in Crook County are part of the Black Hills National Forest (BKNF) and of those lands, approximately 200,000 acres, there are an estimated 13,000 acres identified as Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRA). Wyoming shares the BKNF with South Dakota and IRA acres identified in Wyoming alone equates to an estimated 2% of the forest. While not all of the IRA acres fall within the jurisdictiona boundaries of our County or even our state, the effects of the roadless designation still have real impacts to all neighboring counties within the BKNF

The BKNF Record of Decision (ROD) for the most current land use plan was last completed in March of 1997. The 1997 Black Hills Revised Forest Plan designated two areas for inclusion as IRA: 1) most of Sand Creek as late succession landscape and 2) Inyan Kara Mountain as a special interest area.

The BKNF is currently undergoing the process to revise its land use plan and the County is a cooperating agency on that project. As required under the 2012 Planning Rule, the local assessments have been completed and the NEPA process is poised to begin in early 2026. Pertinent to RACR, Crook County believes that the best forest policy decisions are accomplished through robust local engagement. The County advocates for a tailored approach to forest management, emphasizing the importance of addressing the specific ecological and management needs of individual forest areas.

Further, the County submitted comments regarding the Roadless Area Proposed Rule in 2000 and is on record of strongly opposing the implementation of the Rule claiming the process was “seriously flawed” and the USFS “...totally bypassed the NEPA process when it excluded local stakeholders from participating meaningfully in the planning process."³ Let's learn from history and not repeat our mistakes. The County strongly supports the USFSs recission of the RACR as a national planning approach and urges the federal agency to restore local forest units with more power to address unique management strategies within their individualized land use plans. This local approach would better suit the specialized environmental conditions and community interests of each forest.

## A. Sand Creek Inventoried Roadless Area

The Sand Creek Inventoried Roadless Area (IRA) includes approximately 12,389 acres in the Bearlodge Ranger District portion of the BKNF and as is being managed as “Inventoried Roadless Area where road construction or reconstruction is allowed” (USFS BKNF IRA Map dated Sept. 2000). This area was given an “Inventoried Roadless Area” designation by the Clinton Administration in the late 1990's primarily due to the “old growth” of Ponderosa Pine. The IRA has been identified as lands without existing roads that could be suitable for roadless area conservation as wilderness or other non-standard protections. This designation has resulted in decades of “no” active forest management and has precipitated the spread of the Mountain Pine Bark Beetle (MPB) outbreak which killed a significant portion of the old growth pine inventory over a decade ago. These MPB infected trees present a considerable wildfire hazard not only to the forest, but to the adjacent landowners as has been stated by the USFS regarding this pandemic.

Currently, there are approximately 160 miles of roads identified on the official USFS maps. These roads can range from actual gravel capped to grassed-in logging roads. The area was heavily logged by Homestake Mining in the late 1950's early 1960's and according to the Crook County tax role, valid existing rights in the form of mining claims still exist and are mostly accessed through South Dakota; in fact, there is still a Crook County minor subdivision on the books at one of the mine sites. These roads see extensive use from OHV and vehicle use traveling into the forest to hunt, check grazing allotments recreate, and allows private landowners to access property inholdings. Grazing has occurred in this region since before the USFS was created and therefore, fencing and water improvements are found throughout the area.

A“roadless” or “wilderness" designation can attract travelers and recreationists which leads to the need to develop parking areas, fencing, clear signage, restrooms and good trails for access into the area. With the threat of continued MPB kill and fire exposure from non-management within the IRA, this creates a challenge for fire fighters and emergency response professionals to protect private inholdings and the general public. With already existing roads, trails, OHV use, recreation of all forms, mining claims,

grazing allotments and improvements and private inholdings, this area is not a good candidate preservation.

The County contends that the Sand Creek IRA does not improve the quality of visitor's experience in terms of solitude, primitiveness, and unconfined recreation. This area has been heavily altered by man as discussed, several times above. The area does not complement or improve the IRA where “road construction or reconstruction is allowed” and is not suitable as a stand-alone wilderness designation. There are numerous concerns, conflicts and issues as discussed in the manageability section that face the USFS and the County if the area is managed for preservation

Decisions moving forward regarding roadless or conservation designations must be driven locally through the land use planning process where diverse ecological, social, and economic conditions that vary across different forests, counties, and states, ensure sustainable and context-sensitive forest management practices. Forest managers, in collaboration with state and local partner, must possess the authority to make informed management decisions.

## B. Inyan Kara Mountain IRA

The Inyan Kara Mountain (Mountain) is a stand-alone area managed by the USFS with 1,309 acres. The area is currently being managed as an Inventoried Roadless Area “where road construction or reconstruction is not allowed” (USFS BKNF IRA Map dated Sept. 2000). While the Mountain is primarily federally owned and managed by the USFS, it is completely surrounded by private lands. The USFS has easements with certain landowners for access to the USFS; however, when the Crook County Road and Bridge Department were conducting improvements on the Schlup Road, the County approached surrounding landowners to see if they were interested in extending that portion of the county road to the USFS boundary - the landowners were not interested in that proposal at that time. Therefore, the county road ends ½ mile from that USFS boundary.

The Crook County Fire Department is challenged in fighting fires started by lightening that have occurred there in recent years due to the difficulty in obtaining access across private lands. There are valid existing rights located on and around the Mountain in the form of mainly mining claims. To our knowledge, the Mountain does not have designated hiking trails to the summit, as access is limited due to being entirely surrounded by private property. However, there are plentiful hiking opportunities available, and climbers can choose their own routes once they have permission to cross private lands. The Mountain does have a significant number of active grazing allotments.

Decisions moving forward regarding roadless or conservation designations must be driven locally through the land use planning process where diverse ecological, social, and economic conditions that vary across different forests, counties, and states, ensure sustainable and context-sensitive forest

management practices. Forest managers, in collaboration with state and local partner, must possess the authority to make informed management decisions.

## III.USFS Should Abandon its Top-down One-sized Approach to Roadless Management

The County supports the USFSs reconsideration of its current and misguided nationally driven planning strategy and urges the agency to instead empower local forests with greater authority to modify and update their management plans. This localized approach would better accommodate the unique environmental conditions and community interests associated with each forest.

In stark contrast to the Roadless Rule process established in 2001, Crook County believes that effective forest policy development is best achieved through active engagement with local stakeholders. Recognizing the significant ecological and social differences among national forests and their surrounding communities, a decentralized planning approach ensures that conservation efforts and resource management are more responsive and sustainable, ultimately fostering more effective and context-sensitive forest stewardship.

As a way of background. the USFS issued an “Interim Roadless Rule” that went into effect on March 1, 1999, and imposed an eighteen-month moratorium on road construction in IRAs across the United States. On October 13, 1999, President Clinton directed the Forest Service to initiate rulemaking to protect IRAs. Scoping began on October 19, 1999, with the USFS release of its Notice of Intent (NOI) to prepare an EIS and to initiate rulemaking. The Federal District Court in Wyoming described the rulemaking thus: “In its rush to give President Clinton lasting notoriety in the annals of environmentalism, the Forest Service's shortcuts and bypassing of the procedural requirements of NEPA has done lasting damage to our very laws designed to protect the environment." Wyoming v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., 570 F. Supp. 2d 1309, 1345 (D. Wyo. 2008), rev'd, 661 F.3d 1209 (10th Cir. 2011).

The 1999 NOl did not specify a geographic scope nor did it provide any maps of lands that would be covered by the proposed Rule, Therefore, Wyoming was forced to comment on the Rule NOl without specific information on the extent of the impact of the rule. Neither the state nor local governments were allowed to cooperate in the development of the Rule, and Wyoming actively litigated the RACR for a decade. In the end there was little buy-in from stakeholders who had been barred from involvement in the process.

Wyoming. like many states. boasts a diversity of counties with unigue histories and values based on distinct forests with varying ecology and opportunities. Local governments in Wyoming work tirelessly with USFS partners to develop appropriate management frameworks within the cooperating agency process for forest plans that reflect and appreciate the diversity within our forests and communities. The USFS planning process is worth preserving, empowering, and protecting

One of the many flaws in the rulemaking process was that when the RACR was implemented in 2001, it superimposed roughly drawn maps – developed in the 1970s for potential Wilderness designation – without taking a hard look at the impacts it would have on existing forest plan direction. The Secretary of Agriculture made a conscious decision that the RACR would apply to “all lands within an inventoried roadless area boundary” knowing that thousands of acres within inventoried roadless area (IRA) boundaries already had existing roads and areas with active forest management.

To make matters worse, the Forest Service failed to engage state and local governments as cooperating agencies under NEPA throughout its development of the RACR. Consequently, the RACR sidelined the very governments and people impacted the most by the establishment of the Rule. Despite the RACR providing an opportunity to update or revise the set of inventoried roadless area maps, the Forest Service has failed to make necessary updates or revisions to correct the maps and, in the process, has continued to undermine the credibility of the RACR

Following two decades of implementing the RACR, it is evident that empowering forest managers with greater authority and flexibility is essential for effectively collaborating with all stakeholders, including state and local governments. Such collaboration is vital to addressing current challenges and leveraging opportunities within our forest ecosystems. The original design of the RACR imposed limitations on local authority, restricting the ability of local forest plans to adapt to community needs and priorities Repealing the RACR would restore jurisdiction to local forest managers, enabling them to make informed decisions through forest and project planning processes that incorporate community engagement. This approach fosters sustainable forest management practices, promotes ecological health, and supports the socio-economic well-being of communities nationwide, ensuring that forest policies are responsive to local conditions and stakeholder interests.

The County supports the USDAs initiative to reevaluate and manage the components of roadless and conservation effectively. The basis of our support is grounded not in the assumption that commercial timber roads should not be constructed universally within Wyoming's national forests, but rather in the recognition that forest managers, in collaboration with state and local partners, must possess the authority to make informed management decisions. These decisions should account for the diverse ecological, social, and economic conditions that vary across different forests, counties, and states, ensuring sustainable and realistic forest management practices

Staying the course with RACR as a top-down one-sized approach that was implemented in 2001 does not promote the best management for our distinctive forests or produce the best results for our unique communities. By the USFS's own admission in the preamble to the 2012 Planning Rule, “...more specific requirements were not included in the final rule, because these issues are best identified and determined at the forest or grassland level, reflecting ecosystems and plant and animal communities on the unit." The County agrees with this approach in the Planning Rule. A localized planning approach

recognizes the vast differences between our national forests and the communities that live in and around them.

As the USFS knows, forest plans are required to balance a multitude of challenges, priorities, and interests on our forested lands. Existing plans were established in good faith with the cooperation, data, and input from states, counties and other cooperating agencies. Each of the forest units within the state of Wvoming have direction in their existing plans for identifying areas of roadless or conservation priority. Forcing a national management agenda to layer on top of our existing plans does not strengthen them, it undermines them

The County strongly supports the USFSs recission of the RACR as a national planning approach and urges the federal agency to restore local forest units with more power to address unique management strategies within their individualized land use plans. This local approach would better suit the specialized environmental conditions and community interests of each forest

## IV. The USFS Should Meaningfully Engage with Crook County as a Cooperating Agency under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Forest Management Act and the 2012 Planning Rule

Our County has a history of supporting the USFS in developing, revising, and amending forest plans, providing special expertise on socioeconomic issues, including how amendments will affect jobs and the tax base. The County, has also enjoyed a long history of partnership with the USFS working together through on-the-ground projects and advisory groups to assist with plan implementation. Beyond cooperating agency work, our County has made substantial investments to strengthen the working relationships we enjoy with the Forest Service. Our participation also assists the federal agency to comply with its requirement to coordinate its land management planning with local county land use plans.

## A. National Environmental Policy Act

The County realizes that USDA is currently undergoing revisions to its NEPA procedures for many reasons but one being the issuance of congressional directives⁴ along with new court decisions. Specifically recent federal court cases, along with a Supreme Court Decision, challenged longstanding assumptions regarding the Council on Environmental Quality's (CEQs) authority to issue binding regulations for implementation of the NEPA.

Furthermore, on January 20, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order (E.O.) 14154, rescinding E.O. 11991, which had previously directed CEQ to promulgate NEPA implementing regulations. On February

25, 2025, CEQ published in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) an interim final rule removing existing CEQ NEPA implementing regulations. In addition to Executive Order (E.O.) 14154, the judicial branch's opinions in Marin Audubon v. FAA and lowa v. CEQ demanded the longstanding CEQ regulation framework for cooperating agencies under NEPA be rescinded. However, neither the E.O. nor any court decision mandated that the cooperation our County has enjoyed should be eliminated or impaired. Consequently, the County remains hopeful that much of the clarity and consistency provided by CEQ regulations could survive a move to department regulations.

Additionally, NEPA's commitment to cooperating with local governments in the development of its required analyses plays an outsized role in Wyoming, where nearly half of the state is managed by the federal government along with vast acreage of mineral estate. We are grateful for USDA’s efforts to improve the NEPA process and look forward to seeing the benefits in our communities.

Our goal as cooperating agencies is to help expedite NEPA, provide local and technical data and information, help agencies come to defensible and durable decisions, and support the cooperative principles that distinguishes NEPA from all other acts of congress. It is our goal of safeguarding and furthering NEPA's cooperative code that guides our comments on cooperating agencies.

It cannot be stated strongly enough that state and local government participation in the NEPA process as cooperating agencies is imperative and USDA must include provisions clearly stating inclusion of local governments. In the NEPA process, the USDA must retain similar language in their NEPA procedures that “A lead agency may designate any Federal, State, Tribal, or local agency that has jurisdiction by law or special expertise with respect to any environmental issue involved in a proposal as a cooperating agency." See 40 C.F.R. §§ 1501.7 and 1501.8.

Public lands and the resources on them influence the custom and culture of the County. The relationship between the County and the federal agencies is key to ensuring resources are managed successfully and the County's custom and culture of using public lands for multiple uses remains intact. The County and federal agencies have worked together in the past on resource management concerns and issues and will continue to strengthen and build those relationships to ensure that all stakeholders are at the table when discussing resource management on public lands within the County.

While USDA has the authority to conduct a rulemaking process to create regulations that implement laws and policies that ensures transparency and public involvement in the development of regulations that affect natural resources and public lands, the County contends that more often than not, a departmental “Rule” would have significant impacts on the environment, applies across the Department nationwide and thus warrants an analysis through an environmental impact statement under NEPA. Currently, “Rulemaking” is not required to undergo the same process as NEPA and there is no cooperating agency component, beyond the public comment period, and in this instance, the USFS rightfully chose to conduct EIS to better engage with stakeholders and cooperators; however, it doesn't go far enough and the Forest Service should, at the very least, allow the states to participate as cooperating agencies in this NEPA process.

Further, NEPA is required for all “major federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment." Most federal Rules, if implemented, will undoubtedly impact the socioeconomics of local jurisdictions where federal land exists for example the RACR of which the USFS appropriately conducted a NEPA analysis. The County maintains that Rules impacting states and counties should allow a similar cooperating agency engagement process as NEPA and at the very least, USDA should modify its Rulemaking process to create a “cooperating agency” component similar to NEPA for engagement with states and their agencies. This would ensure better consistency with state and local government plans.

Unfortunately, the USFS is once again attempting to approach the RACR alone. Even though this proposed action is to rescind the Rule, the Forest Service should recognize that it is our forests and communities that will bear the brunt of uncertainty in planning, projects, and litigation that will ultimately result from any modification of the RACR. Serving as cooperating agencies will also benefit us, as we attempt to navigate changes in management and ultimately convey those changes to our constituents.

The USFS would benefit from the meaningful engagement of Wyoming counties in the development of its EIS. Beyond an exhibited commitment supporting the USFS through project and planning efforts for decades. Wvoming counties have local expertise, data, and jurisdiction of the lands impacted by the RACR that would benefit the EIS. While the County cannot demand the Forest Service include our counties and state as cooperators, as governmental partners we are requesting the USFS change its current direction and at the very least allow the state to coordinate as a cooperating agency.

## B. National Forest Management Act

Preceding the NFMA was the Forest and Rangeland Renewable Resources Planning Act of 1974 (RPA), which initially required, among other things, the Forest Service to develop land and resource management plans for units of the National Forest System. Later, the NFMA further expanded the Forest Service planning obligations and established the statutory authority applicable today to the Forest Service and the USDA. The NFMA currently serves as a key statutory backbone for the formation of land management and forest planning regulations. Under the NFMA, 16 U.S.C. §§ 1600-1687, the Forest Service is mandated to promulgate regulations for the development and revision of land management plans to guide management of land within the agency.⁵ The NFMA requires the Secretary of Agriculture to develop regulations under the principles of the Multiple Use and Sustained Yield Act (MUSYA) and to set out further processes for the development and revision of land management plans.⁶

The NFMA guides the development and revision of plans, environmental considerations, resource management guidelines, and general guidelines for land management plans. Further, NFMA requires that the agency's planning regulations must adhere to NEPA and consider the impact to multiple resources, including impacts to wildlife, timber resources, recreation, and grazing under a guidance of multiple use and sustained yield but the Act does not prescribe or dictate to the agency how each resource must be managed beyond a multiple use and sustained yield lens.?

The National Forest Management Act (NFMA) governs the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) and requires the agency to “coordinate”. The NFMA requirements are as follows:

[T]he Secretary of Agriculture shall develop, maintain, and, as appropriate, revise land and resource management plans for units of the National Forest System, coordinated with the land and resource management planning processes of State and local governments and other Federal agencies (16 U.S.C. § 1604(a)).

The fact that the USFS is directed to “coordinate” with local governments implies, by its plain meaning. that the USFS must engage in a process that involves more than simply “considering” the plans and policies of local governments; it must attempt to achieve compatibility between USFS plans and local land use plans. Additionally, the Forest Service is mandated to “engage the public, including State and local governments early throughout the planning process." 36 C.F.R. § 219.4(a)(1)

The USFS is also obligated to perform a consistency review. For development of forest plans, the forest Service shall review the planning and land use policies of State and local governments where relevant to the plan area. The results of the review shall be displayed in the EIS. 36 C.F.R. 219.4(b)(2).

Substantial progress has been made over the past fifty years to build not only the regulatory framework to implement NEPA and NFMA, but also a culture for cooperation and collaboration with local governments throughout the NEPA process. In addition to regulations, agencies have expressed lessons learned from implementing NEPA and best practices to fulfill NEPA’s purposes. The USFS's Guidebook titled “County Governments and the USDA Forest Service: A Guidebook for Working Together” (Guidebook) to discusses the requirement that agencies must provide a meaningful participation and allocate responsibilities to comply with the law.

The Guidebook contains best practices that are not always directly citing NEPA, NFMA, CEQ, or USDA and agency regulations. These best practices have grown out of lived experience working together. The Guidebook illustrates that the outcomes are better when federal agencies and county governments "work together to reach solutions that are politically and socially durable and ensure the long-term

sustainability of communities and natural resources. It is through working together, at multiple stages of planning and project implementation, that we will achieve true success."

Our goal as cooperating agencies is to help expedite NEPA, provide local and technical data and information, help agencies come to defensible and durable decisions, and support the cooperative spirit that distinguishes NEPA from all other acts of congress. It is our goal of safeguarding and furthering NEPA's cooperative code that guides our comments on cooperating agencies under USDA's NEPA procedures.

Public lands and the resources on them influence the custom and culture of the County. The relationship between the County and the federal agencies is key to ensuring resources are managed successfully and the County's custom and culture of using public lands for multiple uses remains intact. The County and agencies have worked together in the past on resource management concerns and issues and will continue to strengthen and build those relationships to ensure that all stakeholders are at the table when discussing resource management on public lands within the County.

## C. USDA 2012 Planning Rule

The 2012 Planning Rule guides the development, amendment, and revision of land management plans on National Forest System lands. Federal law mandates the Forest Service to develop land management plans for units of the National Forest and Grassland System and promulgate regulations to guide the Forest Service planning process. As federal law provides statutory authority for establishing planning regulations, the 2012 Planning Rule sets out the procedural and substantive requirements for land management plans. As discussed, Land management plans set the overall management direction and guidance for each national forest and associated lands. Land management plans should guide the carrving out of projects and activities by providing a general direction of uses within each national forest, prairie, and grassland.

In all stages of land management planning, plans must use the best available scientific information to inform the planning process as reguired by the 2012 Planning Rule. This “best available scientific information” used must be accompanied by documentation that identifies what information was determined to be the best available scientific information, explains the basis for that determination, and explains how the information was applied to the issues considered. Ultimately, the best available scientific information should guide decision making through the planning process.

Furthermore, in the planning process public participation is afforded through specific regulatory requirements of “outreach,” to be conducted by the responsible official of the planning process. Outreach includes engaging Tribes, other Federal agencies, State and local governments, individuals, and public and private organizations or entities.

Additionally, through the development of plans, the responsible official must coordinate with other public planning efforts, including reviewing the planning and land use policies of federally recognized Indian Tribes, Alaska Native Corporations, other Federal agencies, and State and local governments, where relevant to the plan area. This directive to coordinate with other local planning efforts allows for more effective coordination throughout all the planning processes. The result of this coordination in land management review must be displayed in the EIS under NEPA for the associated plan. This coordination with other interests must include specified considerations including

■ The objectives of federally recognized Indian Tribes, Alaska Native Corporations, other Federal agencies, and State and local governments, as expressed in their plans and policies;

■The compatibility and interrelated impacts of these plans and policies;

■ Opportunities for the plan to address the impacts identified or to contribute to joint objectives;

■ Opportunities to resolve or reduce conflicts within the context of developing the plan's desired conditions or objectives

Each plan developed or revised must contain sustainability considerations to provide for social, economic, and ecological sustainability within the Forest Service's authority.8 As part of sustainability considerations, ecological sustainability and social and economic sustainability must both be addressed Both categories require plans and revisions to consider differing factors in the planning process. Providing for cooperating agency status along with consistency review of state and local plans provides the foundation of successful long-term planning and rulemaking implementation

## V. Roadless Areas Conservation Rule Environmental Impact Statement Considerations

## A. Alternatives

The USFS has properly determined it should draft an EIS for its compliance with NEPA. The Notice of Intent describes two alternatives - the No Action (maintaining the RACR) and the Proposed Action (rescission of the RACR). For all detailed statements, under 42 U.S.C. 4332(C)(iii), there must be “a reasonable range of alternatives to the proposed agency action, including an analysis of any negative environmental impacts of not implementing the proposed agency action in the case of a no action alternatives, that are technically and economically feasible, and meet the purpose and need of the proposal."

Over the years, courts have clarified what counts as a reasonable range of alternatives. While agencies have some flexibility, they are not free to ignore important options. Courts have emphasized that agencies should consider a wide and comprehensive set of alternatives, especially for projects they manage directly.

It is important to avoid making the same mistake in this current USFS EIS. However, agencies are not required to consider every possible alternative. The Supreme Court has stated that agencies do not need to include every conceivable option, only those that are reasonable and relevant to the project's goals. For legal sufficiency of the EIS, we encourage the USFS to develop and analyze at least one additional alternative. that is technically and economically feasible, and meets the purpose and need of the proposal.

## B. Impacts of establishing RACR

The Notice of Intent solicits public comments regarding the potential impacts of rescinding the RACR. It is important to clarify that rescinding RACR does not authorize any specific projects, roads, or timber sales. Nonetheless, the implementation of RACR has had observable effects on Wyoming's communities and forest ecosystems. Historically, forest management practices aimed at achieving desired ecological and economic conditions have been limited or foregone, resulting in tangible consequences. These include a decline in timber sale volumes and revenues, reduced financial payments to local counties, and missed opportunities to mitigate fire risks through activities such as salvage logging of trees affected by Mountain Pine Beetles (MPB) or wildfires

Additionally, restrictions have impeded fence maintenance for grazing allotments, and several forest products companies have ceased operations. The absence of proactive management has also led to missed opportunities for fire risk reduction in municipal watersheds, potentially impacting community safety and water guality. Overall, the rescission of RACR could influence forest management strategies economic stability, and ecological health within the region, underscoring the need for a comprehensive review of the Rule's implications since approved in 2001.

## C. Impacts of rescinding RACR

Again, the rescinding of the RACR does not grant authority for additional management decisions beyond existing regulations. Decisions such as constructing roads for commercial timber harvesting remain subject to compliance with the Forest Plan, the NEPA, and other applicable environmental laws. Nonetheless, rescinding RACR could open avenues for proactive landscape management aimed at addressing various ecological and operational challenges, including wildfire mitigation, insect infestations, disease control, watershed health, wildlife habitat preservation, and the resilience of oldgrowth forests.

Furthermore, the implementation of RACR has had notable impacts, particularly in Wyoming, where several mills ceased operations following the rule's enactment. In fact, Crook County is home to one of the last remaining functioning sawmills in the state and rescinding the Rule will only help the future of those mills remain active – if it's not too late. Studies have also indicated correlations between RACR and fire dynamics within IRAs. Data suggest that IRAs experience a higher incidence of fire starts, increased severity of fires, and larger burned areas compared to non-IRA regions. While topography and fire management capabilities significantly influence these outcomes, the data imply that IRAs are more susceptible to high-severity fires and extensive burn areas.

It is important to recognize that, regardless of the management alternative chosen, a substantial portion of roadless areas will remain permanently inaccessible due to inherent topographical features, isolation, resource values, and cost-benefit considerations. These factors inherently limit the potential for development or resource extraction in these regions, ensuring their continued status as roadless landscapes.

## D. Roadless Values

The RACR documents repeatedly characterize IRAs as having the following values – 1) high quality or undisturbed soil, water, and air, 2) sources of public drinking water, 3) diversity of plant and animal communities, 4) habitat for T&E, proposed, candidate, and sensitive species and for species dependent of large, undisturbed areas, 5) Primitive, Semi-primitive, non-motorized, and Semi-primitive motorized recreation, 6) Reference landscapes, 7) natural appearing landscapes with high scenic quality, and 8) traditional cultural properties and sacred sites. While true, these values are not limited to IRAs; in fact, they are part and parcel of multiple use objectives and values across the entire National Forest System

This is an example of why Crook County believes that the best forest policy decisions are accomplished through robust local engagement. The County advocates for a tailored approach to forest management, emphasizing the importance of addressing the specific ecological and management needs of individual forest areas. The County supports the USFSs recission of its current nationally driven planning strategy, which instead empowers local forests with greater authority to modify and update their management plans. This localized approach would better accommodate the unique environmental conditions and community interests associated with each forest.

## E. Roadless Area Conservation Rule Maps Must Be Updated with More Accurate Information

The USFS IRA maps originate from the agency's Roadless Area Review and Evaluation (RARE) RARE Iand RARE Il initiatives conducted in the 1970s. These maps, which served as the basis for designating areas within the RACR, are now considered outdated due to their reliance on antiquated data. Specifically, the use of RARE Il maps to identify IRAs for the RACR has resulted in the inclusion of numerous areas within Wyoming's national forests that feature well-maintained roads, active forest management practices, and lands designated as suitable for timber harvesting according to forest management plans.

The decision at the time by the Secretary of Agriculture to apply the RACR to "all lands within an inventoried roadless area boundary" was made with the understanding that many of these areas already contained existing roads and had been subject to approved forest management projects, including timber harvesting. According to 36 CFR § 294.11, the definition of IRAs allows for the "update or revision" of the RACR maps through the land management planning process. However, the Forest Service has not established a formal process to identify or implement such updates or revisions. Despite the RACR providing an opportunity for map updates, the agency has largely failed to revise or correct the IRA maps, with only minor exceptions, thereby maintaining outdated designations that do not reflect current land use and management activities. This process has been flawed from the beginning and updated mapping through forest level land planning must be the new chartered course of action with the USFS.

## F. RACR disregards local forest plans

Wyoming counties actively participate as cooperating agencies in the development of forest plans. The forest planning process is designed to guide the management direction of forest lands for ten to fifteen years. However, the RACR upset the direction contained in plans by overlaying IRA maps indiscriminately across planning and project areas.

In certain instances, the RACR overlaid IRA maps on areas already identified in the forest plan for certain protections or lands that were not included in the suitable timber base. These lands now have duplicative protections. On the other hand. IRA maps were also overlaid on thousands of acres identified by forest plans as suitable timber base. Sometimes referred to as suitable lands, these acres were identified in the planning process as being available and appropriate for timber production on a sustained vield basis. Lands not compatible with management goals (e.g. set aside for recreation, oldgrowth management, etc.) were excluded, that are biophysically unsustainable (e.g. poor soils, steep slopes, etc.). or economically or operationally impracticable (e.g. inaccessible terrain, extreme harvesting costs, etc.) are excluded from the suitable timber base in the planning process. In other words, the USFS has existing tools at its disposal inside the 2012 Planning Rule to protect, conserve, manage, or develop these lands.

The RACR also overrides Forest Plan direction that would have otherwise allowed the Forest Service to implement ongoing forest management projects. Forest Service Line Officers have minimal authority to implement proactive management projects in IRAs to reduce the risk of catastrophic wildfire and insect epidemics, which include the removal of timber as a byproduct of those treatments. The risk of protracted and expensive litigation has also discouraged line officers from applying the exceptions present in the RACR. This has hampered the Forest Service's ability to implement proactive measures needed to reduce the threat of catastrophic fire and MPB epidemics in municipal watersheds

## G. Private Property Rights

As stated earlier, Crook County is rich in federal resources such as timber harvesting and production, farming, ranching, energy development, tourism and recreation, which all contribute heavily to the heritage of the County. Rangeland used by livestock and agricultural producers continues to be the dominant land use and federal agencies should consider the effects their decisions will have on neighboring private lands.

Furthermore, access to, or restrictions from, crossing federal, state, or county managed lands should not entail encumbrances or constraints on private property. Private property rights are the cornerstone of our County and must be protected to ensure that our continued customs and culture remain intact. When an agency decision or proposed action will have a negative impact to the current use of neighboring private lands, that federal undertaking may not be supported by the County

## VI. Consistency with Crook County Natural Resource Management Plan

As mentioned earlier, the State of Wyoming is unique as County commissions have been charged with the responsibility for the preservation of the custom and culture of Wyoming counties in matters relating to NEPA and federal land planning. Since the customs, culture, and history of the County are inseparably tied to the use of and access to land and resources managed by federal agencies to ensure state and federal agencies manage lands and resources in the County in a way that protects and improves the health, safety, environment, and well-being of our citizens, and improves the performance of the economy without imposing unacceptable or unreasonable costs or impacts to local social structure (Wyoming Statute [W.S.] 18-5-208(a)).

Meaningful cooperating agency engagement, at the earliest practicable time, strengthens informed federal decision making required by NEPA. Congress provided in Section 101 of NEPA, “recognizing the profound impact of man's activity on the interrelations of all components of the natural environment.. declares that it is the continuing policy of the Federal Government, in cooperation with State and local governments... to create and maintain conditions under which man and nature can exist in productive harmony, and fulfill the social, economic, and other requirements of present and future generations of Americans." Therefore, by design, NEPA requires federal decisions to be made in cooperation with state and local partners. Clarity of how federal departments and agencies cooperate with state and local governments remains an essential piece of NEPA implementing regulations, and one that must remain in the agency's NEPA procedures.

The inclusion of special expertise as a basis for our comments corresponds with NEPA’s expressed provision that allows lead agencies to designate “any Federal, State, Tribal, or local agency that has jurisdiction by law or special expertise with respect to any environmental impact..." Counties across the nation have varying authorities to develop or enforce environmental standards, but each county has special expertise. Limiting comments to local agencies that are authorized to develop and enforce environmental standards does not conform to the qualifications required for us to be cooperating agencies NEPA.

Restricting comments to those governments authorized to develop and enforce environmental standards also disregards NEPA's clear interdisciplinary approach expressed in 42 U.S.C. 4332(A) and the Congressional declaration to use all practical means and measures “in a manner calculated to foster and promote the general welfare, to create conditions under which man and nature can exist in productive harmony, and fulfill the social, economic and other requirements of present and future generations of Americans" in 42 U.S.C. 4331.

In addition, federal agencies are required to identify and analyze the impacts to local economies and community culture when making decisions. The County encourages federal agencies to be as consistent as allowed by law with the Converse County Natural Resource Management Plan (County Plan). The County Plan specifically recognizes that the private sector is the best engine for economic growth; regulatory policies should respect the role of state and local governments; and federal land policies and regulations should be effective, consistent, sensible, and understandable. A County Plan, while not required, can aide this analysis.

Although the RACR stands to impact hundreds of communities across the country, the USFS must adeguately consider state and local plans and provide a description of how those plans were given consideration as required by the 2012 Planning Rule and NEPA. At a minimum, the USFS should include a list of the local land use plans that are within the ElS boundary. However, even an impacted county list would not meet the requirements for coordination and consistency

It must be recognized that the USDA and its agencies cannot meet its goals for our Nation’s public lands to continue to provide minerals, energy, forage, timber, and recreational opportunities, as well as habitat. protected water supplies, and landscapes that resist and recover from drought, wildfire, and other disturbances, on its own. Nor can we meet our goals of maintaining our unique cultural heritage with thriving economies on our own. We must work together.

Crook County believes that any federal agencies approach of waiting until the final stage to address inconsistencies in the EIS is flawed. To encourage consistency with the County Plan and for the USFSs convenience, we have identified a few priority policy positions that are impacted by this ElS. This is not a comprehensive list and USFS is encouraged to review the entirety of the County Plan for more details:
