# COUNTYOFWESTON NEWCASTLE, WYOMING 82701

September 19, 2025

Mrs. Brooke Rollins Secretary of Agriculture United States Department of Agriculture 201 14th Street SW Mailstop 1108 Washington, DC 20250–1124 ATTN: Director, Ecosystem Management Coordination

Submitted via Federal eRulemaking Portal Portal: https://www.regulations.goy Docket No. FS-2025–0001

RE: United States Department of Agriculture Forest Service Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement for Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands

Dear Secretary Rollins:

On behalf of the Weston County Board of Commissioners (“County") located in Newcastle, Wyoming, I want to thank you for allowing us the opportunity to submit comments regarding for the United States Forest Service (USFS) Roadless Area Conservation Rule (RACR or Rule) Notice of Intent (NOI) to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS). Weston County's economic viability is highly dependent on federally managed lands for timber production and harvest energy development, livestock grazing, wildlife, tourism, and recreation and this Rule reconsideration initiated by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) will have a significant impact on the socioeconomics, custom and culture of our County and State

In Wyoming, counties serve as a legal arm of the state entrusted with carrying out statutory and regulatory goals at the local level. County governments are actively engaged in the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) processes to assist our federal partners to create management plans that encourage productive and enjoyable harmony between man and his environment. 42 U.S.C. §4321. Weston County takes our responsibility as a local government seriously and

strives to ensure our community is an economically vibrant, safe, and healthy place to live, work, and recreate. Wyo. Stat §18-5-208(b).

Weston County serves as a co-regulator and partner of thousands of acres of USFS federal surface that fall within our jurisdictional boundaries. Our County contains varying percentages of federal, state, and private land, which need thoughtful management at each jurisdictional level. The USFS manages approximately 15% of the total land in Weston County and includes forest lands that are part of the Black Hills National Forest (BKNF) and Thunder Basin National Grasslands (TBNG). Approximately 6,257 acres of the BKNF lie within Weston County. These resources are important for the livelihoods of residents and the attraction of those traveling through. The BKNF and TBNG are included as affected areas and subject to this USFS Rule recission

As co-regulators, Weston County has prepared Weston County Natural Resource Plan² to serve as the basis for communicating and coordinating with the federal government and its agencies on land and natural resource management issues. Wyo. Stat. § 18-5-208(b). Well managed forests are a crucial component to achieving our goals as local governments. Executive Order 14072 "Strengthening the Nation's Forests, Communities and Local Economies" (EO) recognizes this relationship and expressly connects local economies with forest management activities. Our plans, which the USFS should be consistent with, speak specifically about our local economy and the multiple uses within our federal, state, and private forested lands.

As partners, Weston County works diligently to support the work of our federal land managers to overcome shared challenges and achieve mutual goals. Our County actively participates with Wyoming USFS district offices and the regional office on NEPA projects, trainings and presentations, and special initiatives. Although RACR is a substantially different planning effort than is usually contemplated by the agency, we are committed to participate with the USFS and engage in this NEPA process in good faith, to ensure federal agencies understand local environmental and socioeconomic impacts to proposed projects and plans, and that the NEPA documents contain up-to-date local information that only counties can provide.

Weston County also believes that land management decisions for the national forests in Wyoming are best made as close to “on-the-ground" as possible, in coordination and cooperation with state and local governments. The National Forest Management Act (NFMA) recognizes that forest direction should be ecologically sustainable, economically viable, and socially beneficial over the long term. The 2012 Forest Planning Rule operationalizes the NFMA at the local forest level with a commitment to cooperation with state and local governments, protecting our forests and communities from onesize-fits-all rules and decisions from Washington, and strengthening federal decision making that can truly reflect the needs of individual forests and communities that rely on them

While the County fully supports the recission of RACR for reasons detailed below, we submit the following comments for the USFSs consideration as the agency moves forward with development the draft EIS:

## I. General

Wyoming County Commissioners Association (WCCA) – Weston County endorses, and incorporates by reference, comments submitted by WCCA

• State of Wyoming – Weston County endorses, and incorporates by reference, comments submitted by the State of Wyoming and its agencies

## II. Background

Wyoming is home to the first national forest, the Shoshone, and portions, or the entirety, of seven other national forests; the Ashley. Bighorn, Black Hills, Bridger-Teton, Caribou-Targhee, Medicine Bow-Routt, and Uinta-Wasatch-Cache National Forests. National forest lands in Wyoming cover over 9.2 million acres, an area larger than New Jersey, Connecticut, and Delaware combined

As stated above, the USFS lands in Weston County are part of the Black Hills National Forest (BKNF) and of those lands, there are an estimated 13,000 acres identified as Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRA). Wyoming shares the BKNF with South Dakota and IRA acres identified in Wyoming alone equates to an estimated 2% of the forest. While none of the IRA acres fall within the jurisdictional boundaries of our County, the effects of the roadless designation still have real impacts to all neighboring counties within the BKNF

The BKNF Record of Decision (ROD) for the most current land use plan was last completed in March of 1997. The 1997 Black Hills Revised Forest Plan designated one area for inclusion as IRA: 1) most of Sand Creek as late succession landscape and 2) Inyan Kara Mountain as a special interest area

The BKNF is currently undergoing the process to revise its land use plan, and the County is a cooperating agency on that project. As required under the 2012 Planning Rule, the local assessments have been completed and the NEPA process is poised to begin in early 2026. Pertinent to RACR, Weston County believes that the best forest policy decisions are accomplished through robust local engagement. The County advocates for a tailored approach to forest management, emphasizing the importance of addressing the specific ecological and management needs of individual forest areas

Let’s learn from history and not repeat our mistakes. The County strongly supports the USFSs recission of the RACR as a national planning approach and urges the federal agency to restore local forest units with more power to address unique management strategies within their individualized land use plans. This local approach would better suit the specialized environmental conditions and community interests of each forest.

## III. USFS Should Abandon its Top-down One-sized Approach to Roadless Management

The County supports the USFSs reconsideration of its current and misguided nationally driven planning strategy and urges the agency to instead empower local forests with greater authority to modify and update their management plans This localized approach would better accommodate the unique environmental conditions and community interests associated with each forest

In stark contrast to the Roadless Rule process established in 2001, Weston County believes that effective forest policy development is best achieved through active engagement with local stakeholders. Recognizing the significant ecological and social differences among national forests and their surrounding communities, a decentralized planning approach ensures that conservation efforts and resource management are more responsive and sustainable, ultimately fostering more effective and context-sensitive forest stewardship

As a way of background. the USFS issued an "Interim Roadless Rule" that went into effect on March 1, 1999, and imposed an eighteen-month moratorium on road construction in IRAs across the United States. On October 13, 1999 President Clinton directed the Forest Service to initiate rulemaking to protect IRAs. Scoping began on October 19, 1999, with the USFS release of its Notice of Intent (NOI) to prepare an EIS and to initiate rulemaking. The Federal District Court in Wvoming described the rulemaking thus: “In its rush to give President Clinton lasting notoriety in the annals of environmentalism, the Forest Service's shortcuts and bypassing of the procedural requirements of NEPA has done lasting damage to our very laws designed to protect the environment." Wyoming v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., 570 F. Supp. 2d 1309, 1345 (D. Wyo. 2008), rev'd, 661 F.3d 1209 (10th Cir. 2011).

The 1999 NOI did not specify a geographic scope, nor did it provide any maps of lands that would be covered by the proposed Rule. Therefore, Wyoming was forced to comment on the Rule NOI without specific information on the extent of the impact of the rule. Neither the state nor local governments were allowed to cooperate in the development of the Rule, and Wyoming actively litigated the RACR for a decade. In the end there was little buy-in from stakeholders who ħad been barred from involvement in the process

Wyoming, like many states, boasts a diversity of counties with unique histories and values based on distinct forests with varying ecology and opportunities. Local governments in Wyoming work tirelessly with USFS partners to develop appropriate management frameworks within the cooperating agency process for forest plans that reflect and appreciate the diversity within our forests and communities. The USFS planning process is worth preserving, empowering, and protecting.

One of the many flaws in the rulemaking process was that when the RACR was implemented in 2001, it superimposed roughly drawn maps – developed in the 1970s for potential Wilderness designation – without taking a hard look at the impacts it would have on existing forest plan direction. The Secretary of Agriculture made a conscious decision that the RACR would apply to “all lands within an inventoried roadless area boundary" knowing that thousands of acres within inventoried roadless area (IRA) boundaries already had existing roads and areas with active forest management

To make matters worse, the Forest Service failed to engage state and local governments as cooperating agencies under NEPA throughout its development of the RACR. Consequently, the RACR sidelined the very governments and people impacted the most by the establishment of the Rule. Despite the RACR providing an opportunity to update or revise the set of inventoried roadless area maps, the Forest Service has failed to make necessary updates or revisions to correct the maps and, in the process, has continued to undermine the credibility of the RACR.

Following two decades of implementing the RACR, it is evident that empowering forest managers with greater authority and flexibility is essential for effectively collaborating with all stakeholders, including state and local governments. Such collaboration is vital to addressing current challenges and leveraging opportunities within our forest ecosystems. The original design of the RACR imposed limitations on local authority, restricting the ability of local forest plans to adapt to community needs and priorities. Repealing the RACR would restore jurisdiction to local forest managers, enabling them to make informed decisions through forest and project planning processes that incorporate community engagement. This approach fosters sustainable forest management practices, promotes ecological health, and supports the socio-economic well-being of communities nationwide, ensuring that forest policies are responsive to local conditions and stakeholder interests.

The County supports the USDAs initiative to reevaluate and manage the components of roadless and conservation effectively. The basis of our support is grounded not in the assumption that commercial timber roads should not be constructed universally within Wyoming's national forests, but rather in the recognition that forest managers, in collaboration with state and local partners, must possess the authority to make informed management decisions. These decisions should account for the diverse ecological, social, and economic conditions that vary across different forests counties, and states, ensuring sustainable and realistic forest management practices.

Staying the course with RACR as a top-down one-sized approach that was implemented in 2001 does not promote the best management for our distinctive forests or produce the best results for our unique communities. By the US主S's own admission in the preamble to the 2012 Planning Rule, “...more specific requirements were not included in the final rule. because these issues are best identified and determined at the forest or grassland level, reflecting ecosystems and plant and animal communities on the unit." The County agrees with this approach in the Planning Rule. A localized planning approach recognizes the vast differences between our national forests and the communities that live in and around them

As the USFS knows, forest plans are required to balance a multitude of challenges, priorities, and interests on our forested lands. Existing plans were established in good faith with the cooperation, data, and input from states, counties and other cooperating agencies. Each of the forest units within the state of Wyoming have direction in their existing plans for identifving areas of roadless or conservation priority. Forcing a national management agenda to layer on top of our existing plans does not strengthen them, it undermines them

The County strongly supports the USFSs recission of the RACR as a national planning approach and urges the federal agency to restore local forest units with more power to address unique management strategies within their individualized land use plans. This local approach would better suit the specialized environmental conditions and community interests of each forest.

## IV. The USFS Should Meaningfully Engage with Weston County as a Cooperating Agency under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Forest Management Act and the 2012 Planning Rule

Our County has a history of supporting the USFS in developing, revising, and amending forest plans, providing special expertise on socioeconomic issues, including how amendments will affect jobs and the tax base. The County has also enioved a long history of partnership with the USFS working together through on-the-ground projects and advisory groups to assist with plan implementation. Beyond cooperating agency work, our County has made substantial investments to strengthen the working relationships we enjoy with the Forest Service. Our participation also assists the federal agency to comply with its requirement to coordinate its land management planning with local county land use plans.

## A. National Environmental Policy Act

The County realizes that USDA is currently undergoing revisions to its NEPA procedures for many reasons but one being the issuance of congressional directives³ along with new court decisions. Specifically, recent federal court cases, along with a Supreme Court Decision, challenged longstanding assumptions regarding the Council on Environmental Quality's (CEQs) authority to issue binding regulations for implementation of the NEPA

Furthermore, on January 20, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order (E.O.) 14154, rescinding E.O. 11991, which had previously directed CEO to promulgate NEPA implementing regulations. On February 25, 2025, CEQ published in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) an interim final rule removing existing CEQ NEPA implementing regulations. In addition to Executive Order (E.O.) 14154. the judicial branch's opinions in Marin Audubon y, FAA and Iowa v. CEQ demanded the longstanding CEQ regulation framework for cooperating agencies under NEPA be rescinded. However, neither the E.O. nor any court decision mandated that the cooperation our County has enjoyed should be eliminated or impaired. Consequently. the County remains hopeful that much of the clarity and consistency provided by CEQ regulations could survive a move to department regulations

Additionally, NEPA's commitment to cooperating with local governments in the development of its required analyses plays an outsized role in Wvoming, where nearly half of the state is managed by the federal government along with vast acreage of mineral estate. We are grateful for USDA's efforts to improve the NEPA process and look forward to seeing the benefits in our communities.

Our goal as cooperating agencies is to help expedite NEPA, provide local and technical data and information, help agencies come to defensible and durable decisions, and support the cooperative principles that distinguishes NEPA from all other acts of congress. It is our goal of safeguarding and furthering NEPA’s cooperative code that guides our comments on cooperating agencies

It cannot be stated strongly enough that state and local government participation in the NEPA process as cooperating agencies is imperative, and USDA must include provisions clearly stating inclusion of local governments. In the NEPA process, the USDA must retain similar language in their NEPA procedures that “A lead agency may designate any Federal, State, Tribal, or local agency that has jurisdiction by law or special expertise with respect to any environmenta issue involved in a proposal as a cooperating agency." See 40 C.F.R. §§ 1501.7 and 1501.8.

Public lands and the resources on them influence the custom and culture of the County. The relationship between the County and the federal agencies is key to ensuring resources are managed successfully and the County’s custom and culture of using public lands for multiple uses remains intact. The County and federal agencies have worked together in the past on resource management concerns and issues and will continue to strengthen and build those relationships to ensure that all stakeholders are at the table when discussing resource management on public lands within the County

While USDA has the authority to conduct a rulemaking process to create regulations that implement laws and policies that ensures transparency and public involvement in the development of regulations that affect natural resources and publid lands, the County contends that more often than not, a departmental “Rule” would have significant impacts on the environment, applies across the Department nationwide and thus warrants an analysis through an environmental impact statement under NEPA. Currently, “Rulemaking" is not required to undergo the same process as NEPA and there is no cooperating agency component, beyond the public comment period, and in this instance, the USFS rightfully chose to conduct EIS to better engage with stakeholders and cooperators; however, it doesn't go far enough and the Forest Service should, at the very least, allow the states to participate as cooperating agencies in this NEPA process

Further, NEPA is required for all “major federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment." Most federal Rules, if implemented, will undoubtedly impact the socioeconomics of local jurisdictions where federal land exists for example the RACR of which the USFS appropriately conducted a NEPA analysis. The County maintains that Rules impacting states and counties should allow a similar cooperating agency engagement process as NEPA and at the very least, USDA should modify its Rulemaking process to create a “cooperating agency” component similar to NEPA for engagement with states and their agencies. This would ensure better consistency with state and local government plans

Unfortunately, the USFS is once again attempting to approach the RACR alone. Even though this proposed action is to rescind the Rule, the Forest Service should recognize that it is our forests and communities that will bear the brunt of uncertainty in planning, projects, and litigation that will ultimately result from any modification of the RACR. Serving a cooperating agencies will also benefit us, as we attempt to navigate changes in management and ultimately convey those changes to our constituents.

The USFS would benefit from the meaningful engagement of Wyoming counties in the development of its EIS. Bevond an exhibited commitment supporting the USFS through project and planning efforts for decades, Wyoming counties haye local expertise, data, and jurisdiction of the lands impacted by the RACR that would benefit the EIS. While the County cannot demand the Forest Service include our counties and state as cooperators, as governmental partners we are requesting the USFS change its current direction and at the very least allow the state to coordinate as a cooperating agency.

## B. National Forest Management Act

Preceding the NFMA was the Forest and Rangeland Renewable Resources Planning Act of 1974 (RPA), which initially required, among other things, the Forest Service to develop land and resource management plans for units of the National Forest System. Later, the NFMA further expanded the Forest Service planning obligations and established the statutory authority applicable today to the Forest Service and the USDA. The NFMA currently serves as a key statutory backbone for the formation of land management and forest planning regulations. Under the NFMA, 16 U.S.C. §§ 1600-1687, the Forest Service is mandated to promulgate regulations for the development and revision of land management plans to guide management of land within the agency.4 The NFMA requires the Secretary of Agriculture to develop regulations under the principles of the Multiple Use and Sustained Yield Act (MUSYA) and to set out further processes for the development and revision of land management plans.

The NFMA guides the development and revision of plans, environmental considerations, resource management guidelines, and general guidelines for land management plans. Further, NFMA requires that the agency's planning regulations must adhere to NEPA and consider the impact to multiple resources, including impacts to wildlife, timber resources, recreation, and grazing under a guidance of multiple use and sustained yield but the Act does not prescribe or dictate to the agency how each resource must be managed bevond a multiple use and sustained yield lens.º

The National Forest Management Act (NFMA) governs the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) and requires the agency to “coordinate”. The NFMA requirements are as follows:

[T]he Secretary of Agriculture shall develop, maintain, and, as appropriate, revise land and resource management plans for units of the National Forest System, coordinated with the land and resource management planning processes of State and local governments and other Federal agencies (16 U.S.C. § 1604(a))

The fact that the USFS is directed to “coordinate” with local governments implies, by its plain meaning, that the USFS must engage in a process that involves more than simply “considering" the plans and policies of local governments; it must attempt to achieve compatibility between USFS plans and local land use plans. Additionally, the Forest Service is mandated to “engage the public, including State and local governments early throughout the planning process." 36 C.F.R § 219.4(a)(1).

The USFS is also obligated to perform a consistency review. For development of forest plans, the forest Service shall review the planning and land use policies of State and local governments where relevant to the plan area. The results of the review shall be displayed in the EIS. 36 C.F.R. 219.4(b)(2)

Substantial progress has been made over the past fifty years to build not only the regulatory framework to implement NEPA and NFMA, but also a culture for cooperation and collaboration with local governments throughout the NEPA process. In addition to regulations, agencies have expressed lessons learned from implementing NEPA and best practices to fulfill NEPA's purposes. The USFS’s Guidebook titled “County Governments and the USDA Forest Service: A Guidebook for Working Together" (Guidebook) to discusses the requirement that agencies must provide a meaningful participation and allocate responsibilities to comply with the law

The Guidebook contains best practices that are not always directly citing NEPA, NFMA, CEQ, or USDA and agency regulations. These best practices have grown out of lived experience working together. The Guidebook illustrates that the outcomes are better when federal agencies and county governments “work together to reach solutions that are politically and socially durable and ensure the long-term sustainability of communities and natural resources. It is through working together, at multiple stages of planning and project implementation, that we will achieve true success."

Our goal as cooperating agencies is to help expedite NEPA, provide local and technical data and information, help agencies come to defensible and durable decisions, and support the cooperative spirit that distinguishes NEPA from all other acts of congress, It is our goal of safeguarding and furthering NEPA’s cooperative code that guides our comments on cooperating agencies under USDA’s NEPA procedures,

Public lands and the resources on them influence the custom and culture of the County. The relationship between the County and the federal agencies is key to ensuring resources are managed successfully and the County's custom and culture of using public lands for multiple uses remains intact, The County and agencies have worked together in the past on resource management concerns and issues and will continue to strengthen and build those relationships to ensure that all stakeholders are at the table when discussing resource management on public lands within the County.

## C. USDA 2012 Planning Rule

The 2012 Planning Rule guides the development, amendment, and revision of land management plans on National Forest System lands. Federal law mandates the Forest Service to develop land management plans for units of the National Forest and Grassland System and promulgate regulations to guide the Forest Service planning process. As federal law provides statutory authority for establishing planning regulations, the 2012 Planning Rule sets out the procedural and substantive requirements for land management plans. As discussed, Land management plans set the overall management direction and guidance for each national forest and associated lands. Land management plans should guide the carrying out of projects and activities by providing a general direction of uses within each national forest, prairie, and grassland

In all stages of land management planning, plans must use the best available scientific information to inform the planning process as required by the 2012 Planning Rule. This “best available scientific information" used must be accompanied by documentation that identifies what information was determined to be the best available scientific information. explains the basis for that determination, and explains how the information was applied to the issues considered. Ultimately, the best available scientific information should guide decision making through the planning process,

Furthermore, in the planning process public participation is afforded through specific regulatory requirements of “outreach," to be conducted by the responsible official of the planning process. Outreach includes engaging Tribes, other Federal agencies, State and local governments, individuals, and public and private organizations or entities

Additionally, through the development of plans, the responsible official must coordinate with other public planning efforts, including reviewing the planning and land use policies of federally recognized Indian Tribes, Alaska Native Corporations, other Federal agencies, and State and local governments, where relevant to the plan area. This directive to coordinate with other local planning efforts allows for more effective coordination throughout all the planning processes The result of this coordination in land management review must be displayed in the EIS under NEPA for the associated plan. This coordination with other interests must include specified considerations including:

The objectives of federally recognized Indian Tribes, Alaska Native Corporations, other Federal agencies, and State and local governments, as expressed in their plans and policies;

▪ The compatibility and interrelated impacts of these plans and policies;

■ Opportunities for the plan to address the impacts identified or to contribute to joint objectives;

Opportunities to resolve or reduce conflicts within the context of developing the plan's desired conditions or objectives

Each plan developed or revised must contain sustainability considerations to provide for social, economic, and ecological sustainability within the Forest Service's authority.7 As part of sustainability considerations, ecological sustainability and social and economic sustainability must both be addressed. Both categories require plans and revisions to consider differing factors in the planning process. Providing for cooperating agency status along with consistency review of state and local plans provides the foundation of successful long-term planning and rulemaking implementation.

## V.Roadless Areas Conservation Rule Environmental Impact Statement Considerations

## A. Alternatives

The USFS has properly determined it should draft an EIS for its compliance with NEPA. The Notice of Intent describes two alternatives - the No Action (maintaining the RACR) and the Proposed Action (rescission of the RACR). For all detailed statements, under 42 U.S.C. 4332(C)(iii), there must be “a reasonable range of alternatives to the proposed agency action, including an analysis of any negative environmental impacts of not implementing the proposed agency action in the case of a no action alternatives, that are technically and economically feasible, and meet the purpose and need of the proposal."

Over the years, courts have clarified what counts as a reasonable range of alternatives. While agencies have some flexibility, they are not free to ignore important options. Courts have emphasized that agencies should consider a wide and comprehensive set of alternatives, especially for projects they manage directly

It is important to avoid making the same mistake in this current USFS EIS. However, agencies are not required to consider every possible alternative. The Supreme Court has stated that agencies do not need to include every conceivable option, only those that are reasonable and relevant to the project's goals. For legal sufficiency of the EIS, we encourage the USFS to develop and analyze at least one additional alternative, that is technically and economically feasible and meets the purpose and need of the proposal

## B. Impacts of establishing RACR

The Notice of Intent solicits public comments regarding the potential impacts of rescinding the RACR. It is important tc clarify that rescinding RACR does not authorize any specific projects, roads, or timber sales. Nonetheless, the implementation of RACR has had observable effects on Wyoming's communities and forest ecosystems. Historically forest management practices aimed at achieving desired ecological and economic conditions have been limited or foregone, resulting in tangible consequences. These include a decline in timber sale volumes and revenues, reduced financial payments to local counties, and missed opportunities to mitigate fire risks through activities such as salvage logging of trees affected by Mountain Pine Beetles (MPB) or wildfires

Additionally, restrictions have impeded fence maintenance for grazing allotments, and several forest products companies have ceased operations. The absence of proactive management has also led to missed opportunities for fire risk reduction in municipal watersheds, potentially impacting community safety and water quality. Overall, the rescission of RACR could influence forest management strategies, economic stability, and ecological health within the region, underscoring the need for a comprehensive review of the Rule's implications since approved in 2001

## C. Impacts of rescinding RACR

Again, the rescinding of the RACR does not grant authority for additional management decisions beyond existing regulations. Decisions such as constructing roads for commercial timber harvesting remain subject to compliance with the Forest Plan, the NEPA, and other applicable environmental laws. Nonetheless, rescinding RACR could open avenues for proactive landscape management aimed at addressing various ecological and operational challenges, including wildfire mitigation, insect infestations, disease control, watershed health, wildlife habitat preservation, and the resilience of old growth forests

Furthermore, the implementation of RACR has had notable impacts, particularly in Wyoming, where several mills ceased operations following the rule's enactment. Studies have also indicated correlations between RACR and fire dynamics within IRAs. Data suggest that IRAs experience a higher incidence of fire starts, increased severity of fires, and larger burned areas compared to non-IRA regions. While topography and fire management capabilities significantly influence these outcomes, the data imply that IRAs are more susceptible to high-severity fires and extensive burn areas

It is important to recognize that, regardless of the management alternative chosen, a substantial portion of roadless areas will remain permanently inaccessible due to inherent topographical features, isolation, resource values, and cost-benefit considerations. These factors inherently limit the potential for development or resource extraction in these regions ensuring their continued status as roadless landscapes

## D. Roadless Values

The RACR documents repeatedly characterize IRAs as having the following values – 1) high quality or undisturbed soil, water, and air, 2) sources of public drinking water, 3) diversity of plant and animal communities, 4) habitat for T&E proposed, candidate, and sensitive species and for species dependent of large, undisturbed areas, 5) Primitive, Semi primitive, non-motorized, and Semi-primitive motorized recreation, 6) Reference landscapes, 7) natural appearing landscapes with high scenic quality, and 8) traditional cultural properties and sacred sites. While true, these values are not limited to IRAs; in fact, they are part and parcel of multiple use objectives and values across the entire Nationaļ Forest System.

This is an example of why Weston County believes that the best forest policy decisions are accomplished through robust local engagement. The County advocates for a tailored approach to forest management, emphasizing the importance of addressing the specific ecological and management needs of individual forest areas. The County supports the USFSs recission of its current nationally driven planning strategy, which instead empowers local forests with greater authority to modify and update their management plans. This localized approach would better accommodate the unique environmenta conditions and community interests associated with each forest

## E. Roadless Area Conservation Rule Maps Must Be Updated with More Accurate Information

The USFS IRA maps originate from the agency's Roadless Area Review and Evaluation (RARE) RARE I and RARE II initiatives conducted in the 1970s. These maps, which served as the basis for designating areas within the RACR, are now considered outdated due to their reliance on antiquated data. Specifically, the use of RARE II maps to identify IRAs for the RACR has resulted in the inclusion of numerous areas within Wyoming's national forests that feature well-maintained roads, active forest management practices, and lands designated as suitable for timber harvesting according to forest management plans

The decision at the time by the Secretary of Agriculture to apply the RACR to "all lands within an inventoried roadles area boundary" was made with the understanding that many of these areas already contained existing roads and had been subject to approved forest management projects, including timber harvesting. According to 36 CFR § 294.11, the definition of IRAs allows for the "update or revision" of the RACR maps through the land management planning process However, the Forest Service has not established a formal process to identify or implement such updates or revisions Despite the RACR providing an opportunity for map updates, the agency has largely failed to revise or correct the IRA maps, with only minor exceptions, thereby maintaining outdated designations that do not reflect current land use and management activities. This process has been flawed from the beginning and updated mapping through forest level land planning must be the new chartered course of action with the USFS

## F. RACR disregards local forest plans

Wyoming counties actively participate as cooperating agencies in the development of forest plans. The forest planning process is designed to guide the management direction of forest lands for ten to fifteen years. However, the RÂCR upset the direction contained in plans by overlaying IRA maps indiscriminately across planning and project areas.

In certain instances, the RACR overlaid IRA maps on areas already identified in the forest plan for certain protections or lands that were not included in the suitable timber base. These lands now have duplicative protections. On the other hand IRA maps were also overlaid on thousands of acres identified by forest plans as suitable timber base. Sometimes referred to as suitable lands, these acres were identified in the planning process as being available and appropriate for timber production on a sustained yield basis. Lands not compatible with management goals (e.g. set aside for recreation, old-

growth management, etc.) were excluded, that are biophysically unsustainable (e.g. poor soils, steep slopes, etc.), or economically or operationally impracticable (e.g, inaccessible terrain, extreme harvesting costs, etc.) are excluded from the suitable timber base in the planning process. In other words, the USFS has existing tools at its disposal inside the 2012 Planning Rule to protect, conserve, manage, or develop these lands

The RACR also overrides Forest Plan direction that would have otherwise allowed the Forest Service to implement ongoing forest management projects. Forest Service Line Officers have minimal authority to implement proactive management projects in IRAs to reduce the risk of catastrophic wildfire and insect epidemics, which include the removal of timber as a byproduct of those treatments. The risk of protracted and expensive litigation has also discouraged line officers from applying the exceptions present in the RACR. This has hampered the Forest Service's ability to implemen proactive measures needed to reduce the threat of catastrophic fire and MPB epidemics in municipal watersheds.

## G. Private Property Rights

As stated earlier, Weston County is rich in federal resources such as timber harvesting and production, farming, ranching energy development, tourism and recreation, which all contribute heavily to the heritage of the County. Rangeland used by livestock and agricultural producers continues to be the dominant land use and federal agencies should consider the effects their decisions will have on neighboring private lands

Furthermore, access to, or restrictions from, crossing federal, state, or county managed lands should not entail encumbrances or constraints on private property. Private property rights are the cornerstone of our County and must be protected to ensure that our continued customs and culture remain intact. When an agency decision or proposed action will have a negative impact to the current use of neighboring private lands, that federal undertaking may not be supported by the County.

## VI.Consistency with Weston County Natural Resource Management Plan

As mentioned earlier, the State of Wyoming is unique as County commissions have been charged with the responsibility for the preservation of the custom and culture of Wyoming counties in matters relating to NEPA and federal land planning. Since the customs, culture, and history of the County are inseparably tied to the use of and access to land and resources managed by federal agencies to ensure state and federal agencies manage lands and resources in the County in a way that protects and improves the health, safety, environment, and well-being of our citizens, and improves the performance of the economy without imposing unacceptable or unreasonable costs or impacts to local social structure (Wyoming Statute [W.S.] 18-5-208(a))

Meaningful cooperating agency engagement, at the earliest practicable time, strengthens informed federal decision making required by NEPA. Congress provided in Section 101 of NEPA, “recognizing the profound impact of man's activity on the interrelations of all components of the natural environment... declares that it is the continuing policy of the Federal Government, in cooperation with State and local governments... to create and maintain conditions under which man and nature can exist in productive harmony, and fulfill the social, economic, and other requirements of present and future generations of Americans." Therefore, by design, NEPA requires federal decisions to be made in cooperation with state and local partners. Clarity of how federal departments and agencies cooperate with state and local governments remains an essential piece of NEPA implementing regulations, and one that must remain in the agency's NEPA procedures.

The inclusion of special expertise as a basis for our comments corresponds with NEPA’s expressed provision that allows lead agencies to designate “any Federal, State, Tribal, or local agency that has jurisdiction by law or special expertise with respect to any environmental impact..." Counties across the nation have varying authorities to develop or enforce environmental standards, but each county has special expertise. Limiting comments to local agencies that are authorized to develop and enforce environmental standards does not conform to the qualifications required for us to be cooperating agencies NEPA.

Restricting comments to those governments authorized to develop and enforce environmental standards also disregards NEPA's clear interdisciplinary approach expressed in 42 U.S.C. 4332(A) and the Congressional declaration to use all practical means and measures “in a manner calculated to foster and promote the general welfare, to create conditions under which man and nature can exist in productive harmony, and fulfill the social, economic and other requirements of present and future generations of Americans" in 42 U.S.C. 4331.

In addition, federal agencies are required to identify and analyze the impacts to local economies and community culture when making decisions. The County encourages federal agencies to be as consistent as allowed by law with the Converse County Natural Resource Management Plan (County Plan). The County Plan specifically recognizes that the private sector is the best engine for economic growth; regulatory policies should respect the role of state and local governments; and federal land policies and regulations should be effective, consistent, sensible, and understandable. A County Plan while not required, can aide this analysis

Although the RACR stands to impact hundreds of communities across the country, the USFS must adequately consider state and local plans and provide a description of how those plans were given consideration as required by the 2012 Planning Rule and NEPA. At a minimum, the USFS should include a list of the local land use plans that are within the EIS boundary. However, even an impacted county list would not meet the requirements for coordination and consistency

It must be recognized that the USDA and its agencies cannot meet its goals for our Nation’s public lands to continue to provide minerals, energy, forage, timber, and recreational opportunities, as well as habitat, protected water supplies, and landscapes that resist and recover from drought, wildfire, and other disturbances, on its own. Nor can we meet our goals of maintaining our unique cultural heritage with thriving economies on our own. We must work together

Weston County believes that any federal agencies approach of waiting until the final stage to address inconsistencies in the EIS is flawed. To encourage consistency with the County Plan and for the USFSs convenience, we have identified a few priority policy positions that are impacted by this EIS. This is not a comprehensive list and USFS is encouraged to review the entirety of the County Plan for more details;

19. Livestock grazing management decisions shall be made based on the best available scientific information that is applicable to the rangeland resources in Weston County

22. Federal agencies should support livestock grazing where appropriate on federally owned and operated lands as an integral part of habitat management

23. Full site-specific economic and resource analysis of suspending grazing for allotment closures should be completed within one-year of closure,

25. The reduction of domestic livestock grazing animal unit months to provide additional forage for another species or strictly for conservation purposes is not supported by Weston County

31. Federal agencies should review and incorporate legal and credible data collected by a permittee contractors or subcontractors of a permittee, qualified team, or local government for use in management decisions.

33. Grazing rest prescriptions related to either wildfires or prescribed burns should be determined on a site. specific basis. Post-fire grazing will not be limited when unbiased post-fire monitoring and evaluation produces relevant, accurate data demonstrating that grazing will not unduly harm the range

34. Livestock grazing should return to pre-fire levels when post-fire monitoring data shows established objectives have been met or have been achieved to an extent allowed by the site potential. Require the use of credible data as previously defined to make these determinations.

The County cannot state clearly enough the importance of our ability to access federal lands to drive vibrant economic communities. The USFS must adequately consider in the socioeconomic analysis the mineral and timber contributions to the counties and state. The USFS must include a robust socioeconomic analysis clearly demonstrating the differences between management prescriptions in the Alternatives, which includes impacts to the tax base (royalties, rents or bonus bids, severance taxes, ad valorum taxes, sales and use tax employment income, and direct and indirect employment.)

Additionally, Weston County has always been concerned that the Rule's identification process for roadless will ultimately be treated as a form of designation. The designation of wilderness and roadless areas in our national forests will have significant impacts on our ability to access those federal lands; thereby impacting the economics of our communities. The USFS must also consider the cumulative impacts of existing and proposed management restrictions on the local economics, custom and culture. For example, while the County does support proactive stewardship of our forests,

management decisions must be balanced with other resource uses and generally the County does not support overly restrictive management directives such special designations of wilderness, wild and scenic rivers or roadless areas

For the USFSs convenience we have identified a few priority policy positions from our County Plan that are impacted by this EIS. This is not a comprehensive list and USFS is encouraged to review the entirety of the County Plan for more details:

## 3.3.4 Special Management Areas Resource Management Objective (Page 41):

B. No new special designation or management areas are created in Weston County without approval from the County.

## 3.3.4 Special Management Areas Priority Statements (Pages 41-42)

1. Weston County should be a cooperating agency on any action to designate any special management on designation areas.

2. Federal agencies shall consult and coordinate with Weston County as early as possible when considering the designation of new special designation areas and should be consistent with the Weston County Natura Resource Management Plan to the maximum extent possible

3. Any proposed special management area designation shall undergo analysis of the economic and environmental cumulative impact to Weston County's custom, culture, and economy

5. Weston County does not support future designations of new special management or designation areas in the County, including, Wild and Scenic Rivers, Wilderness, or Wilderness Study Areas, lands with wilderness characteristics, Areas of Critical Environmental Concern, Roadless Areas. Any proposed designation shall be coordinated with the County and undergo analysis of the impact to Weston County's economy including a pre-existing condition analysis

7. Federal agencies should consult with Weston County when evaluating whether lands and the multiple uses on them qualify as “conserved lands" under 30x30.

8. Protecting private property rights should be the greatest priority when attempting to fulfill the 30x30 goals outlined in Executive Order 14008.

10. Weston County opposes the America the Beautiful (30x30) program, including its objective of permanently preserving 30% of the Nation's lands in its natural state by 2030, or any similar program that will set aside and prevent the productive use of millions of acres of Weston County's lands

11. Weston County opposes the designation of lands in Weston County for the purposes as expressed in the America the Beautiful (30x30) program which may restrict public access to such land and which may prevent the development of and productive use of the resources on or within such lands.

12. Weston County supports the continued private ownership of land in the County, recognizing the Nation's need for domestic sources of minerals, energy, timber, food, and fiber.

16. Unless lands or waters are given a special management or designation in a respective agency’s planning document, all public lands in Weston County should be managed for multiple use as outlined in the Multiple Use Sustained Yield Act and Federal Land Policy Management Act.

## Vll. Socioeconomics Must Be Adequately Considered in the Environmental Impact Statement

Economic impacts do matter. Access to federally administered lands and resources are critical to ensure the socioeconomic well-being, custom, culture and stability of our communities. In Weston County, lands under federal or state control and decisions made for public land management agencies can directly impact the service and non-service industries, public accessibility, and the demographics of an area. Effective coordination and consultation between the County, federal and state agencies is critical to ensuring that land management agencies thoroughly consider the effects that proposed actions have on custom, culture, and economic stability, conservation and use of the environment and

natural resources in the County along with multiple use. Counties receive revenue from federal lands in many ways including timber harvesting, mineral leasing and development, agriculture, recreation, travel and tourism, etc. Any curtailment of access to public lands will directly impact the socioeconomics of the County, which must be disclosed in the NEPA EIS.

The USFS must analyze for the cumulative impacts to counties specific to the management decisions under each Alternative and how they will affect local and state economic well-being along with impacts to state and private adjacent lands. In addition, the analysis should consider increased costs to state and local communities associated with a higher risk for fire management, disease and insects due to limited management direction in RACR areas.

For the USFSs convenience we have identified a few priority policy positions from our County Plan that are impacted by this EIS. This is not a comprehensive list and USFS is encouraged to review the entirety of the County Plan for more details:

## 7.4.3 Economic and Socioeconomic Resource Management Objectives (Page 143):

A. The socioeconomic and economic viability of Weston County is prioritized, protected, and enhanced in all federal actions or decisions

B. Weston County is included early in the scoping process whenever an agency action or decision may impact the economic or socioeconomic viability of the County

## 7.4.4 Economic and Socioeconomic Priority Statements (Page 143-144)

1. Weston County requires consultation and coordination from federal agencies at the earliest time possible for any proposed action, change of existing activities, newly permitted activities, or changes in regulations that may affect the economic basis of the County

2. Federal agencies should support continued access to natural resources development/use on federal lands to maintain economically viable communities in Weston County

3. Weston County supports “no net loss" in the County economic base due to federal agency decisions

4. Federal agencies should include Weston County in all discussions regarding mitigation, if necessary, to protect the economic base of the County

5. Federal agencies should support the analysis of social and economic factors at the lowest possible level, such as on a County-wide basis, in addition to consideration on a statewide or national scale

6. Federal agencies should promote the economic and socioeconomic growth of Weston County and engage in consultation and coordination between federal agencies and the County regarding any issues and activities on public land that affect or influence the County's economic and socioeconomic viability

8. Weston County supports the achievement of a sustainable balance between economic, recreational, and conservation use of lands for economic growth and quality of life

11. Weston County requires a full analysis by the federal agencies of the impact each proposed decision or federal action wili have on the local economy. If it is determined that the decision wili have significant negative impact on the local economy, the alternative/decision is not supported.

Finally, the USDA must specifically consider and include the following in its socioeconomic analysis components through NEPA

Potential cumulative impacts of reduced mineral development or timber harvesting and overlapping land use restrictions on land allocations that directly eliminate or restrict leasing and development activities that, in turn impact local economies, public services, and labor markets,

Consider an in-depth analysis on where funding streams will be recovered if mineral leasing and development and timber harvesting is eliminated or significantly reduced long-term and where overlapping land allocation occur

Include the effects associated with state and national environmental impacts on programs going forward with the decrease of mineral leasing and development and timber harvesting impacted negatively by reduction of associated royalties, rents, severance taxes, bonus bids, sales and use taxes and property tax collections

## VIII. Conclusion

The County fully supports recission of RACR and returning the decision-making authority for roadless areas to Forest Supervisors through the forest planning process, which empowers states and local governments to work with the USFS to make management decisions that reflect the diverse ecological, social, and economic conditions that exist across national forests, counties, and states.

We appreciate the opportunity to provide input on the Forest Service's intention to prepare an EIS regarding the RACR. As the government entities closest to the land and most impacted by national forest management decisions, Wyoming counties have a deep and sustained interest in ensuring forest policy is flexible, locally tailored, and grounded in contemporary science, land use realities, and legal frameworks.

Should vou have questions or require additional information, do not hesitate to contact Weston County Commissioner Chairman Nathan Todd at ntodd@westongov.com or our natural resource policy advisor Dru Palmer at dru@wyoming.com

Sincerely,
