# September 19, 2025

Director, Ecosystem Management Coordination 201 14thStreet, SW Mailstop 1108 Washington, DC 20250-1124 Submitted via Federal eRulemaking Portal

Re: Notice of Intent to Environmental Impact Statement for Roadless Area Conservation on National Forest System Lands

Dear Director Kinder:

As a Cooperating Agency and the home to the Powder River Ranger District of the Bighorn National Forest, Johnson County registers the following comments on the United States Forest Service (USFS) Notice of Intent to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) regarding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (RACR) on the national forest.

Johnson County serves as a legal extension of the State of Wyoming with statutory and regulatory authority at the local level. County governments are actively engaged in the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) processes to help our federal partners create, revise and amend management plans that encourage productive and enjoyable harmony between man and his environment. 42 U.S.C. § 4321. Wyoming counties take our responsibility as local governments seriously and strive to ensure our communities are economically vibrant, safe, and healthy places tolive, work, and recreate. Wyo. Stat. § 18-5-208(b).

Well-managed national forests are a crucial component of achieving our goals as local governments. Federal Executive Order (EO) 14072 Strengthening the Nation's Forests Communities, and Local Economies, recognizes this relationship and expressly connects local economies with forest management activities. (EO, pg. 24851). As a co-regulator, Johnson County has prepared comprehensive land use and natural resource plans to serve as the basis for communicating and coordinating with the federal government and its agencies on land and natural resource management issues. These natural resource management issues include ecosystem services, water, wildlife habitat, industrial development, and recreation

Communication, coordination, and collaboration with the USFS are vital as management decisions can significantly impact the customs, culture, and socioeconomics of Johnson County We look forward to serving as an active partner throughout the development of the EIS to help the USFS in crafting a reasonable range of alternatives, ensuring a durable management framework, with the overarching goal of advancing locally supported conservation based on the needs of specific forests, community safety, resilient and working forests that meet the USFS's multiple use and sustained yield mission.

## I. Executive Summary

We hold that land management decisions for the national forests in Wyoming are best made as close to “on-the-ground" as possible, in coordination and cooperation with state and local governments. The governing authority concerning the management of national forests in Wyoming should occur under the 2012 Forest Planning Rule in compliance with NEPA. This protects our forests and communities from one-size-fits-all rules and decisions from the Washington office and allows for better, more durable decisions that reflect the needs of the forests and our communities.

Johnson County is supportive of the USFS's efforts to review the RACR. Our support is not based on a perceived need for commercial timber roads to be developed everywhere within the forests of Wyoming, but on the principle that forest managers - and their state and local partners - need to have the authority to make management decisions that reflect the diverse ecological, social, and economic conditions that exist across forests, counties, and states.

Wyoming boasts a diversity of counties with unique histories and values based on distinct forests with varying ecology and opportunities. Local governments in Wyoming work tirelessly with USFS partners to develop appropriate frameworks within the cooperating agency process for forest plans that reflect and appreciate the diversity within our forests and communities. We desperately need forest managers to have the authority and flexibility to work with us to address contemporary challenges and opportunities. The forest planning process is designed to provide flexibility, durability, and community buy-in necessary to promote healthy forests and communities across the nation.

EO 13132 – Federalism, is especially applicable to the concept of local forest planning in which it directs federal agencies to treat state and local governments as collaborative partners. Section 2(a) of the EO states "Federalism is rooted in the belief that issues that are not national in scope or significance are most appropriately addressed by the level of government closest to the people." Section 2(i) of the EO provides, "The national government should be deferential to the States when taking action that affects the policymaking discretion of the States and should act only with the greatest caution where State or local governments have identified uncertainties regarding the constitutional or statutory authority of the national government."

When the RACR was developed in 2001, it superimposed maps drawn in the 1970s for potential Wilderness designation without consideration of the impacts it would have on existing forest plan direction. Additionally, in the development of the RACR, the USFS failed to engage state and local governments as cooperating agencies under NEPA. Consequently, the RACR sidelined the very governments impacted the most by the establishment of the rule

Addressing RACR is the first step to returning forest management tools to millions of acres of national forest lands in Wyoming. Johnson County supports the Department's proposal to evaluate the RACR and return decisionmaking authority to the forests. Doing so will yield more flexible, politically durable, and locally supported outcomes, compared to a one-size-fits-all rule from the Washington Office. This comment letter (1) summarizes Wyoming's on-the-ground experience under RACR, (2) explains why forest-plan-level decisions are the right scale for roadless area management, and (3) offers specific recommendations for coopcrating agency

engagement and the development of reasonable alternatives to ensure a durable outcome and effective EIS.

## II. Background

The Bighorn National Forest is one of the oldest national forests in Wyoming, created February 22, 1887, pre-statehood of Wyoming. It was initially established by President Grover Cleveland as the Big Horn Forest Reserve. Today, the forest spans 1.1 million acres

## A. Roadless Acres in Wyoming

Of the 193 million acres of land across 154 national forests and 20 national grasslands approximately 30% (58.2 million acres) are identified as Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRA) These IRAs are predominantly located in the west, with national forests in Wyoming containing 3,257,000 IRA. The Bighorn has 689,770 IRA acres which is 62% of the forest

## B. RACR Represents a top-down approach to forestry management RACR was developed in DC, not Wyoming

"In just 14 months, the Clinton administration restricted management of 58 million acres — nearly a third of all national forest lands — under a sweeping one-size-fits-all policy. That pace was unprecedented for a decision of such magnitude. And while it made headlines, it trampled carefully developed forest plans that had been crafted under the National Forest Management Act (NFMA). These plans were not abstract exercises; they were the result of years of collaboration among local communities, environmental groups, ranchers, firefighters, water managers, and state agencies. Forest supervisors had worked painstakingly with stakeholders to balance multiple uses and environmental stewardship. All of that was cast aside in favor of a quick national fix. The process also cheated the public by shortchanging the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), which is supposed to ensure honest analysis and meaningful public involvement."(Cables. 2025).

## III. RACR's application in Wyoming

Following are Record of Decision dates for current Forest Plans for the Bighorn National Forest from 9/30/2005:

The 2005 Bighorn NF Forest Plan Revision FEIS (p 3-326) references the revised definition of "Inventoried Roadless Areas" from 36 CFR 294.11, and states that “The 2005 roadless inventory was completed as part of the revision analysis process. This inventory will be used for all Revised Forest Plan implementation activities, and replaces all previous roadless inventories."However, that apparently did not happen as planned (note - we're still researching details)

## A. Conflicts with Wildlife Habitat Restoration

Wyoming Game & Fish Department's (WGFD) Statewide Habitat Plan (SHP, 2020) delineates Restoration Habitat Areas - places that “can and should be actively restored to achieve greater wildlife value,"identified by regional teams of aquatic and terrestrial biologists. WGFD publishes both Terrestrial and Aquatic Restoration Habitat Priority arcas to guide partncrs on

where wildlife habitat treatments are most likely to succeed over the next five years. These priorities apply across ownerships, including National Forest System lands.

Because Johnson County's IRA's, many of WGFD Terrestrial Restoration Habitat Priorities are within IRA's. Where that overlap occurs, RACR's prohibitions on road construction and its tight limits on timber removal materially constrain the very actions the SHP calls “active restoration"- for example, aspen regeneration that depends on conifer removal, sagebrush-mountain-shrub restoration, or targeted fuels work to restore big-game transitional and winter range. The result is fewer acres treated, higher unit costs, and lost windows of ecological opportunity in precisely the landscapes WGFD and local partners have prioritized.

## B. Drinking water infrastructure critical to Wyoming communities

Forests, particularly national forests, are the headwaters for Western communities: the USFS reports that in the West, national forests and grasslands supply drinking water to nearly 90% of people served by public water systems, and USFS lands contribute a disproportionately large share of the region's surface water supply (https://www.fs.usda.gov/about-agency/features/newresearch-reveals-how-critical-forests-are-drinking-water-supply). In Wyoming, the management (or lack thereof) of vast amounts of IRAs in critical watersheds can and have posed considerable complications with source water protection for local communities. The City of Buffalo and six of our neighbor community's municipal watersheds are in the Bighorn National Forest where and 2/3 of the acreage in those watersheds is in IRAs. These three watersheds (HUC 100901010101 100901010102, 100901010103) consists of 75% IRA's or Federally Designated Wilderness That is 75% of those watersheds that have limited management tools to effectively manage lands to prevent catastrophic wildfire and reduce treatment costs for safe drinking water.

RACR complicates scaling the kind of proactive, plan-consistent source-water protection where priority acres lie inside IRAs - precisely where road access for treatment corridors may be needed to reach stands, install control lines, or remove hazardous fuels. The water-quality stakes are not hypothetical: federal science agencies document that severe wildfire can trigger years of elevated turbidity, sediment, nutrients, and metals in drinking-water supplies, driving costly emergency operations, dredging, and treatment upgrades (https://www.usgs.gov/missionareas/water-resources/science/water-quality-after-wildfire#overview). Given that RACR restricts the very tools (mechanical fuels work, strategic access) needed to pre-empt such impacts in certain watersheds, its one-size-fits-all constraints are misaligned with local needs in Wvoming

## C. Effects on Wyoming's Forest Products Companies

The volume of timber sold from all national forest lands in Wyoming dropped 55% from FY 1999 to FY 2000 and continued at approximately that reduced level through FY 2003: it wasn't until FY 2004 that the volume of timber sold from national forest lands in Wyoming exceeded the FY 1999 level. That decline in timber sale volumes was the cumulative result of several factors, of which the 2001 RACR decision was notably significant. Four sawmills in Wyoming shut down permanently during the period 2005 to 2009 including a mill in the county immediately adjacent to Johnson County and the Bighorn National Forest. Each of those sawmills depended heavily on timber sales from the national forests and their closure can be

attributed almost entirely to the uncertainty about timber quantity and quality from the adjacent national forests

## D. Risk of Fires

As pointed out in the NOI, nearly half of all Inventoried Roadless Areas are now rated as High or Very High wildfire risk. In Wyoming, according to Forest Service data, 2.1 million of the 3.3 million acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas are mapped as High or Very High wildfire risk and identified as Forest Health and Fuels Emergency Lands

## E. Built on Outdated Maps

In 2001, the Forest Service promulgated the Roadless Area Conservation Rule to prohibit road building and timber harvest within IRA's as identified on RARE I and RARE II mapping from the 1970s with no adjustments to the boundaries to reflect management actions that had occurred in the interim.

In today's world, with modern mapping and remote sensing technology available to anyone willing to learn and an emphasis on using "best available science" in the 2012 Planning Rule, it's hard to imagine that the US Forest Service is still relying on 50-year old roadless area maps that were hand-drawn with no intention of them being used as a basis for national policy and restrictions half a century later.

Because the RACR used outdated RARE II maps to identify Inventoried Roadless Areas, the national forests in Wyoming contain numerous areas within "Inventoried Roadless Areas" that. in fact, have well-used and maintained roads, areas with historic forest management, and have been identified as suitable timberlands for ongoing forest management. There is also at least one developed Forest Service campground within an Inventoried Roadless Area. In particular, the RACR Inventoried Roadless Areas for the Bighorn National Forest contain areas with approximately 390 miles of Forest Service System Roads and associated history of forest management. The following photograph shows a well-established Forest Service Road within an Inventoried Roadless Area on the Bighorn National Forest.

![](images/f2fc988ea9ea11d80af7d95809f4267a0ce38b7462bf97521691ba818fc1ca58.jpg)

## F. Technical Corrections

Theoretically, the updated definition of Inventoried Roadless Area in the RACR includes an opportunity to update or revise the maps through the land management planning process. The results have been mixed.

In 2021, the Bridger-Teton proposed, and the Chief authorized, corrections to IRA boundaries on the Washington Office IRA maps in 4 areas for a reduction of 13,092 acres.

As previously discussed, however, the Washington Office failed to update the RACR IRA maps to reflcct the Bighorn National Forest's updated Inventoried Roadless Area maps completed as part of the 2005 forest plan revision

Wyoming Governor Matt Mead sought to address the issue in the Bighorn by funding the Bighorn National Forest Roadless Collaborative which prepared a correction to the maps. This recommendation was recently presented to the Chief of the National Forest and the four counties in Wyoming who host the Bighorn were requesting a technical correction to the map.

## G. RACR disregards local forest plans

The RACR gives Forest Service Line Officers very little ability to implement proactive management projects in IRAs to reduce the risk of catastrophic wildfire and insect epidemics, including removal of timber as a byproduct of those treatments. The RACR also overrides Forest Plan direction that would have otherwise allowed the Forest Service to implement ongoing forest management projects. Finally, the RACR has limited the Forest Service's ability to implement proactive measures needed to reduce the threat of catastrophic fire and mountain pine beetle epidemics in municipal watersheds.

## IV. Changes in conditions in Wyoming's Forests since RACR

-many more acres of fire

Wildfire across the western US has increased in size, frequency, and severity since the 1950s. These changes are closely linked with increases in temperature and an increased frequency and intensity of drought. (Wasserman 2020) 161,966 acres of NFS lands in WY burned in 2024, in particular, the 98,000 Elk Fire in the Bighorn National Forest. (NIFC 2024 Annual Report) Although roadless areas in the western United States experienced fewer fire ignitions over the last three decades and are generally cooler, moister, and higher elevation landscapes less conducive to fire, wildfire extent was greater in these areas than in roaded areas. (Johnston 2021)

-many more acres of insect epidemics

There were approximately 1,207,000 acres of mortality attributed to insects and disease from 2001 to 2024 within national forest IRAs in Wyoming.

Approximately 814,000 acres of national forest IRAs in Wyoming are considered at risk of a 25% loss in standing live basal area over the next 15 years due to insect and disease mortality.

-expansion of WUI

A 2022 paper (Mockrin et al, 2022) found that national forests are a focal area for WUI growth, within and around national forests, rates of WUI growth were higher than WUI growth in the rest of conterminous United States.

-the benefits of proactive management have become more evident, not just in WUI, but including entire ecosystems

-An increase in the pace and scale of forest treatments is necessary to mitigate for the increased wildfire activity across the West (Wasserman, 2020)

-the Forest Service approved and is implementing the 2012 Forest Planning Rule, which, among other things, requires the use of best available science, emphasizes public and local government participation, and changes the Responsible Office from Regional Foresters to Forest Supervisors (i.e., closer to the ground and to the people who live, work, and play in the national forests) for forest plan revisions.

\- Higher demand for recreation

## V. Specific Comments

Johnson County supports returning the decision-making authority for roadless areas to Forest Supervisors through the forest planning process. Empower states and counties to work with the

USFS to make management decisions that reflect the diverse ecological, social, and economic conditions that exist across national forests, counties, and states.

## A. Cooperating agency involvement:

The USFS would benefit from the meaningful engagement of Wyoming counties in the development of its EIS. Beyond an exhibited commitment supporting the USFS through project and planning efforts for decades, Wyoming counties have local expertise, data, and jurisdiction of the lands impacted by RACR that would benefit the EIS.

## B. Alternatives Evaluated

The Notice of Intent identified two alternatives - the No Action and the Proposed Action (rescission of the RACR). For all detailed statements, under 42 U.S.C. 4332(C)(iii), there must be “a reasonable range of alternatives to the proposed agency action, including an analysis of any negative environmental impacts of not implementing the proposed agency action in the case of a no action alternatives, that are technically and economically feasible, and meet the purpose and need of the proposal."

Therefore, for legal sufficiency, we encourage the USFS to develop and analyze additional alternatives, that are technically and economically feasible, and meet the purpose and need of the proposal. While the WCCA is not advocating for any particular alternative, such alternatives may include:

The USFS could propose to modify the boundaries of IRAs to remove specific areas (such as the WUI, areas adjacent to or between existing roads, municipal watersheds etc.)

The USFS could also propose an alternative to empower USFS supervisors to consider amendments to IRAs through forest plan amendments and revisions. Additionally, technical corrections to IRAs could be resolved by USFS supervisors, instead of needing to be adopted by the Chief of the USFS. Provisions could contain county and state signoff as well, to ensure that changes to IRA boundaries are in accord with local and state plans.

It is also worth noting in the EIS that whatever alternative is selected, millions of acres of "roadless areas" will continue to be "roadless" in perpetuity due to topography, isolation resource values, cost/benefits, etc.

## C. Impacts of establishing RACR

The Notice of Intent requests public comment on the “impacts of rescinding RACR." However, rescinding RACR will not authorize any specific project, road, or timber sale. Wyoming communities and forests have seen impacts from the implementation of RACR.

## D. Impacts of rescinding RACR:

Rescinding RACR does not authorize any additional management decisions. Building roads or not building roads for commercial timber harvest is still a management decision that must comply with a Forest Plan, NEPA, and other environmental laws.

However, rescinding RACR would create opportunities to address a host of challenges and objectives across landscapes through proactive management. Fires, insects, disease, watershed health, wildlife habitat, resiliency of old growth stands etc.

Additionally, there are impacts we saw from the implementation of RACR. In Wyoming, we saw several mills close after the RACR was created. There are also studies concerning the number of fires in IRA areas, severity of fires, where fires start, and burned acreages. While topography and the ability to address fires play a significant role, we have seen higher percentages of fires starting in IRA, a higher percentage of high-severity fires in IRA, a larger percentage of IRA acreage being burned than non-IRA acreage

## E. Roadless Values:

The RACR documents repeatedly characterize IRAs as having the following values – 1) high quality or undisturbed soil, water, and air, 2) sources of public drinking water, 3) diversity of plant and animal communities, 4) habitat for T&E, proposed, candidate, and sensitive species and for species dependent of large, undisturbed areas, 5) Primitive, Semi-primitive, nonmotorized, and Semi-primitive motorized recreation, 6) Reference landscapes, 7) natural appearing landscapes with high scenic quality, and 8) traditional cultural properties and sacred sites. Those values, however, are not limited to IRAs and we urge you to be clear about that in your analysis.

## F. Maps.

Retire the RARE I and RARE II Maps: Considering that the RARE I and II maps are now approximately half-a-century old, we recommend that you include, as part of the preferred alternative, "retiring" the set of maps referred to in 294.11 along with direction clarifying that RARE I and II maps are not for further use.

## VI Conclusion.

Johnson County looks forward to participating in the rule recission process as a Cooperating Agency and ensuring the interests of Johnson County are considered.

Sincerely,

September 19, 2025

WER 9567.06 U.S. Department of Agriculture Forest Service Notice of Intent FS–2025–0001

The Honorable Brooke Rollins Secretary of Agriculture Washington, DC

Dear Madam Secretary:

The Wyoming Game and Fish Department (Department) has reviewed the proposed Notice of Intent to prepare an environmental impact statement (EIS) and rulemaking for Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands. We offer the following comments for your consideration.

The Department supports locally based decision-making regarding management of roadless areas. In Wyoming, inventoried roadless areas overlap with areas we have identified as Terrestrial Habitat Restoration Areas. This overlap has, at times, limited our ability to cooperatively implement certain types of habitat improvement projects on Forest Service lands. We encourage the USDA to consider alternatives and rules which allow for state wildlife agencies to engage with the Forest Service to plan and implement projects that benefit wildlife in areas currently identified as roadless.

The Department is also supportive of the development of alternatives and rules which continue to maintain the long-term functionality of wildlife habitat within roadless areas. These areas are particularly valuable to wildlife because the lack of motorized access provides essential security, cover, and connectivity for numerous wildlife species. While we support project activities that benefit wildlife and forest health in the inventoried roadless areas, we encourage close collaboration on post-treatment travel management to help ensure long-term habitat values such as security, cover, and connectivity remain intact.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. If you have any questions or concerns please contact me at (307) 777-4501.

Sincerely,

Doug Brimeyer

Deputy Director

Brad Kinder, Acting Director Ecosystem Management Coordination United States Forest Service 201 14th Street SW, Mailstop 1108 Washington DC, 20250-1124

September 19, 2025

Re: USDA-FS-2025-0001 : Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement – Roadless Area Conservation

## Dear Director Kinder,

The Department of Wyoming State Parks & Cultural Resources, Division of State Parks, Historic Sites, and Trails and the Office of Outdoor Recreation (State Parks), respectfully submits comments on the Notice of Intent (NOI) to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) published in the Federal Register on August 29, 2025 (Vol. 90, No. 166) which would prompt rulemaking to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule).

Wyoming State Parks seeks opportunities to enhance our state’s cultural and recreational amenities and networks while supporting their appropriate management. Our mission emphasizes the need for education, responsible use, and dedicated maintenance programs that enable strong partnerships between government agencies, non-profit organizations, and loca communities. State Parks advocates for a balanced approach to all types of recreation, protecting the natural and cultural resources they influence. We work closely with the United States Forest Service (USFS) at all levels to ensure continued education and on-the-ground enforcement.

State Parks recognizes the power of cooperation and supports forest management that is influenced by local data and collaborative decision-making. Planning efforts that acknowledge the benefit of cooperating agencies, public input, and the diversity of Wyoming’s resources and recreational opportunities provide the best opportunity to balance the needs of multiple use and achieve lasting success.

Recreation in Wyoming relies on the protection of natural and cultural resources. We support other state agencies and local cooperators in protecting the resources under their purview and influencing policy that impacts wildlife, wildfire, water quality, and other critical aspects of forest management.

With that in mind, Wyoming State Parks aligns with other Wyoming agencies to support the rescission of the Roadless Rule. We encourage an EIS that includes additional options to meet the requirement of a reasonable range of alternatives. These alternatives should address allowing the state, with forest supervisors, to analyze forest management conditions and to evaluate roadless areas. This would lead to better understanding of what treatments are needed where, allowing for roadless or similar treatments as a viable use of the forest.

Both roadless and developed recreation areas are beneficial for recreation. While Wyoming has historically opposed the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (RACR), the original goal of the rule to protect forests should be considered. If the 2001 Roadless Rule is removed, better management practices will be needed to protect certain areas, a point supported by several recreation groups. Some have argued that roadless management is a valid multiple use, especially when it aligns with regional and local plans and preferences. Roadless management can be supported outside of RACR with tools like the Recreation Opportunity Spectrum, statewide comprehensive outdoor recreation plans, county land use plans, and other public feedback including collaborative recreational planning efforts.

Other considerations include a need for well-planned trails connectivity, including loop trail connections that encourage natural resource protection and responsible recreation use. There are miles of snowmobile trails and backcountry use in and around roadless areas. Off-highway vehicle routes often terminate at the roadless boundary; loop trails provide a logical turnaround are proven to be a successful management tool by providing routes and discouraging user created trails. Temporary logging roads show huge potential as converted trails, reducing expenses both for decommissioning and for constructing new recreation trails. Durable travel management plans should be developed in conjunction with updated forest management plans and prepared with adequate local engagement and consideration in mind. Partnerships with state agencies, local governments, and NGOs will continue to be important in achieving success, particularly whenever there are federal staffing and funding challenges.

We welcome any questions and can provide further details; please contact Carly-Ann Carruthers, Planning Manager, at 307-777-6968 or CarlyAnn.Carruthers@wyo.gov.

Sincerely,

Chris Floyd Deputy Director

# U.S. House of Representatiues Committee on Natural Resources Washington, DC 20515

September 19, 2025

<table><tr><td>The Honorable Brooke RollinsSecretary</td><td>The Honorable Tom SchultzChief</td></tr><tr><td>U.S. Department of Agriculture</td><td>U.S. Forest Service</td></tr><tr><td>1400 Independence Avenue, S.W.</td><td>1400 Independence Avenue S.W.</td></tr><tr><td>Washington, D.C. 20250</td><td>Washington, D.C. 20250</td></tr></table>

Re: Docket (FS-2025-0001) Environmental Impact Statements; Availability, etc.: Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands

Dear Secretary Rollins and Chief Schultz,

The Roadless Rule provides a critical and commonsense safeguard for the nearly 60 million acres of roadless areas on National Forest System lands. I write to voice my strong opposition to its repeal, as increased logging and development of these areas jeopardize abundant outdoor recreational opportunities, clean drinking water for millions of Americans, and essential habitat for a wide range of wildlife.

On August 29, 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) publicized a Notice of Intent (NOI), the first step in its formal rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule. USDA provided just 21 days for public comment; however, typical public comment processes run anywhere from 30 to 90 days, making three weeks insufficient for members of the public to prepare adequate responses. Notably, when the original Roadless Rule was developed in 2001, the Forest Service hosted approximately 430 public meetings, collaborated with seven other federal agencies, and consulted with more than 180 Tribes and Tribal Governments. During these public comment periods, 1.6 million public comments were collected, over 95% of which were strongly supportive of protections for roadless areas. Extensive public engagement should inform a consequential decision that impacts nearly 60 million acres of our national forests, and I urge you to extend the comment period to a full 45 days for public comment and 120 days for Tribal consultation.

California has more national forest acreage than any other state in the lower 48,<sup>1</sup> and within California, around 4 million acres are protected under the Roadless Rule.<sup>2</sup> In California’s Second Congressional District, rescinding the Roadless Rule would remove critical environmental protection for hundreds of thousands of acres in the Shasta-Trinity National Forest, the Mendocino National Forest, and the Six Rivers National Forest. In the Six Rivers National Forest alone, 150,000 acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) would be at risk of development.<sup>3</sup> About 1.4 trillion gallons of water per year come from the Six Rivers National Forest, providing clean water to communities, homes, and wildland habitats with an estimated wholesale market value of over \$428 million. Over 165,000 people visit Six Rivers National Forest to recreate annually, spending about \$7.8 million during their trips and contributing more than \$2.4

# U.S. House of Representatiues Committee on Natural Resources Washington, DC 20515

million towards the wages and income of local businesses.<sup>4</sup> Logging and development in these areas threaten the clean water and recreational opportunities that drive rural economies and sustain healthy communities in my district. Additionally, 154,332 acres of IRAs would lose protection in the Mendocino National Forest, including nearly 30,000 acres within the Berryessa Snow Mountain National Monument.<sup>5</sup> Given the importance of these areas, prominent local environment groups like CalWild, the Environmental Protection Information Center, and Tuleyome have joined to condemn the Administration’s actions.

Stakeholders throughout California understand the importance of the Roadless Rule. In California alone, National Forests make up 20% of the state and supply 50% of the runoff for drinking water.<sup>6</sup> Roadless areas provide key sources of clean drinking water for communities. According to the Forest Service’s own preamble issued as a part of the original rule’s promulgation, “Although the inventoried roadless areas comprise only 2% of the land base in the continental United States, they are found within 661 of the over 2,000 major watersheds in the nation.”<sup>7</sup> National Forest System lands also save downstream communities millions of dollars in water filtration costs. Repealing the Roadless Rule risks the loss of clean water for millions—an especially misguided move as the West faces continued megadrought and water crises.

The intact ecosystems found in roadless areas are also working landscapes that sustain critical fish and wildlife habitat<sup>8</sup> and riparian areas,<sup>9</sup> fueling local economies with tourism, fishing, and recreation. In fact, 70% of the public land within roadless areas is home to native trout or salmon, including cutthroat trout in the Rockies, brook trout in Appalachia, and salmon and steelhead in the Pacific Northwest and Alaska.<sup>10</sup> Repealing the Roadless Rule would put these critical watersheds at risk of degradation from erosion, sedimentation, and contamination, compromising the local communities that depend on healthy roadless ecosystems for the health of their economies or for foraging and subsistence rights of Tribal Nations.

Supporters of rescinding the Roadless Rule argue that it is a barrier to active forest management and wildfire prevention.<sup>11</sup> This is not accurate. The Roadless Rule has allowances for fuels management and timber harvest under certain circumstances, including to reduce fuel loads in the wildland-urban interface and to improve habitat for threatened, endangered, or sensitive species. In fact, the Forest Service’s own research shows that roadless areas have historically received a larger proportion of fuels management projects than other areas of the National Forest System.<sup>12</sup> Additional research shows that fire ignitions are more likely to

VIVIAN MOEGLEIN STAFF DIRECTOR

# U.S. House of Representatiues Committee on Natural Resources Washington, DC 20515

ANA UNRUH COHEN DEMOCRATIC STAFF DIRECTOR

occur near roads than in the backcountry. A recent report examining all fire ignitions across the country on national forest lands from 1992 to 2024 found that ignitions are far more likely to occur near roads and are far less likely in roadless and wilderness areas.<sup>13</sup> Notably, the original Roadless Rule also allows road construction for wildfire response. Claims that repealing the Roadless Rule would improve forest management or community safety clearly ignore the evidence and would only serve to increase wildfire risk.

Roads are also expensive to maintain and a drain on taxpayer resources. The nearly 370,000 miles of Forest Service roads that cross the national forests have resulted in a \$4.85 billion backlog of road maintenance.<sup>14</sup> This fiscal irresponsibility will only continue with increased logging and development in the 45 million acres at risk if the Roadless Rule is rescinded. Instead, the Administration should prioritize preserving and maintaining existing roadless areas to provide outstanding dispersed recreation opportunities such as hiking, cross-country skiing, mountain biking, hunting, and fishing, which contribute to a \$1.2 trillion outdoor economy. Rescinding the Roadless Rule would roll back protections on 25,121 miles of trails, 8,659 climbing routes, 768 miles of whitewater, and 10,794 miles of mountain biking—risking continued access to treasured recreation areas across the nation.<sup>15</sup>

For over two decades, the Roadless Rule has protected 58 million acres of high-quality and unfragmented National Forest System lands, ending decades of unsustainable road building and spiraling maintenance costs while still permitting fuels treatment, fishing, hunting, OHV use, mining, grazing, oil and gas leasing, and timber projects to improve forest health and prevent wildfire. Repealing the Rule would be a profound mistake, locking in a future of increasingly severe wildfires, fiscal irresponsibility, and water scarcity. I urge you to abandon this reckless course and uphold the Roadless Rule’s protections.

Sincerely,

# Congress of the United States

Washington, DC 20515

September 9, 2025

The Honorable Brooke Rollins Secretary of Agriculture U.S. Department of Agriculture 1400 Independence Ave Washington, D.C., 20250

The Honorable Tom Schultz Chief U.S. Forest Service 1400 Independence Ave Washington, D.C. 20250

Dear Secretary Rollins and Chief Schultz,

We write with concern that, in affording just 21 days for public comment, the U.S. Forest Service is not providing an adequate opportunity for meaningful public participation on its Notice of Intent to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (NOI) for the proposed repeal of the Roadless Rule. We respectfully request that you extend the comment period by at least thirty days. We also encourage you to conduct more robust stakeholder engagement, including by holding public hearings in all states with Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) and consulting proactively with Tribal governments.

The Roadless Rule is a landmark public-lands rule that has ensured the responsible management of nearly 60 million acres of National Forest System land and the irreplaceable resources they provide since its inception. Its repeal represents a major shift in the longstanding management of lands in virtually all federal forests across the country – forests that our constituents care deeply about. This includes protections of over half of the 17 millionacre mature and old-growth Tongass National Forest in Alaska – America’s largest forest and last remaining temperate rainforest – which offers critical opportunities for Tribal subsistence, tourism, outdoor recreation, and carbon sequestration. Twenty-one days is simply not enough to provide the opportunity for meaningful participation that the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) requires.

This is an issue with broad public interest from conservationists, recreationists, Tribal communities, and more. When the Roadless Rule was first adopted, more than 1.6 million comments were submitted in favor of the rule. Everyday Americans have a real stake in this issue, and twenty-one days is simply not enough time for individuals to take time out of their busy lives to research, prepare, and submit meaningful comments on such a complex and significant issue. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) held more than 400 public meetings across the country during the 2001 Roadless Rule rulemaking process and has a responsibility to similarly ensure adequate opportunity for the public to weigh in on the proposed repeal.

Additionally, it is the responsibility of the U.S. Government to hold robust and meaningful Tribal consultation with any impacted Tribal governments. Considering the breadth of the Roadless Rule’s purview, numerous Tribes will be impacted, and to our knowledge there has been virtually no Tribal consultation on this significant and sudden policy shift. This is contrary to the Forest Service’s protocol, which requires a minimum tribal consultation period of 120 days for national-level decisions.

Participation by Tribes, local governments and by the public, “in cooperation” with the federal government, is central to the democratic process, and execution of the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”)<sup>1</sup>. As the U.S. Supreme Court has explained, NEPA guarantees that “relevant information will be made available to the larger audience that may also play a role in both the decision-making process and the implementation of that decision.”<sup>2</sup> Allowing the public to participate early on addresses NEPA’s “manifest concern with preventing uninformed action,” because it is through the “broad dissemination of information” that “the public” can “react to the effects of a proposed action at a meaningful time.”<sup>3</sup>

Considering the complex nature of this proposal and the widespread local and national interests likely to be affected, we strongly urge you to provide a minimum of 45 days for the public to comment and participate in public hearings, and 120 days for Tribal consultation.

## Sincerely,

Andren Selinas Andrea Salinas Member of Congress

Re: Request for Extension of Time on Proposed 2001 Roadless Rule Recission, 90 Fed. Reg. 42179 (August 29, 2025) and Government-to-Government Consultation

Dear Secretary Rollins,

The Swinomish Indian Tribal Community (“Swinomish”) writes to request that the deadline to submit comments on the above-referenced Federal Register notice be extended to October 10, 2025. Recission of the 2001 Roadless Rule would result in major impacts to affected tribes and the nation at large, yet the current due date for comments is a mere three (3) weeks after the publication date—which fell on the Friday before Labor Day, a federal holiday. In practical terms, this results in a two-and-a half week comment period for a wholesale reversal in federal policy that could have potentially catastrophic effects on Swinomish Treaty resources and rights. Because this truncated timeline is insufficient for the Tribe to properly and fully respond to the enormity of the federal rule change proposed, we respectfully request that you:

n Republish the Federal Register notice this Friday, September 12<sup>th</sup> announcing that an extended public comment period will be open until Friday, October 10<sup>th</sup>;

n Offer tribal nations, including Swinomish, the opportunity for government-togovernment consultation on the proposed rule through Friday, December 12<sup>th</sup>.

We believe this time extension in the near-term will enable greater collaboration with the Forest Service as our federal trustee and minimize the need for appeals of any final rule later in the process.

We intend to provide the U.S. Forest Service with the necessary information to assure that the environmental impact statement and resulting final rule are in accordance with the federal government’s trust responsibility to Swinomish. To ensure a fair, transparent and thorough process that enables us to meaningfully engage, we believe that a timeline extension for study requests and related comments is necessary and warranted. We hope that you will agree to extend the public comment period and offer tribes like Swinomish the opportunity to have meaningful consultation on this natural resource priority for salmon recovery, hunting, gathering, and other Treaty-protected rights.

We look forward to a constructive consultation with our federal partners to discuss this important matter. Please contact Amy Trainer, Swinomish Indian Tribal Community, (360) 399- 5804 atrainer@swinomish.nsn.us, to schedule a consultation in the near future.

Sincerely,

Steve Edwards, Chairman

Subject: Public Comment on Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement for Rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Docket Number: FS-2025–0001

Dear Director:

The Craig Tribal Association (Craig Tribe), a federally recognized Tribe representing the Indigenous peoples of Craig, Alaska, respectfully submits this public comment in strong opposition to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Notice of Intent (NOI) published in the Federal Register on August 29, 2025 (Vol. 90, No. 166, pp. 42179–42182), to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) and propose rulemaking to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule) (66 FR 3244; 36 CFR Part 294 Subpart B (2001)).

The current regulations at 36 CFR Part 294 (as of September 5, 2025) affirm the essential protections provided by the 2001 Roadless Rule, prohibiting road construction, reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas, including those in the Tongass National Forest, with limited exceptions designed to preserve roadless character while accommodating necessary stewardship activities. Rescinding this rule would undermine these safeguards, adversely affecting our Tribal sovereignty, subsistence rights, cultural heritage, and the ecological health of our ancestral lands

We strongly urge the USDA to withdraw this proposal and maintain the 2001 Roadless Rule in full. As a federally recognized Tribe with profound historical, cultural, and subsistence connections to the Tongass National Forest, the Craig Tribe depends on these roadless areas for essential activities such as hunting, fishing, gathering, and spiritual practices that sustain our communities and way of life. The NOI acknowledges the vital attributes of inventoried roadless areas, stating that 63% are forested with at least 10% canopy cover, supporting critical habitats for fish and wildlife (p. 42179). It further recognizes their contributions to "soil, water and air; plant and animal communities, including threatened, endangered, sensitive species; scenid integrity; recreation settings and opportunities; and cultural resources, traditional cultural properties, and sacred sites" (p. 42181). These statements highlight the indispensable role of roadless areas in upholding biodiversity and cultural values, which are integral to our subsistence practices. However, the proposal favors short-term economic development over these enduring benefits, disregarding the disproportionate adverse effects on Alaska Native subsistence users and directly contravening key federal laws, including but not limited to the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) (16 U.S.C. §§ 3101 et seq.), the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) (42 U.S.C. §§ 4321 et seq.), and the federal trust responsibility to federally recognized Tribes.

The proposed rescission directly conflicts with ANILCA, which requires the protection of subsistence uses on public lands in Alaska. ANILCA Section 810 (16 U.S.C. § 3120(a)(3)) mandates that federal agencies evaluate the impacts of proposed actions on subsistence uses and needs, including whether such actions would significantly restrict subsistence opportunities. This assessment must address

1. effects on subsistence uses and needs;

2. availability of alternative lands for the intended purposes; and

3. options to minimize or eliminate the use of public lands needed for subsistence

The NOI does not sufficiently fulfill these obligations, particularly for the Tongass National Forest, where roadless areas include vital habitats for salmon, deer, and other species central to Craig Tribe's subsistence economy. Under the current 36 CFR Part 294 Subpart B, road construction and reconstruction are prohibited (§ 294.12), and timber cutting, sale, or removal is restricted (§ 294.13), with exceptions that prioritize conservation—aligning with ANILCA's subsistence priorities by maintaining undisturbed habitats.

Rescinding the rule would facilitate road construction and industrial logging, leading to habitat fragmentation and disrupted migration patterns, as indicated by the NOI's data that 31% of these areas are within 0.5 miles of existing roads, heightening development risks (p. 42179). This would diminish fish and wildlife populations, impairing our ability to harvest traditional foods Subsistence is fundamental to our cultural identity and self-determination, safeguarded by ANILCA Title VIII (16 U.S.C. §§ 3111–3126), which grants priority to rural Alaska residents subsistence uses over other consumptive activities. The proposal's shift to "local decision making" via land management plans (p. 42180) overlooks ANILCA's federal subsistence priority, potentially subordinating Tribal needs to timber interests. Past exemptions in the Tongass, like the 2020 Alaska Roadless Rule (85 FR 68688), have caused habitat degradation and reduced subsistence harvests—impacts prevented by the current 36 CFR Part 294 Subpart B through its national prohibitions

Moreover, the proposal breaches ANILCA's no-net-loss policy for fish and wildlife habitats (16 U.S.C. § 3/0/(b)), as expanded development would cause permanent losses to biodiversity and ecosystem services essential for subsistence. The NOI notes that 13% of inventoried roadless areas experienced high or moderate severity wildfire between 1984 and 2024 (p. 42179), yet rescission would intensify such vulnerabilities through fragmentation, contrary to the rule's exceptions for forest health under § 294.13(b)

This proposal sharply contrasts with the Department of the Interior's (DOI) Secretarial Order 3403 (Joint Secretarial Order on Fulfilling the Trust Responsibility to Indian Tribes in the Stewardship of Federal Lands and Waters, November 15, 2021), which promotes Tribal costewardship and meaningful consultation in land management, mandating integration of Tribal knowledge, prioritization of Tribal interests, and avoidance of adverse impacts without mitigation. DOI has implemented this order to bolster Tribal roles, yet the USDA's NOI marginalizes similar duties for the Tongass, viewing Tribal input as supplementary rather than essential (p. 42182). This discrepancy reveals interagency inconsistencies and weakens the federal trust responsibility, rooted in treaties, statutes, and precedents (e.g., Seminole Nation v. United States, 316 U.S. 286 (1942)). The proposal's deregulatory "one-size-fits-all" approach disregards site-specific Tribal contexts. There are 19 federally recognized tribes in Southeast Alaska, all of whom live in or near the Tongass National Forest. Unlike Order 3403's collaborative framework. The current 36 CFR Part 294 facilitates such collaboration by restricting exceptions to non-compromising activities, enabling Tribal participation in planning (p. 42180). Proceeding with rescission would widen federal-Tribal disparities and prompt challenges under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (5 U.S.C. §§ 551 et seq) for arbitrary decision-making

The NOI understates the ripple effects on Tribal subsistence. This cannot be overstated. The Tongass roadless areas offer pristine habitats for anadromous fish, berry patches, and game trails relied upon by our people for millennia. Greater road density would cause stream sedimentation, degrading water quality and salmon spawning—key to our food security and economy. The NOI indicates 9.3 million Tongass acres are protected under the 2001 Roadless Rule (p. 42179), and the 2001 Final EIS forecasted up to 30% wildlife population declines from road development due to fragmentation and access

These effects are amplified by climate change, stressing resources with warmer waters and shifted migrations. The NOI observes heightened wildfire activity in roadless areas since 2000 (p. 42179), yet rescission would worsen threats by eliminating prohibitions on risk-increasing activities. This violates ANILCA subsistence safeguards and Executive Order 13175 (Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments), requiring meaningful Tribal consultation on actions impacting Tribal rights. The NOI's 21-day comment period (August 29 to September 19, 2025) inadequately allows for thorough Tribal engagement, violating these mandates and the rule's public involvement structure under 36 CFR Part 294 Subpart B § 294.14.

Should the USDA advance this rescission, it could invite litigation on several fronts:

1. ANILCA Violations: Inadequate Section 810 subsistence evaluation could support APA claims, as in Amoco Production Co. v. Village of Gambell (480 U.S. 531 (1987)), where courts halted actions harming Alaska Native subsistence. The NOI's issues list addresses cultural resources and sacred sites (p. 42181) but omits specific ANILCA analysis

2. NEPA Deficiencies: The EIS must rigorously examine alternatives, including the "no action" retention of the 2001 Rule (p. 42181), and cumulative subsistence impacts. Insufficient analysis, as in prior Tongass cases (e.g., Organized Village of Kake v. USDA, 746 F.3d 970 (9th Cir. 2014)), would deem the decision arbitrary. The NOI's use of outdated 2001 EIS fire predictions (p. 42180) disregards current data, breaching NEPA's science requirements.

3. Trust Responsibility Breaches: Overlooking Tribal subsistence and co-stewardship violates fiduciary duties, actionable per United States v. Mitchell (463 U.S. 206 (1983)) The Tongass's explicit targeting (p. 42179) discriminates against Alaska Natives prioritizing deregulation over trust duties.

4. APA Claims: Dependence on deregulatory executive orders (e.g., EO 14153) without adequate reversal rationale could be arbitrary, given the rule's judicial affirmations (e.g., Kootenai Tribe v. Veneman, 313 F.3d 1094 (9th Cir. 2002)). Retaining Idaho and Colorado state rules under Subparts C and D (p. 42179) raises Fifth Amendment equal protection issues.

5. ESA and Related Laws: Effects on threatened species (e.g., Alexander Archipelago wolf) may violate the Endangered Species Act (16 U.S.C. §§ 1531 et seq.), necessitating Section 7 consultations. The NOI's 40 percent high wildfire hazard note (p. 42179) underscores risks to sensitive species absent current § 294.13(b) mitigations.

The NOI's retention of state-specific rules for Idaho (Subpart C) and Colorado (Subpart D) while singling out the Tongass further discriminates against Alaska Natives and overlooks the rule's protections for Tribal resources.

In summary, the Craig Tribe respectfully request that the USDA withdraw this NOI and preserve the 2001 Roadless Rule as codified in 36 CFR Part 294. The NOI's data and recognitions confirm the rule's critical role in conserving resources vital to our subsistence, culture, and spiritual connection with the forest. We seek immediate government-to-government consultation. Absent this, we will pursue all available legal avenues to safeguard our rights and sovereignty.

Sincerely,

Clunt 2.cun s

Clinton E. Cook Sr., President

Craig Tribal Association

Comments on Notice of Intent to provide an environmental statement for the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rules

Secretary Rollins,

The Organized Village of Kasaan (OVK), a federally recognized Tribal government, submits these comments in strong opposition to the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. This rule has protected over 9 million acres of ancestral forest homelands in the Tongass National Forest—lands that are vital to our cultural identity, subsistence practices, and ecological integrity.

## Our Homeland Is Not a Commodity

The Tongass is not merely a forest—it is a living, breathing extension of our people. It is where our children learn the stories of our ancestors, where our elders gather traditional medicines, and where our families harvest salmon, crab, deer, and berries to nourish our bodies and spirits. The proposed rollback of roadless protections threatens to fragment these sacred lands, disrupt wildlife habitats, and accelerate the degradation of ecosystems that have sustained the Haida people for millennia.

## Wildlife and Ecosystem Impacts

The Tongass is home to over 400 species, including:

Brown and black bears that rely on salmon runs

• The Alexander Archipelago wolf, found only in Southeast Alaska

• Bald eagles, which thrive in greater numbers here than anywhere else in the world

Sitka White Tailed-Deer, whose habitat is severely impacted by roadbuilding and forest transitions to the stem exclusion phase, making movement and survival difficult

Roadbuilding and logging fragment wildlife corridors, increase erosion and pollution, and disrupt salmon-bearing streams. These activities push deer closer to roads, increasing predation by wolves and reducing food security for tribal citizens. Old growth and riparian buffers are essential for salmon populations, providing shade and invertebrate food sources that sustain aquatic ecosystems.

## Subsistence Use and Cultural Sites

Kasaan qualifies as a food desert according to the USDA definition, with the nearest grocery store located in Thorne Bay. This designation underscores the critical importance of subsistence activities such as hunting, fishing, and gathering for the survival and well-being of Kasaan residents.

Access to hunting, fishing, and harvesting is not optional—it is essential for survival. The Tongass sustains a way of life rooted in subsistence, including:

• Salmon harvesting from over 19,000 miles of streams

• Crab and shrimp gathering, with declining populations due to warming waters and acidification

• Deer hunting and berry picking, critical for food security and cultural continuity

Culturally significant sites include Karta Bay, Kendrick Sound, and the Kasaan Bay shoreline, as well as adjacent terrestrial areas that support invertebrate populations vital to salmon and other species. These areas are living archives of our history, spirituality, and identity.

## Legal and Procedural Concerns

Consultation protocols have not been adequately observed. The USDA is required to follow up in writing detailing how tribal comments will be included in assessments and planning trajectories. The proposed rescission raises serious concerns regarding tribal consultation and environmental justice. The USDA must uphold its trust responsibility and ensure that tribal governments are co-developers of alternatives in the EIS process. The inclusion of Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) is not optional—it is essential.

## Recommendations

• Retain the 2001 Roadless Rule to protect the ecological and cultural integrity of the Tongass

• Include tribal governments as co-developers of EIS alternatives

• Integrate TEK and local data from Southeast Alaska tribes into all environmental assessments

• Ensure robust consultation with tribal governments prior to any decision-making

• Recognize the Tongass as a cultural landscape, not just a resource base

• Address indirect and cumulative impacts on traditional ways of life and subsistence species

## Conclusion

The Organized Village of Kasaan stands united with other Southeast Alaska tribes in defense of our forest homelands. We call on the USDA to honor its trust responsibility and uphold protections that preserve the Tongass for future generations. The forest is our teacher, our provider, and our sacred relative. We say clearly and unequivocally: No to the rescission. Yes, to tribal stewardship.

Respectfully submitted,

Re: Request for Cooperating Agency Status Pursuant to 40 CFR § 1501.6 and Executive Order 13175 (Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments) - Docket ID: FS-2025- 0001 (Proposed Rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule as Applied to the Tongass National Forest)

Dear Mr. Kinder:

The Craig Tribal Association (CTA) hereby formally requests designation as a cooperating agency in the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process for the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule as applied to the Tongass National Forest (Docket ID: FS-2025-0001). CTA qualifies for cooperating agency status due to our jurisdiction by law as a federally recognized Tribe with sovereign interests in the affected region, including ancestral lands and resources on Prince of Wales Island within the Tongass National Forest.

Additionally, CTA possesses special expertise relevant to the environmental impacts of the proposed action, including but not limited to:

Traditional ecological knowledge and subsistence practices reliant on intact roadless areas.

• Cultural resource management and protection of sacred sites potentially affected by increased road construction, timber harvesting, or mining.

• Assessment of cumulative impacts on fish, wildlife, and water quality critical to Tribal health and economy.

Granting CTA cooperating agency status would enhance the NEPA process by ensuring robust government-to-government consultation, incorporating Tribal perspectives early in scoping and Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) development, and avoiding potential delays or litigation through collaborative analysis. CTA is prepared to commit resources to this role, including participation in interdisciplinary teams and review of draft documents, and we request the development of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to outline the terms of our cooperation, as recommended in Forest Service directives (FSH 1909.12, Chapter 10).

We urge the USDA Forest Service to respond to this request promptly and invite further discussion to facilitate our involvement. CTA is available for a meeting at your earliest convenience and can be reached at the contact information above.

Sincerely,

Dear Ecosystem Management Coordination Director

The Organized Village of Kake (OVK), a federally recognized Tribe in Southeast Alaska, submits this letter of response to the Notice of Intent published by the Department of Agriculture in the Federal Register on August 29, 2025. The USDA is initiating a rulemaking process concerning the management of inventoried roadless areas on national forest system lands, including those in Alaska and on the Tongass National Forest. The proposed rule would rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule) nationwide. OVK is writing to strongly oppose rescinding or weakening the 2001Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule) and urge the Department of Agriculture to maintain and strengthen protections for the Tongass National Forest.

The traditional territory of OVK stretches across over 3 million acres of the Tongass National Forest, including Kupreanof Island, Kuiu Island, Baranof Island, Admiralty Island, and parts of the mainland. The Tongass is more than forested land—it is our home, our traditional territory, and a living source of identity, culture, and sustenance for our people. For countless generations, our way of life has depended on the health of these lands and waters, which sustain salmon, deer, berries wild plants, and countless other resources essential to our survival. The Roadless Rule is essential to safeguarding these resources from the damage of large-scale industrial logging and road building.

Weakening these protections would harm cultural and spiritual sites, damage salmon and wildlife habitat, and reduce access to subsistence hunting and gathering. Industrial logging has already left deep scars on our traditional lands, and further development threatens the environment that has supported our people for millennia. Additionally, the Tongass is a globally important carbon sink vital in combating climate change. Protecting its old-growth and mature forests is essential not only to our Tribe's well-being but to climate stability for future generations. Given the overall lack of clarity regarding how the Forest Service intends to honor its trust responsibilities to consult with Tribal Governments, and whether the agency intends to conduct another rulemaking addressing roadless areas on the Tongass and Chugach National Forests in Alaska, OVK has written this letter to inform the federal decisionmaker that our Tribe has numerous concerns and questions pertaining to the proposal to rescind the Roadless Rule. including but not limited to those mentioned above.

As a sovereign Tribal government, OVK has consistently opposed efforts to remove protections for the Tongass, and we continue to call for durable safeguards. Our limited resources should not be spent repeatedly fighting proposals that make it easier to log, mine, and build roads across critical landscapes; federal policy should instead prioritize the protection of these lands, cultural heritage and the health of ecosystems for all people. OVK has passed resolutions since 2001 in support of the rule, with the most recent being passed July 2025 (2025-11). Our Tribe also participated as a cooperating agency during the 2018 Alaska Roadless Rulemaking process and withdrew when the full exemption alternative was chosen in 2020. This alternative ignored our input and the time we had committed to finding solutions for the areas important to us. We have frequently engaged in consultation on the 2001 Roadless Rule and attempts to both repeal and reinstate it. We demand that in accordance with the agency's trust responsibilities to federally recognized sovereign tribal governments, the USDA Forest Service must provide tribal consultation and the opportunity for individual tribal governments to act as cooperating agencies during this process. We have already written with our district ranger to formally request Government-to-Government consultation on the proposal to repeal the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, and this rulemaking must not move forward before consultation requirements are fulfilled.

We further request that the U.S. Forest Service conduct a full ANILCA Title VIII, Section 810 analysis of the impacts that rescinding the Roadless Rule would have on subsistence resources and the way of life of Tribal citizens and rural residents. Protection of subsistence is one of the primary purposes of ANILCA and Title VIII, Section 810, subtitled Subsistence and Decisions, outlines very specific requirements for analyzing impacts to subsistence uses of resources in federal land use decision-making, including hearings. Section 810 analyses must be performed regardless of what level of analysis an agency may or may not be completing under other statutes, such as the National Environmental Policy Act, and it is not subject to time limits imposed by other direction an agency may be following. This analysis is critical to ensuring that decisions regarding the Tongass comply with federal law and do not erode the rights and protections guaranteed to rural subsistence users. In ANILCA, Congress found that continuing opportunity for subsistence is “essential." The impacts that the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule would have on the Tongass are significant due to how many rural communities across the Tongass NF rely on national forest lands to meet their subsistence needs.

The US Forest Service has already determined that ANILCA Title VIII, Section 810 hearings and analysis are relevant to the Roadless Rulemaking process, as evidenced by the previous hearings conducted during the 2018 Alaska Roadless Rulemaking process. There is significant subsistence use in the OVK's traditional territory: tribal citizens and rural community citizens hunt Sitka blacktail deer and moose, beach seine for sockeye salmon and fish for all five species of Pacific salmon that spawn in the lakes and rivers of the surrounding area, and harvest plants and medicines from the surrounding lands, including Roadless areas in Central Kupreanof Island, Gut Bay, Portage Bay, Port Camden, Kuiu Island, and other nearby areas. The 2001 Roadless Rule protects the ecological integrity of this habitat and the productivity of fish and wildlife within it, and it is highly likely that the rescission of the2001 Roadless Rule will have a significant impact on subsistence.

Please respond to this letter with an estimated timeline for the ANILCA public meetings and when the community will have an opportunity for input during the process. Additionally, we would like the opportunity to review the 810 draft analysis before its inclusion into the final record to make sure it is accurate.

We urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture to reject any action to rescind or weaken the 2001 Roadless Rule and to adopt policies that strengthen protections for old-growth forests in the Tongass National Forest. This national proposal, which has the potential to affect millions of acres of our ancestral land and thousands of miles of waterways now managed by the Forest Service.

requires careful review. We take our responsibility as the current and future stewards of these landscapes seriously and it is critical that public land management:

• Prioritize the protection and productivity of subsistence resources to meet local food security needs and fulfill the requirements of ANILCA

• Integrate Indigenous Knowledge at every stage of forest management to enhance ecological stewardship and cultural preservation

• Protects sacred sites, treaty-reserved resources, and culturally significant species through enforceable measures and mandatory consultation protocols

• Prioritizes Tribal-led restoration and economic development initiatives that align with our cultural values and traditional practices, and provide local community benefit

Gunalcheesh,

(Federally Recognized Tribal Government serving the Kake, Alaska area)

Resolution No. 2025-11 Urging the U.S. Department of Agriculture to not rescind the Roadless Rule and to include strong protections for old-growth forests in the Tongass National Forest.

WHEREAS, the Organized Village of Kake (hereinafter OVK) is a federally recognized Indian Tribe under federal law and is empowered under its Constitution and By-Laws to adopt ordinances to govern its members and its activities on behalf of its members; and,

WHEREAS, OVK is further defined as an Indian Tribe in the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act, PL 93-638 and as such is entitled to contract with the Federal Government for the operation of any federal programs, services, activities or functions serving it's members and,

WHEREAS, OVK's traditional territory includes lands on Kupreanof, Kuiu, Eastern Baranof, and southern Admiralty Islands, and along the mainland, including Port Houghton and as far as Taku River south to Port Houghton; and

WHEREAS, protection of our inherent right to harvest and use our traditional and customary foods requires careful cultural stewardship and protection of our environmental and natural resources; and

WHEREAS, our care of the lands now classified as “inventoried roadless areas" (IRA) and within the Tongass National Forest stretches for millennia; and

WHEREAS, our traditional territory holds sacred, cultural, and spiritual significance to us because these lands provide our people with salmon, deer, wild foods, traditional medicinal plants, and trees important for our traditional arts and cultural uses that define who we are and where we come from; and

WHEREAS, protecting the old-growth and mature forests and trees in our traditional territory is of critical importance to protecting and preserving our gathering practices ("subsistence") activities; and

WHEREAS, logging old-growth and mature trees has detrimentally affected our tribal citizens by decreasing subsistence hunting opportunities near Kake, damaging fish habitat, causing landslides, desecrating sacred and cultural sites, and making it more difficult to encounter places in the forest where we can still find the healthy habitat that sustains our people spiritually and culturally; and

WHEREAS, OVK has long advocated for the protection of old-growth trees in our traditional areas of the Tongass by participating in the Forest Service's planning processes, government-to-government consultation, administrative appeals, and litigation challenging timber sales, supporting measures like the Roadless Rule that protect our forests, and other advocacy (OVK Resolution No. 2018-24, see attached); and

WHEREAS. fighting to protect our traditional territory takes significant time and staff resources that OVK could devote to other important programs to benefit our tribal citizens if we did not need to fight logging proposals; and

WHEREAS, the United States Department of Agriculture (the Department) is preparing an environmental impact statement that will rescind the Roadless Area Conservation Rule nationwide, including in the Tongass National Forest; and

WHEREAS, OVK does not support this action by the Department as it would cause significant harm to the ways of life of our citizens and force OVK to continue to use its resources to fight logging proposals and advocate for durable protection of our traditional territory; and

WHEREAS, durable protection for old-growth and mature trees in the Tongass is needed and the Roadless Area Conservation Rule provides our community, and others in Southeast Alaska, with such safeguards

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that OVK supports protecting the remaining old-growth and mature trees in the Tongass from any large-scale commercial logging and urges the Department to keep the Roadless Area Conservation Rule in place; and

FINALLY BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that OVK opposes any rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule both nationwide and, in particular, in the Tongass National Forest

RE: Sitka Tribe Comments on Tongass Roadless Rule Recission

Dear Ms. Miranda,

I write on behalf of the Sitka Tribe of Alaska (STA), tribal government in Sitka, Alaska, with over 4,846 tribal citizens. As a tribal government, STA is responsible for the health, safety, welfare, and cultural preservation of its tribal citizens. STA provides the following comments regarding the rescinding of the 2oo1 Roadless Rule on the Tongass National Forest

STA's traditional territory is defined in its secretarial approved constitution as;

"The jurisdiction of the Sitka Tribe of Alaska shall extend to all lands constituting the Native Village of Sitka and the areas commonly known as “Indian Possession" and "Cottage Settlement", and to all surrounding areas of Indian Country, if any, including all customary and traditional use and access areas in the vicinity of Baranof Island, Chichigof and surrounding islands, and all fee lands and allotments and lands owned by Sealaska, Inc. or Shee-Atika, Inc. located therein (the Native corporations established pursuant to the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (Pub. L. 92-2o3) as amended to hold the land and other benefits provided by Congress in partial compensation for extinguishment of the Tribe's aboriginal land rights), to the fullest extent permitted by federal and tribal law."

These sovereign ancestral lands are more discernible in the attached map and include the lands and waters of the outer coast of Baranof and Chichagof Island and the greater reaches of Peril Strait. No other federally recognized tribe has sovereign jurisdiction over this area.

STA and its tribal citizens rely heavily on these lands and waters to provide healthy subsistence foods not only to offset the extremely inflated cost of living in a remote rural community like Sitka but also as an ingrained part of the Native culture that connects the people to the land. This reliance is acknowledged and supported by the federal government through Sitka's rural status under Title VIII of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) that provides STA tribal citizens priority access to subsistence resources on federal lands and navigable waterways.

The importance of subsistence resources to STA was reinforced in its Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy – Forest Management (SASS-FM) and Tongass Forest Plan Revision comments (both attached). In these comments STA stressed its desire to engage the Forest Service in co-stewardship and co-management of lands, waters, and Native cultural sites within its traditional territory.

Administrative mandates to increase timber production from our national forests is undoubtedly going to have an impact on non-timber related resources. STA is concerned that the rescission of the Roadless Rule on the Tongass will have a negative impact on the ability of the lands and waters to provide the Native community with healthy and culturally appropriate foods as they've done since time immemorial. Due to those impending impacts, STA opposes the rescinding of the Roadless Rule on the Tongass National Forest

While STA is fully aware that its opposition and that of other tribes or US citizens will have little to no impact on the on the final Roadless Rule decision, it encourages the Forest Service not to lose sight of the heavy reliance the community and region have on subsistence resources originating from federal lands on the Tongass, continue to engage tribes in a meaningful and productive dialogue on resource management, and continue to support co-stewardship and comanagement of federal lands and resources on the Tongass.

If you have any questions regarding these comments, contact STA's Resource Protection Department Director Jeff Feldpausch at jeff.feldpausch@sitktribe-nsn.gov or call (9o7)747-7469

Sincerely,

Dionne Brady-Howard

Council Chairwoman

## Ancestral Lands
