Re: Sitka Tribe Comments on the Tongass Forest Plan Revision

Dear Ranger Garner,

I write on behalf of the Sitka Tribe of Alaska (STA), a tribal government in Sitka, Alaska, with over 4,583 tribal citizens; as a tribal government, (STA) is responsible for the health, safety, welfare, and cultural preservation of its tribal citizens. STA respectfully submits the following comments in regard to the proposed Tongass Forest Plan Revision.

## Tribal Engagement

## Sovereignty

There are 19 federally recognized Native Tribes in Southeast Alaska and while they may have overlapping priorities or missions, they are all unique and not from the same cookie cutter mold. The citizenship of each tribe is composed predominantly of Alaska Natives (Aleut, Alutiiq, Athapaskans, Eyak, Haida, Inuit, Inupiat, Tlingit, and Yupik) but many have non-Alaska Natives on their rolls. All but one of these tribes, Metlakatla, are deemed landless under the Alaska Natives Claim Settlement Act (ANCSA) and all but one, the Central Council of Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska (T&H), have federally recognized sovereign traditional territories.

T&H is a federally recognized regional tribal government with limited jurisdiction (as described in its constitution) in relation to other tribal governments. That distinction is further reinforced in the CentralCouncilofTlingitand Haida Indian Tribes ofAlaska Clari� . Under the Act T&H is identi� a subordinate role to other southeast Alaska tribes. The Act states;

“Nothing in this title shall be interpreted to diminish or interfere with the government-to-government relationship between the United States and other federally recognized Alaska Native tribes, nor vest any power, authority, or jurisdiction in the Central Council of Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska over other federally recognized Alaska Native tribes."

STA is a federally recognized tribal government with a sovereign territory de� approved constitution as;

“all lands constituting the Native Village of Sitka and the areas formally known as “Indian Possessions” and “Cottage Settlement” and to all surrounding areas of Indian Country, if any, including all customary and traditional use and access areas in the vicinity of Baranof Island, Chichagof and surrounding islands, and all fee lands and allotments and lands owned by Sealaska, Inc. or Shee Atika, Inc. located therein (the Native corporations established pursuant to the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (Pub. L. 92-2o3) as amended to hold the land and other befits provided by Congress in partial compensation for the extinguishment of the Tribe’s aboriginal land rights), to the fullest extent provided by federal and (territorial map attached).

STA maintains its full sovereignty over these lands and its resources and has not relinquished sovereignty nor given any other tribe or Native-NGO the authority to represent it on resources management issues.

## Tribal Processes/Timelines

Tribal vetting processes for providing comments or making oficial decisions can vary signi� ’s review and decision making process involves vetting topics or issues through its various committees (Natural Resources, Health, Transportation and Community Development, Governance, Finance, Enrollment) or commissions (Kayaani and

Marine Mammal). Committees and commissions make recommendations to the Tribal Council, with the Council making the �

This process is very thorough and allows for input from staf, committees, and tribal citizens. Unfortunately, it doesn’t � committees meet once a month, which, combined with seasonal subsistence con� participation in the vetting process, make it challenging at best for tribes to provide input on issues that impact them or their citizens. The federal government acknowledges tribes in Southeast Alaska as sovereign nations then it’s time to treat them as such and not hold them to mandated public comment period timelines. If this is something that requires a policy change then those eforts should be pursued.

## Forest Service Staf

Recently federal agencies have been using contractors for engagement with tribal governments. STA prefers to engage directly with Forest Service employees rather than staf from contracted NGOs. If the Forest Service wishes to continue this practice, STA suggests requiring the contractor to commit a nondisclosure agreement to protect sensitive information that may be shared.

It’s not uncommon to see signi� and regional level. Unfortunately, new staf coming from other parts of the country don’t have the knowledge to successfully engage with tribal governments in Southeast Alaska. STA recommends all Forest Service staf (Line Oficers, Tribal Liaisons, Forest Supervisors, rct..) who engage with tribal governments take a mandatory course on tribal engagement.

## Co-Stewardship/Co-Management

The distinction between co-stewardship and co-management seems to be a grey area that is allusive and dificult to de� . STA believes maintaining the lands and resources within its traditional territory are its inherent responsibility. Sharing that responsibility through a comanagement agreement is a legitimate action that brings traditional knowledge and values, culture, and ways of life that would bene� .

STA proposes a shared management structure that allows the both parties to take an active role in the management of the lands and resources within it traditional territory. This management structure would be very similar to how STA and the SRD currently work and would not negate the public process. STA hopes to engage the Forest Service’s Sitka Ranger District in comanagement of; all aspect of the Redoubt sockeye program (weir, resource, and habitat), cultural resources, and special forest products.

## Redoubt Sockeye Management

Historically the Redoubt sockeye return has been an important resource for subsistence users in the Sitka area. The management plan for this salmon stock along with the freshwater productivity of the system have created outstanding returns that should be the model for Southeast Alaska. Had the weir not been operational in 2024 the local subsistence harvesters and commercial fishermen would not have been able to benefit from the outstanding returns STA has experience managing weirs and brings additional knowledge and resources to the management “table”.

## Cultural Resource Management

STA has an inherent interest in the preservation of Native cultural properties both on and of federally managed lands within its traditional territory. Public access to these remote sites requires routine monitoring to assess impacts from public use. STA has an agreement with Sealaska Corp. to manage its ANCSA 14(h)(1) sites in the Sitka area. A co-management agreement with the Forest Service would follow suit.

## Special Forest Products and Invasive Species Management

STA’s Kayaani Commission has been working with Forest Service for several years to develop a special forest products management plan and are hopeful it will be complete by spring of 2025. The plan is a living document that prioritizes protection of subsistence access to nontimber related forest products (plants, berries, etc..) while providing for small scale commercial use through an expedited permitting process.

STA has also begun working with Forest Service and State staf to address invasive plants on publicly managed lands (federal, state, and municipal). The Tribe hopes to take a more active role in managing invasives, including education and public outreach.

## Co-Management Funding

While co-stewardship and co-management have their bene� they aren’t much use unless both parties are � Tribes have the ability to secure outside funding to assist with implementing management agreements, but new management options brought forward by the federal government should come with identi� are categorized by priority, overall funding need (costs), and required funding timeline (short, medium, or long term).

## Aquatic Ecosystem Management

All salmon systems should be managed to prioritize production to enhance subsistence opportunities. Management actions include habitat assessments (stream and limnological), escapement monitoring, stream restoration, habitat expansion (� etc...

## Terrestrial Ecosystem Management

Providing subsistence and cultural opportunities should be a priority when making management decisions on a terrestrial level. Subsistence resources include � plants, berries, roots, moss, etc..) and fauna (Sitka Blacktail Deer, Mountain Goat, etc..) that are used as food and medicine. Cultural resources include Spruce roots, Cedar bark, trees (for carving), etc...

## Subsistence Resource Management

Sitka underwent its last decennial review to determine the fate of its rural status in 2010. Its population exceeded the primary rural status criteria of 2,500 residents. Due to it exceeding the primary population cap, a secondary set of criteria were used that included:

1) Use of subsistence resources

2) Proximity to the road system

3) Economic base (rural economy)

4) Infrastructure

5) Military presences

In 2017 the rural determination process was amended so that a community would retain its rural status until it is proven to be non-rural. The current process uses the secondary criteria listed above. The Forest Service should not take any actions that jeopardize Sitka’s rural status.

## Heritage, Cultural and Historic Site Management

Working with tribes is critical to the protection of cultural resources. STA was made aware of a large number of cultural sites listed on a map that was published on Facebook. Many of the sites were Sealaska Corporation’s 14 (h)(1) cultural heritage land selections. Unfortunately, even with pressure from the Forest Service, there’s been no luck getting the map removed. Now that the locations of these sites are available for the world to see its imperative for tribes, Sealaska, and the Forest Service enter into management agreements to provide additional protections.

## Roads and Other Infrastructure

Before any roads or other construction occurs on federal lands, there needs to be a clear assessment of all impacts on cultural and subsistence resources. This assessment should include impacts on access to these resources, including loss of access due to state or federal regulations and the risk to a community's rural status.

## Tourism/Recreation Management

Before any roads or other construction occurs on federal lands, there needs to be a clear assessment of all impacts on cultural and subsistence resources. This assessment should include impacts on access to these resources, including loss of access due to state or federal regulations and the risk to a community's rural status.

Past Forest Service assessments of the impacts of commercial tourism on coastal federal lands focused on impacts within its jurisdiction (above mean hightide line). While the assessment may have provided proception to federal lands it failed to assess the impact to the marine environment used to access these locations. The explosion of cruise ship tourism in Southeast Alaska has resulted in a comparable explosion in the number of local tour operators using the marine waters around Sitka to access Forest Service approved commercial use areas. All past and future commercial tourism assessments and permitting should extend into surrounding environments.

## Climate Change

The increasing threat of landslides brought about by climate change has increased the threat that these events could impact the communities and lives of Southeast Alaska residents. All municipal, state, and federal governments should revisit their policies or codes to allow construction on slopes above residential areas. This would include structures, roads, trails, etc... Unfortunately, landslides will be part of our everyday lives now and in the distant future. It’s time to prepare for this reality.

If you have any questions regarding these comments, please contact STA’s Resource Protection Director, Jef Feldpausch, at (907)747-7469 or email jef.feldpausch@sitkatribe-nsn.gov.

Sincerely,

Re: Comments on Notice of Intent to Rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

Dear Secretary Rollins:

The Coeur d'Alene Tribe appreciates the opportunity to comment on the United States Department of Agriculture Forest Service's (FS) Notice of Intent (NOI) to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule). This proposal lifts prohibitions on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting on 44.7 million acres, and has potentially profound impacts on ecological health and cultural resources across the nation,

The Coeur d'Alene Tribe recognizes that Idaho lands are exempted from this action because of the state-specific roadless rule adopted in Idaho in 2008. However, as we noted in 2004 when the Idaho Roadless Area Management Rule was first proposed, and again in 2008 when it was adopted, we are concerned about the reliance on the State of Idaho to ensure that our ancestral lands will be protected, and the continued vulnerability of these lands to over-development and over-harvest. Recent and past claims by state proponents that opening forests to construction and harvest are necessary for wildfire prevention contradict research that demonstrates that roadless areas protect biodiversity, water quality, and wildlife habitat, and actually reduce wildfire risk.

Additionally, the Coeur d'Alene Tribe's aboriginal territory outside of Idaho, as well as its larger interests in fisheries habitat restoration, extends into eastern Washington and western Montana. These lands, too, have been sources of the Tribe's physical, cultural, and spiritual sustenance since Time Immemorial, and we are concerned about impacts of the Roadless Rule's rescission on these areas and the protection of our interests for our Tribe's future generations. We are especially concerned that opening roadless areas in the Kettle and Sanpoil Rivers will hinder or reverse our collaborative efforts to protect and restore critical fish habitat.

Finally, we are concerned about the lack of clarity in the commitment of the Forest Service for Tribal engagement and consultation, and the lack of consultation with Tribes prior to issuing the NOI. Should the FS move forward with the rescission process, we strongly urge you to ensure that the agency uphold its trust responsibility, and ensure Tribes have adequate time to review and respond to potential impacts to our homelands.

Respectfully,

Sincerely,

Chifgorn

Chief J. Allan

Chairman, Coeur d'Alene Tribe

Date: 16th of September 2025

To: U.S. Department of Agriculture Attn.- Brook Rollins, Secretary of Agriculture From: Klawock Cooperative Association

Re:Comment- Roadless Rule, Docket Number FS-2025-0001

To Whom It May Concern,

The Klawock Cooperative Association is a federally recognized Tribe, located on Prince of Wales Island in southern southeast Alaska. Prince of Wales Island is the US's 4th largest island and were surrounded by the Tongass National Forest.

Please accept our written comment regarding the proposed initiation of an environmental impact statement and rulemaking concerning management of inventoried roadless areas on approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System lands, including in Alaska. This proposed rule would rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule

Klawock Cooperative Association formerly opposes this proposed rule. Our island was heavily impacted by commercial logging, that happened before and after implementing the National Environmental Policy Act, or “NEPA”

Areas that were logged without any environmental protections allowed for logging to occur right up to river and stream banks, causing potential negative effects to anadromous streams. We witnessed an increase in water temperature, a decrease in annual salmon returns, and unstable river/stream bank erosion.

As decades past, we started to see a dramatic increase in landslides. One fall storm had 55 landslides occur that damaged water ways, our highway, we lost electricity, and our entire infrastructure came to a screeching halt. Logging roads that were constructed, often used culverts that are insufficient and restricts water flow. This can damage the land above the culvert, and cause perching below the culverts, restricting the migratory path of our anadromous streams.

Another “unintended consequence" from commercial logging is low water level events. Once trees get established after logging, a tree would dominate an area, and smaller trees would start growing exponentially underneath the canopy. These smaller trees would suck up any rainwater that would typically make it into our rivers and streams.

The high density of trees, both large and small would stop under growth and forage from prospering, causing wildlife, from the bumblebee to the Alexander Archipelago Wolf, to struggle finding food. This shift negatively affected our food security, since our berries and Sitka black tail deer have reduced over time.

Commercial logging nearly halted on our island and were seeing programs and projects that promote the welfare of our land, strengthen stewardship & partnerships, support “qualified local hire or preference", and increase safety of our infrastructure. We have a vast highway system that connects 12 communities on our island, and most receive electricity via our hydro project at Black Bear Creek and Reynolds Creek.

Our Tribe is part of the Prince of Wales-Tribal Conservation District, which has equal representation from all 4 POW federally recognized Tribes, and all 4 POW Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, or “ANCSA”village corporations. This program has been able to secure funding/agreements to create “qualified local hire”. Our population has a lot of loggers, fisher persons, and harvesters. They all rely on pristine land & water for economic and food security.

Approximately 30% of our island is in “stem exclusion”, meaning it can't produce harvestable timber, or have the capacity to support wildlife. We recommend this be the starting point for projects, instead of initiating the process to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule.

Indigenous Science and stewardship being part of our projects have shown that we can assist the land & water. By removing some of these smaller trees, we can open access to areas that would be uninhabitable for decades or generations. This would allow access for wildlife, improve undergrowth & forage, and can reduce low water level events.

These smaller trees can create products that we can use, such as sawdust chips for recreation & trails, biomass for wood energy, and can supplement a compost project. This win-win scenario will satisfy economists and environmental activists, which is a truly rare opportunity in today's political landscape.

Klawock Cooperative Association recommends that stewardship or “good neighbor agreements" be implemented- with sources of funding through partnerships between federally recognized Tribes, ANCSA corporations and USForest Service occur. This would allow for residents to be deployed at areas we intend to improve.

We can demonstrate that by working together so our forests benefit the most amount of people and wildlife for generations to come. These efforts will allow for our economy to strengthen, address landslides & low-water level events, provide food security, decrease wildfires (in other areas besides the Tongass National Forest)- as well as begin efforts to absorb more carbon, since our dominant trees will absorb more carbon in the future,

Please consider these actions, before any decision making occurs that can cause further negative effects within the Tongass National Forest. This balanced approach can attract both sides of today's political spectrum.

Klawock Cooperative Association is grateful that our Indigenous Science, Commerce and Stewardship has an opportunity to play a positive role in the future of the TongassNational Forest.

Thank you for this opportunity to comment on this proposed rule making process.

Respectfully,

Re: Comments on Notice of Intent to Prepare Environmental Impact Statement for Rescission of 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Docket No. FS-2025-0001)

The Pit River Nation submits this letter in response to the Notice of Intent (NOI) published by the Department of Agriculture in the Federal Register on August 29, 2025, initiating an environmental impact statement (EIS) and rulemaking concerning the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule). This proposed action would affect approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System lands, including what appears to be around 280,000 acres within our Pit River ancestral territories.

Our Tribal Government, located in the four Northeastern counties of California, Lassen, Shasta, Modoc, and Siskiyou counties, have stewarded these lands since time immemorial. The Modoc, Klamath, Shasta-Trinity, and Lassen National Forests affected by this federal action are integral to our ancestral homelands, containing sacred sites, traditional use areas, and resources essential to our cultural, spiritual, and physical survival. Our traditional ecological knowledge and stewardship practices have preserved these ecosystems for millennia, maintaining the ecological integrity that the Roadless Rule has protected since 2001.

We have continued to maintain our Cultural properties for traditional use and ceremonial activities in these four counties since time immemorial. Some examples include the Medicine Lake Highland Traditional Cultural District and Sáttítla Highlands National Monument, which is located in existing roadless areas. The potential impacts to lands adjacent to or near Tribal lands will directly affect our resources and communities.

We meet quarterly with the Modoc, Klamath, Shasta-Trinity, and Lassen National Forests. In our September 3, 2025 meeting there was no mention of this potential action that affects these areas. Despite our extensive history that demonstrates our enduring connection to these lands, as well as our consistent engagement in federal decision-making processes affecting roadless areas. Any changes to roadless area management must acknowledge and build upon our existing relationships and investments.

## The Pit River Nation hereby formally requests immediate initiation of government-to-government consultation regarding the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule pursuant to:

● Executive Order 13175 on Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments

● USDA Departmental Regulation 1350-002 on Tribal Consultation (April 30, 2024)

● Forest Service Manual 1563 on Tribal Relations

● Secretarial Order 3403 on Joint Stewardship

● Our inherent sovereignty

## We specifically request:

1. Leadership-Level Consultation: Direct consultation between Tribal Council leadership and the Secretary of Agriculture and/or Chief of the Forest Service, not delegation to staff-level briefings

2. Consultation Timeline: A minimum 120-day consultation period beginning immediately, consistent with the USFS "Strengthening Tribal Consultations and Nation-to-Nation Relationships Action Plan"

## 3. Consultation Format:

○ Initial consultation session within 30 days

○ Follow-up sessions as needed to address complex issues

○ Written documentation of all consultation outcomes

○ Adequate time between sessions for Tribal Council review and community input

## 4. Consultation Scope to Include:

○ Impacts to trust resources

○ Effects on cultural resources and sacred sites

○ Alternatives to complete rescission

○ Potential co-management opportunities

○ Mitigation measures if rescission proceeds

○ Monitoring and adaptive management provisions

○ Requirement for consultation at both the programmatic level for this rulemaking AND commitment that EVERY individual road construction project that may follow will require separate, project-specific Tribal consultation

## 5. Consultation Support:

○ Funding for Tribal participation including travel, technical assistance, and capacity building

○ Access to all relevant documents and analyses

○ Maps and GIS data for affected areas

○ Other support as identified

6. Cooperating Agency Status: Designation of Pit River Nation as a cooperating agency under National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) for the EIS development

Point of Contact for Consultation is our Tribal Chairman & Tribal Historic Preservation Officer:

## Yatch Bamford, Pit River Tribal Chairman

36970 Park Ave

Burney, CA 96013

530-335-5421

Chairman@pitrivertribe.gov (Hard copy always required for consultation)

We request written confirmation within 14 days acknowledging this consultation request and proposing initia consultation dates. Failure to engage in meaningful consultation before proceeding with this rulemaking will constitute a violation of federal law and trust responsibilities.

We note that other Tribal leaders were sent an email notification on July 22, 2025, regarding this significant federal action. But please note that we did not receive this email notification, and always require a hard copy. Further, an email does not constitute meaningful consultation as required by federal law and policy. The NOI indicates that the Department has determined "the 2001 Roadless Rule is no longer the best approach to managing inventoried roadless areas" and proposes to return management authority to local decision-makers. The forthcoming EIS will analyze only two alternatives: the proposed rescission and a "no action" alternative maintaining current protections. This limited scope fails to consider reasonable alternatives that would address stated management concerns while preserving critical protections for Tribal interests.

Of particular concern is the abbreviated 21-day comment period ending September 19, 2025, which is wholly inadequate for meaningful Tribal engagement and engagement by Tribal members on a decision affecting millions of acres of ancestral territories. The NOI's vague promise that "Tribal governments and Alaska Native Corporations will have an opportunity to be engaged during rulemaking and EIS development" provides no concrete timeline, process, or commitment to substantive government-to-government consultation as required by law and policy.

Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRA) encompass numerous Traditional Cultural Properties (TCPs), Traditional Cultural Districts (TCDs), sacred sites, and cultural landscapes integral to our identity and spiritual practices. These areas include:

● Ceremonial and prayer sites used for specific purposes

● Traditional gathering areas for medicines, foods, and materials

● Burial grounds and ancestral village sites

● Cultural landscapes that embody our creation narratives and oral traditions

The proposed rescission fails to address how these irreplaceable cultural resources would be protected from:

● Physical destruction through road construction and logging operations

● Desecration through increased public access and industrial activity

● Loss of privacy and sanctity necessary for ceremonial practices

● Looting, vandalism, and unauthorized artifact collection

● Increased wildfire risk from human-caused ignitions that threaten cultural and sacred sites

Existing protections under the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), American Indian Religious Freedom Act, and Cultural Heritage Cooperation Authority (CHCA) are insufficient without the baseline protection provided by the Roadless Rule. Project-level consultation cannot replace landscape-level protection of interconnected cultural resources.

Roadless areas protect the headwaters and riparian systems that sustain our world renown fisheries and provide clean water for our Tribal communities and millions downstream.

● Spawning and rearing habitat

● Cold, clean water essential for fish survival in a warming climate

● Intact riparian vegetation maintaining stream temperatures and preventing sedimentation

● Natural hydrology supporting traditional and subsistence fishing

● Clean drinking water for Tribal communities, many of which lack adequate water infrastructure

● Water quality for ceremonial and cultural practices

● Protection of medicinal plant habitats that require pristine water sources

Scientific evidence demonstrates that road construction is the primary source of sediment pollution in forest streams, with roads contributing up to 90% of total sediment yield. The proposed rescission would:

● Increase sedimentation, destroying spawning gravels and smothering eggs

● Elevate stream temperatures beyond tolerance levels for cold-water species

● Fragment aquatic habitats through culverts and stream crossings

● Introduce pollutants from vehicle traffic and industrial operations

## Our people depend on roadless areas for:

● Traditional foods

● Medicinal plants requiring undisturbed forest conditions

● Materials for traditional arts, utilitarian objects, crafts, regalia, and ceremonial items

● First Foods central to our nutritional, cultural, and spiritual health

## Industrial development in these areas would:

● Reduce abundance and accessibility of subsistence resources

● Introduce invasive and noxious weed species through roads and ground-disturbing activities, which harm traditional plants and wildlife habitat

● Introduce competition from non-tribal commercial and recreational users

● Contaminate traditional foods through chemical applications and pollution

● Disrupt traditional harvest cycles and ecological relationships

● Directly threaten our food security and sovereignty

IRAs serve as critical climate refugia and carbon sinks, storing approximately 445 million tons of sequestered carbon. For the Pit River Nation, climate resilience is inseparable from cultural survival. The proposed rescission would:

● Release stored carbon through logging and soil disturbance

● Reduce forest resilience to climate impacts including drought, fire, and disease

● Eliminate migration corridors essential for species adaptation

● Undermine Tribal climate adaptation strategies

The proposed rescission raises serious environmental justice concerns, as Tribal communities would bear disproportionate impacts while receiving none of the economic benefits. Our communities already face:

● Higher rates of poverty and unemployment

● Higher risk of developing chronic health issues

● Limited access to proper healthcare and clean water infrastructure

● Cumulative impacts from historical and ongoing environmental degradation

● Loss of traditional lifeways from past federal actions

● Direct threats to food security through degradation of subsistence resources

## EXPECTATIONS AND REQUIREMENTS

## A. Government-to-Government Consultation Requirements

The announced decision to rescind the Roadless Rule without prior Tribal consultation violates multiple lega and policy requirements:

## Legal Obligations:

● Executive Order 13175 requiring "meaningful and timely input by tribal officials"

● USDA Departmental Regulation 1350-002 mandating consultation "early in the process"

● Secretarial Order 3403 on fulfilling trust responsibilities

● Forest Service Manual 1563 on Tribal Relations

The Department's April 2024 Departmental Regulation 1350-002 specifically prohibits promulgating any regulation with Tribal implications without first consulting "with Tribal officials early in the process of developing the proposed regulation." The June 2025 announcement and August 2025 NOI were issued without any documented Tribal consultation, representing a fundamental breach of trust responsibilities.

## Consultation Standards Required:

● Nation-to-nation engagement at the leadership level, not merely staff briefings

● Minimum 120-day consultation period as specified in USFS Action Plan

● Regional and local consultation sessions accessible to affected Tribal Governments

● Written documentation of how Tribal input influenced decision-making

● Tribal summary impact statement in Federal Register notices

● Consideration of negotiated rulemaking per DR 1350-002

## B. Timeline Inadequacy

The 21-day comment period is grossly inadequate for the following reasons:

## Capacity Constraints:

● Many Tribal Governments lack dedicated NEPA staff to analyze complex federal actions

● Tribal Councils meet monthly or bi-monthly, preventing timely review

● Cultural protocols require elder consultation and community input

● Geographic isolation and limited internet access and cell phone service impede participation

## Complexity of Issues:

● Eliminating management direction across 44.7 million acres across multiple states require site-specific analysis

● Interconnected impacts requiring holistic analysis - Treaty rights, cultural resources, and subsistence uses overlap within the same landscapes, making it impossible to assess impacts to one without understanding effects on all three, requiring extensive internal Tribal consultation and coordination that cannot be completed in 21 days

● Need to coordinate with multiple Tribal Governments sharing ancestral territories

● Requirement to analyze interactions with existing forest plans and agreements

## Precedent and Fairness:

● Original 2001 Rule provided multiple comment periods over 18 months

● State-specific rules (Idaho, Colorado) included extended consultation

● Environmental justice requires additional time for affected communities

● Complexity exceeds typical NEPA actions warranting extended timeline

## Minimum Requirements:

● Extend scoping comment period to at least 90 days

● Provide 120-day formal consultation period before proposed rule

● Schedule regional consultation sessions in culturally appropriate venues

● Fund Tribal participation including travel and technical assistance

## C. Conflicts with Existing Agreements and Laws

The proposed rescission creates unresolved conflicts with multiple existing authorities:

## Tribal Forest Protection Act (TFPA):

● Existing TFPA agreements addressing fire and forest health in IRAs

● Tribal proposals pending for managing threats across boundaries

● No analysis of how rescission affects TFPA implementation

## National Historic Preservation Act:

● Section 106 requirements for undertakings affecting historic properties

● Programmatic agreements covering TCPs and TCDs in roadless areas

● Landscape-level impacts cannot be mitigated through project consultation

## Cultural Heritage Cooperation Authority:

● Temporary closures for traditional and cultural purposes under 25 U.S.C. §3054

● Reburial sites protected under 25 U.S.C. §3053

● Confidentiality protections that would be compromised by development

## 2012 Planning Rule:

● Areas of Tribal Importance designated under 36 CFR §219.10(b)(1)

● Plan components specifically referencing Roadless Rule protections

● Integration of Indigenous Knowledge requirements

## Recent Forest Plan Revisions:

● Modoc, Shasta-Trinity, Lassen and Klamath National Forest Plan components dependent on roadless protections

● Co-stewardship agreements assuming continued IRA designations

● Monitoring commitments based on roadless area baseline conditions

The Pit River Nation unequivocally opposes the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule. This action represents an unconscionable breach of trust responsibilities, a violation of our inherent rights, and an existential threat to our cultural survival. We demand:

1. Immediate Withdrawal of the proposed rescission based on failure to conduct required Tribal consultation

2. Full Compliance with all consultation requirements before any further action

3. Comprehensive Analysis of impacts to treaty rights, cultural resources, and trust responsibilities

4. Alternative Development including Tribal co-management and enhanced protection options

5. Free, Prior, and Informed Consent for any changes affecting our ancestral territories

The Roadless Rule has provided essential protections for the lands and resources that sustain our people. We will utilize all available means—legal, political, and social—to prevent this destructive reversal of three decades of conservation policy. We stand ready to work with the Administration on genuine forest management improvements that respect Tribal sovereignty and enhance ecological resilience, but wholesale rescission is unacceptable.

The Pit River Nation requests written acknowledgment of receipt of these comments and a detailed response addressing each concern raised. We further request designation as a cooperating agency under NEPA and inclusion in all government-to-government consultation sessions.

Any failure to adequately address these concerns will be considered a violation of federal trust responsibilities and may result in administrative appeals, litigation, and requests for congressional intervention. We look forward to meaningful engagement that honors our government-togovernment relationship and protects the irreplaceable natural and cultural heritage of these lands for future generations.

Sincerely, yBf Yatch Bamford (Sep 19, 2025 10:24:37 PDT)

Yatch Bamford, Pit River Tribal Chairman

Mr. Brad Kinder Acting Director Ecosystem Management Coordination 201 14th Street SW Mailstop 1108 Washington, DC 20250-1124

RE: FS-2025-0001-0001 – Retain the 2001 Roadless Rule

Dear Mr. Kinder,

Chickaloon Native Village (CNV) is a federally-recognized Ahtna Dene Tribal government in southcentral Alaska, governed by Chickaloon Village Traditional Council (CVTC). CNV’s ancestral territory includes much of southcentral Alaska including upper Cook Inlet and the Susitna Watershed, and our traditional area of influence overlaps neighboring Dena’ina Dene and Ahtna Dene Tribal governments. Actions that occur within CNV’s traditional ancestral territory and customary area of use may impact our environment, our cultural resources, and the health of our Tribal citizens and community members. CVTC opposes the repeal of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. Rescinding this rule would open public lands up to harmful development and road construction, decreasing the amount of habitat for wildlife, and increasing wildfire risk.

The 2001 Roadless Rule protects 58 million acres of forested lands throughout the United States, including 14.7 million acres in Alaska alone. 99% of the Chugach National Forest, located in southcentral Alaska, within CNV’s traditional Tribal territory, is included in the inventoried Roadless Area. The Chugach National Forest contains salmon habitat for five species of Pacific salmon: chum, pink, coho, Chinook, and sockeye salmon. These salmon populations support commercial, subsistence, sport, and personal use fisheries that benefit all Alaskans. Chickaloon Native Village stewards salmon populations in Cook Inlet, which will be affected by development to lands currently protected by the Roadless Rule. In particular, lands protected under the Roadless Rule in Turnagain Arm include salmonbearing Resurrection Creek, Sixmile Creek, and Twentymile River. Resurrection Creek was degraded by historic placer mining in the early 20<sup>th</sup> century, but a 20 year, \$10+ million partnership between federal, local, and non-government partners has restored salmon habitat. Repealing the Roadless Rule will open the door for future development to degrade these salmon habitats.

Wildfire is a natural and essential process for keeping Alaska’s forests healthy, yet proposals to repeal the federal Roadless Rule—often justified by claims that more roads are needed for fire suppression—do not match how fire is managed in the state. Across much of Alaska, wildfires are monitored and frequently allowed to burn because they recycle nutrients, reduce pests and disease, and create a mosaic of habitats that supports biodiversity and forest resilience, especially in Interior Alaska. In contrast, Southeast Alaska’s cool, wet coastal rainforest rarely experiences large or frequent burns. Building roads in currently undeveloped areas would fragment habitat, increase erosion, and invite more human-caused ignitions without meaningfully improving fire control. Maintaining the Roadless Rule therefore safeguards the ecological benefits of natural fire and the longterm health and productivity of Alaska’s forests.

In fact, roads can increase the risk and number of wildfires in Alaska. A study of Interior Alaska from 1988–2005 showed human-caused fire ignitions were 11 times higher within 5 km of highways, and 6-fold between 5–10 km, compared to farther away. Areas within 10 km of roads and settlements have many more fire starts by people than do remote areas. Roads facilitate access by people—more chance of campfires, discarded cigarettes, equipment sparks or other ignition sources. They also alter the landscape: creating edges where vegetation dries faster, accumulating flammable fuel in road verges, and increasing wind exposure. These combined factors make roads a significant contributor to wildfire risk, especially when fire suppression is cited as a reason for building more roads. Another study by the U.S. Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station (2020) found that “non-native plants are twice as common within 500 feet of a road as they are farther away” and found that “speculation that eliminating road prohibitions would improve forest health is not supported by nearly twenty years of monitoring.” In other words, increased development and expansion including road construction would lead to detrimental effects to our protected forested lands, increasing non-native plant species and wildfire risk.

Furthermore, granting more land access allows for permissive activities without responsibilities. Alaskan communities are often faced with access that is not consented causing deleterious effects to the environment and wildlife. Tribes, especially, feel development projects acutely in their care for land and waters, as opening more land leads to more vulnerability of the land and waters in which they steward.

In conclusion, we urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture to retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. We thank you for the opportunity to submit these comments.

May Nek’eltaeni (Creator) Guide our Footsteps,

## Re: Comment of the Ketchikan Indian Community (KIC) on USDA Forest Service Proposal to Rescind the National Roadless Rule Protections on the Tongass National Forest, Docket No. FS-2025-0001 (filed electronically at: https://www.regulations.gov/commenton/FS-2025-0001-0001).

Dear Secretary Rollins and Acting Director Kinder

On behalf of the Ketchikan Indian Community (KIC), we submit these comments in strong opposition to the rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule as it applies to the Tongass National Forest¹, especially in regards to the rights of indigenous people in Southeast Alaska to exercise their rights and sovereignty in connection with the land

## Our Homeland and Connection to the Tongass

KIC's traditional homelands span what is now known as the Tongass National Forest (or “Tongass"). Our rights to self-determination are intertwined with the resources the Tongass provides, as an inextricable means to practice, preserve and exercise our culture as a sovereign Tribe. Our people have been here for more than 10,000 years. Roadless areas are integral to our identity and our survival. We hunt, fish, gather medicines, and harvest spruce root and cedar bark from old growth trees to weave hats and baskets and build canoes to revitalize our traditiona practices and ways of life. This interdependence cannot be separated from our culture and is embedded in our exercise of sovereignty as a federally recognized Tribe. Healthy old-growth forests are our churches, our classrooms, and our grocery stores. They heal us. When they are logged, we lose that connection and our health suffers.

In a 1977 interview with attorney Mr. Ellis, Tlingit Elder Albert Shields (Teikweidi, Taanta Kwaan) recounted the Forest Service's seizure of his ancestral land within now Ketchikan Indian Community jurisdiction. Mr. Shields described how his family had a smokehouse and a log cabin

OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT

near the mouth of Thorne Arm, by a creek and lake, the Forest Service arrived, burned their structures, and forcibly removed them. The agency's stated reason was to install a water gauge.According to Mr. Shields, the Forest Service proceeded to sell some of the ancestral land and clear-cut the old-growth trees. This was the same land where his family had hunted deer and fished for coho salmon, since the beginning of his time and his grandfather's time and before that. He lamented the resulting devastation, stating that after the timber was removed, only stumps remained where they once hunted, leaving nothing, meaning there is no longer deer in the area. Mr. Shields stressed that this was his grandfather's land and expressed his desire to see it preserved. Mr. Shields was filing a claim to get his families land back. The old growth forest of the Tongass is essential to sustaining our ecosystem. It preserves carbon, maintains necessary temperatures and habitat for salmon to spawn and return to our oceans (where we remind you aboriginal rights remain intact) and provide livelihood for the animals, plants and traditional medicine indigenous peoples of these lands have stewarded for thousands of years as part of a reciprocal existence.

We would like to specifically voice the impact of Senate Bill 25542 — the Alaska Native Landless Equity Act in the 119th Congress (introduced July 30, 2025 by Sen. Lisa Murkowski with Sen. Dan Sullivan as cosponsor) currently reviewed in the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. It recognizes the Southeast Alaska Native communities of Ketchikan, Haines Petersburg, Tenakee Springs, and Wrangell as "landless" under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act³ and authorizes equitable land conveyances from the Tongass National Forest by amending ANCSA to include newly formed Alaska Native urban corporations. Should Roadless rescission proceed, the status quo of these lands currently preserving indigenous interests will be detrimentally altered from the risk of being logged, mined or degraded before transfer destroying their value and violating the promise of equity embedded in the bill. Because the bill may pass by the end of the 119th Congress (January 3, 2027), any administrative move that undermines land conditions prejudices Congressional intent and violates principles of fairness and trust. This will cause undue burden on the Tribe to spend unnecessary time, funds and resources to mitigate these risks from this federal action

## Tribal Consultation Failures

We must place on the record that there has been no meaningful Tribal consultation in this process. The July forum was canceled without notice after we engaged our Tribal Council, who were on call and in anticipation of immediate engagement, but received none. Additionally, the August 5th meeting was, in fact, nothing more than a Tribal forum—a setting where the Forest Service talked at Tribes instead of a government-to-government dialogue, as required by law.

OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT

That is not consultation. It violates Executive Order 131754, USDA's Tribal Consultation policy, and the federal trust responsibility. Since then, we have communicated our request for formal consultation but have had no material action taken by the forest service. This procedural failure alone provides grounds for legal challenge. It is also important to note that this expedited timeline of 21 days between USDA's notice of rulemaking on the Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) reflects inconsistent federal policy and does not provide sufficient time for Tribe's to adequately be engaged on the matter or for the federal government to provide the required analysis by the laws this decision implicates.

## Procedural & Legal Concerns with Rescission

NEPA (National Environmental Policy Act⁵) Violations: The Forest Service must analyze the cumulative, site-specific, and cultural impacts of rescinding the Roadless Rule, including harm to Tribes, their subsistence rights and impacts on federally protected waters (such as the inter-continental shelf where aboriginal rights are implicated, and is directly and indirectly impacted by changes to the Tongass) and congressional actions. A draft EIS cannot lawfully proceed without this analysis.

NHPA (National Historic Preservation Act6) violations: The NHPA mandates meaningful government-to-government consultation and an evaluation of the impacts to areas covered within the Tongass National Forest. Namely, Duke Island, which has been formally recognized as Traditional Cultural Property. This requires a consideration of the cultural significance of this land by the USDA prior to any rule making. This cannot occur without required consultation with Tribes.

ANILCA (Alaska National Interests Land Conservation Act7) & Rural Subsistence Rights: Under ANILCA, rural and Alaska Native subsistence8 uses must be prioritized Logging roads fragment deer habitat and salmon watersheds, directly undermining KIC's subsistence rights. This burdens KIC and its Citizens by forcing them to pursue longer distances and expend more energy and funds to steward and reach their dwindling wildlife and ecosystems that are currently available in their immediate surroundings

Landless Communities: KIC is a landless community under ANCSA. The Alaska Delegation's bill would allow for the creation of a Ketchikan Native corporation and transfer of lands from the Tongass. Some of those lands are within areas protected by the roadless rule. With rescission occurring while the bill is being passed, these lands could be logged, destroying their value and violating the trust obligation to transfer intact, viable lands. This creates a legal conflict between these congressional efforts and administrative agency action.

•Irreparable Harm: Once old-growth is logged, it cannot be restored for centuries9. Tha irreparable harm would form the basis for seeking injunctive relief if USDA proceeds without resolving these conflicts. Clearing trees impede the sustainability of interconnected ecosystems that indigenous people preserve by simply practicing their ways of life. Any further removal from these systems will exacerbate the loss of culture

## Practical Realities of Nonexistent Infrastructure

Repealing the Roadless Rule will not bring jobs or community stability. The pulp mills have been closed for decades, shipping costs are prohibitive, and trained timber personnel are gone Most raw logs are shipped overseas, often to China, rather than supporting local housing. By contrast, the Roadless Rule already contains exceptions for genuine community infrastructure needs. With it in place, KIC has successfully partnered with the Forest Service on restoration work—bringing jobs, restoring watersheds, and supporting Tribal citizens.

## Our Position and Request

• KIC reaffirms our opposition to rescission of the Roadless Rule.

We demand government-to-government consultation10not forums, not webinars, but consultation in the meaning of federal law for each statute and federal trust responsibility that has been implicated

• We ask the Forest Service to halt this process until Congress resolves the Landless issue Until then, the lands in question remain in dispute and must be protected

## Legal Foundation Prompting Injunctive Relief

KIC reserves the right to pursue injunctive relief before or after the draft EIS. Grounds include:

Failure to conduct lawful Tribal consultation (E.O. 13175, APA (Administrative Procedure Act), NEPA, NHPA).

• Failure to consider subsistence rights (ANILCA§810)

Risk of irreparable harm to disputed lands concerning congressional action (equitable settlement for communities unjustifiably left out by ANCSA)

• Arbitrary and capricious agency action under the APA by ignoring cultural environmental, and economic realities

OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT

## Conclusion

Until the land dispute is resolved, those are our Trees. They are part of our homeland, our health, and our future. We ask USDA and the Forest Service to keep the Roadless Rule in place in the Tongass and respect our rights as a sovereign Tribal government

The Forest Service's proposed timeline issuing a Draft Environmental Impact Statement (EIS), is expected by March 2026, and a final decision by late 2026, demonstrates an expedited process that fails to honor the depth of consultation and analysis required under federal law and EO 1415311, which only authorizes agencies to only take "legal actions."Compressing review into this shortened window undermines the government's obligations underNEPA, which requires a thorough and good-faith analysis of impacts and alternatives, and under theNHPA, which demands early, meaningful engagement with Tribes to protect cultural and historic resources Moreover, proceeding on the accelerated track while Senate Bill 2554 is legislated in Congress prejudices the legislative process and risks irreparable harm to lands that would soon, and of right ought to be conveyed to landless Alaska Native communities. This creates a violation of both federal trust responsibilities and the APA, as it would be arbitrary and capricious to finalize a rule that overlooks legal requirements and ignores unresolved land claims by foreclosing on Congress'ability to deliver a just remedy. Coupled with the federal government's inconsistent policy on this rule and the undue burden imposed on Tribes to navigate this shifting framework is an illegal exercise of federal action

We request a review and adjustment to the current course of action and urgently petition the federal government to uphold these federal trust responsibilities to Tribal Nations.

Respectfully submitted,

RE: Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule) (66 FR 3244, 36 CFR Subpart B (2001)), Docket No. FS-2025-0001-0001

Dear Secretary Rollins,

The Snoqualmie Indian Tribe (“Snoqualmie Tribe”), a federally recognized sovereign Indian tribe and signatory to the Treaty of Point Elliott of 1855 with reserved rights thereunder, appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (“Roadless Rule”).

The Snoqualmie Tribe, known as the People of the Moon - sdukʷalbixʷ in our Native language – is a federally recognized tribe in the Puget Sound region of Washington State. When our ancestors signed the Treaty of Point Elliott, trading our former lands for the right to continue our culture and our way of life, they did so with the understanding that all those things that support and sustain us and our culture would remain available to us. Specifically, as a signatory to the Treaty, the Tribe reserved to itself, among other things, the right to fish at usual and accustomed areas and the “privilege of hunting and gathering roots and berries on open and unclaimed lands” off-reservation throughout the modernday state of Washington (Treaty of Point Elliott, art. V, 12 Stat. 928). To this end, the government of the United States, with whom we made that agreement, has a trust responsibility to ensure that we continue to have access to clean water, land and air across our traditional lands in perpetuity.

We write in a spirit of partnership, but with a firm expectation that the United States will honor its obligations to respect Tribal sovereignty, include tribes as co-equal decisionmakers, and uphold the trust duty in all actions. The proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule directly threatens the rights guaranteed under treaties by opening up to destruction the lands and habitats that support the species and practices that comprise our cultural inheritance. We ask that the proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule be withdrawn and the Rule remain in place as currently written. Tribal Consultation with the Snoqualmie Indian Tribe did not occur prior to the announcement that the Roadless Rule would be rescinded, and the Tribe requests a suspension of the rescission and meaningful government-to-government consultation.

![](images/4697397c5700f26f2131b4bfa06b6353d54f77ca25a39a090bb25f862c45b25b.jpg)

## Environmental Impacts

The 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule restricts road construction and development across approximately 60 million acres of national forests and grasslands, 2 million of which is located in Washington State. Roadless areas protect fish and wildlife habitats, clean drinking water, and wild forests. Road construction and logging have been shown to have significant negative environmental impacts by fragmenting ecosystems, disrupting wildlife migration and negatively impacting biodiversity, allowing for the spread of invasive species, and degrading water quality with road run off and increased erosion and sedimentation<sup>1,2</sup>. Furthermore, logging can lead to increased flood severity and landslides, creating large-scale negative impacts on watershed health<sup>1</sup>. Intact forests also provide valuable ecosystem services, serving to regulate temperature and mitigate climate change.

National Forests in Washington support more than 1,600 plants and animal species, 39 of which are endangered<sup>3</sup>. Lack of adequate habitat is a major limiting factor in recovering these species, which are not only central to Tribal cultural practices and ways of life but many of which, such as Pacific Salmon, support billion-dollar commercial and recreational industries. Protecting these areas is necessary for species recovery and sustaining the culture and lives of the Snoqualmie people.

## Wildfire hazard management

The argument that rescinding the Roadless Rule will lead to reduced wildfire risk and increased protection for surrounding communities and infrastructure is flawed. Approximately 85% of all wildfires are human-caused<sup>4,5</sup> and the majority of human-caused fires on National Forests start within a half a mile of a road<sup>2,</sup> <sup>6</sup>. Fire suppression activities are already explicitly allowed in roadless areas and there is no evidence that fires spread more quickly in roadless areas than managed forests<sup>2,6</sup>. Rescinding the Roadless Rule will not lead to a reduction in wildfire threat nor the protection of neighboring communities and will instead create additional risk by increasing opportunity for the leading driver of wildfires, human activity.

## Economic impacts

Areas protected under the Roadless Rule generate significant and sustainable economic benefits for local communities through outdoor recreation. These areas contain pristine and high-quality fishing and hunting grounds and are popular for other types of backcountry recreation. In Washington state, an estimated \$290 million is spent annually in communities around national forests lands<sup>7</sup>. The economic benefits of rescinding the Roadless Rule and increasing industry will largely be concentrated with private companies, while tribes and tribal environmental and cultural resources and local communities will bear the costs.

![](images/b0a60084a866f293bb467334eb2390bc3a3fd4e6627a5307c10797fccb5d6775.jpg)

Expanding Forest Service Roads throughout roadless areas is also not economically viable. The U.S. Forest Service already manages a 380,000-mile road system with an estimated \$8.6 billion backlog, largely due to dilapidated roads<sup>8</sup>. New construction of roads in roadless areas will just further add to the maintenance issues and financial burden of the Forest Service.

## Impacts on Tribal Rights and Usual and Accustomed Places

National Forest lands hold culturally significant areas, including sacred sites, ancient trail networks and travel routes, and usual and accustomed hunting, fishing, and gathering areas. Roadless areas help to protect these places; allowing new construction and increased industry could lead to their destruction and disrupt access to tribal members, and thus the ability to exercise treaty-protected rights.

It is both fiscally and environmentally responsible to protect these roadless areas and undeveloped forest lands. This proposed recission is a step backwards and will not only threaten the tribe’s hard-earned progress to restore local habitats and preserve Tribal ways of life for future generations but will also compromise the ecological advancements gained from federal, Tribal, state, and local agencies who have dedicated time and resources to serve their communities for the benefit of all Americans.

## Alternatives to the Roadless Rule

If the process to rescind the Roadless Rule moves forward, alternatives to replace the rule already exist. The U.S.D.A. Forest Service and Department of Interior sign co-management and co-stewardship agreements with tribes for federal lands and waters<sup>9</sup>. The federal trust and treaty responsibility to tribal nations includes co-management of tribal ancestral homelands. For example, through the Tribal Consultation process, the areas that were previously protected by the Roadless Rule can be discussed with co-management as a viable alternative framework. Both tribal and federal governments can discuss how to prevent foreseeable hazards, while protecting, restoring, and respecting lands for the benefit of all.

![](images/a7ea66cf4c53d7322f7a05f8a7209fbde8860e1b0997033448f711c488f88dd5.jpg)

Please listen to the science and indigenous knowledge gained from the stewardship of these lands from time immemorial and keep the 2001 Roadless Rule in place as it is currently written. Thank you for considering these comments.

Sincerely,

—DocuSigned by: Michael Ross

Michael Ross

Deputy Executive Director of Government Affairs and Special Projects

Subject: Comments on Notice of intent to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement on a proposed rule to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule

Dear Mrs. Rollins:

The Big Pine Paiute Tribe of the Owens Valley (“Tribe”), a federally recognized tribe, respectfully requests that the federal government keep the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (“2001 Roadless Rule”) intact. There is no need to rescind it or prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (“EIS”).

The 2001 Roadless Rule has served the Tribe well for more than two decades. Owens Valley is almost completely surrounded by lands managed by the Inyo National Forest. These lands span the Tribe’s traditional territory and remain extremely important as places of cultural preservation, watershed health, good air quality, and more. Tribal members frequently visit nearby Forest lands to access food (such as pinenuts and game), medicines, fiber, fuelwood, and places of spiritual renewal. When the rule was introduced, Tribal leaders and staff worked with Forest Service staff to advise on roads important for Tribal access as well as on “roads” and routes that were redundant and difficult (and expensive) to maintain. The Tribe desires access to Forest lands, but too many roads leads to too many recreationalists gaining access to remote areas where mischief—or worse--may occur. Although modern people need roads, all roads alter the natural ecosystem. Roads change the patterns of wildlife, emit dust (such as particulate matter that degrades air quality and human health), collect and channel water thus increasing soil erosion, cause pollution in creeks, and damage plant roots sometimes leading to plant and tree death. Roads lead vehicles to places where people knowingly or carelessly damage archaeological sites, pillage artifacts, leave waste, trample vegetation, risk starting fires, disturb wild creatures, collect rocks and crystals, and more. On poor or unmaintained roads, vehicles get stuck or damaged, and this typically leads to road widening, which leads to further erosion, dust, and ecological degradation.

Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule would be an affront to the people who, two decades ago, worked long and hard on this challenging project. The rule was controversial when introduced, but once the stakeholders looked more closely at the problems and potential solutions, people went to work studying, mapping, and evaluating. For the Inyo National Forest, the result was a satisfactory balance between conservation objectives and the desire for access. Now, there are ample roads used by Tribal members, and there are fewer redundant, resource-damaging roads. Many of the unnecessary routes

have been obscured and have gradually recovered from past use. In fact, volunteers, including some Tribal youth, helped to obscure illegal routes and tracks by scattering downed wood or dead vegetation debris to make them less obvious, thereby allowing recovery to begin.

The 2001 Roadless Rule is compatible with the need to manage forest fuels, and it serves to lessen the chances of igniting a forest fire. Many fires start when vehicles come in contact with dry plant material, and a high percentage of fires result from improperly extinguished campfires or other human actions. Obviously, these chances are reduced if sites cannot be reached by roads. There are many effective methods for fuels reduction that do not require “roads” in the true sense. Fire can help renew most forest ecosystems, so wildfires that burn in roadless areas should be allowed to burn, within reason, because if there are no roads, there are unlikely to be structures in need of protection. Airborne methods and other fire-fighting approaches may be deployed if there are concerns. More roads are not the solution to protect the Wildland Urban Interface (“WUI”) from wildfire, and legal roads typically already exist within these edges. There is no need to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule to protect the WUI; rather, appropriate fuel management should be implemented, and communities must refrain from allowing further encroachment into wild lands.

The Tribe hopes your agency will drop the idea of rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule rather than waste the time and money to prepare an EIS to arrive at the obvious conclusion that roads damage the environment. Should an EIS or other National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”) process commence, it is imperative that your agency conduct early and meaningful consultation with tribes.

## Subject: Hoopa Valley Tribe's Comments on the Proposed Roadless Area Conservation Rule

The Hoopa Valley Tribe appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed Roadless Rule. Portions of the land that could be impacted by this action are adjacent to the Hoopa Valley Indian Reservation which are within our ancestral territory. Forest Management Decisions by the Federal Government in our ancestral territory must be justified by sound science and by meaningful Government to Government consultation. Our people have stewarded these lands for millennia and our knowledge of this unique ecosystem is based upon management principles that have insured the Hupa Peoples survival.

The Hoopa Valley Tribe is opposed to any Federal actions that would rescind the existing Federal Roadless Conservation Rule. The current proposal would circumvent the NEPA process, and the proposed timeline will not allow for meaningful consultation on actions that will affect the Hupa people and our way of life.

Existing Scientific data demonstrates that intact, roadless landscapes provide significant ecological benefits. These areas protect headwater streams and reduce fine sedimentation critical for sustaining anadromous fish populations central to our culture, ecosystem health, and survival of our people. Roadless areas also serve as important wildlife corridors, help to preserve biodiversity and support sensitive species like Northern Spotted Owl (Strix occidentalis) and Northern Harrier (Circus hudsonius) on the landscape. Further, these landscapes contribute to carbon sequestration helping to mitigate the effects of accelerating climate change.

We support adaptive management as defined in the US Department of Interior handbook and we are currently partnered with the US Forest Service, Six Rivers National Forest to be co-stewards of significant portions of these landscapes. This collaboration has the potential to promote forest health, enhance ecosystem resilience, and reduce wildfire risk

The Tribe urges the Forest Service to engage us as co-equal partners in all aspects of roadless area management. Doing so ensures that roadless designations integrate both indigenous knowledge ecological science and that policies remain flexible enough to address site-specific conditions while safeguarding the health of forests and watersheds for generations to come.

Sincerely, Aoe Davo Joe Davis, Chairman Hoopa Valley Tribe

Re: LVD Comments on Notice of Intent to Prepare Environmental Impact Statement for Rescission of 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Docket No. FS-2025-0001)

Dear Director,

The Lac Vieux Desert Band of Lake Superior Chippewa Indians, a federally recognized Indian Tribe (Tribe) located in Watersmeet, Michigan, submits this letter in response to the Notice of Intent to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Proposed Recission). This Proposed Recission directly affects the Ottawa National Forest, among many other forests located within the Tribe’s treaty-ceded territories under the Treaties of 1842 and 1854. These forests hold sacred sites, traditional use areas, and treaty-reserved resources that are central to our survival, identity, and responsibilities as a sovereign Nation.

The Tribe carries out stewardship in these forests through Manoomin restoration, water quality monitoring, cultural site protection, native plant cultivation and monitoring and fisheries management. Any reduction in roadless protections would damage these responsibilities. New road construction and logging would fragment wildlife habitat, increase sediment in rivers and streams, and degrade the clean water and medicines our people depend on. Scientific evidence shows that forest roads are the single greatest source of sediment pollution in streams, contributing up to 90 percent of sediment loads and seriously disrupting the safety and stability of watersheds<sup>1</sup>. Intact forests also serve as carbon sinks, storing an estimated 445 million tons of carbon across inventoried roadless areas<sup>2</sup>, which are critical for climate resilience and for the survival of fish, wildlife, and people in a changing world.

Roadless areas safeguard treaty-reserved hunting, fishing, and gathering. Their destruction would reduce the abundance and accessibility of traditional foods and medicines, introduce invasive species, contaminate subsistence resources, and disrupt ecological relationships that our knowledge systems have stewarded for generations. These areas also contain sacred sites, burial places, ceremonial grounds, and cultural landscapes that cannot be replaced. Increased roads and industrial activity threaten these sites with desecration, looting, loss of privacy for ceremonies, and greater fire risk.

These ecological and cultural harms are inseparable from the process failures we are now witnessing, because rushing this decision without full Tribal input compounds the risks to our people and our homelands. The Forest Service sent an email to Tribal leaders on July 22, 2025, regarding this Proposed Recission. However, email notice does not constitute Tribal consultation. Government-to-government consultation must be meaningful, timely, and respectful of our sovereignty. Proceeding without such consultation violates Executive Order 13175, USDA Departmental Regulation 1350-002, Forest Service Manual 1563, Secretarial Order 3403, and the federal government’s trust and treaty responsibilities.

The Tribe formally requests immediate in-person, government-to-government consultation related to the Proposed Rescission. Consultation must occur at our Tribal headquarters in Watersmeet, Michigan, with our Tribal leadership. We request a minimum 120- day consultation period, consistent with the Forest Service’s “Strengthening Tribal Consultations and Nation-to-Nation Relationships Action Plan.” The scope must include impacts to treaty rights, trust resources, cultural and sacred sites, water resources, fish and wildlife, and climate. Alternatives to full rescission, opportunities for co-management, and mitigation measures must all be part of the discussion. If this Proposed Rescission proceeds, we also require a commitment that every individual road construction or logging project will trigger separate project-level Tribal consultation.

Furthermore, we request designation as a cooperating agency pursuant to National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) is 42 U.S.C. § 4321 et seq., Public Law 91–190 for the Environmental Impact Statement. The current 21-day comment period is wholly inadequate. Tribal governments cannot analyze complex federal actions within this timeframe, especially when our Tribal leadership manages so many additional responsibilities, cultural protocols require community and elder input, and multiple Tribes must coordinate to assess the individual impacts on their Tribal communities. The original 2001 Roadless Rule involved extended comment and consultation periods; this process demands no less.

The Tribe unequivocally opposes the Proposed Rescission. This action represents an unconscionable breach of trust responsibilities, a violation of our treaty rights, and an existential threat to our cultural survival.

The Tribe demands:

1. Full compliance with all consultation requirements pursuant to Executive Order 13175, USDA Departmental Regulation 1350-002, Forest Service Manual 1563, Secretarial Order 3403, and the federal government’s trust and treaty responsibilities before any further action on the Proposed Rescission.

2. Immediate withdrawal of the Proposed Rescission based on failure to conduct required Tribal consultation.

3. Comprehensive analysis of impacts to treaty rights, cultural resources, and trust responsibilities implicated by the implementation of the Proposed Rescission.

4. Alternative development of enhanced protection option including Tribal co-management as it relates to implementation of the Proposed Rescission.

5. Free, Prior, and Informed Consent for any changes affecting Tribal ancestral territories.

The 2001 Roadless Rule has provided essential protection for the lands and resources that sustain our people. We stand ready to work with the Administration on genuine forest management improvements that respect Tribal sovereignty and enhance ecological resilience, but wholesale rescission is unacceptable.

Our point of contact for consultation on this matter is:

Dr. Lara A. Jacobs Natural Resources Director Lac Vieux Desert Cultural Preservation and Natural Resources Divisions Lara.Jacobs@LVD-nsn.gov

We expect written confirmation of receipt of this letter within 14 days, along with proposed dates for initiating in-person consultation with our Tribal Council.

Sincerely,
