RE: Technical Comments on the Notice of Intent (NOI) to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) for the Proposed Rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule Reinstatement – Tongass National Forest

Dear Secretary Rollins and Forest Service Planning Staff:

The undersigned Southeast Alaska Tribal Governments, as federally recognized sovereign nations whose ancestral homelands encompass what is now known as the Tongass National Forest, respectfully submit the following technical comments on the Notice of Intent (NOI) issued by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to develop an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) concerning the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule) as applied to the Tongass National Forest.

For the Tribes of the Tongass, these forests are not merely resources—they are our homelands. Our communities rely on them for cultural, nutritional, spiritual, and economic sustenance. Accordingly, any federal proposal that alters the management regime of these lands, particularly one involving the potential expansion of industrialscale development into currently protected areas, constitutes a matter of significant tribal concern. We therefore offer the following comments in three primary domains:

I. Priority Considerations and Alternatives to the Proposed Recission of the 2001 Roadless Rule

II. Effects That Should Be Analyzed in the EIS and Relevant Scientific Studies, Indigenous Knowledge, and Local Data Legal and Procedural Concerns Affecting Tribal Rights and Interests

III. Legal and Procedural Concerns Affecting Tribal Rights and Interests

## I. Priority Considerations and Alternatives to the Proposed Recission of the 2001 Roadless Rule

A central shortcoming of the NOI is its apparent framing of management options through a limited and binary lens—one that positions the complete rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule as necessary to facilitate economic vitality and the development of a sustainable forest-based economy within the Tongass National Forest (Green, 2007; Trump, 2025). Such framing fails to reflect the range of scientifically and culturally grounded management strategies that have emerged from decades of tribal, regional, and intergovernmental planning efforts (Organized Village of Kasaan et al., 2020; Portner, 2021; Sustainable Southeast Partnership, 2020). Additionally, the continued reliance on timber-volume mapping as the primary means of measuring forest diversity, ecosystem function, conservation priorities, and potential effects is fundamentally flawed. Accordingly, the following alternatives and priority issues must be fully developed, considered, and analyzed within the EIS process:

## Priority Consideration

## A. Transition to Culturally Aligned Young-Growth Forestry in Previously Logged Areas

• Focus considerations on restoration-based second-growth timber harvest within the existing road matrix (Hanley, 2005; Sustainable Southeast Partnership, 2020).

• Avoid expansion into roadless or unfragmented old-growth areas (Carroll et al., 2025; DellaSala et al., 2022; Martin et al., 2021).

Implement Indigenous Knowledge and science-based restoration forestry to improve habitat quality and connectivity, and understory diversity (Garibaldi & Turner, 2004; Kübler & Günter, 2024; Lee et al., 2021; Long et al., 2020; Wickham et al., 2022).

Support the continued work of regional working groups (Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy, Tongass Transition Collaborative) whose efforts have resulted in planning frameworks that have garnered community support (Portner, 2021).

## B. Investment in Deferred Maintenance and Existing Infrastructure to Support Regional Economic Objectives

Allocate funding toward backlogged maintenance of existing forest roads, culverts, and bridges, particularly for fish passage and erosion control, and towards the development of durable, culturally aligned young growth active management. Currently, there are approximately 5,000 miles of roads within the National Forest system, approximately 3,100 miles of which are not maintained for passenger vehicles (Escamilla, 2024) and a \$10.8 billion dollar backlog in deference maintenance costs.

Develop funding strategies, allocations, and mechanisms that do not rely on the sale of timber to maintain infrastructure maintenance and invest in restoration.

Prioritize contracting for upgrades using Good Neighbor Authorities with southeast Alaska Native Tribes, 638 contracting and compacting mechanisms, and the Tribal Forest Protection Act to ensure tribal involvement in project development, oversight, and implementation.

## C. Indigenous-Led Forest Stewardship

Establish a co-management framework in which federally recognized tribes assume lead roles in determining local land use designations, consistent with principles of Indigenous self-determination (Johnson et al., 2021; Mills & Nie, 2021, 2022).

Embed Indigenous Knowledge and cultural-use mapping in the development of adaptive management zones and protected areas (Berkes et al., 2000; Blevins, 2024; Cuerrier et al., n.d.; Fatorić & Seekamp, 2017; Johnson et al., 2021; Lander & Mallory, 2021).

These priorities reflect our traditional cultural values, ecological imperatives, and durable regional consensus on economic trajectories that should be given full analytical weight in the scoping and subsequent NEPA phases of this rulemaking.

Alternatives to the Proposed Rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule

Tribal Alternative for the Protection of Traditional Homelands In the Tongass National Forest

## Overview

In recognition of the inherent sovereignty and government-to-government relationship between federally recognized Tribes and the United States, and in light of the longstanding, well-documented traditional and customary uses of the Tongass National Forest by the indigenous peoples, we propose the development and adoption of a Tribal Alternative as part of the Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) process for the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule. This alternative is rooted in the protection of tribal homelands, cultural lifeways, and ecological stewardship responsibilities.

## Purpose and Need

One of our sovereign Tribes’ highest priorities is the protection and continuation of traditional and customary hunting, fishing, and gathering practices within our traditional tribal territories. These lifeways are directly threatened when large-scale industrial activities—such as road construction, logging, mining, and mineral leasing—are allowed to further degrade the lands and waters of the Tongass, especially without the informed consent or full participation of affected Tribes.

Despite participating in consultations and serving as cooperating agencies during the Alaska Roadless Rulemaking processes, our sovereign input has been repeatedly ignored or marginalized (Organized Village of Kasaan et al., 2020). This failure amounts to collective disenfranchisement and undermines the federal government’s trust responsibility and its obligations under Executive Order 13175 (Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments), among others.

## Core Components of the Tribal Alternative

## 1. Creation of a Traditional Homelands Conservation Rule

The USDA and U.S. Forest Service (USFS), in partnership with the sovereign Tribal governments of Southeast Alaska, shall initiate an independent rulemaking process to establish a Traditional Homelands Conservation Rule that is:

o Separate from the Alaska Roadless Rule and any current or future efforts to modify or rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule.

o Centered on protection of areas identified as critical to traditional and customary tribal use.

o Structured around co-management principles that fully integrate Tribal ecological knowledge, cultural priorities, and land stewardship values.

## 2. Identification and Mapping of Traditional and Customary Use Areas This process shall include:

o Development of a transparent and culturally appropriate methodology for the identification, documentation, and protection of traditional and customary use areas.

o Direct participation of Tribal knowledge-holders and governments in the designation of these areas.

o Ensuring that identified areas are permanently protected from industrialscale logging, roadbuilding, mining, and other extractive practices.

## 3. Implementation of Forest-Wide Conservation Measures

o Prohibit large-scale industrial development in identified traditional and customary use areas.

o Maintain and expand roadless protections within the Tongass National Forest in areas of Tribal significance.

o Promote restoration of previously impacted sites in partnership with Tribal governments, utilizing Indigenous stewardship principles.

## 4. Government-to-Government Consultation and Mutual Concurrence

o Enforce the established formal government-to-government consultation framework based on mutual concurrence, ensuring that no major decision affecting traditional lands proceeds without the informed agreement of affected Tribes.

## 5. Utilization of Existing Authorities and Cooperative Agreements

o Expand the use of stewardship contracting, cooperative agreements, and other authorities to empower Tribal co-management of lands and resources.

o Fund Tribal natural resource departments to carry out ecological monitoring, cultural site management, and sustainable development planning.

o Authorize tribes to assume the development of the environmental impact statement for the Tongass National Forest Plan Revision and associated NEPA processes with predicted impacts to homeland forests.

## 6. Cultural and Environmental Justice Protections

o Recognize and address the disproportionate impacts of environmental degradation on Alaska Native communities.

o Embed principles of Tribal cultural continuity, ways of life, and subsistence rights into all planning and decision-making related to the Tongass.

## Conclusion

The Tribal Alternative represents a path forward that honors the sovereignty, culture, and deep ecological knowledge of the Indigenous peoples of Southeast Alaska. It seeks to ensure that any changes to federal land management policies in the Tongass do not replicate the historic injustices of exclusion, exploitation, and environmental harm. We call on the USDA and USFS to adopt this alternative in good faith, and to begin a new chapter of respectful, collaborative, and government-to-government partnership in the stewardship of our shared forest homeland.

## Additional Proposed Alternatives and Considerations

The ultimate test of any policy is its durability. While this NOI requests input on national alternatives, one of the primary justifications for the proposed rescission is the desire for decision-making power to be placed in the hands of regions and communities. On this front, the Idaho Roadless Rule has proven remarkably successful. Following its promulgation, the rule was challenged in federal court by a coalition of conservation groups who argued that it illegally weakened the protections of the 2001 rule and failed to comply with environmental laws. These groups pointed to Forest Service projections that the Idaho rule would triple road construction and nearly double logging compared to the 2001 rule.

Despite these objections, the rule was upheld first by the U.S. District Court for Idaho and then, in 2013, by a unanimous (3-0) decision from the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals. This legal validation, from a court often seen as environmentally leaning, is a powerful testament to the rule's sound legal and procedural construction.

Politically, the rule has been equally resilient. Because it was forged through a state-led, collaborative process with broad stakeholder and tribal buy-in, it has not faced the persistent threats of administrative reversal that have plagued the national rule. Idaho Senator Jim Risch continues to champion it as a successful, common-sense model that other states should emulate to resolve their own public land disputes.

The Idaho rule's success demonstrates a critical principle: by localizing the decisionmaking process, as this proposal claims it wants to do, it transforms the debate from a national, ideological conflict to a series of local, community-based and science-based evaluations. The Idaho rule itself does not authorize a single project; it establishes a rigorous but workable framework for evaluating projects that would have been nonstarters under the 2001 rule, including all of the fire management issues the Administration now claims are necessary to address with the current proposal.

Still, more than 95% of the roadless acres under the Idaho Roadless Rule enjoy similar or stronger protections than under the 2001 national rule while still providing the management flexibility this Administration claims to want. This shift in the locus of conflict resolution is perhaps its most important and replicable feature, and it should get serious consideration here with this current proposal. If this Administration truly believes in solutions for our National Forests, its preservation of the Idaho Roadless Rule is definitive as to what does, and does not, work on our public lands.

A Tribal and State co-led process could have equally similar successful results for all parties involved as the Idaho Roadies Rule. Failure to consider an "Idaho Rule”-like solution for the Tongass would be a grave violation of the APA, NEPA and common sense. Doing so would be a triumph of this Administration’s wisdom.

Per the extensive tribal and community engagement during the 2020 Alaska rulemaking process, which advocated for “long-term, durable approach to roadless areas management...that accommodates the unique biological, social, and economic situation found in and around the Tongass”. We submit the proposed alternatives taken verbatim from the Alaska Roadless Rulemaking Regulatory Impacts Assessment and Cost Benefit Assessment (2020) for consideration. The proposed alternatives reflect the results of extensive public engagement and alternative building work that took place during the development of the Alaska Roadless Rule. While these alternatives are specific to Alaska, we submit them as durable, community-developed alternatives that can be scaled up to accommodate the multiple uses under which National Forests are managed or reconsidered as components of an updating of the 2020 Alaska Roadless Rule under one of the community-supported alternatives which would advance national strategy.

## Alternative 1 (Southeast Tribes Alternate Priority)

Maintain and strengthen the 2001 Roadless Rule (No Action Alternative)

• Retain all current protections for inventoried roadless areas (IRAs) in the Tongass.

• Strengthen conservation provisions by identifying ecologically critical and culturally significant subunits (e.g., karst, high-volume stands, cultural and sacred sites) for enhanced protection (Betts et al., 2018; Birdsey et al., 2025; Carroll et al., 2025; DellaSala et al., 2022).

## Alternative 2 (Watershed Priority)

Alternative 2 maximizes roadless area protection, by adding an additional 133,000 acres as Alaska Roadless Areas, while providing for additional timber harvest opportunities by removing areas generally known as “roaded roadless” areas but also include additional areas considered to be substantially altered. Alternative 3 provides more timber harvest opportunities than Alternative 2 by removing substantially-altered roadless areas (including roaded roadless, similar to Alternative 2) and extending the bounds of these areas to logical end points of existing road and timber harvest systems (212,000 acres), generally defined as the nearest watershed boundary (i.e., ridgeline of 14th-field hydrologic unit) from an existing road system. Removing these areas from the roadless inventory represents the logical extensions of substantially altered acres from existing infrastructure and likely encompasses the more economically feasible locations for future timber harvest with the least impact to roadless characteristics.

## Alternative 3 (Community Priority + Watershed Priority)\*

Alternative 3 also provides additional timber harvest opportunity by designation of Community Priority areas around affected communities. Community Priority areas allow for small-scale timber harvest and associated road construction and reconstruction.

\*This management category was developed to address specific desires of some communities to retain roadless protections while also allowing for small timber operators in the community, infrastructure development to support the communities, and provide for traditional Alaska Native cultural uses. The provision allows for road building to accommodate small commercial sale less than one million board feet (which does not exclude larger operators but designed to reduce barriers to entry for smaller operators). The Forest Service is seeking public input on this management category, specifically with respect to whether this designation should be applied to other communities/areas. The Forest Service proposes to consider applying the Community Priority land management category to ARAs either adjacent to communities or within Community Priority areas as requested by non-profit community associations organized under State of Alaska law (Alaska Statute 10.20.005), municipal governments, or tribal governments.

## II. Effects That Should Be Analyzed in the EIS and Relevant Scientific Studies, Indigenous Knowledge, and Local Data

Any serious examination of the implications of rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule must include comprehensive and interdisciplinary analyses of cumulative, long-term, and place-based effects. The following categories of impacts are of relevance:

## A. Impacts to Alaska Native Ways of Life and Subsistence Resources

Diminished access to and availability of subsistence resources such as Sitka black-tailed deer, anadromous fish, berries, and food, fiber, and medicinal plants due to habitat fragmentation, loss of old-growth, and the degradation of productive understory (Buonanduci et al., 2025; Johnson et al., 2021; Long et al., 2020; Shanley et al., 2021; Ulaski et al., 2025).

Disruption of spiritual and ceremonial use areas embedded in intact forest landscapes (Dixon et al., 1997; Freedman & Fridgen, 2007; Isa, 2018).

Declining intergenerational transmission of traditional knowledge due to ecological degradation of culturally vital gathering and hunting grounds and associated learning opportunities (Bussey et al., 2016; Chamley et al., 2008; Charnley et al., 2007; Cheveau et al., 2008; Huntington, 2000; Kimmerer, 2002; Todd et al., 2023).

Federal law (Section 810 of ANILCA) requires that federal agencies specifically consider these impacts. See 16 U.S.C. § 3120(a). Thus, as in the promulgation of Alaska-specific roadless rules in 2020 and 2023, the USDA must conduct such analysis, as noted below.

## B. Biodiversity, Wildlife, and Forest Integrity

Loss of contiguous habitat for endemic, threatened, and culturally critical wildlife species, including but not limited to the Chinook, Sockeye, Coho, Pink, and Chum salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha, O. nerka, O. kisutch, O. gorbuscha, O. keta), Sitka Black-Tailed Deer (Odocoileus hemionus sitkensis), the Alexander Archipelago wolf (Canis lupus ligoni), and the Queen Charlotte goshawk (Accipiter gentilis laingi) (Brooks et al., 2024; Flitcroft et al., 2022; Haddad et al., 2015; Hanley, 2005; Kravitz & Blair, 2019; Moore et al., 2024).

Reduction of critical ecosystem functions such as nutrient cycling, watershed regulation, and the maintenance of robust populations of ANILCA-protected traditional and customary use species, habitats, and Alaska Native lifeways (Brandt et al., 2014; DellaSala et al., 2011; Dietz et al., 2021; Healey, 2020; Lader et al., 2023; Loucks et al., 2003; Seiler, n.d.; Talty et al., 2020; Tanyaş et al., n.d.; Van Der Ree et al., 2011).

Edge effects, habitat fragmentation, and microclimate alterations due to increased road density and canopy removal (Rykken et al., 2007; Sperry et al., 2008; Valente et al., 2023).

## C. Climate Change Resilience and Carbon Accounting

Net increase in carbon emissions due to removal of large-diameter, high-carbonvalue old-growth trees (Besnard et al., 2025; Birdsey et al., 2025; Buotte et al., 2020; Farinacci et al., 2024; Law et al., 2023; Leighty et al., 2006).

• Loss of carbon storage capacity in soils and hydrological systems affected by road building (Booth et al., 2023; Dellasala et al., 2022; Fellman et al., 2017; McNicol et al., 2023).

Reduced climate buffering capacity of intact forests under intensifying regional precipitation events and landslide risks (Betts et al., 2018; Frey et al., 2016; Lindenmayer & Laurance, 2017; Wolf et al., 2021).

## D. Geophysical and Hydrological Risk Factors

Increased landslide and sedimentation risk associated with road construction on steep, rain-saturated slopes (Tanyas et al. 2022; Lader et al. 2023).

Disruption of fish habitat and passage due to road stream crossings (Kravitz 2019).

Accelerated deterioration of karst hydrology systems and groundwaterdependent ecosystems (Bryant et al., 1998; Dixon et al., 1997; Hendrickson & Groves, 2011).

Our tribes emphasize that Indigenous Knowledge is best available science and must be used as the foundation on which assessments are based (Blevins 2024). Indigenous Knowledge recognizes and safeguards the integrity of ecological systems over generational timeframes and thus must be integrated into baseline condition assessments and scenario modeling. Community-level data should be integrated to construct an accurate picture of environmental and cultural consequences (Blevins, 2024). Please reference the bibliography at the end of this letter for a full list of the specific citations used to inform our comments.

## E. Indigenous Knowledge (IK)

• Community documentation and oral histories identifying:

◦ Seasonal migration patterns of culturally significant wildlife.

◦ Long-term observations of forest health and change.

Indigenous management, harvest, and land-use practices adapted to the specific ecology of homeland forests which encompass and include the Tongass National Forest.

## F. Local and Tribal Data

• Harvest monitoring reports from tribal and state subsistence programs especially as information relates to effects observed in proximity to roads and roaded areas vs those less proximate to roads and roaded areas.

• Where available and allowable, maps of traditional use areas and cultural and sacred sites within tribal homelands.

• Road maintenance and cost data by district.

Each of these impact domains and knowledge sources requires thorough spatial, temporal, and cumulative analysis under NEPA, including disclosure of mitigation measures, tradeoffs, and irretrievable losses. A thorough ANILCA 810 analysis is a required component of the evaluation of environmental impacts. Taken together this information significantly contributes to our tribes’ ability to understand the effects of federal actions on traditional ways-of-life and subsistence resources. We strongly urge that these sources inform both the selection of alternatives and the EIS analytical framework.

## III. Legal and Procedural Concerns Affecting Tribal Interests

## A. Inadequate Consultation and Federal Trust Responsibility

The NOI does not satisfy the consultation requirements outlined in Executive Order 13175 and the USDA’s Departmental Regulation 1350-002, which requires early and substantive tribal engagement in policy development. Various other federal laws, such as the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA, National Environmental Policy Act, and ANILCA, also require consultation and engagement. Despite these requirements, our current experience of recent consultation processes continues to appear more procedural than meaningful. Per a June 26<sup>th</sup> comment letter from Tlingit & Haida:

“This decision was made without tribal consultation and therefore violates the federal government’s legally mandated trust responsibility to tribal nations. As such, we do not recognize the legitimacy of this action until meaningful, government-to-government consultation has occurred. This unilateral rescission disregards the inherent sovereignty of tribes, undermines the rights of the Indigenous peoples of Southeast Alaska, threatens the health of the land that our communities have stewarded for millennia, and disregards the foundational government-to-government relationship that should guide all federal actions involving tribal homelands”.

This follows an unfortunate pattern of failed communication and breaches of trust articulated in the 2020 APA Tribal Homelands Petition submitted by twelve federally recognized Alaska Native tribes (Organized Village of Kasaan et al., 2020).

We therefore request:

• Co-development opportunities on topics of tribal priority (see above) during the development of the EIS.

Formal, government-to-government consultation prior to finalization of the environmental impact statement, and written documentation articulating how our points have been included in the final EIS.

A detailed and comprehensive analysis of potential impacts on subsistence resources, pursuant to ANILCA Section 810.

Co-development of project-level consultation protocols tied to proposed road construction or timber sales.

• Regular tribal briefings, including both consultation and engagement, during the EIS process and inclusion of tribal representatives on interdisciplinary review teams.

## B. Potential Violations of Environmental and Cultural Protection Statutes

The proposed action may implicate several statutes, including:

• National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) – Incomplete scoping, failure to consider reasonable alternatives, and insufficient cumulative impact analysis.

• Endangered Species Act (ESA) – Inadequate consideration of the effects of habitat loss on listed species and their critical habitat.

• National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) – Risk to unrecorded sacred and cultural sites.

• ANILCA Section 810 – Consideration and priority of traditional and customary use species and the potential impacts of federal actions.

Failure to address these concerns in the EIS may render the final rule legally vulnerable.

## V. Conclusion and Requests for Follow-Up

The undersigned Tribes urge the USDA to reconsider the rationale and direction of this rulemaking. The proposed rescission appears to privilege extractive economic interests and broad generalizations about wildfire risk—conditions that are inapplicable to the temperate rainforest systems of the Tongass. Our forest requires management grounded in place-based knowledge, tribal sovereignty, and a recognition of the ecological complexity of the Tongass, not administrative uniformity. While this is the ostensible motivation behind the proposed recission, we submit that federal oversight and standardization of environmental review is still urgently needed: Despite the multiple use mandate and reliance on forest plans for direction and governance, the USFS still affords a privileged position to the timber industry via agency reliance on timber receipts to complete mandated work including restoration actions and infrastructure maintenance.

## We request:

1 Full development and consideration of the alternatives outlined above.

2 Comprehensive ecological, cultural, and climate-related impact analysis including indirect and cumulative impacts.

3 Integration of TEK and tribal data as required by NEPA and Executive Orders.

5 Formal documentation of how tribal comments will be addressed and incorporated into the Draft EIS.

The undersigned tribes stand ready to support a collaborative and scientifically grounded planning process—one that respects Indigenous governance, sustains local communities, and ensures the integrity of the Tongass for future generations.

By sianing below, the undersigned Tribe affirms support for these technical comments on the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule as applied to the Tongass National Forest.

Secretary Brooke L. Rollins Secretary of Agriculture U.S. Department of Agriculture 1400 Independence Avenue SW Washington DC 20250

September 18, 2025

Re: Notice of Intent to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement on Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule (Docket Number FS-2025-0001)

The Tulalip Tribes of Washington (Tulalip) is a federally recognized sovereign Indian government, successor in interest to the Snohomish, Snoqualmie, and Skykomish, and as well as other allied tribes and bands, signatory to the 1855 Treaty of Point Elliott. Members of Tulalip, together with other Coast Salish tribes, have strong historical and spiritual ties and treaty reserved rights to hunt, fish and gather in all usual and accustomed places and on all opened and unclaimed land, which includes the forest lands and waters that comprise what is now a part of the National Forest system managed by the U.S. Forest Service (USFS). The Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (MBS) lies entirely within the Treaty of Point Elliott area.

As their original stewards, we have nurtured these forest landscapes for millennia, maintaining balance and resilience through our deep connection to and reliance on these lands. Lands within the MBS constitute some of the last undeveloped areas within the Pt. Elliot Treaty tribes territory, where tribes like Tulalip, can exercise our treaty-reserved fishing, hunting, and gathering rights. These lands continue to provide water, foods, medicines, and places that sustain our people, our lifeways, and livelihoods. As such, we have a profound interest in how these federal forest lands are managed and protected for future generations

In 2007, Tulalip and the MBS entered into a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) to serve as an ongoing framework for our government-to-government relationship and partnership in forest stewardship. Through an amendment to this MOA, we most recently incorporated Tulalip's Uplands Strategic Plan (2023), which speaks to our historical and continued connection to and reserved treaty rights on these forest lands, our vision for their future, and the strategic actions we believe are needed to sustain them. It is through this lens that we offer our comments, which are summarized below and expanded upon later in this letter.

The Tulalip Tribes is opposed to the Notice of Intent to prepare an Environmental impact Statement on rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule (Docket Number F-2025-0001)(NOI) which proposes to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule in its entirety.

However, if the Forest Service moves ahead with the creation of an EIS to analyze its proposed action to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule, Tulalip requests that the Forest Service engage in meaningful consultation to address the concerns stated herein on a government-to-government basis. This will allow for, among other things, engagement at a local level with Tulalip, which is one of the goals and purposes stated in the NOI. When analyzing the various alternatives, Tulalip urges the Forest Service to address the lack of consultation leading to the 2001 Roadless Rule and the current rulemaking process and ensure access to treaty resources, cultural sites, and sacred areas for federally recognized treaty tribes, including Tulalip. The Forest Service must engage at the local level with those treaty tribes that have management authority as secured through a treaty, to determine impacts to natural and cultural resources and their habitats, and for which roadless areas shall remain so as not to diminish treaty-reserved resources. Finally, if any alternative other than the “no action" alternative, i.e., maintaining the 2001 Roadless Rule, is selected, the Forest Service must ensure that future actions in these roadless areas only occur upon the informed and express consent of federally recognized treaty tribes, such as Tulalip, with federally protected property rights within such areas.

## I. THE 2001 ROADLESS RULE AND TREATY RIGHTS

When promulgated, the 2001 Roadless Rule noted that inventoried roadless areas often encompass traditional cultural properties and sacred sites² but, the Environmental Impact Statement prepared (EIS) for the 2001 Roadless Rule provided relatively little discussion or analysis of tribal issues. Indeed, the EIS and mostly recited background information about legal status and consultation requirements, for which tribes were minimally consulted with outside of the public comment period.

Reflective of this general approach, the language of the 2001 Roadless Rule exception allows that road construction when a "road is needed pursuant to reserved or outstanding rights, or as provided for by statute or treaty."3

The Kootenai Tribe of Idaho was a lead plaintiff challenging the 2001 Roadless Rule, based in part on the Forest Service's failure to engage in substantive tribal consultation.4 A central concern consistently expressed by tribes was that “traditional uses of the land and access to

cultural and sacred sites be allowed to continue." The Forest Service responded to this concern by pointing to the flexibility of the 2001 Roadless Rule, including the exception quoted above.6

Therefore, it is absolutely crucial to leave the 2001 Roadless Rule untouched, in place, and engage in meaningful consultation, as a legal obligation of the Forest Service for its current rulemaking.

The 2001 Roadless Rule is not otherwise outdated as stated in the NOI. In fact, it is crucial in upholding the inherent rights recognized by and explicitly reserved in the 1855 Treaty of Point Elliott; which created a trust responsibility that the Forest Service, as our federal trustee, is legally required to protect. While the Forest Service has a trust obligation to all federally recognized Indian tribes, the Forest Service has a unique fiduciary duty to treaty tribes to protect tribal rights reserved by treaty-a treaty right without the resources to support it, is an abrogation of the right.

Many non-timber and timber products on National Forest lands are incredibly important resources to the culture of tribes such as Tulalip. Our culture depends on their abundance, and our ability to access them at sustained levels. However, the impacts of growing public use, commercial practices, and recreation are taking their toll on these significant cultural resources and properties, and thus, tribal member access for the exercise of treaty and other tribal rights and traditional, cultural, and religious practices.

Rescinding the Roadless Rule will diminish natural and cultural resources, leading to abrogation of these rights.?

The NOI's proposed recission will diminish and in some cases, eliminate these natural and cultural resources on which our treaty-reserved rights depend on because:

1. Roads encourage industrial encroachment on treaty rights and the landscape.

2. Roadless areas are critical for ecological integrity in the landscape setting:

A. Salmon habitat is negatively impacted by roads due to the amplification of magnitude, frequency, and duration of sediment and hydrology delivery to stream channels.

B. Roads severely fragment already declining wildlife habitat.

C. Roads play an enormous role in creating hydraulic repercussions on the landscape in terms of continuity, magnitude, frequency, and amplification of flood events All of which are exacerbated by environmental shifts and climate change.

D. Roads, via harvest and other land use impacts, increase the effects of soil desiccation during extreme heat events, compounding the impacts of drought and impacting forest health.

Further, the recission of the 2001 Roadless Rule does not and cannot meet its stated goals because:

3. The recission is fiscally irresponsible- the Forest Service already struggles to maintain its existing road system- which is the largest for any federal agency- and increasing the miles of road will exacerbate this problem, at great cost to the federal government;

4. The recission exacerbates wildfire risk. Roads are a source of ignition, not a solution; and

5. This will not lead to the local prescription that addresses wildfire abatement, forest health, or upholding trust responsibilities, but instead nationally directs the Forest Service to prioritize timber production exacerbating risks on public lands.

Finally, we request clarity about opportunities to engage in the consultation process. Tribes must be consulted with in accordance with Executive Order 13175 and USDA's Tribal Consultation Policy. The Forest Service is legally obligated to engage in early and meaningful government-togovernment consultation with federally recognized tribes that affect tribal resources. To date, the Forest Service has failed to engage in meaningful consultation with the Tulalip Tribes, which contravenes federal law and trust obligations. Further, no clear or meaningful plan for consultation has been otherwise outlined or communicated to tribes.

## 1. EXPANDING ROADS FOR PURPOSE STATED IN THE NOI ENCOURAGES ANDFACILITATES INDUSTRIAL ENCROACHMENT ON TREATY RIGHTS & THELANDSCAPE

Continuation and/or expansion of extractive economies should be based on ecological sustainability, to allow otherwise, is to facilitate the abrogation of treaty-reserved rights.

Despite the NOI stating that recission will allow for local direction of land use, the Forest Service has been given the directive to “exploit our domestic timber supply" and “full[y] utilize[e] these resources...and increase domestic timber production"8 as well as other mineral exploration directives on forest service land in Executive Orders regarding energy development.9 This is explicitly a call to allow industrial encroachment upon treaty rights and the landscape that those rights depend upon. It contradicts a “local direct of land use" within treaty territories.

Opening roadless areas encourages damaging extractive industries. The expansion of roads facilitates industrial logging, mining, and other large-scale uses that threaten the ecological integrity of forests, rivers, and uplands. Such industrial encroachment directly conflicts with and diminishes the exercise of treaty-reserved hunting, fishing, and gathering rights, and irreparably harms the cultural and spiritual connections that Tulalip maintains with these lands.

## 2. ROADLESS AREAS ARE CRITICAL FOR ECOLOGICAL INTEGRITY IN THE LANDSCAPE SETTING

The MBS roadless areas are among the last intact ecosystems within the Treaty of Point Elliott territory. These areas function as interconnected systems of plants, animals, waters, and uplands that sustain both natural and cultural resources. Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule in its entirety would repeatedly expose natural and cultural resources to ecological degradation in perpetuity abrogating our treaty rights.

These natural and cultural resources impacts include critical treaty resources such as salmon, wildlife, various plants, and their habitats.

## A. Severe Impacts on Anadromous Salmon and Aquatic Habitats

Roadless areas protect cold, clean water, intact riparian forests, and stable stream networks— conditions essential to the survival of salmon throughout their life cycles. By contrast, roads increase water run-off and sedimentation, impede fish migration, and degrade water quality through road stabilization additives. The Forest Service itself has acknowledged these impacts for decades.'º Expanding the road network exponentially increases both ecological harm and the fiscal burden of attempting to mitigate it—mitigation that is already lagging behind on the roads that currently exist.

## B. Creating Roads Severely Fragments Already Rapidly Declining Wildlife Habitat

Creating roads also fragments wildlife habitat, which is particularly devastating in the Pacific Northwest where certain species have already lost much of their historical range. Research demonstrates that wildlife species including elk, mountain goat, bear, lynx, and wolverine avoid roads, even little-used ones, altering movement patterns and reducing available habitat."1 Large, connected tracts of roadless forest are critically important and increasingly rare refuges for these species, and their continued existence is essential to maintaining healthy ecosystems essential to upholding treaty rights

## C. Hydraulic & Hydrologic Repercussions: Flood Frequency, Magnitude, and Continuity

Roads profoundly alter natural water flow, increasing the risk, frequency, and severity of flooding, risks that will only be magnified under drought conditions, transcontinental atmospheric events, and other environmental shifts. Forest roads, have highly compacted surfaces with very low infiltration rates. These surfaces generate overland flow—even under moderate rainfall—rather than allowing water to soak into soils, slowing it, or spreading it across the landscape.12

Roads also intercept subsurface flow: cuts and fills transform how groundwater moves, often diverting it toward the surface or into roadside ditches, which then deliver large pulses of water quickly into streams. This increases peak stream discharge, erodes stream banks, incises channels, amplifies sediment delivery, and worsens flood peaks. All of which increase risk to downstream communities; human and ecological alike. In Western Washington and similar forested mountain landscapes, studies show that when forest roads are directly hydrologically connected to streams (via ditches, gullies, or through road-stream crossings), there is a measurable increase in flood flows——sometimes on the order of 10-12% increase in annual discharge in certain catchments.'3

Further, during high-rain events or extreme storms, roads act to concentrate runoff. Natural terrain spreads and slows water; roads collect it, route it, sometimes block its natural pathways, leading to abrupt overflow, greater erosion, and downstream flooding. The severity and frequency of such flood events are exacerbated by local environmental shifts: more intense precipitation, more rapid snowmelt, and more frequent storms. Without the buffering effect of undisturbed, roadless terrain, communities, aquatic habitats, and treaty-protected resources downstream will be increasingly at risk

## D. Soil Desiccation, Extreme Heat & Land Use Impacts

Roads via harvest and land use impacts, significantly contribute to soil desiccation during extreme heat events.

Heavy machinery compacts soils, reducing their porosity and water-holding capacity; as a result, infiltration rates drop and soils dry out more quickly during heat or drought.'4At the same time canopy and vegetative cover are removed, eliminating the shade and evapotranspiration functions that moderate soil temperatures. Without this protection, soils are exposed to greater

solar heating, further accelerating moisture loss which leads to further heating of the air and even to deadly heat domes, as happened in our region in 2021.15

In addition, roads create “edge effects," where adjacent soils develop warmer and drier microclimates compared to interior forest soils. These altered conditions extend outward from roads, disrupting soil moisture, organic matter decomposition, and the ecological functions of plants and microbes.16

Taken together, these processes reduce the resilience of forest soils under environmental stress, threatening the survival of culturally significant plants, berries, roots, and medicines relied upon by the Tulalip Tribes. Under extreme heat, soils that are already compromised (compacted exposed, with lower organic matter) dry out faster, which reduces resilience: plants cannot access deep water, seedlings and understory species suffer, riparian zones may lose moisture, and overall landscape recovery is harder after disturbances. For treaty-reserved resource plant and animal species, these changes threaten medicinal plants, roots, berries, and undergrowth that depend on stable moisture, and exacerbate heat stress in aquatic systems (e.g., by reducing shading), which further impact fish and stream organisms.

## 3. FISCAL MANAGEMENT OF ROAD SYSTEMS

The recission is fiscally irresponsible. The Forest Service manages more roads than any other federal agency,'7 and fails to maintain them, facing chronic shortfalls in both staffing and financial resources.

In the 2026 Forest Service budget, appropriations for roads are down \$23,000,000 and are completely cut for legacy roads and trails.18 Adding more roads to the forest system does not make economic sense and can lead to taking funds from critical habitat, treaty rights, fire management, and other forest management. Moreover, the current rule already allows roadbuilding and logging of smaller trees to reduce fire risk and protect public safety. Allowing the expansion of roads will only deepen that burden while diverting scarce resources away from habitat protection, treaty obligations, and wildfire management

Given the Forest Service's directive to “exploit our domestic timber supply" and “full utilization of these resources...and increase domestic timber production"19there is concern that road construction may increasingly be financed through timber company activities. Such an approach risks prioritizing industrial access over treaty-reserved rights and could effectively sideline the

federal government's trust responsibility to uphold those rights, a violation of the United States Constitution.

## 4. WILDFIRE MANAGEMENT AND RESPONSE

The NOI suggests that rescission will support wildfire management. In reality, the opposite is true. The 2001 Roadless Rule already contains an exception to construct roads for wildfire (and other emergency) response, negating the need to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule in its entirety to address this growing need.20

Further, roadless areas experience fewer human-caused ignitions, which account for approximately 80% of all wildfires—and 90% of those begin within a half-mile of a road.²1 Increasing road density, will increase ignition risk and the costs of fire suppression. Roadless areas also provide the safest settings for allowing natural wildfire to play its ecological role in restoring forest structure and composition. Rescission would diminish this natural resilience, undermining forest health and adaptation to changing conditions.

Moreover, the 2026 Forest Service budget slashes agency funding by more than 60%, and zeroes out funding for Wildland Fire Management, the Wildfire Suppression Operations Reserve Fund, and State, Private, and Tribal Forestry.22 USDA's stated rationale for rescission—addressing wildfire risk and giving states more decision-making power—rings hollow when no funding is allocated to meet those goals

## 5. REPEALING THE 2001 ROADLESS RULE IN ITS ENTIRETY WILL NOT LEAD TO LOCAL CONTROL

The NOI states that "the Department believes that the one-size-fits-all' approach to roadless area management is no longer appropriate and proposes to use local land management planning processes to administer inventoried roadless areas," and that rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule would allow local land managers to tailor management to local conditions. However, this rings hollow because: (1) recent actions directly contradict this stated commitment to locally based decision-making; (2) the Forest Service is approaching the Roadless Rule in another “one-sizefits-all" approach with an all or nothing recission proposal; and (3) there are exceptions in the 2001 Roadless Rule which allow for local land management control.

The Executive Order establishing a national policy of Immediate Expansion of American Timber Production, together with the Secretarial Memo on Increasing Timber Production, reflect a national, top-down directive that prioritizes resource extraction at the expense of treaty-reserved rights and healthy forests. Such a mandate undermines any discretion of local managers and

threatens the values safeguarded by the 2001 Roadless Rule including clean water, ecosystem services, and forest habitats. Rather than advancing local interests and values, the proposed action would impose a national policy that abrogates treaty rights

We reiterate that the 2001 Roadless Rule should not be rescinded. However in preparing an EIS, in order to truly meet the “local decision-making" directive stated in the NOI and consultation requirements, the Forest Service must engage in meaningful consultation with the treaty tribes with management authority for those lands, to determine impacts on natural and cultural resources and their habitats and for which roadless areas shall remain so as not to diminish treaty-reserved resources. .

Further, this EIS should conduct a thorough analysis of what specific, targeted changes might improve the balance between ecological protection, treaty-reserved rights, and multiple uses of National Forest System lands. This would be more consistent with the Forest Service's obligations which require the Forest Service to identify tribal interests and impacts to them than wholesale rescission, which jeopardizes both ecological integrity and treaty rights.

The Draft EIS should carefully assess the anticipated impacts and benefits of any future action, including those reasonably foreseeable at both the project and landscape scale on treaty resources and the habitats that support them. While site-specific analysis is essential, it is not sufficient: fish, wildlife, water, and other ecological systems do not observe forest or project boundaries For example, salmon populations are affected by activities across watersheds, meaning that road building in one area, such as the Tongass, can have consequences for fisheries and tribal treaty rights in Washington state

In short, the Forest Service should not rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule or continue the NEPA process to do so, however, if an EIS is pursued it should look to thoughtful, targeted adjustments that protect treaty rights and ecological integrity, rather than a broad recission. Also, the Forest Service must ensure that future actions in these roadless areas only occur upon the informed and express consent of federally recognized treaty tribes, such as Tulalip, with federally protected property rights within such areas.

Thank you again for allowing us to comment on this Notice of Intent. Please contact Libby Nelson at Inelson@tulaliptribes-nsn.gov with any questions

Sincerely,

Teri Gobin

Chair

Tulalip Tribes

# BISHOP TRIBAL COUNCIL

![](images/b48c9af32d5cd35b1251583250798985ce2a8577db898c8b50aef3458e7de767.jpg)

To: Department of Agriculture- Forest Service

Re: Strong Opposition to FS-2025-0001– Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule) (66 FR 3244, 36 CFR Subpart B (2001)) (Submitted on Behalf of the Bishop Paiute Tribe)

September 19<sup>th</sup>, 2025

Manahuu (Hello),

The Bishop Paiute Tribe submits this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule) as proposed in docket number FS-2025-0001. The Bishop Paiute Tribe’s ancestral homeland and present-day reservation border the Inyo National Forest. We submit this formal comment in strong opposition to any proposal to rescind or weaken the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. The protection of these roadless areas is not merely an environmental issue; it is a matter of cultural survival, indigenous rights, and environmental justice for our people.

The Inyo National Forest, at approximately 2.1 million acres, is not a separate entity from our community; it is an extension of our homeland. For generations, our people have maintained a deep, reciprocal relationship with these lands. Proposals to open these areas to road construction, logging, and industrial development directly threaten this relationship in the following critical ways from disrupting our cultural practices of gathering pine nuts and hunting our traditional foods as well as threatening the quality and quantity of our already limited waters. Increased road access, habitat fragmentation, noise, and pollution from industrial activity would severely degrade the quality and productivity of the pinion trees and would displace wildlife by disrupting migration patterns, and diminishing the populations we depend on, violating our reserved hunting rights on our ancestral homelands. These operations also have the potential to violate our established Water Quality Standards [Clean Water Act §303(c)].

This proposal claims that this recission of the 2001 Roadless Rules is meant to reduce decades and, in turn, centuries of fire suppression which has been the direct result of taking native peoples away from these lands and stalling cultural fire practices. The Bishop Paiute Tribe agrees that the forests are unhealthy, however, it is also evident that opening these lands to private, for-profit logging and mining companies reduces transparency, and threatens tribal sovereignty. There are ways to go about enhancing forest health and increasing climate resiliency, for instance, the ongoing Eastern Sierra Climate and Communities Resilience Project (ESCCRP) project in the Inyo National Forest aims to manage 65,000 acres for wildfire resiliency. This project is in collaboration with the tribes of the Owens Valley and the greater Eastern Sierra, as well as other partners. Crucially, the 2001 Roadless Rule already contains provisions allowing for road construction to address emergencies [36 CFR § 294.12(b)(1)], demonstrating that rescinding the rule is not required to protect public safety.

Furthermore, the headwaters of Bishop Creek originate in the roadless areas of the Inyo National Forest and flow directly onto our reservation. This water is essential for our people for ceremonial use, and agriculture. The Roadless Rule is a key tool in protecting the integrity of these waters.

CWA Section 303(c): Our Tribe has established its own Water Quality Standards under the authority of the Clean Water Act. Road construction, logging, and associated erosion would lead to significant sedimentation, polluting our waters and violating these designated uses.

CWA Section 401: The Tribe asserts its authority under Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. Any federal permit or license that may result in a discharge into our waters (such as a permit for road construction or a timber sale) requires a certification from our Tribe that the activity will comply with our Water Quality Standards. We will not certify any project that jeopardizes the purity of our waters, and the Roadless Rule is the most effective preventative measure to avoid such conflicts.

The 2001 Roadless Rule functions as an essential buffer, protecting our cultural practices, subsistence resources, and water quality from irreversible harm. It aligns most with our Tribe's long-held ethic of stewardship and respect for the land.

Thank you for your attention to this significant matter.

Sincerely,

—Signed by:

Steven Orihuela

BLACKFEET TRIBAL BUSINESS COUNCILRODNEY R GERVAIS, JRSHELLY HALLPATRICK D. ARMSTRONG. JRMICHEAL COMESATNIGHTKRISTY BULLSHOECLEO BULLSHOEEVERETT D. ARMSTRONGSCOTT “ILIFF"KIPP SRTHOMAS L. RUTHERFORD, JR

Director, Ecosystem Management Coordination 201 14th St. SW, Mailstop 1108 Washington, DC 20250-1124

Re: Public Comment from the Blackfeet Nation Opposing the Repeal of the Roadless Rule

To whom it may concern:

The Blackfeet Nation stands in firm opposition to any effort to repeal or weaken the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. This policy has been a critical safeguard for our sacred lands, including the Badger-Two Medicine region, which holds profound cultural, spiritual, and ecological significance for our people

For over 18,000 years, our ancestors have lived in harmony with the mountains, rivers, and forests of what is now called Montana. These lands are not merely wilderness—they are living cultural landscapes, home to our origin stories, ceremonial sites, traditional medicines, and the spirits of our people. The Roadless Rule has helped protect these areas from fragmentation, industrialization, and desecration. Repealing this rule would open the door to roadbuilding, logging, and energy development that threaten to destroy irreplaceable cultural heritage. It would violate our treaty rights, undermine federal trust responsibilities, and disregard the principle of free, prior, and informed consent that is essential to tribal sovereignty.

Moreover, more roads, means more noxious weeds being spread throughout the National Forests and beyond. At a meeting on August 28, 2025, representatives from the United States Forest Service met with the Blackfeet Tribal Business Council and representatives from various Blackfeet Nation departments at Blackfeet Nation headquarters in Browning, Montana and stated that the most concentrated areas of noxious weeds in the Lewis and Clark National Forest (Badger Two-Medicine region) are on the roadways. Noxious weeds outcompete native vegetations for sunlight, water, nutrients and space that leads to a decline or extinction of native plant species, some of which are used for traditional medicines. Further, native animals often depend on native plants for food, nesting and shelter. When noxious weeds takeover food sources disappear, habitat quality declines and some species may be forced to migrate or die out. Noxious weeds also alter soil and water supply systems, and lead to an increase in wildlife. Therefore, lifting the Roadless Rule will ultimately lead to a spread of noxious weeds, devastating the environment.

We call on the United States Department of Agriculture and all federal agencies to uphold their legal and moral obligations to Indigenous Nations. The Roadless Rule must remain intact not only to protect wildlife and clean water, but to honor the sacred relationship between Native peoples and the land.

Sincerely,

Rodney Gervais, Jr., Chairman

Blackfeet Tribal Business Council

Comments on 2001 Roadless Rule Rescission, FS-2025-0001-0001 Submitted by: Chugach Regional Resources Commission (CRRC) Date: 9/19/2025

To: Forest Service, Agriculture (USDA)

## RE: Tribal Comments on the Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) for the 2001 Roadless Rule Rescission

The Chugach Regional Resources Commission (CRRC) submits these comments in response to the U.S. Department of Agriculture initiating an environmental impact statement (EIS) and rulemaking concerning management of inventoried roadless areas on approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System lands, including the Chugach National Forest. CRRC is an inter-Tribal natural resource organization representing the seven Tribes of the Chugach Region. Our mission is to protect, maintain, and enhance the natural resources of the region to support subsistence practices, food security, cultural continuity, and Tribal sovereignty. Cook Inlet and its marine and coastal ecosystems are deeply tied to the lifeways of our member Tribes. Natural resource extraction and development such as logging and mining pose serious risk to these interconnected systems and the people who rely on them.

## Background:

Chenega, a sovereign federally recognized tribe in the Chugach Region, is a coastal community on Evans Island in Prince William Sound. Eyak, a federally recognized tribe based in Cordova, represents descendants of the Eyak people whose traditional homelands extend across the Copper River Delta and eastern Prince William Sound. Qutekcak, a federally recognized tribe located in Seward at the head of Resurrection Bay, is part of the Chugach Region and maintains deep ties to both land and sea resources. Tatitlek, another sovereign federally recognized tribe in the Chugach Region, is a small Native village on Prince William Sound accessible only by boat or plane. Valdez, home to the federally recognized Valdez Native Tribe, is at the head of Prince William Sound, where coastal resources have long supported subsistence lifeways. For members of Chenega, Eyak, Qutekcak, Tatitlek, and Valdez, their culture and survival remain rooted in the continued health of traditional resources that have sustained them for generations.

## 2. Protection of Cultural Resources

Prince William Sound is home to ancestral village sites, travel routes, and areas of deep cultural and spiritual significance. These sites are not always documented in federal or state registries but are known through oral history and continued use.

• USDA and USFS must consult directly with the CRRC and its member Tribes to identify cultural resources.

• Archaeological sites that may be impacted by logging or associated activities should be surveyed in collaboration with Tribal Historic Preservation Officers.

• Risk assessments should be conducted for flooding and associated land/rock/mud slides from logging and associated development plans.

![](images/0c6bb3575bbc3022525253518cc39cf4133794343821bd90ab985b4d0214ba8a.jpg)  
Figure 2: Variation in physical characteristics of rivers due to logging activity. Source: Wootton JT (2012) Effects of Timber Harvest on River Food Webs: Physical, Chemical and Biological Responses. PLoS ONE 7(9): e43561. doi:10.1371/ journal.pone.0043561

## 5. Cumulative Impacts

The EIS must provide a realistic and community-centered analysis of cumulative effects, including:

• Long-term impacts to food sovereignty, cultural practices, and community health that are often not captured by narrow technical assessments.

• The impact on natural resources throughout the Chugach National Forest. These locations are extremely important to the livelihood of Tribal members from Chenega, Eyak, Qutekcak, Tatitlek, and Valdez.

## 6. Consultation and Tribal Co-Stewardship

Consultation must be more than procedural and with the capability of influencing outcomes.

We urge the USDA and USFS to establish formal co-stewardship agreements with Chugach region Tribes and CRRC as a regional coordinating body.

The USDA and USFS should support capacity-building for Tribal governments to meaningfully participate in environmental reviews, data collection, and monitoring efforts tied to any lease activities.

## 7. Economic Impacts

• USDA and USFS should conduct economic impact assessments regarding the impact of logging, mining, damming, and other development activity on the communities along and neighboring the roadless area in Chugach National Forest.

• These Tribal communities directly and indirectly depend upon tourism and fishing to support themselves, both sectors are intertwined with natural resource health.

The USDA and USFS must also assess the impact of development to the greater Alaska and United States economy. This assessment must touch on how degrading Pacific salmon rearing and breeding grounds located within the Chugach National Forest will alter the quality and quantity of fishing yields.

## Recommendations Summary:

1. Fund a Traditional Knowledge study in collaboration with Chugach Tribes to inform EIS revisions and future management decisions.

2. Establish a Tribal Co-Stewardship Working Group with representation from CRRC and our member Tribes.

3. Invest in Tribal-led baseline and ongoing environmental monitoring to safeguard resources within the Chugach National Forest.

4. Assess the Economic, Cultural, and Ecoligical Impacts of Natural Resource Development and Extraction on the Tribal communities surrounding and within the Chugach National Forest.

RE: FS-2025-0001-0001 EIS Rescind of 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule

Dear Mr. Kinder:

Please accept this letter as the written comments of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes of the Flathead Reservation (CSKT or Tribes) regarding the proposed federal decision to rescind the 2001Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule) and a request from the CSKT to engage in formal government-to-government consultation. The Tribes are aware that the US Department of Agriculture-Forest Service (USFS or Forest Service) will initiate an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) to evaluate impacts a rescission of the rule would have upon public access, forest health and management, and local and regional economies. The Tribes are more specifically concerned with how rescinding the Roadless Rule will impact the Forest Services’ ongoing federal trust responsibility to recognize and safeguard tribal reserved treaty rights, and preserve and protect the natural and cultural resources located within areas of national forests currently designated as roadless under the current rule.

## CSKT Treaty Reserved Rights

From time immemorial the aboriginal homeland of the CSKT reached from what is now British Columbia, down through parts of what are now the states of Washington, Idaho, Montana and Wyoming. A large portion of the aboriginal lands the Tribes once inhabited are now public lands managed under the national forest system. As a federal agency, the USFS has a unique trust obligation to Indian tribes as a matter of federal Indian law. Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, 30 (Pet) 1, 19 (1831). This trust obligation carries with it a duty to consult with Indian tribes when a federal action could impact tribal interests. Over the years this duty has been recognized through Executive Orders and agency policy documents (See, e.g. E.O. 13175 (Nov. 9, 2000) stating federal agencies should “ensure meaningful and timely input by tribal official in the development of regulatory policies that have tribal implications"; USDA Departmental Regulation N. DR 1350-002, Tribal Consultation (issued April 30, 2024); Forest Service Manual 1563.01, Tribal Relations, describing authorities that support agencies’ consultation requirements; See also, Professors Monte Mills and Martin Nie, PotentialTribal Implications of the Proposed Rescission of 2001 Roadless Rule, included as an attachment to this letter). The duty to consult in a government-to-government manner between two sovereigns is a key component of the CSKT goal of protecting treaty reserved access to, and use of, the natural and cultural resources located on the national forests land the Tribes utilize.

There are no rights more profound in the field of federal Indian Law, and no rights have come at more of a cost to Indian Nations then the rights guaranteed by treaties. In exchange for the promise of an exclusive homeland and other rights retained through the treaty process, tribes ceded vast tracts of lands to the United States. As the courts have observed, treaties are not grants of rights from the United States to Indian Tribes. They are agreements negotiated between sovereign nations. Treaties are grants of rights from tribes, to the United States, with a reservation of rights – often a homeland and other rights expressly held by a tribe. The importance of treaty rights to an Indian Nation cannot be understated. Tribes may hold their treaty as a sacred connection to their history and traditional lifeways. Tribal treaty rights are the cornerstone of federal Indian Law and serve as the documents upon which the federal government's relationship and trust duty to Indian Nations was established.

The CSKT have reserved (among other things) hunting, fishing, and gathering rights, both on and off the Flathead Reservation. These rights have been secured through the “Treaty with the Flatheads, Etc." 12 Stat.975 (The Hellgate Treaty). The Hellgate Treaty was signed near present day Missoula, Montana on July 16, 1855. The Hellgate Treaty is a “Stevens Treaty" negotiated by Governor and Superintendent for Indian Affairs for the Washington Territory, Isaac I. Stevens. Governor Stevens was tasked with making peace with the tribal nations along the Oregon Trail. He negotiated a majority of the treaties with Indian Nations throughout the northwest, and those treaties contain similar language securing off-reservation rights. In exchange for accepting what were often smaller reservations, the Stevens Treaty tribes reserved to themselves significant rights to hunt, fish, and gather off-reservation in the places they traditionally pursued those activities. The Flathead Reservation in northwest Montana was created through the Hellgate Treaty.

The specific language in the Hellgate Treaty reserving the right to hunt, fish, and gather is found in Article III, which states in relevant part:

The exclusive right of taking fish in all the streams running through or bordering said reservation is further secured to said Indians; as also the right of taking fish at all usual and accustomed places, in common with all citizens of the Territory, and of erecting temporary buildings for curing; together with the privilege of hunting, gathering roots and berries, and pasturing their horses on all open and unclaimed lands.

Stevens Treaty language has been the subject of much litigation, and has resulted in some of the landmark cases of federal Indian Law. The courts have recognized the term“open and unclaimed" to include federal public lands such as USFS national forest system lands now located within the CSKT aboriginal territory. The roadless areas within these national forests remain some of the last places Tribal members can exercise their treaty rights to hunt, fish, and gather on lands that are undisturbed or undeveloped, providing prime habitat for game the Tribes rely upon for subsistence and protection for cultural sites.

While ensuring the Tribes have access and use of these roadless areas in order for Tribal members to exercise their treaty reserved rights, and protecting resources is a critical interest for the CSKT, the Tribes have other concerns with the proposal to rescind the Roadless Rule. The Tribes are prepared to discuss these concerns in detail at a formal government-to-government consultation on this matter, but the Tribes include the following points in our written comment letter.

## Cultural Resource Management & Religious Practices

This proposal endangers natural and cultural resources of fundamental importance to our people. The United States is obligated to protect those resources as part of its treaty-based trust responsibilities to the CSKT. Past failures to meet those trust responsibilities have resulted not only in the government having to compensate the CSKT, but also—far worse from our perspective—the permanent degradation of irreplaceable resources of importance to our people and all Americans. We appeal to you to reconsider this unwise, destructive proposal, which would reverse decades of incremental progress in our government-to-government relations and our ability to work together to ensure the health and well-being of our shared environment.

Outside of wilderness areas and other places given the strongest protections, the great majority of the federal lands within our aboriginal territories have already been roaded, and many of them logged, with most of those impacts having occurred since World War II.

The 2001 Roadless Rule has given protection to a relatively small percentage of remaining roadless federal lands. Those lands hold an outsized importance to the CSKT and our ability to continue to exercise our rights, guaranteed in the 1855 Treaty of Hellgate, to practice our cultural ways in “open and unclaimed" parts of our ceded territories. Inherent in those reserved rightsis the continued health and well-being of the lands and waters, and the native plants, animals, fish, birds, and other resources of cultural importance. For our continued ability to practice our cultural and spiritual traditions, it is also crucial that these places provide quiet and solitude, qualities that are directly harmed by road-building. Roads also harm the connectivity of wildlife habitat and the health of wildlife populations, many of which are already declining or imperiled.

To illustrate the direct threat to our people posed by the proposed rescission, we offer maps of the aboriginal territories of two of our three tribal groups (the Salish and Kalispel or Pend d’Oreille) and of USFS roadless areas within that area.
