![](images/b150211c81271adb4b29f5934681dd9bcf661878fe10b398a811d7f82367b2c4.jpg)

These maps clearly indicate that the impacts of this proposed rescission on the CSKT would be massive. For many thousands of years, our people have held an intimate knowledge and understanding of these places. We continue to use them for many purposes, including hunting, fishing, gathering plants, and spiritual practices. They are places that bear Salish place-names referring to certain resources of cultural importance or even to our Creation stories, reflecting the depth of our connection to these areas

According to oral history, our CSKT aboriginal territory extends from the northern plains to present-day Edmonton, Alberta, Yellowstone Park, Lake Pend Oreille in north Idaho, parts of British Columbia, and to the west coast. The mountains and forests are essential to the CSKT, not only for harvesting wildlife, food, and medicines, but also as the heart of our spiritual way of life. The rescission of Roadless Rule would have a direct impact on all these elements that are integral to tribal lifeways.

Our right to practice our religion and our existence as a people depend on our ability to preserve and nurture this relationship with the land. A vast majority of the Selis, Ksanka, and Qlispe people continue to practice their traditional religions and maintain a deep, sacred connection to the land. Our religion is at the heart of our sovereignty as Indian people. The U.S. Department of

Agriculture, as a federal agency, has a responsibility under the American Religious Freedom Act (AIRFA) to ensure that Tribal spiritual places are kept in their natural condition and that our religious practices are not interfered with. The rescission of Roadless Rule would open up pristine lands that otherwise remain untouched by modern development, which would have a direct effect on Tribal spiritual and religious practices

Since 2001, the Roadless Rule, implemented by the Forest Service, has protected undeveloped roadless regions within National Forests by banning logging and road construction. There are approximately 6 million acres of uninhabited and undeveloped areas in Montana forests that are protected under the Roadless Rule. These areas are vital for conserving natural habitats and preserving the wilderness character, as well as for maintaining habitats of old-growth forests. which holdsignificant ecological and cultural value. For example, portions of the Yaak Valley located within the Kootenai National Forest, remain wild and undeveloped, with at least 15 areas protected from road development and logging, preserving essential natural resources. Among these resources are sacred sites to the CSKT people. These sites are vital for the well-being, cultural preservation, and sometimes even the survival of our communities. Any disruption to these pristine wilderness areas could harm the health and well-being of our people

Rescission of the Roadless Rule will not only have a direct impact on the resources that the tribes of the CSKT utilize, including wildlife, medicinal, and food plants, but also will affect areas that hold religious and spiritual significance. It is important to acknowledge that these places cannot be replicated, and opening them up to development, including the construction of roadways and the exploitation of natural resources, will cause detrimental impacts in these areas.

## Ongoing Forest Planning and Budget Concerns

Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule at this point is poor timing. Many national forests are still carrying out needed revisions to their current land use planning documents and are doing so with reduced staff capacity. The CSKT is currently consulting with national forests locatedwithin the Tribes’ ceded lands and traditional use area (such as the Lolo National Forest) that are in the process of updating their forest plans. Many of the roadless areas have been incorporated under management plans for uses consistent with roadless designations. As the forest planning processes reach their conclusions, the Tribes want to see the forest planning documents and management projects continue to recognize the roadless designation within each national forest plan. Changing the Roadless Rule at this point in the planning process will upend years of consultation between the Tribes and national forests

Furthermore, the 2001Roadless Rule was developed primarily because of budget concerns and the ballooning cost of road constructions and maintenance.

From 1992 to 1997, the Forest Service’s timber program cost taxpayers over \$2 billion. The Forest Service's system of forest roads operated as a major subsidy for the timber industry--on average, timber sale revenues totaled only eighty-three cents for each dollar spent because of road construction and maintenance costs, which the Forest Service shouldered. In the 1990s, the Forest Service became known as the largest roadbuilding entity in the world, maintaining over 380,000 miles of forest roads. Despite its

efforts to reduce the mileage of forest roads—the Forest Service decommissioned 2,700 miles per year between 1991 and 1997—the demand for new road construction continued....[T]he costs of constructing and maintaining so many forest roads took its toll on the Forest Service budget. With an annual road maintenance budget of about \$90 million, the Forest Service's backlog for road projects ballooned to over \$8.4 billion by 1996. New road construction became unsustainable from an economic perspective, and officials in the Clinton Administration began to examine ways to stop new road construction completely in roadless areas across the country.1

Rolling back the 2001 Roadless Rule, a measure that was designed primarily to address the burgeoning cost of road maintenance and construction, would undoubtedly increase the Forest Service's budget. Yet, the current Administration recently proposed a budget that would cut the Forest Service's budget by 65%.2 Proposing a measure that will dramatically increase costs for the Forest Service while at the same time proposing to greatly reduce the Forest Service budget is not fiscally responsible, and will undoubtedly result in fewer resources for other important Forest Service programs, and will ultimately lead to an increased burden on taxpayers.

## Wildlife and Conservation Implications

For two and a half decades, the Roadless Rule has protected undeveloped, unroaded national forest lands from development and disturbance such as logging and road construction. These roadless areas span over 58.2 million acres of national forest lands. This is a significant amount of critical habitat for species listed under the Endangered Species Act, 16 U.S.C. 1531, et seq (ESA) and other sensitive wildlife (see, e.g. North American wolverine, Canada lynx, grizzly bear, mountain goat and big horn sheep).

Roadless areas also provide habitat for a variety of important wildlife species, including species that are important to the Tribes for subsistence hunting or their cultural significance. Elk, grizzly bear, lynx, and wolverine are a few species that are directly impacted by road density. Increased road density and reduced or fragmented habitat resulting from commercial use and development requiring road construction would be harmful to the conservation of these species.

Habitat fragmentation occurs when large expanses of habitat are intersected and/or removed by activities such as road building, human development and habitat manipulation, all of which can have negative impacts to a wide range of wildlife species. Increased road densities and timber harvest operations reduce the total area of continuous habitat and creates barriers to wildlife movement between habitats. While areas that have been logged may provide temporary benefits for some wildlife species, the great majority of wildlife is negatively impacted by these activities Important high-quality habitat for ESA listed species is often directly related to overall road density in a particular area, or distance to open roads. Species sensitive to the impacts of roads within national forest lands are already pushed to the brink. Rescinding the Roadless Rule would only serve to reduce critical habitat and increase the jeopardy to many ESA listed species, setting back decades of recovery efforts while ensuring those species remain listed.

Along with ESA listed species, road densities can influence the distribution of big game during certain seasons. Rocky Mountain Elk in particular are a species negatively impacted by the density of roads during hunting season. CSKT Tribal members exercising treaty reserved subsistence hunts could experience big game displacement throughout their aboriginal territory if the Roadless Rule is rescinded.

## Summary

Land use planning and development, along with natural and cultural resource management are matters the Tribes undertake through a staff of committed professionals dedicated to keeping the Tribes’ history and values in mind. The Tribes are equally invested in the management of public lands and resources off-Reservation where CSKT members have exercised their right to hunt, fish, gather, and conduct cultural activities for generations. Any impacts to the Tribes' treaty reserved rights and resources located on lands managed by the USFS require formal governmentto-government consultation with the CSKT. Thus, the CSKT urges that the proposed rescission be retracted or at least paused, and that we are afforded the opportunity to have formal government-to-government consultations on this matter.

Please consider this letter as the written comments of the ConfederatedSalish and Kootenai Tribes in opposition to the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule, and a request to engage in formal consultation with Agriculture Secretary Brooke L. Rollins and U.S. Forest Service Chief Schultz, and surrounding regional Forest Supervisors. The Tribes invite the federal team to the CSKT Tribal Complex in Pablo, Montana to meet with the CSKT Tribal Council and staff at a time that is mutually workable but timely enough to be meaningfully considered prior to finalization of the proposed Roadless Rule decision. Please feel free to direct any questions or begin setting a date for formal consultation with Katie MacDonald, CSKT Tribal Relations Specialist, Kathryn.McDonald@cskt.org, (406) 675-2700 ext. 1082.

Thank you for your time and we look forward to our meeting.

September 19, 2025

United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) U.S. Forest Service (USFS) Attn: Brooke Rollins, Secretary of Agriculture

Submitted via Regulations.gov website

RE: Proposed rescinding of the 2001 Roadless Rule, FR Document No. 2025-16581

Dear Secretary Rollins,

On behalf of the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community of Oregon (“Grand Ronde” or “Tribe”), thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rescinding of the 2001 Roadless Rule. As a Sovereign Nation, the Tribe reserves the right to consult government-to-government with the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the United States Forest Service (USFS) regarding this proposed action and future Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) on an ongoing basis, and to make additional and/or updated comments at any time. Grand Ronde Tribal Council reserves the right to make and/or update statements of Tribal policy or position on an ongoing basis.

Grand Ronde is a Tribal nation made up of more than 30 antecedent tribes and bands with homelands in western Oregon, southwest Washington, and northern California. Much of the 2 million acres of Roadless Rule designated forests in Oregon lie within the Tribe’s 14 million acres of ceded land, including sacred forests in the Mt. Hood N.F., Willamette N.F., Umpqua N.F., Siuslaw N.F., and Rogue River-Siskiyou N.F. Since time immemorial, the Tribe’s ancestors have hunted, fished, and gathered cultural resources and First Foods in this area. Today, Tribal members maintain a strong connection to their homelands through traditions, lifeways and practices that remains unbroken.

The Tribe wishes to consult with the USFS on the 2001 Roadless Rule for the following reasons:

1. The Roadless Rule protects important Tribal hunting, fishing, and cultural gathering areas that need protection.

2. The most common cause of fires are human activities which are co-located with roads.

3. Adding roads increases the risk of introduction of invasive plants and insects traveling and dispersed by human activities.

4. Adding roads poses more risk to streams from erosion and turbidity, resulting in long term negative impacts to threatened and endangered salmonids and steelhead. Moreover, roads must be maintained, or they pose even higher risk to streams and the USFS does not currently have the resources to effectively manage the roads within its control.

5. Adding roads poses risks to sacred areas and cultural resources by opening areas to vandalism and illegal artifact gathering.

6. Tribal ancestors evolved with fire as a natural function of the ecosystem and have continually utilized cultural burns to sustainably manage the landscape, as we still do today. U.S. fire suppression strategies over the past 150 years have artificially depressed the natural fire regime; studies have found that commercial timber intensively managed forests are more prone to extreme fire hazard. The Tribe does not support unsustainable practices and does not agree that current strategies are optimizing fire risk reduction where it is most needed in the urban-rural interface2.

7. Roadless Rule areas already allow for forest health treatments such as thinning out small trees. These practices are occurring widely in the Pacific Northwest. Further, the Tribe supports sustainable timber harvesting and replanting with diverse tree species, leaving unfragmented forests that support biodiversity.

Grand Ronde welcomes collaboration with the U.S. Forest Service to sustainably co-manage forests within the Tribe’s ceded homelands and encourages the U.S. Forest Service to host conversations about what sustainable planning and co-management should look like in national forests, including the roadless areas, into the future.

Thank you again for the opportunity to comment on this critically important process in the Tribe’s ceded lands.

hayu-masi (Many thanks),

Michael J. Karnosh

Brooke L. Rollins Secretary of Agriculture United States Department of Agriculture 1400 Independence Ave., SW Washington, D.C. 20250-0100

Comments of the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians on the Proposed Termination of the 2001 Roadless Rule

The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians respectfully submits the following comments in strong opposition to the proposed termination of the 2001 Roadless Rule.

The Roadless Rule prohibits road construction, timber harvest, and oil and gas exploration in many of this country's last wild forests and grasslands. It safeguards nearly 30 percent of national forest lands from damaging extractive enterprises, resulting in significant ecological benefits—cleaner air, protected drinking water sources, carbon storage, and critical wildlife refuges for species requiring large, unfragmented habitats to sustain viable populations. Once these areas are opened to roads and industrial extraction, their wilderness character is lost forever, along with the material, cultural, and spiritual benefits they provide.

One rationale cited for rescinding the rule is wildfire prevention. Yet research shows that more than 80 percent of wildfires occur within 800 meters of roadways. Expanding road construction and timber harvest in these areas would only increase risk and accelerate the loss of high-value old-growth trees—the very trees most resilient to wildfire. Another justification advanced is economic benefit through new opportunities for timber companies. However, this view ignores the broader economic and societal benefits these ecosystems provide, including carbon sequestration, clean water, clean air, biodiversity, and recreation—benefits that serve all Americans, not just the timber industry.

In Oregon alone, the Roadless Rule protects nearly 2 million acres of national forest land managed by the U.S. Forest Service. Many of these Inventoried Roadless Areas—including Mt. Hebo, Drift Creek, Tahkenitch, Tenmile, and Woahink Creeks on the Siuslaw National Forest, and Shasta Costa, Copper Mountain, North and South Kalmiopsis, and Mt. Emily on the Rogue-Siskiyou National Forest—are part of the ancestral homelands of the Siletz Tribe. These areas are central to our mission to care for, protect, enhance, and provide for the wise use of our natural resources in a way that ensures all future generations will benefit. They provide not only physical sustenance and spiritual grounding but also maintain the ecological balance of the region. Our stewardship practices have preserved these ecosystems for millennia, and our continued involvement is essential to their resilience.

The federal government's trust responsibility, as affirmed in Secretarial Order 3403, Executive Order 14072, USDA Departmental Regulation 1350-002, and the U.S. Forest Service Manual (FSM 1563), obligates the Forest Service to treat Tribes as full partners in managing ancestral lands and resources. Weakening the Roadless Rule undermines that responsibility.

For these reasons, the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians strongly oppose the rollback of protections for Inventoried Roadless Areas. We urge the U.S. Forest Service to keep the Roadless Rule in place, ensuring that these irreplaceable wilderness areas—and the cultural, ecological, and spiritual values they embody—are protected for all future generations.

Sincerely,

Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement, Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands

Dear Mr. Kinder:

On behalf of the Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians, we submit the following comments on the Department of Agriculture’s proposal regarding management of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs). Our Tribe has deep ancestral, cultural, and contemporary connections to the forests within what is now the Umpqua National Forest and Rogue River–Siskiyou National Forest. These lands hold sacred sites, subsistence resources, and cultural use areas that remain vital to our people.

## Protection of Cultural Resources and Tribal Access

The Cow Creek Tribe emphasizes that IRAs in the Umpqua and Rogue River–Siskiyou National Forests often overlap with areas of profound cultural, spiritual, and subsistence importance. Policies must ensure continued Tribal access for hunting, fishing, gathering, and ceremonial uses. Road decommissioning, neglect, and categorical restrictions have already impaired Tribal member access to important cultural sites. Any proposed rulemaking must prioritize Tribal rights to access, utilize, and steward these lands in accordance with treaty obligations and federal trust responsibilities.

## Road Maintenance and Legacy Road Impacts

In both the Umpqua and Rogue River–Siskiyou National Forests, legacy road systems are deteriorating, creating significant sedimentation, water quality, and habitat impacts. Neglected roads also impede safe access for Tribal members and land managers. Road maintenance, repair, or strategic decommissioning must be included as part of the environmental review. A comprehensive assessment of road-related environmental impacts is necessary, including the

costs of repairing or removing failing infrastructure. Without investment in road system sustainability, both cultural access and ecological health will remain at risk.

## Fire Prevention and Fuels Management

The Cow Creek Tribe has long recognized that proactive forest management is essential to reduce the growing threat of catastrophic wildfire. The creation and maintenance of strategic fuel breaks, hazardous fuels reduction, and prescribed burning, particularly in the Umpqua and Rogue River–Siskiyou National Forests, are necessary to protect Tribal cultural resources, nearby communities, and ecosystem integrity. We urge the Forest Service to explicitly include Triballed or co-managed fuels management projects within IRAs as allowable activities under any revised rule.

## Financial Costs and Resource Needs

Too often, policies are crafted without a clear recognition of the financial burden associated with deteriorating conditions on the ground. Addressing the backlog of road maintenance, implementing fuels management strategies, and restoring legacy impacts will require substantial, dedicated funding. We urge the agency to assess and disclose the true financial costs of inaction versus proactive management, and to dedicate the necessary resources to improve conditions in IRAs for the benefit of Tribes, local communities, and the environment.

## Tribal Partnership and Co-Management

Finally, the Cow Creek Tribe requests that the Forest Service establish a formal mechanism for Tribes to propose alternative management approaches or co-management arrangements for IRAs within the Umpqua and Rogue River–Siskiyou National Forests. This would allow Tribes to bring traditional knowledge, cultural priorities, and place-based expertise into federal land management decisions, consistent with the federal trust responsibility and Departmental Regulation 1350-002 on Tribal Consultation.

For questions regarding these comments, please contact Jason Robison, Land and Resources Officer, at Jrobison@cowcreek-nsn.gov.

The Cow Creek Tribe calls for policies that protect cultural resources, secure Tribal access, address deteriorating infrastructure, reduce wildfire risk, and provide adequate financial and operational resources to improve conditions on the ground. We urge the Forest Service to meaningfully engage with our Tribe in shaping the future of IRAs in the Umpqua and Rogue River–Siskiyou National Forests.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Sincerely,

Corca Kune

Carla Keene, Chairman

Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians

Dear Secretary Rollins,

The Hopi Tribe's Tribal Historic Preservation Office (THPO) submits the following comments regarding the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) initiation of an environmental impact statement (EIS) and rulemaking concerning management of inventoried roadless areas on approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System lands.

The Hopi Tribe supports the United State Forest Service's (USFS) longstanding commitment to consultation with the Hopi Tribe on projects to determine the potential impacts on cultural resources and sacred places. These efforts reflect USDA's commitment to upholding the United States government-to-government relationships with Tribal Nations.

The Hopi Tribe is concerned that the proposed rescission of the Roadless Rule is a federal agency action that may adversely impact historic properties, including sacred sites, traditional cultural places, and other properties of religious and cultural significance to Indian Tribes. The NHPA requires consultation on such federal agency actions to avoid and mitigate such potential impacts.

Many Hopi Tribal ancestral lands are located in National Forest boundaries that contain numerus tribal cultural historic properties. It is imperative that the USFS follow the law and consult with the Hopi Tribes about activities in these forests. The Roadless Area Conservation Rule, was established to protect unnecessary road development and to protect cultural resources important to tribes and citizens of the United States, including the Hopi people. Many of these resources are only located on National Forest lands. Development and increase access in these areas may adversely impact these resources. Any proposed work in National Forests should be conducted with the utmost respect that reflects the importance of these lands to the Hopi Tribe with an aim to avoid unnecessary destruction of important cultural resources

The importance of engaging in consultation regarding the management of inventoried roadless areas is a reminder that the Hopi Tribe and indigenous communities have used resources in the National Forests long before the establishment of the National Forests.

Consistency and certainty are important for projects that are essential for all Americans. including members of Tribal Nations. We are confident that with nation-to-nation consultation and proper funding for THPOs, the project permitting process can be efficient, while at the same time guaranteeing that Tribal Nations' cultural resources are protected.

Thank you for considering our comments. Please do not hesitate to contact me if you would like to discuss this matter

Sincerely,

Re: Comments of the Inter Tribal Association of Arizona, Inc. (ITAA) on the USDA Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) and Proposed Rulemaking to Rescind 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, FS-2025-0001

To Whom It May Concern:

This letter is submitted by the Inter Tribal Association of Arizona, Inc. (ITAA) regarding the USDA Forest Service’s Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) on the proposed rulemaking to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule), as published in the Federal Register on August 29, 2025.<sup>1</sup>

ITAA is an inter-tribal consortium of 21 federally recognized Indian Tribes with lands in Arizona, California, Nevada, and New Mexico. The Member Tribes of ITAA have advocated together since 1952 on issues of common interest and concern across Indian Country. ITAA is governed by the highest elected Tribal officials from each Tribe, including Tribal chairpersons, presidents, and governors.

The proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule is of particular concern to our Member Tribes in Arizona, as Arizona contains 1.174 million acres of designated inventoried roadless areas.<sup>2</sup> In total, there are nearly 60 million acres of designated roadless areas in our nation, and these areas are overwhelmingly concentrated in the western states. As a result, many if not all of the ancestral homelands of ITAA’s Member Tribes within Arizona and the nearby states include designated inventoried roadless areas.<sup>3</sup>

The 2001 Roadless Rule has endured for nearly 25 years and it reflects important ongoing actions by the U.S. Forest Service to protect undeveloped areas on our public Forest Service lands. Since 2001, the rule has provided much-needed protections for animal and plant habitats and ecosystems, waters, and numerous traditional ancestral areas used by tribal members for traditional, cultural, and religious practices. The consequences of rescinding the Rule could be significant, as it will open millions of acres of our national forests to road construction, logging, mining, and oil and gas drilling, among other purposes, forever changing the character and health of these wild areas.

Accordingly, because the USDA’s proposed rule to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule has the potential to directly implicate the ancestral lands or resources of nearly all of ITAA’s Member Tribes in some way, ITAA has been directed to submit these comments.<sup>4</sup>

## USDA Must Engage in Tribal Consultation On This Matter

ITAA, along with other commenting tribes and tribal organizations, reminds USDA that it has a trust obligation to engage in advanced, direct government-togovernment Tribal consultation with each of our Member Tribes on the EIS and all other activities related to the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule, since this action will have differing but specific impacts on the lands and water resources adjacent to and surrounding our Member Tribes’ reservation lands, including to our Member Tribes’ ancestral homelands and the traditional, religious and cultural sites and practices which are inherently connected to and associated with these homelands.

Consultation with Indian Tribes fulfills the United States’ trust responsibilities and is required by numerous existing laws and policies, including Secretary’s Order 3175 (November 8, 1993) (requiring all agencies, bureaus, and offices within the Department of the Interior to identify potential impacts of Departmental activities upon Indian Trust resources and mandating meaningful consultation with Tribes where activities directly or indirectly affect such resources); Presidential Memorandum of April 29, 1994 titled “Government-to-Government Relations with Native American Tribal Governments” (also requiring proper consultation with Indian tribes to the greatest extent practicable prior to taking any actions that affect such tribes); Department of the Interior Manual Part 512 (discussing and embodying these same requirements in the Department Manual); Executive Order 13175 (November 6, 2000) (requiring all agencies, bureaus, and offices within the Federal Government to establish regular and meaningful consultation and collaboration with tribal officials in the development of Federal policies that have tribal implications); Memorandum for the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies on Government-to-Government Relationship with Tribal Governments (September 23, 2004); Sec. 106 of the NHPA, 16 U.S.C. § 470(f); Memorandum for the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies on Tribal Consultation (November 5, 2009) (supplementing Executive Order No. 13175); see also Presidential Memo titled Tribal Consultation and Strengthening Nation-to-Nation Relationships Memorandum for the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies (January 26, 2021); Uniform Standards for Tribal Consultation, Memorandum for the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies (November 30, 2022), to name a few.

In short, the extremely short 30-day comment period on this consequential EIS and Rule change, coupled with the lack of any informational or stakeholder webinars or meetings, and the overall accelerated proposed rulemaking timeline is grossly insufficient to ensure real Tribal and public input or meaningful tribal consultation. As you may know, early and meaningful tribal consultation on issues potentially impacting Indian Tribes is a legal requirement, not an afterthought.

On behalf of our 21 Member Tribes, ITAA respectfully request that you suspend further action on this EIS and the proposed rulemaking until an opportunity for legally compliant, meaningful, and robust tribal consultation can be fulfilled with all impacted tribes, including the Member Tribes of ITAA.

Thank you for your consideration of the ITAA’s comments. Any questions regarding these comments may be directed to ITAA Executive Director, Maria Dadgar at (480) 258-4822.

Sincerely,

INTER TRIBAL ASSOCIATION OF ARIZONA

Dear Acting Director Kinder,

I am writing on behalf of the Nez Perce Tribe ("Tribe") requesting an extension of the comment period for the Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement concerning the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (“2001 Roadless Rule"), as announced on August 29, 2025, in the Federal Register. The current comment period, which is set to close on September 19, 2025, provides insufficient time for the Tribe to thoroughly consider, analyze, and respond to the notice

The 2001 Roadless Rule applies to hundreds of thousands of acres of the Tribe's homelands now administered by the U.S. Forest Service in the states of Washington, Oregon, Montana, and Wyoming. The proposed recission of the 2001 Roadless Rule will have significant implications not only for these lands, but for rights and resources the Tribe reserved by Treaty with the United States.' They include rights to hunt, fish, gather, and pasture, as well as the wildlife, fisheries, and plant resources necessary for the exercise of the rights.2

The Tribe engaged extensively with the Forest Service in support of the 2001 Roadless Rule, including through government-to-government consultation, and knows well the complexity and potential impacts of the proposed recission. It is thus essential that the Forest Service invite government-to-government consultation on the proposal and allow the Tribe adequate time to provide comprehensive feedback. The Tribe's governmental processes require necessary review and coordination among various departments and officials, including technical staff, and legal counsel prior to formal action by the Nez Perce Tribal Executive Committee, the governing body of the Tribe. This ensures that our comments are well-informed and reflect the collective input of our community.

The provided comment period of just fourteen business days does not allow for meaningful participation during this early and critical stage of the decision-making process and is inconsistent with the Forest Service's "Strengthening Tribal Consultations and Nation-to-Nation Relationships Action Plan:" which specifies a minimum 120-day Tribal consultation period for national-level action. Therefore, we request an extension of the comment period to December 29, 2025. This additional time will enable the Tribe to engage with the Forest Service in à thorough and effective review process and to provide detailed and constructive comments on the Notice of Intent and proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule.

We request a written response approving the extension. Please do not hesitate to contact me directly at (208) 621-4781 or angelab@nezperce.org should you have any questions or require further information.

We appreciate your consideration of this request and look forward to your favorable response.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

Angela R. Jackson

Project Coordinator

RE: Nooksack Tribe comment on the Notice of Intent to prepare an EIS for rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Docket No. FS-2025-0001)

Dear Secretary Rollins and Chief Schultz:

On behalf of the Nooksack Indian Tribe, I respectfully submit these comments on the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. As a sovereign nation with a long history of use of the forest lands affected by this project, we have a strong interest in federal management of forest lands within our traditional area. The Nooksack Tribe retains constitutionally protected, treaty-reserved rights to harvest, hunt and gather, and otherwise manage fish, shellfish, and other treaty reserved resources within their usual and accustomed areas, and on all open and unclaimed lands- both on and off reservations. These rights and resources require intact habitat and functioning ecosystems. Federal public lands, and roadless areas in particular, contain the last best remaining habitats in Washington State and are critical for maintaining ecosystem function for treaty resources, including fish, wildlife and culturally important plant species.

The exercise of Treaty rights is a trust responsibility of the Forest Service and must be a primary consideration in the evaluation of the impacts of rescinding the Rule. Consistent with this responsibility and Executive Order 13175, the federal government must engage in timely, substantive, and meaningful consultation with tribes and proactively ensure that their rights and interests are fully respected in all federal decisions. To this end, the Nooksack Tribe entered into a Memorandum of Understanding with the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest in 2022 to further co-stewardship on Federal lands in the tribe’s traditional areas. Meaningful consultation with the Nooksack Tribe and tribal participation in and review of any proposed changes are critical to protecting our resources.

Further opening roadless areas to increase the lumber supply is short sighted. The Forest Service already manages a road system that they cannot bring up to a modern standard and maintain. According to the 2024 Deferred Maintenance Report, this maintenance backlog currently exceeds \$5 billion. In 2000, the National Forests in Washington State agreed to adopt the forest road standards met by private and state landowners, but they so far have not begun to meet that commitment. In the Nooksack Watershed, we have seen continued environmental damage caused by forest road failure, fish passage obstructions and sediment delivery to our aquatic resources. We believe that extending the road network into steeper, more challenging ground will only further degrade our treaty resources. This threatens not only tribal treaty reserved rights and treaty trust resources but would also undermine decades-long work to recover salmon and steelhead populations in these watersheds, many of which are home to species already threatened or endangered.

The claim presented in the Federal Register Notice that new roads reduce wildfire risk is counter to the fire statistics. Roads contribute to higher ignition risk, while roadless areas experience significantly fewer ignitions. About nine in ten fires on national forest lands are caused by people, and 80% of those occur nears roads. Building more roads will only increase the likelihood of human-caused fires. Further, the Roadless Rule does not hinder firefighting; agencies retain authority to cut temporary fire breaks or develop emergency access roads. It also allows for forest health treatments, such as thinning and undergrowth control, that can help reduce fire risk and restore healthy forests. This work in roadless areas has already been ongoing across western states in compliance with the existing Rule.

For these reasons, the Nooksack Tribe firmly opposes rescission of the Roadless Rule. Its protections are essential to supporting tribal treaty rights, sustaining salmon populations, preventing invasive species spread, reducing wildfire ignitions, and ensuring responsible management of public lands. The Nooksack Tribal Council will follow this correspondence with a letter seeking leadership-level consultation on the potential impacts to treaty rights and trust resources, including cultural resources.

Sincerely,

Gary Kentner Natural Resources Director Nooksack Indian Tribe garyk@nooksack-nsn.gov

Re: FS-2025-0001 – Response to notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule - Shoshone-Bannock Tribes

Dear Secretary Rollins,

On behalf of the Fort Hall Business Council, the governing body of the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes (Tribes) of the Fort Hall Indian Reservation, I write to express the Tribes' opposition to USDA's notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement (EIS) and conduct rulemaking to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule). The Tribes acknowledge that this action would not affect state-specific roadless rules for Idaho, to which the Tribes voiced opposition in 2008. However, with our vast homelands that include parts of Wyoming, Montana, Washington, Oregon, and Idaho, the recission will have impacts on our Treaty rights, our traditional cultural practices, and our rights reserved in land cessation agreements.

The designation of inventoried roadless areas (IRAs) within a less protective theme than they currently receive under the Roadless Rule will result in unacceptable management practices of public lands and violate mandates of the USDA to preserve the national forests' biological diversity and ensure a truly sustainable yield' of the resources within a forest ecosystem. Under legislation and acts of Congress, the Forest Service (FS) must maintain biological diversity within any given forest system. Thus, the agency must refrain from approving activities that will diminish the capacity of the system to maintain native plant and animal species. Likewise, the FS has an obligation to provide habitat for wildlife and watershed health. Rescinding the Roadless Rule will undo FS actions to meet these mandates and provide a physical path to harm delicate ecosystems.

It is clear that the underlying intent of the recission of the 2001 Roadless Rule is to enhance the economic opportunities for a select group of interests at the expense of the nation's roadless areas. The Tribes can easily see that USDA's emphasis on rescinding the Roadless Rule stated in Release No. 0141.25, “...for fire prevention,"and to give, “...more flexibility to take swift action to reduce wildfire risk..." is a literal smokescreen' to justify rescinding the rule to enable economic development of public lands.

The Tribes oppose development within an IRA because of the unique characteristics found in each roadless area. These remaining parcels of forest provide countless opportunities for ecosystem sustainability, refuge for wildlife, habitat for fish, solitude, and botanical diversity. They also hold the memories of the past generations for the future. The opportunities for exercising treaty rights and ceremony, while preserving watershed health, ecological diversity and wildlife habitat far outweigh the fleeting benefits that would be realized from the unscrupulous practices of development.

To: The Honorable Brooke L. Rollins Re: FS-2025-0001 – Response to notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule – Shoshone-Bannock Tribes

Of note, notice 2025-16581 (90 FR42179) states, "No Cooperating or Participating Agencies have been designated. The USDA Forest Service does not anticipate designating any Federal, State, Tribal, or local agencies as cooperating or participating agencies."Tribes and other stakeholders must be designated as participating organization in any rulemaking. This goes beyond consultation. Tribes must have a seat at the table in the rulemaking process to provide our expertise on how to best manage the land. The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes are ready and willing to participate.

Also of grave concern are the recent changes to National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) policies and rules to conform to Executive Order 13175. NEPA historically served as a vital tool to ensure that the voices of Tribal communities are heard in the federal decision-making process, and enabled Tribes to advocate for our rights and interests in relation to environmental protection and sustainability. USDA's new NEPA rules represent a severe rollback of environmental protections, and is a direct threat to our Tribal sovereignty, environment, lands, natural resources, cultural heritage, and public health. It also reduces government transparency.

The NEPA process approved and authorized prior to Executive Order 13175 is also critical in ensuring that archaeological resources that are of historic, religious, and cultural significance to Indian tribes are protected in accordance with the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). Moreover, the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) requires agencies to consult with Indian Tribes regarding planned activities on Federal and Tribal lands that might result in the excavation of Native American human remains or other cultural items. These are essential provisions of the NEPA process. Opening up IRAs to roads will require adherence to NHPA and NAGPRA, while new NEPA regulations do not have sufficient emphasis to ensure NHPA, NAGPRA, and other provisions are followed. Likewise, shortened timelines for response are impossible to meet. No rulemaking should marginalize the importance of NHPA and NAGPRA. Furthermore, the Tribes require 90 days to respond to USDA's draft EIS projected to be released in March of 2026.

The roadless areas of the United States are among the last features that are still intact and functioning as a reminder of the world that pre-dated the United States. From time immemorial the Shoshone and Bannock peoples utilized the forests of our ancestral homelands for subsistence. The Tribes continue to hunt salmon and game and to gather medicinal plants for sustenance and ceremony. IRAs are key components of the ecosystem. They play a pivotal role in the holistic relationship we have with our ancestors. The Tribes expect our Trustees at the USDA and FS to uphold their Trust responsibilities, and to utilize the highest standard in determining what are acceptable levels of the IRAs

Please acknowledge receipt of these comments. We look forward to your response. If you have any questions, please contact our Tribal Policy Analyst, Michael Steele at michael.steele@sbtribes.com.

DomaOhompson Donna Thompson Donna Thompson

Chairwoman Fort Hall Business Council Shoshone-Bannock Tribes

Re: Comments on Proposed 2001 Roadless Rule Recission, 90 Fed. Reg. 42179 (August 29, 2025) (“Proposed Rule”) and Government-to-Government Consultation

Dear Secretary Rollins and Chief Schultz,

The Swinomish Indian Tribal Community (“Swinomish” or the “Tribe”) strongly objects to the proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule because it amounts to a wholesale reversal in federal policy that would remove long-standing protections within the Tribe’s Treaty area resulting in catastrophic effects on Swinomish Treaty natural and cultural resources, rights and practices as described below. These potential direct, indirect, individual and cumulative impacts must be avoided to the maximum extent practicable and must be accounted for in the EIS.

It is unclear why neither the Department of Agriculture nor the U.S. Forest Service adhered to their tribal consultation policies and regulations, and it is concerning. Swinomish respectfully requests a formal government-to-government consultation with you so that Swinomish Tribal Leaders have the opportunity to meaningfully consult on this natural and cultural resource priority for salmon recovery, hunting, gathering, and other Treaty-protected rights and practices.

## I. The Swinomish Tribe Has a Long History as a Leader on Salmon Recovery and Reliance on Inventoried Roadless Areas For Fishing, Hunting and Gathering In the Skagit River Watershed.

The Swinomish Indian Tribal Community is a federally recognized Indian tribe and political successor in interest to certain tribes and bands that signed the 1855 Treaty of Point Elliott, which among other things reserved fishing, hunting and gathering rights and established the Swinomish Reservation on Fidalgo Island in Skagit County, Washington. The Swinomish Reservation sits at the mouth of the Skagit River, the largest river system draining to Puget

Sound and the only river in the Lower 48 states that still has all species of wild Pacific salmon and steelhead spawning in its waters.

Since time immemorial, the Swinomish Tribe and its predecessors have occupied and utilized vast areas of land and water to live, hunt, fish and gather to support the Swinomish Tribe’s cultural and traditional lifeways. In the Treaty, Swinomish reserved its right to take fish at its usual and accustomed fishing places in perpetuity, including throughout the entirety of the Skagit River watershed and beyond and to hunt and gather on open and unclaimed lands, including Federal- and state-owned forest lands and private industrial timberlands. These reserved rights are to be treated as the “supreme Law of the Land” pursuant to U.S. Constitution Art. 6, Cl. 2. They function akin to easements running with the lands or places they attach to, and are protected from federal, state, and private interference. See United States v. Winans, 198 U.S. 371, 381 (1905); United States v. Oregon, 718 F.2d 299, 304 (9th Cir. 1983); United States v. Washington, 20 F. Supp. 3d 828, 889 (W.D. Wash. 2007). These are not privileges granted by the federal government but rather were and are retained sovereign rights that predate the United States itself.

The Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest has Inventoried Roadless Areas (“IRAs”) all across the Tribe’s adjudicated Treaty area in the Skagit River watershed, including along the mainstem Skagit River, Baker River, Cascade River, and the Suiattle River that drains into the Sauk River. Removal of IRA protections over these important salmon rivers and their many tributaries, and over ecologically important wildlife corridors that connect public lands for wildlife migration could result in catastrophic direct, indirect, individual and cumulative impacts to the Tribe’s Treaty rights and Traditional Cultural Properties – all of which must be accounted for in the EIS.

The rescission of the Roadless Rule would undermine the Tribe’s Treaty rights by:

n Reversing long-standing federal rule protections for wildlife habitat and corridors, including salmon streams for ESA-listed species;

n Opening Treaty-protected areas to road construction and industrial logging that would fundamentally alter and harm ecosystems upon which the Tribe’s Treaty resources depend;

n Degrading, destroying and fragmenting habitat for Treaty-reserved species, including salmon, steelhead, lamprey, deer, elk, and traditional plants and foods;

n Restricting access to traditional use areas through privatization and industrialization; and

n Violating the federal government's obligation to protect Treaty resources in perpetuity.

The EIS must provide a comprehensive assessment of the direct and indirect individual and cumulative effects of the Proposed Rule to the exercise of these Treaty protected rights that are essential to the Tribe’s cultural lifeways and identity.

The 2001 Rule's exception allowing roads "needed pursuant to reserved or outstanding rights, or as provided for by statute or treaty" has provided essential flexibility while maintaining baseline protections. The Proposed Rule’s complete rescission eliminates this balanced approach. In fact, the Federal Register notice announcing the Proposed Rule states that “flexibility to respond to local land and resource conditions is paramount.”<sup>1</sup> The Proposed Rule’s blanket approach to drastically opening all IRAs across the country fails to make any mention of tribal treaty rights and cannot be adopted in its current form. The Tribe strongly urges the USFS not to adopt the Proposed Rule, and assess an alternative in the EIS to remove all IRAs from the final rule that include lands and waters where Treaty tribes have adjudicated treaty rights.

## II. The U.S. Department of Agriculture and the U.S. Forest Service Violated Their Formally-Adopted Tribal Consultation Policies and Regulations.

Both the U.S. Department of Agriculture (“USDA”) and the U.S. Forest Service (“USFS”) ignored their tribal consultation policies ahead of publishing the Proposed Rule. The Tribe was not provided advanced notice of 2001 Roadless Rule nor was it provided with the opportunity for consultation prior to the issuance of the Proposed Rule. See Attachment A.<sup>2</sup> Swinomish filed a request for a 30-day extension of time to submit comments on September 8<sup>th</sup> which was rejected without any explanation. See Attachment B. This is very concerning.

The USDA issued Departmental Regulation 1350-002 last year regarding Tribal Consultation.<sup>3</sup> That regulation defines consultation as “the timely, meaningful, and substantive dialogue between USDA officials who have delegated authority to consult, and the elected leadership of federally recognized Tribes or their designated representative(s), pertaining to USDA policies that may have Tribal implications.”<sup>4</sup>

The regulation continues by defining “Policies with Tribal Implications” as “Regulations, legislative comments or proposed legislation, and other policy statements or actions that have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes, treaty rights, Tribal jurisdiction, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes.”<sup>5</sup>

Consistent with these definitions, the regulation requires that:

[w]hen formulating and implementing policies that have Tribal implications, the

Department will, to the extent practicable and permitted by law:

1) Encourage Tribes to develop their own policies to achieve program objectives;

2) Where possible, defer to Tribes to establish standards;

3) Honor Tribal treaty rights, respect Tribal sovereignty and Tribal jurisdiction; and 4) In determining whether to establish Federal standards, consult with Tribal officials as to the need for Federal standards and any alternatives that would limit the scope of Federal standards or otherwise preserve the prerogatives and authority of Tribes.<sup>6</sup>

At the sub-Department level, agencies, including the USFS, are directed to collaborate with Tribes at the state and regional level to “establish regular, meaningful consultation and collaboration relationships.”<sup>7</sup> In addition, where issues arise that implicate important tribal interests, such as “Tribal treaty and other rights,” agencies are to “explore where appropriate and in consultation with the Office of the General Counsel, using consensual mechanisms for developing regulations, including negotiated rulemaking.”<sup>8</sup>

The regulation also prohibits agencies from:

promulgat[ing] any regulation or policy that has Tribal implications … unless

(b) The … agenc[y] …, prior to the formal promulgation of the regulation or policy, has:

1) Consulted with Tribal officials early in the process of developing the proposed regulation or policy;

2) Provided a Tribal summary impact statement in a separately identified portion of the of the preamble to the regulation as it is to be issued in the Federal Register, which consists of a description of the … agency’s … prior consultation with Tribal officials, a summary of their concerns, the … agency’s… position supporting the need to issue the regulation or policy, and a statement of the extent to which the concerns of Tribal officials have been met; and

3) Made available to the Secretary and the Director of OMB any written communications submitted to the … agency … by Tribal officials.

The regulation also prescribes specific standards for how consultation is to occur, who is authorized to consult on the part of the Department and agencies, how conflicts are to be resolved, and, for regulations, what must be published with regard to the consultation when the rule is published.<sup>9</sup> These standards include additional specifics, such as requiring that Tribes be given one month after consultation occurs to submit additional information for the record.<sup>10</sup>

USDA and USFS purportedly sent an email notification on July 22, 2025, regarding the Proposed Rule, but as my staff recently discovered, Swinomish did not receive the notification because the USFS sent it to the wrong email address. Even if we had received the July 22<sup>nd</sup> email notification, an email does not constitute meaningful consultation as required by federal law and policy. The USDA and USFS ignored, and thus violated, their own tribal consultation regulations and policies to the detriment of Swinomish because no consultation was offered or held prior to the publication of the Proposed Rule.

As a result, of particular concern is the truncated 21-day comment period ending September 19, 2025. As I noted in my September $8 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ letter requesting an extension of time to comment until October 12<sup>th</sup>, the USDA published the Proposed Rule on the Friday of a federal holiday weekend, the practical effect of which is a two-and-a-half (2.5) week comment period. This greatly reduced public notice period – on top of the failure to offer consultation – is wholly inadequate for meaningful Tribal engagement and consultation on this massive reversal of federal policy that will affect tens of thousands acres of the Swinomish Tribe’s ancestral territories and adjudicated Treaty area. The Proposed Rule includes a vague statement that "Tribal governments and Alaska Native Corporations will have an opportunity to be engaged during rulemaking and EIS development" but this provides no concrete timeline, no details about the process, nor any actual commitment to substantive government-to-government consultation as required by law and policy. The USDA and USFS have a trust responsibility to Swinomish - this is the U.S. government’s permanent legal obligation to exercise statutory and other legal authorities to protect tribal land, assets, resources, and treaty rights, as well as a duty to carry out the mandates of federal law with respect to American Indian and Alaska Native tribes.<sup>11</sup> The EIS must address how and to what extent the USDA and USFS believe that they have fulfilled their legal trust responsibility to Swinomish, and how they intend to do so throughout the rest of the rulemaking process.

The Tribe believes that because the USDA and USFS failed to adhere to the basic tenets of their own tribal consultation policies and regulations, these agencies have completely failed in their trust responsibility to Swinomish and other Tribes. The Inventoried Roadless Areas (“IRAs”) within the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest overlap with areas where the Swinomish people have hunted, fished and harvested plants and other resources to meet their subsistence, ceremonial, spiritual, cultural, and medicinal needs, and for the purposes of trade and commerce, since time immemorial. With significant recent changes to USFS NEPA regulations, deferring these questions would delay, if not sidestep, further and more detailed consideration of the impacts of rescinding protections mandated by the 2001 Roadless Rule.

Because the USDA and USFS did not engage Swinomish or other Tribes prior to publishing the Proposed Rule on August 29<sup>th</sup> as required by their own tribal consultation policies, the Proposed Rule does not include any consideration of its impacts on Treaty rights and resources – a clear violation of USDA and USFS adopted policies and regulations. The complete lack of tribal consultation results in the failure to assess compliance with the Protection of Historic Properties under 36 CFR 800. These regulations implement the National Historic Preservation Act Section 106 and define how federal agencies take into account the effects of their undertakings on historic properties. These regulations identify consulting parties, and identify the goal of consultation: to identify historic properties potentially affected by the undertaking, assess its effects, and seek ways to avoid, minimize or mitigate any adverse effects on historic properties. The EIS must address the lack of acknowledgement of NHPA Section 106 and include specific and comprehensive plans to fully adhere to it.

The USDA has conveniently determined that "the 2001 Roadless Rule is no longer the best approach to managing inventoried roadless areas" and proposes to return management authority to local decision-makers. The forthcoming EIS will analyze only two alternatives: the proposed rescission and a "no action" alternative maintaining current protections.

This limited scope fails to consider reasonable alternatives that would address stated management concerns while preserving critical protections for Tribal Treaty rights and interests. As a result, Swinomish strongly objects to the adoption of the Proposed Rule and believes that unless and until the USDA and USFS honor their trust responsibility to Swinomish and other tribes by following long-standing tribal consultation policies and regulations that require meaningful involvement in federal regulation and policy changes like the Proposed Rule, the “no action” alternative must be adopted.

In addition, the EIS must assess to what extent are Tribally-focused designations, such as areas of tribal importance, found within IRAs covered by the 2001 Roadless Rule? The EIS should also assess how the rescission of the 2001 Rule would impact Tribal treaty-based resources, areas of tribal importance, or other areas of tribal interest—and the related plan components in revised forest plans—especially where those plans and the relevant components cross-reference or rely upon the protections provided by the 2001 Rule?

## III. The Proposed Rule Violates the Terms and Spirit of the 2013 Memorandum of Agreement Between the U.S. Forest Service and the Swinomish Tribe.

In 2013, Swinomish and the USFS entered into a Memorandum of Agreement (“MOA”) to facilitate their shared responsibility to protect and enhance the USFS lands, especially the traditional aboriginal territories and treaty protected use areas of Swinomish within the boundaries of the lands administered by the USDA’s Forest Service within the Mt. Baker –

Snoqualmie National Forest.<sup>12</sup> See Attachment C. The MOA acknowledged that Swinomish are “successors in interest to signators of the Treaty of Point Elliott of 1855” and that:

The Tribe views the continued availability and use of resources within the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest as critical to perpetuating its culture and identity as a distinct Tribe. The water, the plants and the trees all serve a purpose that helps the Swinomish people, as a distinct tribe, to continue their cultural life ways that have been rooted for thousands of years upon this land and waters flowing through and adjacent thereto. The Swinomish Tribe understands that this land and waters, this place, as well as its language connect it and its people to all things and must be conserved and nurtured. The Swinomish Tribe and the Forest Service also recognize that the Tribe’s cultural continuity is tied to the constant ebb and flow of natural resources. Therefore, this Agreement is much more than a piece of paper when it comes to the Swinomish peoples historical relationship to the land, waters and resources within the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest as understood and valued by their ancestors. It is an instrument to acknowledge their historical legacy of respect for the lands, waters and resources.<sup>13</sup>

Regarding the USFS trust responsibility to Swinomish, the MOA acknowledges that:

The Forest Service shares in the United States Government’s trust responsibilities to protect the rights of federally recognized Indian Tribes. Facilitating the exercise of treaty-reserved rights on National Forest System lands is a part of the overall management function of the agency under the broad range of federal laws that authorize National Forest (“NF”) activities and programs.<sup>14</sup>

In the MOA, the Tribe and USFS agreed, among other things, that:

1.1 The predecessors to the present day Swinomish Tribe entered into a treaty with the United States by which they reserved tribal hunting, fishing and gather rights in lands that include the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest, and the waters and resources therein. Since time immemorial, the Swinomish people have hunted, fished and harvested plants and other resources found on lands, and in waters flowing through lands, now managed by the Forest Service to meet their subsistence, ceremonial, spiritual, cultural, and medicinal needs, and for the purposes of trade and commerce. The Forest Service recognizes the Swinomish Tribe’s rights to continue to practice these treaty-reserved rights within the boundaries of the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest.<sup>15</sup>

1.2 The Swinomish Tribe has a continuous interest in the activities taking place within the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest that affect the Tribe’s cultural and archeological resources. A significant portion of the Tribe’s traditional aboriginal territory and areas used for the exercise of treaty-reserved rights overlap the boundaries of the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest.<sup>16</sup>

1.3 Further, the Forest Service recognizes a) The Tribe’s inherent sovereignty and retained regulatory authority regarding its treaty-reserved rights; and b) The Tribe’s ability to implement and administer a system of effective tribal selfregulation regarding tribal member exercise of those rights.<sup>17</sup>

1.4 The Tribe and the Forest Service have an ongoing government-to-government relationship pursuant to federal Indian law and policy, including but not limited to the trust responsibility of federal agencies to tribes to protect the Tribe’s rights.<sup>18</sup>

The MOA included agreement that the Parties would “[i]mplement Forest Service programs and activities consistent with and respecting Indian treaty rights and fulfilling the Federal government’s legally mandated trust responsibility with Tribes,” as well as “[m]anage NFS-administered lands and resources on which tribal treaty rights exist in coordination with Tribes.”<sup>19</sup> In the MOA, the USFS agreed to consult with the Tribe in order to “[c]omply with laws and regulations in a manner consistent with the special and unique legal and political relationship with Tribes” and to “[c]ollaboratively involve Tribes, as early as possible, in the development of regulatory and management policies . . . plans and actions that may have tribal implications.”

The “Objectives” in the MOA include, among other things, to:

3.2 Facilitate consistent and timely communication between Parties at the appropriate levels of government;

3.3 Provide for the effective participation by the Tribe in the management of the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest, including . . . all other proposed activities within the National Forest that may affect the Tribe, and the natural and cultural resources of interest to the Tribes;

3.4 Facilitate the exercise of the Tribe’s treaty hunting, fishing and gathering rights.

3.5 Facilitate through collaboratively developed management plans access to NF lands within the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie Forest to enable the exercise of the Tribe’s treaty hunting, fishing and gathering rights as well as the protection and conservation of natural and cultural resources as well as the habitats of these resources subject to the Tribe’s treaty rights.

3.7 Ensure that Forest Service officials, programs and activities respect tribal selfgovernment and sovereignty and honor tribal rights and interests.

These and other Objectives are reaffirmed in the “Commitments” section of the MOA. Since 2013 the USFS has worked in good faith to implement the MOA to honor, uphold, protect and enhance Swinomish Community Members’ exercise of Treaty rights to hunt, fish, gather and practice cultural and spiritual ceremonies throughout the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest. Unfortunately, the Proposed Rule completely disregards this good faith effort and work, including the significant substantive and procedural commitments to Treaty resource protection that implementation of the MOA has accomplished.

The EIS must address and account for the Tribe’s Treaty rights in and to the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest as well as the numerous natural and cultural resources that the Proposed Rule would put at immeasurable risk. The EIS must address and account for the direct and indirect individual and cumulative impacts of the Proposed Rule on the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest staff’s ability to continue to facilitate the exercise of treaty-reserved rights on National Forest System lands that is a part of the overall management function of the USFS.

## IV. The Proposed Rule Lacks Any Credible Scientific Basis and Would Result in Significant Harm to Treaty Protected Natural and Cultural Resources.

For Swinomish, the IRAs within Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest provide important ecological functions, including landscape habitat connectivity for wide-ranging terrestrial species, clean cold water for salmon and downstream communities, and the ability to exercise traditional cultural ceremonies and visit sacred sites. The Proposed Rule would eliminate the protections to IRAs and usher in a wholesale policy reversal to allow new roads in sensitive ecological areas. The Proposed Rule thus directly undermines the Tribe’s Treaty rights to the continued existence and protection of these natural and cultural resources. The EIS must address the direct and indirect individual and cumulative adverse impacts to these resources.

## A. New Roads Cause Harmful Impacts to Skagit Watershed Salmonid Species.

Native salmonid species, including ESA-listed threatened Puget Sound Chinook salmon and steelhead trout, are extremely sensitive to habitat conditions in the freshwater stages of their life cycles.<sup>20</sup> Excess sedimentation due to the failure of forest roads is a primary cause of aquatic habitat destruction in forest lands.<sup>21</sup> <sup>22</sup> Habitat destruction, in turn, results in severe impacts to the persistence and recovery of salmon and trout.

Excess sediment from new roads has a multitude of harmful effects, including that it:

n fills spawning gravels,<sup>23</sup>

n restricts the flow of oxygenated water around incubating eggs,<sup>24</sup>

n fills and simplifies pools which are critical for salmon rearing,<sup>25</sup>

n widens channels and destroys riparian vegetation,<sup>26</sup> which leads to increased stream temperature hazards,<sup>27</sup> and

n scours and destroys in-channel structures formed by wood,<sup>28</sup> which are critical habitat elements for a range of life history stages of salmon and trout.

Expanding the USFS road network in Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest will lead to further habitat destruction, degradation and fragmentation, threatening the recovery of ESAlisted species. The experiment invited by the Proposed Rule has already been run and we have
