Each year, road washouts occur that go unfixed due to a lack of funding and staffing capacity. These road washouts restrict treaty-protected access to Tribal hunting, gathering and ceremonial practices and sites. High-risk road segments remain on the landscape in an un-decommissioned state,<sup>29</sup> waiting for the next large storm to send overwhelming sediment volumes into creeks and rivers below. To fully comply with its trust responsibilities to Tribes for access and environmental protection, the USFS should be developing a plan to fix all remaining high- and medium-hazard road segments and maintain access throughout the remaining network, not paving the way for an unmanageable expansion of risky roads.

The EIS must address how these scientifically-based direct and indirect individual and cumulative adverse impacts to salmon habitat would affect the recovery of both ESAlisted and non-listed salmonids in the Skagit River watershed from the new road building impacts listed above.

## B. The Tribe Has Significant Economic, Subsistence and Cultural Interests in Protecting the Inventoried Roadless Areas that ESA-listed Salmonids and the SRKW that Rely Upon Them Need to Recover.

Anadromous fish, and particularly Chinook salmon, have played a central role in the Tribe’s subsistence, economic, cultural, spiritual lifeways, and day-to-day existence for thousands of years. The Tribe has witnessed the precipitous decline of Puget Sound Chinook salmon even before they were listed in 1999. Even though the Tribe has been a leader in responsibly managing and using the threatened salmon resource, it has watched its members livelihoods deteriorate as fishing runs have plummeted and fishing seasons have been shortened and closed.

What harms salmon harms Swinomish. The loss of fishing opportunities has strained the Tribe’s cultural lifeline and diminished Tribal members’ economic opportunities and overall well-being. To Swinomish members, fewer Chinook salmon means less harvest for subsistence, ceremonial, and commercial purposes. With salmon populations plummeting since the 1990s, some of the Tribe’s children are no longer following in the footsteps of their fathers, uncles and mothers as fishers – with the result that we, as a Tribe, as People of the Salmon, are threatened with losing a way of life that has been with us for thousands of years.

Swinomish is a primary guardian of the Skagit and Samish River basins and surrounding coastal areas. For decades, the Tribe has invested in scientific research which increasingly indicates that without reversing some of the past degradation to salmon habitat, and without protecting the remaining intact, functioning habitat, recovery of ESA-listed salmonids and the Southern Resident Killer Whale (“SRKW”) that depend upon them is not possible. Among other efforts, Swinomish has advocated for decades to protect instream river flows, ensure federal,

state and local regulations are enforced and policies and plans adhere to best scientific and technical data, including to restore riparian, floodplain and estuary habitats, remove roads causing harm to salmon and hunting habitat within the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest, and protect nearshore habitat for salmon recovery in the Skagit basin, through significant policy, scientific, and legal efforts.

The Tribe is an adjudicated co-manager of Washington fisheries along with the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) and in this capacity has worked with WDFW and NOAA Fisheries for decades to ensure protection and restoration of fishery habitats and resources in the Skagit and Samish basins, as well as shellfish resources in Washington’s coastal zone. The Tribe was a founding member of the Skagit River System Cooperative (“SRSC”) (established as the Skagit System Cooperative in 1976 and renamed in 2003), a fisheries and environmental science and research consortium between Swinomish and the Sauk-Suiattle Indian Tribes. SRSC is considered a center of excellence in fisheries science, research and restoration. It has more than 25 highly qualified scientists and biologists with expertise in fish biology, hydrology, hydrogeology, restoration ecology and environmental permitting and regulatory compliance and works closely with Swinomish staff to pursue salmon recovery goals.

As explained in the attached declaration of Tandy Wilbur,<sup>30</sup> Swinomish is today, and always has been, very much a fishing community. For context, in 2023, 101 members registered for salmon fishing, and 187 for Dungeness crab. In 2024, 93 members registered for salmon fishing, and 275 for Dungeness crab. That is around 20% of the Swinomish membership, one in five of every Swinomish man, woman and child. Some of the fishers are engaged full time in the various tribal fisheries, while others fish part time during certain seasons to supplement their income. Most hire deckhands, who must be Swinomish members. The total income to the Tribe from commercial, ceremonial and subsistence finfish fisheries was \$1,035,522 in 2022; \$484,956 in 2023; and \$584,748 in 2024. The total income to the Tribe from commercial, ceremonial and subsistence shellfish fisheries was \$8,904,014 in 2022; \$6,864,508 in 2023; and \$7,522,739 in 2024.

The act of fishing, the circulation of harvest within the community, the dietary reliance upon the harvest, and the importance of salmon and other species to the Swinomish culture and spiritual life, give treaty fishing rights a value that far transcends the economic value as a commodity. The treaty fishing right was meant to preserve our culture and way of life revolving around fishing and the fish harvest. However, since 1978, the Tribe has not issued a regulation opening a direct wild spring Skagit Chinook fishery because of the severe decline in Skagit Chinook populations and the concomitant need for a conservation closure. As a result, tribal members have been unable to harvest the prize of all salmon species.

The tribes have a right to engage in subsistence fishing, meaning fishing for personal or household consumption and not for sale. Commercial fishing has a subsistence component, since all commercial fishers reserve from their catches fish for their families and to distribute to extended family, elders and others in need in the community. Sharing of the bounty of the sea is a deeply ingrained cultural tradition of the Coast Salish tribes. It is particularly strong at Swinomish, where the bounty of the Skagit River, the adjacent tidelands, and the strong marine fisheries close to the Swinomish Reservation presented an abundance of fisheries riches. The people thrive as a community around the sharing offish.

The Treaty fishing right also includes the right to take fish for ceremonial purposes. This harvest directly addresses the ceremonial, religious and spiritual values of the treaty fishing right. The Swinomish Fisheries Manager also manages these fisheries. They take place under permit and the catch counts toward our allocation share. As a community member and leader, I greatly appreciate the significance of the ceremonial fishery.

The Tribe has taken an important leadership role in working to maintain and recover salmon stocks in the region through habitat protection and restoration efforts because the best available science from the 2005 Skagit Chinook Recovery Plan (“Recovery Plan”) over two decades ago made clear that habitat degradation and destruction have caused the decimation of our ESA-listed Chinook and other salmon runs. Degradation to these habitats affects Chinook recovery directly as well as the entire food web that they depend upon to feed and grow strong enough before they journey to the ocean. The Tribe is very concerned that the Proposed Rule would remove these key habitat protections in IRAs for ESA-listed Chinook, Steelhead, and Bull trout, among other salmon species.

There are many Treaty resources that the Tribe depends upon for its commercial, subsistence and ceremonial fisheries, including sockeye, coho, pink and chum salmon that depend upon the same habitats in the Skagit River as ESA-listed species. The Tribe has benefited from the 2001 Roadless Rule protections against habitat degradation in the upper portions of the Skagit watershed. The Tribe is very concerned that if the Proposed Rule is adopted, and these important protections are diminished or eliminated, many ESA-listed and non-listed species may suffer and decline.

The Swinomish community also benefits from the tribal commercial fishery in another way. Since 1968 a fish processing plant has been operating on the Swinomish Reservation. The plant began as a tribal operation, but after a few years was leased out to a private operator. In 2009, Swinomish formed the Swinomish Fish Company and took over operation of the plant. Swinomish Fish Co. is also major producer of salmon roe caviar primarily for export to Europe and Asia. The plant purchases crab and other local harvests as well. It is a major purchaser of tribal member harvest, and its wholesale purchasing activities help to support the price fishers obtain for their fish. The plant also purchases fish from other sources, tribal and non-tribal alike, including fish from British Columbia. Swinomish Fish Company generated several million dollars in sales in recent years. The plant would most likely close if there were no tribal treaty harvest to process.

We know that scientifically, roadless areas protect the headwaters and riparian systems that sustain our treaty-reserved fisheries and provide clean water for our communities. The Skagit River watershed contains tens of thousands of acres of IRAs that are critical for:

n Spawning and rearing habitat for salmon, steelhead, bull trout;

n Cold, clean water essential for fish survival in a warming climate;

n Intact riparian vegetation maintaining stream temperatures and preventing sedimentation;

n Natural hydrology supporting traditional and subsistence fishing;

n Water quality for ceremonial and cultural practices; and

n Protection of medicinal plant habitats that require pristine water sources.

The EIS must provide a comprehensive assessment of the direct and indirect individual and cumulative effects to these ecological functions that are essential to protect and recover the Tribe’s Treaty resources and rights.

Scientific evidence demonstrates that road construction is the primary source of sediment pollution in forest streams, with roads contributing up to 90% of total sediment yield. The Proposed Rule would:

n Increase sedimentation, destroying spawning gravels and smothering eggs

n Elevate stream temperatures beyond tolerance levels for cold-water species

n Fragment aquatic habitats through culverts and stream crossings

n Introduce pollutants from vehicle traffic and industrial operations

The EIS must provide a comprehensive assessment of these direct and indirect individual and cumulative effects resulting from the Proposed Rule that would remove long-standing protections against road building in sensitive ecological systems and allow the impacts above to the Tribe’s Treaty resources and rights.

In summary, the Swinomish treaty fishery generates significant economic, subsistence and spiritual value for tribal members and our tribal community, but would be far less if current protected IRAs become open to the substantial amount of direct and indirect individual and cumulative adverse effects from new roads that will degrade, fragment and diminish key salmon habitat. Since almost every Swinomish household includes a fisher, that income is diffused through the whole tribal community. A decline in tribal fishing would cause serious and immediate adverse effects on the tribal economy and community.

C. The Proposed Rule Threatens the Tribe’s Treaty Right to Hunting and Would Cause Immeasurable Harm to the Tribe’s Ability to Protect Cultural Resources, Exercise Cultural and Spiritual Ceremonies, and Protect Sacred Sites.

As explained in the attached declaration of Valentino “Tino” Villaluz,<sup>31</sup> Swinomish’s Wildlife Program Manager, there has been a continued struggle to exercise Swinomish’s Treatyprotected hunting and gathering rights throughout the Skagit River watershed, including the

IRAs, because of current levels of human impact.

Mr. Villaluz and Tribal members are familiar with the Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) in the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest, especially the IRAs surrounding Baker Lake, those northeast of Concrete and along the mainstem Skagit River, those bordering North Cascades National Park, the Cascade River and the Suiattle River. They have regularly practiced their Treaty rights to hunt, gather and practice spiritual ceremonies in these IRAs. There is serious concern that numerous Swinomish tribal members who also engage in the exercise of their Treaty rights in these areas will be substantially harmed by the removal of Roadless Rule protections. The EIS must account for the impacts to the exercise of these rights.

Today, Swinomish can harvest far fewer plants and animals than previous generations, which impacts my and the Tribal Community’s ability to feed our families and practice our cultural lifeways. Recovering native plant and animal populations is high on the Tribe’s list of priorities because we are starting to lose hunters and gatherers as opportunities to hunt and gather decline. This loss breaks the generational cycle that has existed for millennia. Before, our earliest thoughts were on the water, with our parents, uncles and grandparents catching salmon, and also on the land, hunting and gathering. If our children are no longer following in our footsteps, we— as a Tribe, as a people—are threatened with losing a way of life that has been with us for thousands of years.

Equally impactful, habitat degradation, fragmentation and destruction already represent an existential threat to the plants and animals that form part of the foundation of the Tribe’s Treaty rights. Simply put, our fish, plants, and animals are experiencing a homelessness crisis. After more than a century of population growth, recreational impacts and resource extraction in the greater Skagit River watershed, as well as the Mt. Baker - Snoqualmie National Forest and its IRAs, overall the remaining habitat does not come close to meeting conservation needs, much less meeting the Tribe’s needs in terms of access to and availability of multiple species. Recreational impacts are finally beginning to be studied and understood, but without question, shifting from a federal policy of having tens of thousands of acres of IRAs in the watershed to a wholesale removal of those protections will absolutely bring more impacts, including from more recreation, which has direct and indirect, as well as individual and cumulative, impacts to the Tribe’s ability to exercise Treaty rights to hunt and gather.<sup>32</sup>

This level of habitat degradation is also harmful on a cultural level to a people whose teachings and beliefs are so tied to the land. From an early age Swinomish youth are taught that life begins in the Upper Watershed—fishing, hunting, and everything else depends on the cold, clean water of the Skagit River flowing downstream from the Cascade Mountains. We have a saying that our existence occurs “from whitecap to whitecap”—meaning, from the snow and glaciers atop the Cascade mountains to the whitecaps of waves breaking in the Salish Sea. We may be the “People of the Salmon,” but we are not just that—for example, the Swinomish story pole features a mountain goat, a species only found in the alpine and sub-alpine areas of the Upper Watershed. The purpose of a roadless area is a vital one: maintaining connectivity and species diversity in critical habitats. Rescission would paint a target on the remaining untrammeled critical habitat when the species dependent on that habitat are already desperate for more.

Swinomish has a system of issuing permits and tags to Tribal members for the subsistence harvest of game. These harvests are small due to conservation needs and the dwindling availability of many species for harvest, but are nonetheless very important to Tribal members’ health, tradition, and cultural practices. In the 2024-2025 subsistence and ceremonial hunting season, Tribal hunters harvested 16 deer (approximately 800 pounds), 27 elk (approximately 7,290 pounds), one bear (approximately 100 pounds), and an estimated 200 geese (approximately 1200 pounds) and 500 ducks (approximately 1500 pounds).

Subsistence hunting and gathering is much more important to Swinomish and other treaty tribes than it is to the general population. Game and harvested foods like berries, in addition to fish and shellfish, have been a major part of the Swinomish diet since time immemorial. All of these foods, and in particular game, have declined as a share of Swinomish member’s diets due lack of access, fragmented habitat, falling abundance due largely to inadequate or degraded habitat, and harvest time restraints.

The IRAs within the Mt. Baker Snoqualmie National Forest, particularly in the Skagit River Watershed, encompass numerous Traditional Cultural Properties (TCPs), sacred sites, and cultural landscapes integral to our identity and spiritual practices. These areas include:

(1) ceremonial and prayer sites,

(2) traditional gathering areas for medicines, foods, and materials, and

(3) cultural landscapes that embody our stories and oral traditions.

The EIS must provide a comprehensive assessment of the direct and indirect individual and cumulative effects to the exercise of these Treaty protected rights that are essential to the Tribe’s cultural lifeways and identity.

The Proposed Rule does not, but the EIS must, address how these irreplaceable Tribal cultural resources would be protected from:

n Physical destruction through road construction and logging operations;

n Desecration through increased public access and industrial activity;

n Loss of privacy and sanctity necessary for ceremonial practices;

n Looting, vandalism, and unauthorized artifact collection; and

n Increased wildfire risk from human-caused ignitions that threaten cultural, sacred sites and culturally modified trees.

Existing protections under the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), American Indian Religious Freedom Act, and Cultural Heritage Cooperation Authority (CHCA) are

insufficient without the baseline protections provided by the Roadless Rule. Project-level consultation cannot replace landscape-level protection of interconnected cultural resources. The EIS must address the direct and indirect individual and cumulative impacts to Treaty-protected sacred cultural sites and resources.

Section 101(b)(4) of the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”) declares that one objective of the environmental policy is to “preserve important historic, cultural, and natural aspects of our national heritage.” Accordingly, NHPA Section 106 studies are coordinated with the NEPA process. Identification and evaluation of historic properties and determination of effects on them takes place as NEPA documents are developed. How will the EIS account for the preservation of the important historic, cultural and natural aspects of the nation’s heritage that are fundamentally part of the Tribe’s Treaty rights and resources? How will the EIS account for compliance with the American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978 (AIRFA), that protects the rights of American Indian people to believe, express, and exercise their traditional religions? AIRFA allows access to sites, use and possession of sacred objects, and freedom of worship through traditional ceremonies and practices. The EIS must provide a comprehensive assessment in response to these questions and applicability of these important tribal cultural laws.

V. The Proposed Rule Is Economically Illogical, Subjects National Forest Lands to Undue Pressure Based on H.R. 1, and Not Supported by the USFS’s Own Research and Monitoring.

A. The Proposed Rule is Economically Illogical Because it Does Not Account for the Financial Inability of National Forests to Currently Manage Their Current Extensive Road Systems.

For decades, there have been more roads in national forests than can be maintained by the USFS. The USFS has a massive 380,000-mile road system and a growing \$10.8 billion dollar maintenance backlog that has persisted for decades. The Forest Service receives funding to maintain only a fraction of their road system. Roads are expensive to build and maintain, fragment and degrade wildlife habitat, serve as vectors for human fire ignitions, and annually dump many tons of sediment onto fish habitat and breeding sites. The EIS must assess this multibillion dollar backlog in existing road maintenance and explain in detail how it proposes to allow new road development without externalizing significant costs onto local communities and tribes like Swinomish.

The USFS has already expended significant resources to successfully reduce its road network, and it makes no economic sense to redo these past failings. Largely in response to the overwhelming evidence linking forest road building and clearcutting to landslides and aquatic habitat destruction, the USFS initiated a program of road improvements and decommissioning that was most active during the lead up to and directly following the enactment of the Roadless

Rule in 2001. Similarly, the 2005 Travel Management Rule<sup>33</sup> required National Forests to specify a ‘minimum road system’ which would be both financially sustainable and environmentally sound. The bottom line was that, in addition to the aquatic hazards explained above, the USFS recognized it could not adequately maintain its road network or ensure public safety and resource protection. Therefore, protections afforded to habitat by regulating roadless areas have been complementary to an active program of reducing past harms in watersheds that already contained forest roads. Road decommissioning projects implemented during this period of road network reduction, many of which cost millions of dollars and took years to plan and complete, were hugely successful at reducing road failures and sedimentation impacts.<sup>34</sup>

In the local process to satisfy the requirements of the Travel Management Rule, the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest ranked 41% of its road network as medium or high from a resource concern perspective.<sup>35</sup> The data used to support that finding were derived in part from multiple watershed analyses conducted to support NEPA review for specific project areas, which focused on road decommissioning and improvements as integral components of the action alternatives.<sup>36</sup> <sup>37</sup> These action alternatives used a risk-based framework in which the highest-risk road segments were targeted for decommissioning, closure or improvements, with the goal being reducing or eliminating the risk of failure and damage to aquatic habitats while simultaneously bringing the USFS road network to a more manageable size.

As a result of this work by the USFS, the Tribe has seen few landslides originating from USFS roads following the completion of many of these decommissioning projects, leading to a quantifiable reduction in sediment delivery to salmon streams.<sup>38</sup> We commend the USFS for the good work it has completed over multiple decades to mitigate damage to aquatic resources from USFS roads within the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest. We believe that the tenets of good government should be adhered to so that the real risks and consequences of road building in sensitive habitats does not resurrect the harmful impacts to the Skagit River watershed and beyond.

The EIS must provide a comprehensive analysis of the current inability of the USFS to manage and maintain its vast network of roads based on the lack of federal appropriation for such work and the lack of staff resources for such work due to this Administration’s budget cuts. The EIS must provide a comprehensive financial analysis of the how the Proposed Rule will open millions of acres of sensitive habitat to new roads, including the standards those new roads will be held to, particularly if non-governmental entities could be given authority for new road construction.

## B. The USDA and USFS Must Provide an Economic and Legal Analysis of How the Proposed Rule Intersects with the Mandates for Substantially Increased Timber Harvest on USFS Lands in H.R. 1.

On July 4, 2025, H.R. 1 was signed into law.<sup>39</sup> Section 50301, sub-section (a) of H.R. 1 contains the following language:

```txt
(2) Timber sales on public domain forest reserves.-- (A) In general.--For each of fiscal years 2026 through 2034, the Secretary shall sell timber annually on National Forest System land in a total quantity that is not less than 250,000,000 board-feet greater than the quantity of board-feet sold in the previous fiscal year. (B) Limitation.--The timber sales under subparagraph (A) shall be subject to the maximum allowable sale quantity of timber or the projected timber sale quantity under the applicable forest plan in effect on the date of enactment of this Act. (3) Long-term contracting for the forest service.-- (A) Long-term contracting.--For the period of fiscal years 2025 through 2034, the Secretary shall enter into not fewer than 40 long-term timber sale contracts with private persons or other public or private entities under subsection (a) of section 14 of the National Forest Management Act of 1976 (16 U.S.C. 472a) for the sale of national forest materials (as defined in subsection (e)(1) of that section) in the National Forest System. (Emphasis added).
```

This section of H.R. 1, read in conjunction with the Proposed Rule, would add significant new pressure for vastly increased timber harvest on national forest lands, potentially in sensitive IRAs. The EIS must provide a comprehensive assessment of how the Proposed Rule intersects with the new mandates in H.R. 1 that the USFS must sell a minimum of 250,000,000 board-feet greater quantity than it sold in the previous fiscal year. In the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest, the applicable forest plan has timber harvest targets, not maximum allowable amounts, and so to the extent the Proposed Rule would seek to utilize this new mandate for timber harvest, the EIS must address and account for impacts to the abovementioned Treaty rights to natural and cultural resources.

## C. The USFS’s Own Research and Monitoring Supports Maintaining Roadless Protections.

The USFS has published research that completely contradicts the claims made in the Proposed Rule notice of intent that the Proposed Rule is necessary “to achieve its multiple use conservation mission, including timber production, recreation, wildfire suppression and fuel reduction treatments.”<sup>40</sup> As summarized in the “Long-term forest health implications of roadlessness,” a USFS published research paper, concludes that:

Agency management records show that a lack of roads has not stopped fire prevention measures; fuel management activities in roadless areas have actually been more numerous on a per-square kilometer basis than elsewhere in the National Forest System, although activities in areas with roads cover larger areas. Historical fire maps indicate that forests with and without roads have burned at similar rates since the Rule took effect. The apparent neutrality of roads with respect to fire occurrence may be due to higher rates of human caused ignition near roads offsetting advantages related to more agile positioning of fire-fighting assets. Beyond the fire dimension of forest health, analysis of over 15 000 inventory plots showed that while tree root disease is only weakly correlated with proximity to roads, roads are strongly associated with the spread of invasive plant species in national forests. Non-native plants are twice as common within 152 meters (500 feet) of a road as farther away. Speculation that eliminating road prohibitions would improve forest health is not supported by nearly twenty years of monitoring data.<sup>41</sup>

It is clear that the Proposed Rule would not be beneficial to the overall health of national forest lands based on the USFS’s published research. The EIS must address and account for the direct and indirect individual and cumulative impacts to the health of national forest lands in general, and the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest specifically, should the Proposed Rule be adopted in its current form.

## VI. Conclusion

The Swinomish Tribe unequivocally opposes the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule. Removing roadless protections in the Mt. Baker – Snoqualmie National Forest will, without a doubt, allow more roads, which leads to innumerable adverse impact from increased human impact and habitat fragementation, and thus impairs the Tribe’s ability to exercise its Treaty rights to hunt, fish, gather and practice cultural and spiritual ceremonies. The

Proposed Rule represents a substantial breach of trust responsibilities, a violation of Swinomish’s Treaty rights, and an existential threat to the Tribe’s cultural survival.

The Tribe respectfully requests and demands the following:

1. Immediate Withdrawal of the proposed rescission based on failure to conduct required Tribal consultation;

2. Full Compliance with all consultation requirements before any further action is taken;

3. Comprehensive Analysis of the numerous impacts to the Tribe’s Treaty rights, cultural resources, and USDA and USFS trust responsibilities to Swinomish;

4. Alternative Development including Tribal co-management and enhanced protection options; and

5. Negotiated Rulemaking for any specific changes proposed in the Mt. Baker - Snoqualmie National Forest.

The Roadless Rule has provided essential protections for the lands and resources that sustain the Swinomish Tribe’s people and way of life since time immemorial. We stand ready to work with the Administration on genuine forest management improvements that respect Tribal sovereignty and enhance ecological resilience, but the Proposed Rule’s wholesale rescission and reversal of federal policy is simply unacceptable.

Thank you for your consideration of our comments. We look forward to having a government-to-government consultation with you. Please contact the Tribe’s environmental policy direct, Amy Trainer [atrainer@swinomish.nsn.us] to schedule it.

Sincerely,
